schema.problem: Current AI scientist systems generate research end-to-end but suffer from execution errors, hallucinated results, and logical inconsistencies that evade post-hoc evaluation. While emerging systems integrate closed-loop feedback, there is no systematic characterization of which in-process verification strategies most effectively catch errors during research generation.
schema.motivation: A systematic characterization would make it possible to choose effective verification strategies and improve the reliability of AI scientist workflows.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work introduces a modular verification architecture for AI scientist workflows that embeds staged checks for code executability, output reproducibility, claim-evidence alignment, and logical consistency at key decision points. It defines an evaluation methodology measuring verification sensitivity as error detection rate, specificity as false positive rate, and cost as computational overhead. The framework is instantiated across three research domains to compare domain-specific validators, such as statistical correctness checks for empirical research, against generic LLM-based validation. The work also derives design principles for integrating verification into AI scientist architectures and releases a benchmark for evaluating verification strategies.
schema.research_plan: Evidence consists of an empirical instantiation across three research domains measuring verification sensitivity, specificity, and cost. Claim (1) is tested by comparing the proposed architecture against systems without in-process feedback on critical-error reduction; claim (2) is tested by comparing domain-specific validators with generic LLM-based validation. No explicit failure conditions or matched-resource constraints are stated in the abstract.

items.title: In-Process Verification Architectures for AI Scientist Workflows
items.abstract: Current AI scientist systems generate research end-to-end but suffer from execution errors, hallucinated results, and logical inconsistencies that evade post-hoc evaluation. While emerging systems integrate closed-loop feedback, there is no systematic characterization of which in-process verification strategies most effectively catch errors during research generation. This paper introduces a modular verification architecture for AI scientist workflows that embeds staged checks—code executability, output reproducibility, claim-evidence alignment, and logical consistency—at key decision points. We propose an evaluation methodology that measures verification sensitivity (error detection rate), specificity (false positive rate), and cost (computational overhead), then instantiate this framework across three research domains to characterize the trade-offs between verification depth and research quality. Our results show that multi-stage verification reduces critical errors by 40–60% relative to systems without in-process feedback, and that domain-specific validators (e.g., statistical correctness checks for empirical research) outperform generic LLM-based validation. We provide design principles for integrating verification into AI scientist architectures and release a benchmark for evaluating verification strategies.

schema.problem: As LLMs move toward end-to-end manuscript production, fluent output can hide fabricated citations, numerical drift from source tables, and unmet reporting-guideline items; existing tools generate without verifying, and self-critique inherits the blind spots that produce confident fabrication.
schema.motivation: Verification, not generation, is becoming the bottleneck, and making checks auditable and re-executable would expose the evidence a human needs to check an LLM-assisted manuscript.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework decomposes the manuscript production workflow into self-contained skills, gates every stage transition with halt-on-failure, and resolves each integrity question with the cheapest sufficient mechanism: a deterministic, re-executable check where one suffices and a prose-level probe only where interpretation is unavoidable. The preference for deterministic checks over prose-level probes is organized as a taxonomy of verification gates. It is realized as an open-source toolkit of 43 skills with a 21-detector deterministic tier, released under an MIT license and archived.
schema.research_plan: (1) The feasibility and reproducibility claim is evaluated on three public-dataset pipelines (STARD, PRISMA, STROBE) by running the workflow and verifying content-hash manifests and whether gates surface real defects. (2) A seeded-defect ablation injects identical defects and compares the deterministic gate tier against a single-prompt LLM reviewer on matched clean fixtures; the implied success condition is that the deterministic gates detect the seeded defects with no false positives, including code, bibliography, and style defects that prose-level review tends to miss. (3) The evidence is explicitly scoped as feasibility and reproducibility rather than human-competitive quality, with a separate blinded study addressing the latter.

items.title: Deterministic Integrity Gates for LLM-Assisted Clinical Manuscript Preparation: An Auditable Biomedical Informatics Architecture
items.abstract: As autonomous research agents and AI co-scientist systems push large language models (LLMs) from drafting toward end-to-end manuscript production, the bottleneck shifts from generation to verification. Fluent LLM output can hide fabricated citations, numbers that drift from source tables, and unmet reporting-guideline items; existing tools generate without verifying, and self-critique inherits the blind spots that produce confident fabrication. We describe an architecture pairing generation with verification, resting on three principles: decompose the workflow into self-contained skills, gate every stage transition with halt-on-failure, and resolve each integrity question with the cheapest sufficient mechanism, a deterministic, re-executable check where one suffices and a prose-level probe only where interpretation is unavoidable. This determinism-where-possible split, organized as an integrity-gate taxonomy, is the core contribution. It is realized as MedSci Skills, an open-source toolkit of 43 skills with a 21-detector deterministic tier, evaluated on three public-dataset pipelines (STARD, PRISMA, STROBE) and a seeded-defect ablation. Across the three pipelines every content-hash manifest verified clean and the gates surfaced real defects; on 27 identical injected defects the deterministic gates detected all 27 with no false positives on the matched clean fixtures, whereas a single-prompt LLM reviewer detected 11, its misses in code, bibliography, and style defects the prose hides. Determinism-where-possible verification yields an auditable, re-executable trail that exposes the evidence a human needs to check an LLM-assisted manuscript: feasibility and reproducibility evidence, not a claim of human-competitive quality, which a separate blinded study addresses. MedSci Skills is MIT-licensed and archived (v3.8.0).

schema.problem: Current AI-driven scientific automation systems can generate hypotheses, design experiments, and execute them, but they cannot integrate resulting experimental findings into publication-ready manuscripts that withstand peer scrutiny.
schema.motivation: Automating this gap would reduce manual manuscript preparation and revision effort while producing evidence-grounded manuscripts ready for peer review.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a multi-agent workflow combining result analyzers, evidence retrievers, critic agents, and revision synthesizers. It grounds revision suggestions in actual experimental outcomes and supporting literature, simulates structured peer review that identifies and justifies critiques using evidence from the paper and experiments, and iteratively refines manuscripts through multiple rounds of evidence-backed revision cycles.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is collected on a benchmark derived from withdrawn arXiv papers with experimental protocols. Critique quality and specificity are measured for the simulated peer review, and coherence of revisions to experimental findings is measured for evidence grounding. Manuscript quality improvement across revision rounds and acceptance likelihood under domain-expert simulation are also measured, with independent reasoning LLMs used for quality checks. Failure would be indicated if critique quality/specificity, revision coherence, or manuscript quality/acceptance do not improve across revision cycles.

items.title: Evidence-Guided Iterative Manuscript Refinement Through Simulated Peer Review and Experimental Grounding
items.abstract: Current AI-driven scientific automation systems excel at hypothesis generation, experimental design, and execution, but struggle to integrate experimental findings into publishable manuscripts that withstand peer scrutiny. We propose VERIFY, a system that automates the critical gap between raw experimental results and publication-ready manuscripts by: (1) grounding revision suggestions in actual experimental outcomes and supporting literature; (2) simulating structured peer review feedback that identifies and justifies critiques using evidence from the paper and experiments; and (3) iteratively refining manuscripts through multiple rounds of evidence-backed revision cycles that mirror human review processes. We will implement this as a multi-agent workflow combining result analyzers, evidence retrievers, critic agents, and revision synthesizers. Unlike prior work that treats peer review and manuscript writing as separate tasks, our approach integrates them—the peer review simulation is evidence-driven, the revisions are rooted in experimental data, and both are evaluated on whether manuscripts pass quality checks from independent reasoning LLMs. We will evaluate on a benchmark derived from withdrawn arXiv papers with experimental protocols, measuring: critique quality and specificity, coherence of revisions to experimental findings, improvement in manuscript quality across revision rounds, and acceptance likelihood under domain-expert simulation.

schema.problem: End-to-end research paper generation requires more than text generation: it also requires literature retrieval, experiment design and execution, evidence-based claim revision, publication-ready figure production, and consistency over a long generation process, and it is not established how to supply these capabilities reliably in a lightweight, composable workflow.
schema.motivation: Reliable end-to-end paper generation would make research workflows faster and cheaper while keeping experimental evidence central to how claims are accepted, revised, or abandoned, rather than producing plausible but unsupported manuscripts.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an end-to-end research paper generation workflow implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant, with no separate agent platform or orchestration service. It separates model-based judgment from deterministic operations that can be directly executed and checked, and separates experiment planning from reporting so that required evidence is specified before results are observed and manuscript claims are revised according to measured outcomes. For reliability over long trajectories, it combines deterministic integrity checks with self-critique and bounds the described failure mode in which repeated experiments reject the original research objective. It produces editable vector figures through programmatic plotting for experimental results and code-based reconstruction for generated method diagrams.
schema.research_plan: (1) The system-level claim is evaluated across eight controlled research topics using citation validity and figure editability audits. (2) The reliability claim is evaluated by a controlled ablation that compares fabrication detection for a single-pass draft against the full integrity and review stack, plus an adversarial review precision measurement. (3) Resource practicality is characterized by token usage, monetary cost, and time per manuscript. Failure would be if the full stack did not improve fabrication detection over the single-pass draft or if the workflow were not usable inside the existing coding assistant.

items.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
items.abstract: Turning a research idea into a complete paper requires more than text generation: the system must retrieve literature, design and execute experiments, revise claims according to evidence, produce publication-ready figures, and maintain consistency across a long generation process. We present Spark-to-Paper, an end-to-end research paper generation system implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant, without requiring a separate agent platform or orchestration service. Spark-to-Paper separates model-based judgment from deterministic operations that can be directly executed and checked. It further separates experiment planning from reporting, so that required evidence is specified before results are observed and manuscript claims are revised according to measured outcomes. To improve reliability over long research trajectories, the system combines deterministic integrity checks with self-critique and bounds a failure mode we call the Self-Refutation Loop, in which repeated experiments continue to reject the original research objective. Spark-to-Paper also produces editable vector figures through programmatic plotting for experimental results and code-based reconstruction for generated method diagrams. Across eight controlled research topics, Spark-to-Paper achieves 99.5% citation validity and 96.4% figure editability. A controlled ablation increases fabrication detection from 14% for a single-pass draft to 92% with the full integrity and review stack, while adversarial review achieves 74% precision. The full system uses 11.9M tokens, costs $8.1 per manuscript, and requires 3.2 hours on average. These results show that end-to-end research paper generation can be implemented as a lightweight, composable workflow inside existing coding assistants while keeping experimental evidence central to how claims are accepted, revised, or abandoned.

schema.problem: Existing peer-review evaluation tools for AI-generated manuscripts rely solely on text inspection or generic LLM evaluations, leaving them blind to internal discrepancies between textual claims and ground-truth execution artifacts such as code execution logs and quantitative artifact logs.
schema.motivation: Bridging this gap would preserve scientific integrity in fully automated discovery pipelines by enabling empirical claims to be verified against actual execution artifacts.
schema.proposed_approach: A multi-agent framework programmatically and semantically cross-verifies empirical claims in AI-generated manuscripts against immutable execution traces, raw MLflow/artifact logs, and reproducibility pipelines. It extracts explicit quantitative assertions from manuscript text, maps them to corresponding execution run IDs and code blocks using structured lineage tracking, and flags inconsistencies.
schema.research_plan: The proposed framework is evaluated on benchmark suites of AI-generated papers by comparing its detection of manuscript-execution inconsistencies against text-only peer review and baseline hallucination detectors.

items.title: Trace-to-Text Audit (T2TA): Automated Cross-Verification of Execution Traces and Textual Claims in AI-Generated Research
items.abstract: Autonomous AI scientist systems are increasingly capable of executing the full research lifecycle, from hypothesis generation and code execution to manuscript writing. However, recent studies demonstrate a critical vulnerability: these systems frequently generate internal discrepancies between their actual code execution logs, quantitative artifacts, and the final textual claims reported in papers—manifesting as metric misuse, unfaithful reporting, or selective omission of failed trials. Existing peer-review evaluation tools rely solely on text inspection or generic LLM evaluations, which remain blind to ground-truth execution artifacts. To bridge this accountability gap, we propose Trace-to-Text Audit (T2TA), a multi-agent framework that programmatically and semantically cross-verifies empirical claims in AI-generated manuscripts against immutable execution traces, raw MLflow/artifact logs, and reproducibility pipelines. T2TA extracts explicit quantitative assertions from the manuscript text, maps them to corresponding execution run IDs and code blocks using structured lineage tracking, and flags inconsistencies. Evaluations on benchmark suites of AI-generated papers demonstrate that T2TA significantly outperforms text-only peer review and baseline hallucination detectors, ensuring that scientific integrity is preserved in fully automated discovery pipelines.

schema.problem: Language-model agents increasingly produce quantum-science results, but it is not established that the same agentic paradigm can scrutinize those results in an auditable, reproducible, and cost-transparent form.
schema.motivation: Quantum-science outputs from language agents need scrutiny that is auditable, reproducible, and cost-transparent before they can be trusted; deterministic checkable gates make such scrutiny possible without requiring human labels.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper presents an open-source skill-orchestrating language agent that generates quantum-computing artifacts—papers, Pareto-front ansatz candidates, and patent drafts—and reviews them through simulated referee and patent-examiner panels. Its audit-and-falsify layer uses deterministic gates: strict Pareto domination, numerical recomputation from on-disk artifacts, Wilson small-sample intervals, and a cross-vendor consensus guard; these constrain the claims allowed to survive rather than generating them. Every model call is logged with backend, token count, and cost. The framework is positioned as decision support, not a replacement for peer review or patent examination, and reports where its mechanisms remain unexercised on real inputs.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is organized around the two central claims. (1) For the claim that the deterministic gates can constrain claims to checkable ones without human labels, the paper uses a planted adversarial corpus; success requires catching every planted overclaim with no false positives, and any missed overclaim or false positive would count as failure. (2) For the claim that the panels provide cost-transparent decision support, the paper reports a first deployment on six manuscripts and one granted patent, with per-call backend/token/cost logging and a comparison of panel decisions against the public acceptance record on a one-sided sample; the work also reports where its mechanisms remain unexercised on real inputs.

items.title: QuantumNovelty: A Skill-Orchestrating Language Agent for Referee-Style Review and Patentability Screening of Quantum Papers and Patents
items.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly produce quantum-science results; we ask whether the same agentic paradigm can also scrutinize them in an auditable, reproducible, and cost-transparent form. We present QuantumNovelty, an open-source skill-orchestrating language agent that both generates quantum-computing artifacts (papers, Pareto-front ansatz candidates, and patent drafts) and reviews them through simulated referee and patent-examiner panels. Its design contribution is an audit-and-falsify layer of deterministic gates -- strict Pareto domination, numerical recomputation from on-disk artifacts, Wilson small-sample intervals, and a cross-vendor consensus guard -- that constrains, rather than generates, the claims allowed to survive; every model call is logged with backend, token count, and cost. We make no accuracy claim against human experts, and validate only what is checkable without human labels: on a planted adversarial corpus the deterministic gates catch every planted overclaim with no false positives, and on a first deployment (six manuscripts and one granted patent, at a measured cost of about twenty-four US dollars) the panels are directionally more conservative than the public acceptance record, on a one-sided sample. The framework is decision support, not a replacement for peer review or patent examination, and we report in full where its mechanisms remain unexercised on real inputs.

schema.problem: Existing methods for automated scientific hypothesis generation with LLMs either produce coarse-grained, high-level research directions that lack actionable experimental details or rely on flat multi-agent brainstorming that is prone to hallucinations.
schema.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to automate scientific hypothesis generation, and producing fine-grained, grounded, and actionable hypotheses would make these systems more useful for downstream experimental work.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework decomposes hypothesis generation into a coarse-to-fine trajectory, progressing from conceptual research directions to specific parameter configurations. It employs specialized agents—generators, method critics, and execution-feasibility simulators—in an adversarial multi-agent refinement loop that iteratively prunes and shapes the latent reward landscape. The loop is driven by combinatorial recombination over knowledge graphs, and generation is grounded in external knowledge graphs to reduce factual drift. The design is framed in terms of dual-space search and combinatorial innovation.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is empirical: (1) the framework's generated hypotheses are compared with those of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse scientific benchmarks, evaluated on novelty and methodological actionability. Support for the single claim requires the framework to show improvement on both criteria; the abstract does not specify the baselines or a matched-compute or failure condition.

items.title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Fine-Grained Hypothesis Discovery via Combinatorial Knowledge Recombination and Execution-Feasibility Simulation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been employed to automate scientific hypothesis generation, yet existing methods predominantly produce coarse-grained, high-level research directions lacking actionable experimental details, or rely on flat multi-agent brainstorming prone to hallucinations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework for Fine-Grained Hypothesis Discovery that combines hierarchical search with an adversarial multi-agent refinement loop driven by combinatorial knowledge graph recombination. Specifically, our approach decomposes hypothesis generation into a coarse-to-fine trajectory—progressing from conceptual directions to specific parameter configurations—while employing specialized agents (generators, method critics, and execution-feasibility simulators) to iteratively prune and shape the latent reward landscape. Grounded in principles of dual-space search and combinatorial innovation, the system leverages external knowledge graphs to ground ideas and avoid factual drift. Empirical evaluations across diverse scientific benchmarks demonstrate that our hierarchical multi-agent framework significantly enhances both the novelty and the methodological actionability of generated hypotheses compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

schema.problem: Hypothesis generation, central to scientific discovery, remains one of the least formalized and least automated components of the research process; while automation and self-driving laboratories have transformed how hypotheses are tested, their formulation has largely remained a human endeavor.
schema.motivation: Recent progress in AI, particularly large language models, enables large-scale generation of novel, plausible, and actionable hypotheses by recombining existing knowledge, making it timely to pursue end-to-end automated scientific discovery by coupling this generation with agentic reasoning and autonomous laboratory platforms.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper advocates integrating AI-driven hypothesis generation with agentic reasoning systems and autonomous laboratory platforms into closed-loop experimental workflows. It develops criteria for what defines a good scientific hypothesis, assesses the opportunities and limitations of contemporary AI systems for generating such hypotheses, and outlines how hypothesis generation can be integrated into experimental loops. It concludes by identifying key challenges that must be addressed for this approach to accelerate materials science.
schema.research_plan: The paper supports its position through conceptual discussion: it assesses what defines a good scientific hypothesis and evaluates the opportunities and limitations of contemporary AI systems for hypothesis generation, then outlines integration into closed-loop experimental workflows and identifies key challenges. No experimental, formal, or quantitative evaluation is described; the evidence is argumentative and review-based.

items.title: AI-Generated Hypotheses and the Emergence of Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: Hypothesis generation plays a central role in scientific discovery, yet it has remained one of the least formalized and least automated components of the research process. While advances in automation, machine learning, and self-driving laboratories have transformed how hypotheses are tested, their formulation has largely remained a human endeavor. Recent progress in AI, particularly LLMs, challenges this assumption by enabling the large-scale generation of novel, plausible, and actionable hypotheses through computational recombination of existing knowledge. We argue here that coupling AI-driven hypothesis generation with agentic reasoning systems and autonomous laboratory platforms opens a realistic pathway toward end-to-end automated scientific discovery. We discuss what defines a good scientific hypothesis, assess the opportunities and limitations of contemporary AI systems, and outline how hypothesis generation can be integrated into closed-loop experimental workflows. We conclude by identifying key challenges that must be addressed for such a Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Discovery System (HADS) to truly accelerate material science.

schema.problem: LLM-based equation-discovery agents generate physically plausible symbolic hypotheses from scientific priors, but they treat data as fixed and search within an existing dataset. Classical active symbolic-regression methods decide where to measure next from genetic-programming populations or learned query networks, yet they have no access to scientific semantics, and no retrieved system couples an LLM hypothesis proposer with a quantitative, discrimination-driven experiment-selection criterion.
schema.motivation: The strengths are complementary: an LLM proposer can supply scientific semantics and physically plausible candidates, while quantitative active selection can reduce the experiments needed to identify a symbolic form, so coupling them may make equation discovery more sample-efficient and semantically coherent.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop agent consists of two parts. An LLM proposes, refines, and maintains a small pool of fitted candidate symbolic models, using scientific priors and code-based evaluation. A Bayesian acquisition function computes the expected information gain about which candidate is correct, rather than about any single model's parameters, and chooses the next experimental input. The LLM never chooses the numeric query; a verifiable expected-information-gain computation disambiguates the maintained pool.
schema.research_plan: (1) The division-of-labor claim is tested through controlled-prior ablations and through comparisons against LLM self-design and statistics-only query strategies. (2) The fewer-experiments prediction is evaluated on the anti-memorization LLM-SRBench protocol converted to an online query budget and on Feynman-style transfer cases. (3) The baselines - random design, LLM self-design, uncertainty sampling, and GP query-by-committee - share the same proposer, holding candidate proposal fixed to isolate the query-selection mechanism. The success condition is that the agent identifies correct symbolic forms in substantially fewer experiments than any LLM-only or statistics-only variant on every benchmark where querying inputs is permitted; failure would be any such benchmark where this does not hold.

items.title: Propose-then-Discriminate: Coupling an LLM Equation Hypothesizer with Bayesian Model-Selection Acquisition for Data-Efficient Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: LLM-based equation-discovery agents generate physically plausible symbolic hypotheses from scientific priors, but they treat data as fixed: once a dataset exists, they search for equations within it . Conversely, classical active symbolic-regression methods decide where to measure next from genetic-programming populations or learned query networks, yet they have no access to scientific semantics . These strengths are complementary, and no retrieved system couples an LLM hypothesis proposer with a quantitative, discrimination-driven experiment-selection criterion. We propose Propose-then-Discriminate (PtD), a closed-loop agent in which (i) an LLM proposes, refines, and maintains a small pool of fitted candidate symbolic models using scientific priors and code-based evaluation, while (ii) a Bayesian acquisition function — the expected information gain about which candidate is correct, not about any single model's parameters — chooses the next experimental input. The division of labor is the falsifiable claim: LLMs keep proposing semantically coherent candidates, but never choose the numeric query, because LLM intuition about information value is demonstrably unreliable ; instead, a verifiable EIG computation disambiguates the maintained pool. We evaluate PtD on the anti-memorization LLM-SRBench protocol converted to an online query budget, plus Feynman-style transfer cases and controlled-prior ablations, against random design, LLM self-design, uncertainty sampling, and GP query-by-committee sharing the same proposer. The prediction is that PtD identifies correct symbolic forms in substantially fewer experiments than any LLM-only or statistics-only variant, on every benchmark where querying inputs is permitted.

schema.problem: Most approaches to scientific discovery reduce it to supervised learning over fixed datasets, where limited observations can support multiple plausible mechanisms that fit locally but fail to generalize; the unresolved challenge is selecting informative observations to resolve uncertainty through adaptive data acquisition.
schema.motivation: Closing the loop between hypotheses and experiments would enable robust mechanism recovery under constrained observation budgets, avoiding reliance on passively collected data that cannot distinguish locally plausible mechanisms.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework iteratively proposes plausible hypotheses, selects informative experiments to distinguish or refine them, and updates its state using the resulting evidence; rather than fitting models to passively collected data, it couples hypothesis generation with hypothesis-conditioned experiment selection and mechanism refinement. The work also releases a benchmark suite with two datasets: 57 enzyme-kinetics tasks and 45 gene-regulatory-network tasks, modeling discovery as a budget-constrained process requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms. Code and data are made available.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation for the framework-performance claim compares the proposed framework against prior methods on NewtonBench, the 57-task chemistry dataset, and the 45-task gene-regulatory-network dataset; reported metrics are symbolic accuracy and exact graph recovery. Evaluation for the sample-efficiency claim compares hypothesis-guided experimentation against the strongest competing baselines under a budget constraint. Evaluation for the benchmark-adequacy claim rests on the design of the tasks as requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms in two domains. Success conditions are implicitly superiority on the reported metrics and improved sample efficiency; no explicit failure thresholds or matched-compute controls are stated.

items.title: LLM-AutoSciLab: Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery via Active Experimentation with LLMs
items.abstract: Scientific discovery is a closed-loop process in which hypotheses guide data acquisition and observations refine the hypothesis space. Yet most approaches reduce discovery to supervised learning over fixed datasets, where limited observations can support multiple plausible mechanisms that fit locally but fail to generalize. Thus, the key challenge is selecting informative observations to resolve uncertainty, shifting the focus from static inference to adaptive data acquisition. To address this, we propose LLM-AutoSciLab, a closed-loop framework that couples hypothesis generation with hypothesis-conditioned experiment selection and mechanism refinement. Rather than fitting models to passively collected data, LLM-AutoSciLab iteratively proposes plausible hypotheses, selects informative experiments to distinguish or refine them, and updates its state using the resulting evidence. To evaluate dynamic, closed-loop scientific discovery with active data acquisition, we introduce ActiveSciBench, comprising two datasets: ActiveSciBench-Chem with 57 enzyme-kinetics tasks and ActiveSciBench-GRN with 45 gene-regulatory-network tasks. These datasets model discovery as a budget-constrained process requiring adaptive experiment design, variable selection, and recovery of true mechanisms. Across NewtonBench, ActiveSciBench-Chem, and ActiveSciBench-GRN, LLM-AutoSciLab outperforms prior methods, achieving 67.6% and 35.1% symbolic accuracy on NewtonBench and ActiveSciBench-Chem, respectively, and 31.1% exact graph recovery on ActiveSciBench-GRN. Moreover, hypothesis-guided experimentation is 2-5x more sample-efficient than the strongest competing baselines. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-AutoSciLab

schema.problem: There is no evaluation of autonomous idea-generation systems that is not mediated by human or LLM judgment, and both are unstable, self-serving, and weakly predictive of executed research outcomes.
schema.motivation: An objective, longitudinal benchmark for AI ideation would remove the field's central methodological weakness and answer recent calls for drift-aware idea evaluation.
schema.proposed_approach: Fit a dynamic neural topic model over a time-stamped paper corpus to produce per-topic, per-year density and velocity estimates of the research landscape. Condition an LLM ideation agent to place hypotheses in cells characterized by low density and positive velocity, and on bridges between topic pairs that rarely co-occur but are both rising. Evaluation projects ideas generated from the corpus up to year T into topic coordinates and scores them against the topic cells and concepts of papers actually published in the held-out T+1..T+3 window, alongside a cheap executability check.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a backtest design: ideas generated from the corpus up to year T are projected into topic coordinates and compared with topic cells and concepts of papers published in the held-out T+1..T+3 window, with an executability check. (1) The objectivity and leakage-resistance claim is supported by training only on data up to year T and scoring against future publications. (2) The anticipation claim is supported only if the proposed signal outperforms a frequency prior that predicts the currently hottest topics; failure to do so would show the landscape control signal is worthless.

items.title: Backcasting the Frontier: Temporal Topic-Landscape Conditioning and Retrodictive Evaluation for LLM Research Ideation
items.abstract: Autonomous idea-generation systems now match or exceed human experts on apparent novelty, yet the field has no evaluation that is not mediated by human or LLM judgment — and both are known to be unstable, self-serving, and only weakly predictive of executed research outcomes. This proposal reframes AI ideation around a single falsifiable question: given only the literature published up to year T, can an ideation agent generate research directions that anticipate what the community actually publishes in T+1…T+3? The method fits a dynamic neural topic model over a time-stamped paper corpus to produce a per-topic, per-year density–velocity field of the research landscape, then conditions an LLM ideation agent to place hypotheses in emerging-sparse cells (low density, positive velocity) and on bridges between topic pairs that rarely co-occur but are both rising. Evaluation is a temporal retrodiction backtest: ideas generated from the ≤T corpus are projected into topic coordinates and scored against the topic cells and concepts of papers actually published in the held-out window, alongside a cheap executability check. This turns the field's central methodological weakness (no ground truth for idea quality) into an objective, leakage-resistant, longitudinal benchmark, and it directly answers recent calls for drift-aware, longitudinal idea evaluation. The proposal is falsifiable: a frequency prior that simply predicts the currently-hottest topics must be beaten, or the landscape control signal is worthless.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-driven scientific discovery systems are generally limited to one-shot prompting on static literature snapshots and are validated only against contemporary judges, leaving open whether they can anticipate future trends.
schema.motivation: Identifying promising research directions in fast-moving subareas is cognitively expensive, and predictive validation against future literature would provide a falsifiable, low-cost alternative to contemporary-judge evaluation protocols.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed workflow maintains an evolving knowledge state by continuously ingesting literature through sliding windows. It generates hypotheses and grades them against papers published after the generation window. A failure-detection component diagnoses workflow failure modes from its outputs. A lightweight variant is evaluated on a 50-topic machine learning benchmark.
schema.research_plan: Claims (1) and (2) are evaluated on a 50-topic machine learning benchmark by matching generated hypotheses to papers published after the generation window and comparing yield, per-topic cost, and token cost against a one-shot prompting baseline. The temporal gap between each validated hypothesis and its matched paper is recorded. The failure-detection capability is assessed by diagnosing failure modes from workflow outputs. The abstract does not state an explicit predefined failure threshold beyond topic-level validation counts.

items.title: Continuous Knowledge Metabolism: Generating Scientific Hypotheses from Evolving Literature
items.abstract: Identifying promising research directions in fast-moving subareas is one of the most cognitively expensive tasks in modern AI research. Existing LLM-driven scientific discovery systems are typically limited to one-shot prompting on static literature snapshots and are validated only against contemporary judges such as human reviewers, agent peer review, wet-lab assays, or self-evaluation, leaving open whether they can anticipate future trends. We present Continuous Knowledge Metabolism (CKM), an AI workflow for hypothesis generation with three key capabilities: (i) continuous literature metabolism via sliding windows that maintain an evolving knowledge state; (ii) predictive evaluation, which grades hypotheses against papers published after the generation window; and (iii) practitioner-grade failure detection that diagnoses workflow failure modes from its outputs. On a 50-topic machine learning benchmark, CKM-Lite produces at least one validated hypothesis on 72% of topics (36 out of 50), more than doubling a one-shot baseline (30%) at approximately 3 dollars per topic and achieving 91% lower token cost. Validated hypotheses precede their matched papers by an average of 404 days (55 hits across 36 topics; median 399 days, range 66-757 days). Broadly, predictive validation against future literature provides a falsifiable, low-cost alternative to contemporary-judge evaluation protocols and can be applied wherever a corpus has dated publication records.

schema.problem: Existing benchmarks for AI research-idea systems score ideas for static plausibility or text alignment, but no benchmark asks whether those scores predict realized future impact.
schema.motivation: The community's central open question of whether idea-evaluation scores mean anything about future outcomes is currently unmeasured, and time-stamped bibliographic indexes now make retrospective outcome measurement tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark constructs candidate ideas in three classes: historical realized ideas mined from accepted papers, ideas replayed from open generation agents against a frozen literature snapshot, and counterfactual rejected ideas from the same era. All working literature is cut off at a timestamp t0, so generation and evaluation see exactly what a researcher at t0 could see. Realized outcomes are measured at t1 using time-stamped bibliographic indexes as field- and age-normalized forward citations over a 3–5 year window plus community uptake. The protocol's core quantity is predictive validity: the rank correlation between each evaluation scheme's t0 scores and t1 realized outcomes, tested against shuffled-label and citation-text baselines.
schema.research_plan: For each evaluation scheme, the protocol computes rank correlation between its t0 scores and t1 realized outcomes under the frozen-literature cutoff, and compares it with shuffled-label and citation-text baselines. The three candidate idea classes are scored under the same hard cutoff, so predictive validity is measured across historical realized, replayed, and counterfactual ideas. An evaluation scheme fails if its correlation does not exceed the shuffled-label or citation-text baselines.

items.title: IdeaAudit: A Time-Stamped Benchmark for the Predictive Validity of AI Research-Idea Evaluation
items.abstract: AI research-idea systems are now benchmarked, reviewed, and tuned against evaluation scores—but no existing benchmark asks whether those scores predict what actually happens to an idea. We propose IdeaAudit, a retrospective evaluation protocol and benchmark whose ground truth is realized future impact rather than static plausibility or text alignment. Candidate ideas—historical realized ideas mined from accepted papers, ideas replayed from open generation agents against a frozen literature snapshot, and counterfactual rejected ideas from the same era—are scored under a hard evidence constraint: all working literature is cut off at a timestamp t₀, so generation and evaluation see exactly what a researcher at t₀ could see. Realized outcomes (field- and age-normalized forward citations over a 3–5 year window, plus community uptake) are measured at t₁ using time-stamped bibliographic indexes. The protocol's core quantity is the predictive validity of each evaluation scheme: the rank correlation between its t₀ scores and t₁ realized outcomes, tested against shuffled-label and citation-text baselines. IdeaAudit thereby converts the community's central open question—do idea-evaluation scores mean anything about future outcomes?—into a measurable quantity, and gives every existing evaluation method (LLM-as-judge rubrics, expert panels, reference-based metrics, generator self-scores) a common, outcome-based validity readout.

schema.problem: Large language models are increasingly used to assess and forecast research ideas, but there is no scalable way to evaluate the quality of their judgments about scientific ideas.
schema.motivation: Linking scientific idea judgments to downstream signals that become observable later, such as citations and shifts in researchers' agendas, makes verifiable and scalable evaluation possible, while agent-based research judgments need controlled testbeds.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework freezes a pre-cutoff snapshot of evidence in an offline sandbox and asks models to forecast post-cutoff outcomes tied to downstream signals such as citations and shifts in researchers' agendas. It supports verifiable evaluation when ground truth arrives, scalable benchmarking without exhaustive expert annotation, and analysis of human-model misalignment against signals such as peer-review awards. It also provides a controlled testbed for agent-based research judgments, comparing tool-using agents to non-agent baselines under prompt ablations and budget scaling, across 30,000+ instances in four benchmark domains.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of benchmarking across 30,000+ instances spanning four benchmark domains, with comparisons of tool-using agents against non-agent baselines under prompt ablations and budget scaling. The analysis also examines human-model misalignment against signals such as peer-review awards. Support for the framework's verifiability and scalability rests on its offline sandbox and future-verifiable targets as ground truth arrives.

items.title: Proof of Time: A Benchmark for Evaluating Scientific Idea Judgments
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used to assess and forecast research ideas, yet we lack scalable ways to evaluate the quality of models' judgments about these scientific ideas. Towards this goal, we introduce PoT, a semi-verifiable benchmarking framework that links scientific idea judgments to downstream signals that become observable later (e.g., citations and shifts in researchers' agendas). PoT freezes a pre-cutoff snapshot of evidence in an offline sandbox and asks models to forecast post-cutoff outcomes, enabling verifiable evaluation when ground truth arrives, scalable benchmarking without exhaustive expert annotation, and analysis of human-model misalignment against signals such as peer-review awards. In addition, PoT provides a controlled testbed for agent-based research judgments that evaluate scientific ideas, comparing tool-using agents to non-agent baselines under prompt ablations and budget scaling. Across 30,000+ instances spanning four benchmark domains, we find that, compared with non-agent baselines, higher interaction budgets generally improve agent performance, while the benefit of tool use is strongly task-dependent. By combining time-partitioned, future-verifiable targets with an offline sandbox for tool use, PoT supports scalable evaluation of agents on future-facing scientific idea judgment tasks.

schema.problem: In large-scale automated science the bottleneck is deciding which candidate hypotheses are worth the cost of an experimental test; existing systems rank hypotheses by pre-experiment plausibility or filter them for binary feasibility, but none selects hypotheses by the predicted informativeness of the test relative to its cost.
schema.motivation: Experimental testing is the scarce and expensive step, so selecting tests by information value per unit cost would allocate budgets to the experiments most likely to advance discovery and avoid wasting resources on plausible but uninformative or infeasible tests.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed stage decomposes each candidate hypothesis into measurable implications, plans a concrete test via an LLM agent, filters out infeasible or non-executable tests using claim verification plus an executability model, scores survivors by estimated expected information gain per unit cost, and executes them sequentially under a knowledge-gradient-style policy that updates informativeness predictions from observed outcomes. The proposed benchmark comprises parametric simulated discovery environments calibrated against literature results and a temporal backtest set of historically tested hypotheses with known outcomes.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation tests the central claim by measuring discoveries-per-experiment-budget for the proposed information-value triage against plausibility-ranked and feasibility-gated baselines on the proposed benchmark's simulated environments and temporal backtest set. The stated failure condition is that if information-value-based triage does not discover more true discoveries at every research budget than plausibility-based ranking, the selection objective rather than the pipeline components should be reconsidered.

items.title: TriageWorth: Selecting Hypotheses for an Autonomous Scientist by Expected Information Gain per Unit Cost
items.abstract: The bottleneck in large-scale automated science is no longer generating or ranking hypotheses by plausibility — it is deciding which hypotheses are worth the expense of a test. Existing systems either rank hypotheses by pre-experiment plausibility (MOOSE-Chem3's baselines, ResearchBench, Sybrandt-style candidate ranking) or filter them for binary feasibility (Matter-of-Fact), but none selects hypotheses by the predicted informativeness of the experiment that would test them relative to its cost. We propose TriageWorth, a test-worthiness selection (TWS) stage for the AI-scientist pipeline: given a pool of candidate hypotheses, the system (i) decomposes each into measurable implications, (ii) plans a concrete test via an LLM agent, (iii) filters out infeasible or non-executable tests using claim verification plus an executability model, and (iv) scores and ranks survivors by estimated expected information gain per unit cost (EIG/cost), then executes sequentially under a knowledge-gradient-style policy that updates its informativeness predictions from observed outcomes. We introduce TriageMax, a benchmark of parametric simulated discovery environments calibrated against literature results plus a temporal backtest set of historically tested hypotheses with known outcomes, on which we evaluate selection by discoveries-per-experiment-budget against plausibility-ranked and feasibility-gated baselines. Our central, falsifiable claim is that information-value-based triage discovers more true discoveries at every research budget than plausibility-based ranking across heterogeneous domains; if it does not, the selection objective — not the pipeline components — is what needs rethinking.

schema.problem: Across AI-driven science, generative capacity has outpaced investigative judgment: it is now possible to produce millions of plausible candidates in hours, but not yet to decide which of them merit expensive validation.
schema.motivation: This asymmetry is described as the central bottleneck of scientific discovery for the next decade; resolving it is necessary to convert generative capacity into scientific progress without wasting expensive validation.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper formalizes the principle as a multi-fidelity Markov decision process in which agents maximize the value of information purchased relative to its cost; the formulation is pluralistic, admitting reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and multi-armed bandits. The framework is developed in protein design, where the vendor hierarchy runs from sequence embeddings to wet-lab assays and spans several orders of magnitude, and the same structure is argued to recur in materials science and autonomous chemistry. Three grand challenges concerning cross-modal calibration, asynchronous decision logic, and interpretable strategy are proposed as anchors for a 2030 benchmark.
schema.research_plan: The paper's evidence is its conceptual framing and formalization, together with the claimed recurrence of the same structure across protein design, materials science, and autonomous chemistry. Progress is anchored by a 2030 benchmark whose success condition is an agent discovering a functional protein at 1% of the compute and 10% of the lab cost of human-designed pipelines; failure is falling short of that target. The three grand challenges are proposed as criteria for tracking progress, but the abstract does not specify concrete experiments or ablations.

items.title: The Autonomous AI Scientist of 2030 Needs Inferential Arbitrage
items.abstract: Across AI-driven science, generative capacity has outpaced investigative judgment. It is now possible to produce millions of plausible candidates in hours, but not yet to decide which merit expensive validation. This asymmetry defines the central bottleneck of scientific discovery for the next decade. This blue sky paper casts scientific investigation as an information market. A strategically intelligent agent must exploit cost-information asymmetries across fidelity levels, purchasing cheap inferences to decide whether expensive ones are worth acquiring. The paper formalizes this principle as Inferential Arbitrage: a multi-fidelity Markov Decision Process in which agents maximize inferential return on investment. The formulation is pluralistic by design, admitting reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and multi-armed bandits. The framework is developed in protein design, where the vendor hierarchy from sequence embeddings to wet-lab assays spans several orders of magnitude, but the same structure recurs in materials science and autonomous chemistry. Three grand challenges (cross-modal calibration, asynchronous decision logic, interpretable strategy) anchor a 2030 benchmark: an agent that discovers a functional protein at 1% of the compute and 10% of the lab cost of human-designed pipelines. The ultimate measure of an autonomous AI scientist is not what it can compute, but what it chooses not to.

schema.problem: Current LLM-based systems for scientific research focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities.
schema.motivation: The rapid advancement of LLMs makes it timely to integrate their strengths with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation to enable more complete automation of scientific research.
schema.proposed_approach: An integrated framework that uses LLMs for hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, combined with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools for experiment execution and analysis, aimed at end-to-end autonomous AI scientists.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and its performance will be assessed in real-world scientific research scenarios; no failure condition or held-matched comparison is specified.

items.title: End-to-End Autonomous AI Scientists: An Integrated Framework for Scientific Research Automation
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shown potential in automating various stages of scientific research. However, current LLM-based systems primarily focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities. This proposal aims to design and develop an integrated framework that enables end-to-end autonomous AI scientists by combining LLMs with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools. The proposed framework will leverage the strengths of LLMs in hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, while integrating them with AI tools for experiment execution and analysis. We will evaluate the framework using benchmarks such as LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and assess its performance in real-world scientific research scenarios.

schema.problem: Automated research systems today operate primarily as hidden prompt-to-paper pipelines centered on a single agent or a fixed serial workflow, with limited real-time steerability, monitoring, or connection to local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints.
schema.motivation: Making autonomous research interactive and laboratory-like would let users inspect artifacts, roll back or resume runs, and faithfully transfer experiments into papers, reducing common failure modes such as partial runs and malformed result reporting.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an interactive autonomous research platform. From a single user prompt it instantiates a full research team with customizable roles, collaborative workflows, real-time monitoring, artifact inspection, and rollback/resume control through a unified dashboard. It offers distinct research modes for exploration, multi-agent discussion, and reproduction. A code harness connects local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints to runnable experiments and feeds execution artifacts back into the research loop.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is an internal evaluation on five AI research case studies, comparing the proposed platform with the AutoResearchClaw baseline; AI expert judges rate idea novelty, experiment completeness, and paper presentation quality. The harness is assessed through its connection of local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints to runnable experiments and the feeding of execution artifacts back into the loop, with experimental completion and result integrity as stated dimensions. The abstract does not specify explicit failure conditions or matched compute/parameter settings.

items.title: Claw AI Lab: An Autonomous Multi-Agent Research Team
items.abstract: We present Claw AI Lab, a lab-native autonomous research platform that advances automated research from a hidden prompt-to-paper pipeline into an interactive AI laboratory. Rather than centering the system around a single agent or a fixed serial workflow, we allow users to instantiate a full research team from one prompt, with customizable roles, collaborative workflows, real-time monitoring, artifact inspection, and rollback/resume control through a unified dashboard. The platform also supports distinct research modes for exploration, multi-agent discussion, and reproduction, making autonomous research substantially more steerable and laboratory-like in practice. A key practical contribution of Claw AI Lab lies in its Claw-Code Harness, which connects local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints to runnable experiments and feeds execution artifacts back into the research loop. As a result, the harness improves not only execution integration, but also experimental completion and result integrity: experiments are easier to inspect, iterate on, and faithfully transfer into final papers, reducing common failure modes such as partial runs and malformed result reporting. In our internal evaluation on five AI research case studies, using AutoResearchClaw as the baseline, Claw AI Lab is consistently preferred by AI expert judges on idea novelty, experiment completeness, and paper presentation quality. We view Claw AI Lab as an early step toward a new paradigm: autonomous research as usable, interactive, and reliability-aware scientific infrastructure.

schema.problem: Autonomous materials discovery and experimental design remain limited by dependence on high-quality data, the opacity of LLMs, and difficulty handling complex material systems.
schema.motivation: Accelerating the full materials research lifecycle from knowledge mining to intelligent design would reduce time and cost, and the availability of LLMs and automated experimental platforms makes such a system newly tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The system is a multi-agent architecture that couples LLMs to automated experimental platforms. It applies retrieval-augmented generation and multi-modal information retrieval to extract and construct material data from large scientific literature and experimental record repositories. It is intended to operate across the research lifecycle from knowledge mining to intelligent design, with human-AI collaboration as a design focus.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation is planned through benchmark construction and evaluation metrics for LLMs in scientific research, with a focus on human-AI collaboration; no explicit failure condition or matched-compute trade-off is stated.

items.title: Advancing Autonomous Materials Discovery and Experimental Design with Multi-Agent Systems and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: This proposal aims to develop a novel multi-agent system that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with automated experimental platforms for autonomous materials discovery and experimental design. The proposed system will leverage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multi-modal information retrieval to efficiently extract and construct material data from vast repositories of scientific literature and experimental records. The system will be evaluated using benchmark construction and evaluation metrics for LLMs in scientific research, with a focus on human-AI collaboration. The goal is to accelerate material design throughout the entire research lifecycle, from knowledge mining to intelligent design, and address the challenges of dependence on high-quality data, the “black-box” nature of LLMs, and limitations in handling complex material systems.

schema.problem: The application of large language models in complex materials science remains limited.
schema.motivation: Large language models offer new possibilities for accelerating materials research by automating time-consuming literature review and experimental planning, freeing researchers for creative thinking.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a knowledge-driven hierarchical multi-agent and robot architecture coordinating 19 large language model agents with 16 domain-specific tools for closed-loop autonomous materials discovery. It combines scientific knowledge with decision-making capabilities and uses retrieval-augmented generation over a customized knowledge base to mitigate hallucination. The system automates literature review and experimental planning and provides a natural-language interface for researchers.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is experimental validation on two materials tasks: closed-loop optimization of perovskite nanocrystal synthesis and design of a water-stable perovskite composite structure. Evaluation compares the system's iteration count and elapsed time against conventional experimental workflows as baselines, holding the target materials fixed. Support would be successful optimization and design with fewer iterations and less elapsed time than conventional methods; failure would be requiring comparable or more time or iterations, or failing to produce the target materials.

items.title: Knowledge-driven autonomous materials research via collaborative multi-agent and robotic system
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide new possibilities for accelerating materials research, yet their application in complex materials science remains limited. Here, we developed the collaborative multi-agent and robot system (MARS), a knowledge-driven hierarchical architecture coordinating 19 LLM agents with 16 domain-specific tools for closed-loop autonomous materials discovery. MARS combines scientific knowledge with decision-making capabilities while mitigating hallucination through retrieval-augmented generation with a customized knowledge base. In experimental validation, the system optimized perovskite nanocrystal synthesis within 10 iterations and designed a biomimetic “core-shell-corona” structure for water-stable perovskite composites in 3.5 h versus conventional methods requiring 4–6 months. This acceleration automates literature review and experimental planning, allowing researchers to focus on creative thinking while interacting through a natural language interface. This work establishes an integrated AI-driven framework for accelerating materials innovation and presents a paradigm for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

schema.problem: Autonomous research systems produce end-to-end reports with unsupported claims—failed or never-run experiments, missing artifacts, and findings with no trace evidence—while existing responses either diagnose these problems after the fact or gate claims only on whether a code run finished, leaving no runtime mechanism that hard-blocks unverified claims inside the agent loop.
schema.motivation: As such systems become more autonomous, unsupported claims entering reports undermine trustworthiness, and re-proposing dead ends wastes compute; making every claim contingent on verifiable evidence is now both necessary and tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: A typed ledger for claims and evidence is inserted as a hard dependency in the agent's reasoning loop. Every claim must carry a pre-registered testable prediction, an executable test or data probe, a bound result artifact, and an explicit support/refute/inconclusive status. A claim is blocked from driving downstream reasoning or entering the report unless its evidence passes a structural and statistical verifier; refuted claims and negative results are retained and re-surfaced to prevent re-proposing dead ends. The paper also releases a claim-support annotation protocol and a planted-claim diagnostic.
schema.research_plan: The central falsifiable claim is tested by comparing the fraction of report claims lacking sufficient, non-contradicted evidence and task success for the ledger-enforced agent against three baselines: a trajectory-only agent, a flat 'cite your evidence' prompt, and an execution-gates-only baseline. Validation uses three ground-truth tracks: synthetic ML-experiment discovery, equation discovery, and literature-to-report with planted unsupported claims. The claim would fail if the reduction in the primary metric is less than 30% relative or if task success drops by more than 5 points relative to the baselines. A claim-support annotation protocol and a planted-claim diagnostic are released to support community auditing.

items.title: Claim–Evidence Ledgers: Falsification-Aware Bookkeeping for Autonomous Research Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous "AI Scientist" systems now produce end-to-end research reports, but independent audits show their outputs are riddled with unsupported claims: experiments that failed or never ran, tasks marked complete with missing artifacts, and findings no trace evidence supports . Existing responses are either diagnostic — showing failures exist and recommending artifact submission — or execution-centric — gating claims on whether a code run finished . We propose a different, runtime mechanism: a typed claim–evidence ledger that is a hard dependency inside the agent loop. Every claim the agent makes must carry (i) a pre-registered testable prediction, (ii) an executable test or data probe, (iii) a bound result artifact, and (iv) an explicit support/refute/inconclusive status; a claim is blocked from driving downstream reasoning or entering the report unless its evidence passes a structural and statistical verifier, and refuted claims and negative results are retained and re-surfaced so dead ends are not re-proposed. Our core, falsifiable claim: enforcing the ledger reduces overclaim rate (fraction of report claims lacking sufficient, non-contradicted evidence) by at least 30% relative while keeping task success within 5 points, versus a trajectory-only agent, a flat "cite your evidence" prompt, and an execution-gates-only baseline. We validate on three ground-truth tracks — synthetic ML-experiment discovery, equation discovery , and literature-to-report with planted unsupported claims — and release a claim-support annotation protocol plus a planted-claim diagnostic as a community "overclaim meter."

schema.problem: AI-assisted research compresses ideation, implementation, evaluation, and manuscript writing into a single interactive loop; while useful, this compression creates a publication risk because paper claims can become easier to state than to audit.
schema.motivation: The compression is useful, so it is worth retaining that speed while making the resulting claims auditable rather than giving up the loop.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is an evidence-gated control plane for AI-assisted computational research. It models research questions, task contracts, evidence objects, claim ledgers, closeouts, and paper bindings as durable project state, realized as a repository-backed runtime. The technical report specifies the protocol, state model, transition rules, claim-admission algorithm, and insight-compounding mechanism.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of a full experimental record across nine versions: a self-hosting case study, a controlled task-suite study with component ablations, a mathematical olympiad evaluation, and a supplementary SciCode boundary experiment using the official generated-code harness; artifacts, manifests, and verification reports are preserved in the project repository.

items.title: ResearchLoop: An Evidence-Gated Control Plane for AI-Assisted Research
items.abstract: AI-assisted research compresses ideation, implementation, evaluation, and manuscript writing into a single interactive loop. This compression is useful, but it also creates a publication risk: paper claims can become easier to state than to audit. We present ResearchLoop, an evidence-gated control plane for AI-assisted computational research. ResearchLoop treats research questions, task contracts, evidence objects, claim ledgers, closeouts, and paper bindings as durable project state, realized here as a repository-backed runtime. This technical report provides the complete protocol specification, state model, transition rules, claim-admission algorithm, and insight-compounding mechanism. It also reports the full experimental record spanning nine versions (V0--V9), including a self-hosting case study, a controlled task-suite study with component ablations, a mathematical olympiad evaluation, and a supplementary SciCode boundary experiment evaluated with the official generated-code harness. All artifacts, manifests, and verification reports are preserved in the project repository.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI scientist agents running multi-session campaigns do not persist their own research state, so they re-encounter failed configurations, re-run near-identical experiments, and forget which hypotheses have already been falsified.
schema.motivation: As such campaigns extend over hours to months, this state loss wastes compute and slows progress toward verified improvements; making research state persist could avoid redundant work and make fixed budgets more productive.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper proposes a schema-enforced, append-only, provenance-bearing persistent store of an agent's research state: hypotheses with predictions recorded before execution; experiment specs keyed by hashes of code, config, and seed; results with evidence pointers to cells, logs, and code; per-experiment costs; and lifecycle statuses (open, confirmed, falsified, dead-end). The store is exposed through a small set of typed query and update tools that the execution harness verifies. On top of the ledger, the agent chooses the next experiment by maximizing expected information gain conditional on the ledger, subject to a per-experiment cost bound, a redundancy penalty, and a hypothesis-diversity floor.
schema.research_plan: The paper tests the single falsifiable claim on three to four baseline-improvement research programs—machine learning, a wet-lab-style prediction task, and a physics-reproduction task—using a pre-registered protocol and at least five seeds per configuration. It compares the proposed ledger plus budget-aware selection against a stateless agent and an unstructured free-text memory agent, both using the same backbone model, and measures redundant-experiment rate, cost-to-first-verified-improvement, final metric, ideation diversity, and trace integrity.

items.title: The Research-State Ledger: Persistent, Provenance-Bearing Memory and Budget-Aware Experiment Selection for AI Scientist Agents
items.abstract: AI scientist agents now run autonomous campaigns spanning hours to months, yet they persistently lose the state of their own research: between sessions they re-encounter the same failed configurations, re-run near-identical experiments, and forget which hypotheses have already been falsified. We propose the Research-State Ledger (RSL), a schema-enforced, append-only, provenance-bearing persistent store of an agent's own research state — hypotheses with predictions recorded before execution, experiment specs keyed by hashes of code, config, and seed, results with evidence pointers to cells, logs, and code, per-experiment costs, and lifecycle statuses (open, confirmed, falsified, dead-end) — exposed to the agent through a small set of typed query and update tools that the execution harness verifies. On top of the ledger we add budget-aware next-experiment selection: the agent chooses the candidate experiment maximizing expected information gain conditional on the ledger, subject to a per-experiment cost bound, a redundancy penalty, and a hypothesis-diversity floor. We make a specific falsifiable claim: under a fixed compute budget split into sequential fresh agent sessions, RSL plus budget-aware selection reduces the redundant-experiment rate and the cost-to-first-verified-improvement, and yields a higher final metric at equal budget, than both a stateless agent and an agent with unstructured free-text memory running the same backbone model. We test this on three to four baseline-improvement research programs (machine learning, a wet-lab-style prediction task, and a physics-reproduction task) with a pre-registered protocol and five or more seeds per configuration, measuring redundancy, cost-to-verified-improvement, final metric, ideation diversity, and trace integrity. The proposal contributes (1) the RSL schema and construction rules, (2) the ledger-conditional budget-aware selection objective, (3) a fixed-budget multi-session evaluation protocol for AI scientist systems, and (4) an empirical account of the efficiency–diversity trade-off, connecting agent memory design to the dual-space (hypothesis-space vs. experiment-space) account of human scientific reasoning.

schema.problem: Autonomous research agents lack a way to carry hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and distilled insights across successive attempts, leaving them as sequences of local experiments rather than a cumulative long-horizon process.
schema.motivation: Making autonomous research cumulative could improve research artifacts over many iterations and reduce the need for step-level human supervision by letting lessons persist and propagate across attempts.
schema.proposed_approach: A long-lived coordinator manages global research strategy, while short-lived executors implement and test individual hypotheses in isolated worktrees. A persistent tree links hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and distilled insights. As results return, the framework updates the tree, propagates reusable lessons, refines the search frontier, and admits verified improvements.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation uses an operational setting in which an agent improves an initial research artifact through iterative experimentation without step-level human supervision. Six real research tasks span model training, harness engineering, and data synthesis; the framework is compared with Codex and Claude Code under the same task interface and resource budget, with support judged by held-out performance. A second evaluation on MLE-Bench Lite with GPT-5.5 uses the Any Medal metric. For the six-task comparison, failure would be not exceeding the baselines' held-out performance under the matched interface and budget; for the benchmark comparison, failure would be not achieving the strongest Any Medal result, though no matching condition is stated. No formal ablation isolating the cumulative memory structure is described.

items.title: Toward Generalist Autonomous Research via Hypothesis-Tree Refinement
items.abstract: Scientific progress depends on a repeated loop of exploration, experimentation, and abstraction. Researchers test candidate directions, interpret the evidence, and carry the resulting lessons into later attempts. We study how an AI agent can run this loop autonomously over long horizons. We introduce Arbor, a general framework for autonomous research that combines a long-lived coordinator, short-lived executors, and Hypothesis Tree Refinement (HTR), a persistent tree that links hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and distilled insights across time. The coordinator manages global research strategy over the tree, while executors implement and test individual hypotheses in isolated worktrees. As results return, Arbor updates the tree, propagates reusable lessons, refines the search frontier, and admits verified improvements. This design turns autonomous research from a sequence of local attempts into a cumulative process in which strategy, execution, and evidence are carried across time. We evaluate Arbor under Autonomous Optimization (AO), an operational setting where an agent improves an initial research artifact through iterative experimentation without step-level human supervision. Across six real research tasks in model training, harness engineering, and data synthesis, Arbor achieves the best held-out result on all six tasks, attaining more than 2.5x the average relative held-out gain of Codex and Claude Code under the same task interface and resource budget. On MLE-Bench Lite, Arbor reaches 86.36% Any Medal with GPT-5.5, the strongest result in our comparison.

schema.problem: Current autonomous scientific research agents generate hypotheses at scale but struggle to validate them rigorously because the hypotheses often lack explicit, measurable falsifiable implications.
schema.motivation: Enforcing falsifiable structure before committing expensive experimentation can avoid wasted experimentation and make rigorous hypothesis validation more tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework has three stages. First, abstract AI-generated hypotheses are converted into operationalized forms with concrete measurable implications and explicit negative outcomes. Second, experiments are synthesized autonomously to disconfirm hypotheses, with a provable minimum set of outcomes that could disconfirm each hypothesis. Third, hypotheses are iteratively refined based on falsification results and unfalsifiable branches are pruned.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on a cross-domain benchmark spanning biology, chemistry, and materials science. It is compared against the Popper falsification-only baseline and the TrustSciAgent trustworthiness-focused baseline. The evaluation measures the defined minimum set of disconfirming outcomes, experimental efficiency, and discovery success. The expected improvement in hypothesis quality and reduction in wasted experimentation would be supported by outperforming those baselines on the relevant metrics; failure to do so would count against that claim. The provable minimum-set property is assessed through the corresponding benchmark metric, though the abstract does not describe a separate formal proof.
