items.title: Falsifiability-Assured Discovery Agents: Structural Enforcement of Falsifiable Hypotheses in Autonomous Scientific Research
items.abstract: Current autonomous scientific research agents generate hypotheses at scale but struggle to validate them rigorously because hypotheses often lack explicit, measurable falsifiable implications. We propose Falsifiability-Assured Discovery Agents (FADA), a framework that enforces falsifiable hypothesis structure before expensive experimentation. FADA operates in three stages: (1) Falsifiability Refactoring—converts abstract AI-generated hypotheses into operationalized forms with concrete measurable implications and explicit negative outcomes; (2) Adaptive Falsification Design—autonomously synthesizes experiments designed to disprove rather than confirm, with provable falsifiability coverage (the minimum set of outcomes that could disconfirm the hypothesis); and (3) Evidence-Driven Refinement—iteratively refines hypotheses based on falsification results, pruning unfalsifiable branches. We evaluate FADA on a cross-domain benchmark spanning biology, chemistry, and materials science, comparing against Popper (falsification-only validation) and TrustSciAgent (trustworthiness-focused) baselines, measuring falsifiability coverage, experimental efficiency, and discovery success. We expect FADA to improve hypothesis quality by 40% and reduce wasted experimentation by 30% relative to baselines.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI scientists currently rely on static knowledge representations or generic retrieval methods, which fail to capture the evolving landscape of scientific topics.
schema.motivation: Capturing evolving topic structures would allow autonomous research pipelines to discover and synthesize emerging research directions in real time.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates dynamic, adaptive topic models into autonomous research pipelines. It learns evolving topic structures as new literature arrives, uses these structures to guide hypothesis generation toward novel intersections of emerging topics, and maintains structured topic relationships that ground literature-discovery agents. The framework will be implemented within an open-ended AI scientist system.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be implemented within an open-ended AI scientist system and evaluated on benchmark datasets from multiple domains. Support for the claims will be measured as improvements in research novelty, relevance, and traceable grounding compared to static topic baselines and dense-retrieval-only approaches; failure would be no improvement on those metrics.

items.title: Dynamic Topic Modeling for Autonomous Research Discovery
items.abstract: Autonomous AI scientists have demonstrated remarkable capability in hypothesis generation, literature review, and experimental design, but they currently rely on static knowledge representations or generic retrieval methods that fail to capture the evolving landscape of scientific topics. We propose DynaTopics, a framework that integrates dynamic, adaptive topic models into autonomous research pipelines to enable real-time discovery and synthesis of emerging research directions. Unlike existing approaches that treat topics as fixed or apply post-hoc topic analysis, DynaTopics learns evolving topic structures as new literature arrives, guides hypothesis generation toward novel intersections of emerging topics, and maintains structured topic relationships that ground literature-discovery agents. We will implement this framework within an open-ended AI scientist system, evaluate it on benchmark datasets from multiple domains, and measure improvements in research novelty, relevance, and traceable grounding compared to static topic baselines and dense-retrieval-only approaches.

schema.problem: Ensuring formal correctness and safety of LLM-generated code remains an open challenge; existing frameworks that integrate program refinement calculus with LLMs either rely on heavyweight interactive theorem provers like Coq or use coarse-grained verification loops that lack localized feedback for partial program components.
schema.motivation: Using refinement checking as a source of fine-grained, compositional feedback could make autonomous code repair tractable while preserving the semantic flexibility of LLM generation and avoiding heavyweight interactive proof.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses refinement types as precise, compositional feedback signals for iterative program repair and synthesis. It parses fine-grained type error traces from a refinement type checker to isolate sub-expression failures, dynamically constructs localized refinement obligations, and guides an agent through targeted patch generation. Static type-checking failures are transformed into actionable agent instructions, combining LLM-based generation with static verification.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation plan is to compare the framework against test-driven and coarse-grained refinement baselines on benchmark synthesis tasks. The abstract does not specify benchmark names, metrics, ablations, held-matched conditions, or explicit failure criteria.

items.title: TypeRefine-Agent: Type-Directed Iterative Refinement Agents for Verified Program Synthesis
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized automated program synthesis, yet ensuring the formal correctness and safety of generated code remains a fundamental challenge. While recent frameworks integrate program refinement calculus with LLMs, they either rely on heavy interactive theorem provers like Coq or operate in coarse-grained verification loops that lack localized feedback for partial program components. To bridge this gap, we propose TypeRefine-Agent, an autonomous LLM agent framework that leverages refinement types (such as Liquid Types) as precise, compositional feedback signals for iterative program repair and synthesis. Instead of treating code generation as a black-box text-to-code translation or relying solely on sparse test suite executions, TypeRefine-Agent parses fine-grained type error traces from a refinement type checker to isolate sub-expression failures, dynamically construct localized refinement obligations, and guide the agent through targeted patch generation. By transforming static type-checking failures into actionable agent instructions, our approach achieves both the semantic flexibility of LLM-based generation and the rigorous guarantees of static verification. We outline a comprehensive experimental evaluation on benchmark synthesis tasks comparing our approach against test-driven and coarse-grained refinement baselines.

schema.problem: Autonomous AI Scientist systems face an implementation gap: they frequently fail during execution due to runtime exceptions, tensor shape mismatches, silent computational failures, and unverified experiment semantics. Current correction strategies relying on naive retry loops driven by raw stack traces or trial-and-error prompting scale poorly to complex, multi-file machine learning codebases and miss degenerate training behaviors.
schema.motivation: The promise of end-to-end autonomous scientific research makes robust execution-phase correction necessary, since unreliable code execution blocks workflows before scientific conclusions can be trusted.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework constructs lightweight program dependency graphs and extracts domain-specific methodological invariants—tensor shape constraints, gradient norm bounds, and loss monotonicity expectations—derived from target baseline papers before full-scale training runs. When execution anomalies or invariant violations occur, it localizes faults by comparing intermediate runtime execution traces against the expected invariants and generates targeted, semantically grounded code patches rather than wholesale rewrites.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is planned across standard machine learning reproducibility benchmarks, comparing the proposed framework against existing LLM agent baselines on execution success rates, scientific validity, and iteration efficiency. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions, ablations, or what is held matched across baselines.

items.title: Bridging the Implementation Gap in AI Scientists via Execution-Trace Verification and Invariant-Guided Self-Correction
items.abstract: Recent advancements in autonomous AI Scientist systems have demonstrated remarkable potential in executing end-to-end scientific research workflows, from hypothesis generation and experimental code implementation to academic manuscript drafting. However, empirical investigations reveal a critical systemic bottleneck: the "implementation gap," where autonomous agents frequently fail due to runtime exceptions, tensor shape mismatches, silent computational failures, and unverified experiment semantics during execution. Current correction strategies rely predominantly on naive retry loops driven by raw stack traces or trial-and-error prompting, which scale poorly to complex, multi-file machine learning codebases and fail to catch degenerate training behaviors. In this paper, we propose TraceGuard, an execution-verification-guided self-correction framework designed specifically for autonomous AI Scientists. TraceGuard constructs lightweight program dependency graphs and extracts domain-specific methodological invariants—such as tensor shape constraints, gradient norm bounds, and loss monotonicity expectations—derived directly from target baseline papers prior to full-scale training runs. When execution anomalies or invariant violations occur, TraceGuard localizes faults by comparing intermediate runtime execution traces against expected mathematical invariants, enabling targeted, semantically grounded code patches rather than wholesale rewrites. Extensive evaluation plans across standard machine learning reproducibility benchmarks demonstrate that TraceGuard substantially improves execution success rates, scientific validity, and iteration efficiency over existing LLM agent baselines.

schema.problem: Two literatures — deployed AI-scientist systems in fluid mechanics and turbulence-closure research — evaluate discovered physical models by proxies such as code executability, draft or peer-review plausibility, or a priori flux correlation; whether a proposed model yields stable, accurate, and out-of-distribution-generalizing forward simulations is left unexamined.
schema.motivation: Models with superb offline a priori accuracy are known to destabilize when run inside a coarse solver, so proxy judgments can hide physically useless closures; because agentic discovery systems are already being deployed and reporting high completion rates, their outputs must be evaluated by forward simulation.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark supplies filtered high-fidelity data from 2D-turbulence and quasi-geostrophic testbeds. Agents must propose, run, and iteratively refine symbolic subgrid-scale closures; each candidate's reward is computed only by executing it in a coarse large-eddy-simulation solver. The reward covers stability over a fixed horizon, spectral fidelity, non-degenerate interscale transfer, and held-out generalization to higher Reynolds number and changed forcing. The construction follows recent agentic-benchmark audit guidance, with pre-registered traps for data leakage, metric misuse, post-hoc selection bias, and reward hacking by trivial stable-but-useless closures.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the claim that offline- and run-completion-gated agents excel on native metrics yet solve few instances, the benchmark records solved-instance yield for such agents; support is few solved instances and failure is many solved instances. (2) For the claim about the verification-gated loop, it compares instance yield from the propose–run–diagnose–revise loop against ungated agents with the same backbone; support requires at least double yield. (3) For the claim about proxy scoring, it compares proxy-scored discovery skill against a posteriori forward-simulation skill and quantifies the overestimation margin; failure is if proxy and simulation-based assessments substantially agree. (4) Audits use pre-registered traps to detect data leakage, metric misuse, post-hoc selection bias, and reward hacking by trivial stable-but-useless closures.

items.title: ClosureBench: A Simulation-in-the-Loop Benchmark for Agentic Turbulence-Closure Discovery
items.abstract: AI-scientist systems are being deployed in fluid mechanics, orchestrating hypothesis generation, CFD runs, and drafting while reporting high completion rates; in parallel, turbulence-closure research has repeatedly shown that models with superb offline (a priori) accuracy destabilize when actually run inside a coarse solver. These two literatures share an unexamined failure mode: discovered physical models are judged by proxies — code executability, draft or peer-review plausibility, or a priori flux correlation — rather than by what physically matters, namely whether the model yields stable, accurate, and out-of-distribution-generalizing forward simulations. We propose ClosureBench, a benchmark that makes a posteriori verification the object of evaluation in agentic turbulence-closure discovery. Agents receive filtered high-fidelity data from 2D-turbulence and quasi-geostrophic testbeds and must propose, run, and iteratively refine symbolic subgrid-scale (SGS) closures whose reward is computed only by executing each candidate in a coarse large-eddy-simulation (LES) solver: stability over a fixed horizon, spectral fidelity, non-degenerate interscale transfer, and held-out generalization to higher Reynolds number and changed forcing. We state three falsifiable predictions: offline and run-completion-gated agents that excel on their native metrics will solve few ClosureBench instances; a verification-gated "propose–run–diagnose–revise" loop will at least double instance yield relative to ungated agents of the same backbone; and proxy scoring will overestimate agent discovery skill by a large, quantifiable margin. ClosureBench is built to the audit standards of recent agentic-benchmark guidance, with pre-registered traps for data leakage, metric misuse, post-hoc selection bias, and reward hacking by trivial stable-but-useless closures.

schema.problem: No benchmark measures whether an agent can choose experiments that discriminate between competing mechanistic explanations of a catalytic reaction; in CO2 electroreduction, closed-loop Bayesian optimization platforms optimize selectivity without maintaining mechanistic hypotheses, and autonomous mechanistic studies test a single pre-specified mechanism family without expanding it.
schema.motivation: Agentic AI scientists are claimed to accelerate mechanistic understanding, and surveys identify experiment selection for mechanistic model discovery as central but unevaluated, so a benchmark is needed to make that capability measurable.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark instantiates ground-truth worlds as generative kinetic simulators reproducing documented CO2RR nonidealities: potential-dependent apparent CO2/bicarbonate orders and electrolyte-poisoning signatures at CoPc/CoTPP/FePc, and opposing pH-dependent OCHO volcanos for single-atom versus polyatomic Sn catalysts. An agent controls a batch experimental executor and is scored on experiments-to-identification, posterior calibration, and transfer of optimal operating conditions, with implementation capability penalized. Baselines include objective-only Bayesian optimization, classic model-discrimination design over a fixed model library, random design, and free-form LLM planning. An evaluated mechanism-expansion module expands the hypothesis library from a literature knowledge base.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the claims that an explicit discrimination objective beats objective-only optimization within known mechanism families and that LLM expansion rescues performance under misspecification, the benchmark compares the baselines—objective-only Bayesian optimization, classic fixed-library model-discrimination design, random design, and free-form LLM planning—on scored trajectories. (2) Support or failure for each claim is read from the benchmark metrics: experiments-to-identification, posterior calibration, and transfer of optimal operating conditions, with implementation capability penalized to isolate planning quality. (3) The misspecification regime is induced by setting the true mechanism outside the initial library; the LLM expansion module is enabled or ablated to test whether it is the responsible component under that regime, holding the rest of the agent fixed.

items.title: MechCO2: Can AI Scientists Choose Experiments That Discriminate CO₂ Electroreduction Mechanisms? A Ground-Truth Benchmark with Literature-Grounded World Models
items.abstract: Agentic AI scientists are claimed to accelerate mechanistic understanding, yet no benchmark measures whether an agent can choose experiments that discriminate between competing mechanistic explanations of a catalytic reaction. In CO₂ electroreduction (CO₂RR) this matters acutely: closed-loop platforms driven by Bayesian optimization optimize selectivity without maintaining mechanistic hypotheses , while the few autonomous mechanistic studies test a single pre-specified mechanism family and never expand it . We introduce MechCO2, a ground-truth benchmark whose worlds are generative kinetic simulators reproducing documented CO₂RR nonidealities — potential-dependent apparent CO₂/bicarbonate orders and electrolyte-poisoning signatures at CoPc/CoTPP/FePc , and opposing pH-dependent *OCHO volcanos for single-atom versus polyatomic Sn catalysts . An agent controls a batch experimental executor and is scored by experiments-to-identification, posterior calibration, and transfer of optimal operating conditions, with "implementation capability" penalized after . Baselines are objective-only BO (the status quo ), classic model-discrimination design over a fixed model library , random design, and free-form LLM planning . The decisive, falsifiable claim is that an explicit discrimination objective beats objective-only optimization within known mechanism families, and that an LLM module which expands the hypothesis library from a literature knowledge base is what rescues performance when the true mechanism lies outside the initial library — the misspecification regime that defeats every fixed-library or objective-only policy. MechCO2 contributes to the agentic-science community a chemically faithful, quantitatively scored testbed for the capability that surveys identify as central but unevaluated : experiment selection for mechanistic model discovery.

schema.problem: Existing autonomous idea-generation loops close within a single, context-clipped snapshot, forming and validating ideas against a fixed literature view, so nothing the system learns during verification ever reshapes what it proposes next.
schema.motivation: Without persistent memory and drift control, recursive batches risk drifting toward the center of a distribution the agent keeps re-sampling from its own outputs, causing novelty decay over long-running discovery.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed loop maintains a persistent time-indexed store of each generated idea together with its novelty-relevance-feasibility annotations, embeddings, and fate (verified-success, verified-failed, or rejected). Candidate ideas are scored against the union of this store and a sliding literature window, a crowding step enforces a collision-radius budget over the full history rather than only the current batch, and a re-ranking step shifts sampling mass toward idea clusters whose past executions realized novelty. The deliverable includes an open-source agent scaffold implementing this loop and a multi-generation evaluation protocol over 10 rounds.
schema.research_plan: (1) The main claim is tested over 10 generation rounds by comparing the proposed loop against three static-context generators (Nova-style planning/search, Chain-of-Ideas literature chaining, and multi-agent critic pools, each with fresh context per batch); support requires statistically significant novelty decline for the static baselines and no decline or a decline under one-third the rate for the loop, as measured by collision rates, RND-calibrated novelty continuity, and reviewer-estimated realized novelty; failure for this claim is any static baseline failing to decline or the loop declining at or above the one-third threshold, with baselines held to fresh context snapshots. (2) The collapse hypothesis is tested directly with a recursive variant whose own outputs re-enter its context, which is expected to fail.

items.title: Landscape-Locked Ideation: A Persistent, Execution-Informed Chronicle Loop for Autonomous Scientific Idea Generation
items.abstract: Autonomous AI-scientist systems now run the full research pipeline, and idea-generation agents convincingly raise novelty and diversity relative to naive prompting—yet every generation loop we retrieved closes within a single, context-clipped snapshot: ideas are formed and validated against a fixed the-agent-can-see-here literature view, and nothing the system learns during verification ever reshapes what it proposes next. We argue this design gap manufactures an agentic analog of model collapse: recursive batches drift toward the center of a distribution the agent keeps re-sampling from its own outputs. We propose a persistent idea chronicle—a time-indexed store of (idea, novelty–relevance–feasibility annotations, embeddings, and fate: verified-success, verified-failed, rejected)—plus a drift-aware novelty gate that scores each candidate against the union of the chronicle and a sliding literature window, crowding suppression that enforces a collision-radius budget over the entire chronicle rather than merely within-batch diversity, and verification-conditioned re-ranking that reallocates sampling mass toward idea clusters whose past executions actually realized novelty. The core, falsifiable claim: across 10 generation rounds, static-context generators (Nova-style planning/search, Chain-of-Ideas literature chaining, and multi-agent critic pools, each with fresh context per batch) will show statistically significant novelty decline, while the chronicle-loop system will not (or will decline at under one-third the rate)—measured by collision rates, RND-calibrated novelty continuity, and reviewer-estimated realized novelty. A recursive variant whose own outputs re-enter its context tests the collapse hypothesis directly and is expected to fail, providing a long-overdue longitudinal instantiation of gaps previously argued only in position papers. The deliverable is the loop mechanism, an open-source agent scaffold implementing it, and the first multi-generation evaluation protocol for AI idea generators.

schema.problem: In AI-scientist pipelines that generate thousands of candidate ideas per run, the decision to promote a candidate idea to execution rests on LLM plausibility judgment, even though pre-execution ratings are known to collapse after execution and LLM claim-to-evidence reasoning is weak.
schema.motivation: Making idea promotion a predictive, error-controlled quantity would avoid relying on uncalibrated judgment and reduce wasted execution on ideas whose pre-execution ratings will not hold up.
schema.proposed_approach: Each candidate idea is compiled into a machine-readable record of its claims and escalated through three nested pre-registered falsification layers: static audits for consistency, leakage, and plausibility; near-zero-cost reanalysis using literature-derived statistical priors that bound reachable effect size (meta-analytic estimates and historical improvement distributions); and capped mini-executions with a pre-registered pass threshold and calibrated per-probe p-values. Promotion requires survival through every layer under pre-committed decision rules with family-wise Type-I error control via Holm allocation; any post-hoc probe reuse or late threshold change is logged as an α-spending violation. The screen is embedded in an existing AI-scientist discovery loop over three fast, fully replicable domains: ML algorithm variants on public benchmarks, symbolic-regression equation candidates, and PDE closures. It is evaluated on a new dataset of about 6,000 generated ideas with hyperverified outcome ground truth.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a pre-registered evaluation on a new dataset of about 6,000 generated ideas with hyperverified outcome ground truth across the three domains. Claim (1) is tested by comparing the screen's precision at k and compute per confirmed finding against the pipeline's LLM judge; it fails if precision at k is lower or compute per confirmed finding exceeds half of the judge. Claim (2) is tested by pooling false-positive rates on null ideas under the pre-committed decision rules and Holm allocation; it fails if the pooled family-wise error rate exceeds nominal α. Claim (3) is tested on held-out execution outcomes, comparing the screen's scores with the LLM judge via area under the curve and with blinded expert review via correlation; it fails if the AUC improvement is below 0.7 or the correlation is below 0.5. Any post-hoc probe reuse or late threshold change is logged as an α-spending violation and treated as evidence against the error-control claim.

items.title: Falsification Gates: Pre-Registered, Statistically Controlled Pre-Execution Screening of AI-Scientist Idea Pools
items.abstract: AI-scientist systems generate thousands of candidate ideas per run, but the promotion decision from "candidate idea" to "worth executing" rests on LLM plausibility judgment — even though pre-execution ratings are known to collapse after execution, and LLM claim-to-evidence reasoning is demonstrably weak. This proposal introduces the Falsification Gate (FG): a pre-execution screen that compiles each candidate idea into a machine-readable Claim Record and escalates it through three nested, pre-registered falsification layers — Level 0 statics (consistency, leakage, and plausibility audits), Level 1 near-zero-cost reanalysis (literature-derived statistical priors bounding reachable effect size, including meta-analytic estimates and historical improvement distributions), and Level 2 capped mini-executions with a pre-registered pass threshold and calibrated per-probe p-values — under pre-committed decision rules with family-wise Type-I error control via Holm allocation. An idea is promoted only if it survives every level; any post-hoc probe reuse or late threshold change is logged as an α-spending violation. We embed FG in a DeepScientist-style discovery loop across three fast, fully replicable domains (ML algorithm variants on public benchmarks, symbolic-regression equation candidates, PDE closures) and test three falsifiable predictions on a new GateBench dataset of ~6,000 generated ideas with hyperverified outcome ground truth: (1) FG matches the pipeline's LLM judge precision@k while spending ≤ half the compute per confirmed finding; (2) pooled FWER on null ideas stays at or below nominal α; (3) gate scores predict held-out execution success (AUC ≥ 0.7 improvement over the judge, r ≥ 0.5 against blinded expert review). If the gate works, idea promotion becomes a predictive, error-controlled quantity rather than an uncalibrated judgment.

schema.problem: Current LLMs lack core chemical knowledge, produce unreliable reasoning trajectories, and exhibit suboptimal performance across diverse chemical tasks, limiting their use for autonomous hypothesis generation and experiment planning in advanced chemical physics.
schema.motivation: LLMs show potential to advance chemical discovery; automating the initial stages of hypothesis generation and experiment planning could assist researchers and accelerate advanced chemical physics studies.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates atomized chemical knowledge and reasoning capabilities into an LLM-based system for hypothesis generation and experiment planning. A benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated hypotheses in advanced chemical physics will be developed, building on existing works such as Chem-R and AOT*.
schema.research_plan: The evidence will center on a benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated hypotheses in advanced chemical physics, built on existing works such as Chem-R and AOT*. The abstract does not state explicit metrics, baselines, or failure conditions for hypothesis quality or experiment planning.

items.title: Advancing LLM-Based Frameworks for Automating Hypothesis Generation and Experiment Planning in Advanced Chemical Physics Studies
items.abstract: This proposal aims to design and develop an LLM-based framework that can autonomously generate hypotheses and plan experiments for specific chemical physics problems. Despite the potential of LLMs in advancing chemical discovery, current models lack core chemical knowledge, produce unreliable reasoning trajectories, and exhibit suboptimal performance across diverse chemical tasks. Addressing these challenges, our framework will integrate atomized chemical knowledge and reasoning capabilities to improve hypothesis generation and experiment planning. We will develop a benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated hypotheses in advanced chemical physics, building on existing works like Chem-R and AOT*. Our expected outcome is a functional LLM agent that can assist researchers in advanced chemical physics studies by automating initial stages of the research process.

schema.problem: Evaluating LLMs' hypothesis generation capabilities across multiple scientific domains is currently difficult due to the lack of comprehensive benchmarks and evaluation metrics.
schema.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for hypothesis generation, and improved cross-domain evaluation would support more effective, domain-agnostic LLM-based scientific research tools.
schema.proposed_approach: Conduct a literature review to identify existing benchmarks and metrics for LLM hypothesis generation; analyze their applicability across scientific domains; evaluate their strengths and limitations; then develop a domain-agnostic benchmarking and evaluation framework from those analyses.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a literature review identifying existing benchmarks and metrics, plus an analysis of their domain applicability, strengths, and limitations. Support for the framework would come from its comprehensiveness and domain-agnostic coverage; the abstract does not specify named baselines, metrics, failure conditions, or matched comparisons.

items.title: Domain-Agnostic Fine-Tuning of LLMs for Research Hypothesis Generation: Benchmarks and Evaluation Metrics
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating scientific research processes, particularly in hypothesis generation. However, evaluating their performance across multiple scientific domains remains challenging due to the lack of comprehensive benchmarks and evaluation metrics. This proposal aims to address this gap by identifying and developing domain-agnostic benchmarks and metrics for assessing LLMs' hypothesis generation capabilities. We will conduct a thorough literature review to identify existing benchmarks and metrics, analyze their applicability across various domains, and evaluate their strengths and limitations. The expected outcome is a comprehensive framework for benchmarking and evaluating LLMs in hypothesis generation, facilitating the development of more effective and domain-agnostic LLM-based scientific research tools.

schema.problem: AI-scientist systems are currently evaluated either by having other LLMs review the papers they write or by measuring how well they reproduce existing code, and neither approach establishes that an agent actually discovered anything.
schema.motivation: A benchmark that grades the experiments agents design against known ground truth would make scientific discovery a measurable, ground-truth-graded question rather than a paper-writing or code-reproduction exercise.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark comprises twelve solvability-certified discovery environments across causal-graph, dynamical-system, and semi-synthetic epidemiology families. Each environment has a designer-known true causal mechanism and planted near-miss decoy mechanisms that produce statistically indistinguishable observational data; agents run the full hypothesis–experiment–conclusion loop under a fixed experimental budget. For each experiment an agent designs, a decisiveness metric is computed from the data-generating process to quantify how well that experiment would separate the true mechanism from the strongest decoy, independent of the agent's beliefs. The release also includes mechanism-recovery, posterior-calibration, and pre-registration-vs-post-hoc trace-audit metrics, an expected-information-gain oracle planner as a benchmark ceiling, and human positive-control validation protocols.
schema.research_plan: (1) The dominance of decisiveness over hypothesis generation is assessed by comparing whether generated hypotheses contain the true mechanism while the experiments agents select fail to separate it from the strongest decoy, as measured by the decisiveness metric and mechanism-recovery F1 under a fixed budget. (2) The explicit candidate-mechanism-space intervention is compared against backbone-model swaps on decisiveness and claim correctness, with the candidate-space condition and model substitutions evaluated in the same task set. (3) Forced pre-registration of a decisive experiment is compared with an equivalent experimental budget spent on post-hoc analysis using claim correctness and trace-log commitment audits as the outcome measures. Success for each claim requires the predicted ordering to hold; failure conditions include finding hypothesis generation, not experiment design, as the limiting factor, or finding model swaps or post-hoc analysis to be equally or more effective than the candidate-space constraint or pre-registration.

items.title: DecisiveBench: Benchmarking AI Research Agents on Planted-Mechanism Discovery with Near-Miss Confounders
items.abstract: AI-scientist systems are evaluated either by having other LLMs review the papers they write, or by measuring how well they reproduce existing code — neither establishes that an agent actually discovered anything. We introduce DecisiveBench, a benchmark of solvability-certified discovery environments in which a designer-known true mechanism and planted near-miss decoy mechanisms produce statistically indistinguishable observational data, and an agent must run the full hypothesis → experiment → conclusion loop under a fixed experimental budget to recover the correct causal claim. Our core contribution is an agent-belief-independent decisiveness metric: for each experiment the agent designs, we compute from the data-generating process how well that experiment would separate the true mechanism from the strongest decoy, independent of the agent's own beliefs. This is complemented by mechanism-recovery F1, posterior calibration over the mechanism space, and a pre-registration vs. post-hoc commitment audit extracted from execution trace logs. Our central, falsifiable claim is that the dominant failure point of frontier LLM agents on such tasks is the decisiveness of experiment design, not hypothesis generation: we predict that agents frequently generate the true mechanism yet select experiments that fail to separate it from its strongest decoy (P1); that constraining agents to an explicit candidate mechanism space improves decisiveness and claim correctness roughly 2× more than any backbone-model swap in our test set (P2); and that forced pre-registration of a decisive experiment yields a larger claim-correctness gain than an equivalent budget of post-hoc analysis (P3). We release 12 environments across three families (causal-graph, dynamical-system, and semi-synthetic epidemiology), the metric and trace-audit suite, an expected-information-gain oracle planner as a benchmark ceiling, and validation protocols including a human positive control. By grading the experiments agents design — not the papers they write — DecisiveBench makes "did the agent do science?" a measurable, ground-truth-graded question.

schema.problem: The scientific integrity of AI-scientist system outputs can currently be checked only by labor-intensive manual tracing; existing automated trace analysis targets which agent caused a task failure, so successful-looking but scientifically invalid runs slip through, and in-loop governance depends on voluntary adoption.
schema.motivation: AI-scientist systems are already producing outputs submitted to venues and read by LLM reviewers, so integrity failures can enter the scientific record unless checking becomes automated and independent of system adoption.
schema.proposed_approach: A post-hoc, system-agnostic auditor converts any research agent's raw logs into a typed event graph whose nodes are code edits, executions, data reads/writes, metric emissions, literature accesses, claims, and paper artifacts, connected by temporal, dataflow, and claim-provenance edges. A statistical check suite of five detectors—for leakage, claim–metric inconsistency, silent execution dropout, trial inflation/selection bias, and evaluation substitution—emits flags with severity and machine-checkable evidence pointers. The work also contributes a seeded-failure benchmark built from clean twin runs with controlled scientific-integrity mutations.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation uses seeded runs from 2–3 open AI-scientist systems and the clean twin benchmark with controlled mutations; per-class recall and precision are measured for each detector. The auditor is compared against a paper-only LLM reviewer and an unstructured LLM reading the same full raw trace, comparing recall at matched precision. Success means meeting the stated recall/precision thresholds and the stated reviewer-comparison margin; failure is falling below those thresholds or not outperforming the reviewers at matched precision.

items.title: IntegrityAudit: A Post-Hoc, System-Agnostic Automated Auditor of AI-Scientist Execution Traces, with a Seeded-Failure Benchmark (IntegrityBench)
items.abstract: Open AI-scientist systems (Kosmos, InternAgent, Jr.-AI-Scientist-style pipelines) now run hundreds of agent rollouts, tens of thousands of lines of code, and thousands of document reads per research cycle, and their outputs are already being submitted to venues and read by LLM reviewers. Yet the scientific integrity of what these systems produce can only be checked today by labor-intensive manual tracing: controlled manual experiments have shown that AI-scientist systems exhibit data leakage, metric misuse, post-hoc selection bias, and inappropriate benchmark selection, and that execution traces reveal what the final paper hides. Meanwhile, existing automated trace analysis targets a different question — which agent caused a task failure — so runs that complete "successfully" yet are scientifically invalid slip through, and in-loop governance frameworks only work when a system voluntarily adopts them. We propose IntegrityAudit: a post-hoc, system-agnostic auditor that converts any research agent's raw logs into a typed Integrity Event Graph (IEG) — code edits, executions, data reads/writes, metric emissions, literature accesses, claims, and paper artifacts connected by temporal, dataflow, and claim-provenance edges — and runs a statistical check suite of five detectors (leakage, claim–metric inconsistency, silent execution dropout, trial inflation/selection bias, evaluation substitution) that emit flags with severity and machine-checkable evidence pointers. We further contribute IntegrityBench, a seeded-failure benchmark built from clean twin runs with controlled scientific-integrity mutations. Core falsifiable claim: on seeded runs from 2–3 open AI-scientist systems, IntegrityAudit reaches ≥80% per-class recall at ≥0.6 precision and beats both a paper-only LLM reviewer and an unstructured LLM reading the same full raw trace by ≥30 absolute recall points at matched precision.

schema.problem: Automatic generation of scientific paper introductions remains difficult because it requires not only linguistic fluency but logical soundness and verifiable faithfulness. Existing AI-assisted methods treat the task as text generation rather than reasoning and structuring, leading to problems such as hallucinated citations.
schema.motivation: With AI systems progressing across other stages of the research pipeline, automatic introduction writing remains a bottleneck in automated scientific writing.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach grounds introduction generation in the paper's core evidence. It first constructs a logic-reasoning graph from the paper's main body to serve as a verifiable logical blueprint. A co-rewarding mechanism then jointly optimizes both the graph's structural fidelity and the final narrative's quality. Evaluation uses a dataset constructed from Nature Communications papers.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is an experimental evaluation on a dataset constructed from Nature Communications papers, using metrics for logic fidelity and introduction generation quality. The abstract does not name baselines, ablations, or failure conditions, nor does it state what is held matched for trade-off claims.

items.title: LECTOR: Joint Optimization of Scientific Reasoning Graphs and Introduction Generation
items.abstract: AI Scientists have shown promising progress across multiple stages of the research pipeline, among which automatic scientific paper writing remains a formidable challenge. The Introduction writing is especially challenging, which demands not only linguistic fluency, but logical soundness and verifiable faithfulness. Most AI-assisted methods treat the task as text generation instead of reasoning and structuring, leading to severe drawbacks, e.g., hallucinating citations. To address this, we first formulate the Content-Conditional Introduction Generation (CCIG) task, which requires grounding the Introduction in the paper's core evidence. We then propose LECTOR, a novel Logic-Expression Co-Reinforcement Learning framework that can strictly follow the scientist's logic, add high-quality citations and keep structured expressions. LECTOR first constructs a logic-reasoning graph from the paper's main body to serve as a verifiable logical blueprint. Subsequently, it employs a Logic-Expression Co-Rewarding mechanism to jointly optimize for both the graph's structural fidelity and the final narrative's quality. We conduct a dataset from Nature Communications papers to assess our method. Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in both logic fidelity and Introduction generation quality metrics, e.g., Graph Quality (+26.7%), Citation Quality (+8.6%), and Paper Consistency (+3.3%). Code and data are available at https://github.com/Xiao-Youth/LECTOR.

schema.problem: In autonomous scientific imaging it is generally assumed that adaptive or Bayesian navigation is the main lever for sample-efficient acquisition, but in dose-limited STEM it is unclear whether navigation or the perception/analysis pipeline actually determines dose efficiency.
schema.motivation: Because every STEM measurement deposits damaging electron dose, knowing whether navigation or perception drives dose efficiency determines where scarce ML effort and beam dose are spent.
schema.proposed_approach: An open-source Gymnasium benchmark is built with 15 physics-simulated STEM worlds spanning five materials, three difficulty levels, and four characterisation tasks. It is scored by a single scalar area under the information-versus-dose Pareto frontier and decouples perception, navigation, and planning under a unified dose budget. The study evaluates 33 agent configurations under realistic dose budgets, including trained CNN analysts with naïve raster scanning, Bayesian navigation, adaptive finite-state-machine navigation, and production-tier vision-language models.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from 33 agent configurations under realistic dose budgets, scored by the information-versus-dose Pareto area. The design isolates perception by comparing a trained CNN analyst with naïve raster scanning against a CNN-free raster baseline, isolates navigation by substituting Bayesian and adaptive finite-state-machine navigation for raster under the same analyst, and isolates analyst type by comparing production-tier vision-language models with task-specific CNNs on crystallographic defect analysis. Support requires the perception comparison to dominate the navigation comparison; the premise that navigation is the principal lever would fail if navigation substitutions yield no statistically significant gains while perception changes dominate.

items.title: STEMGym: Benchmarking Sequential Decision-Making under Dose Budgets in Autonomous Electron Microscopy
items.abstract: A central premise of autonomous scientific imaging is that smarter navigation, whether Bayesian, RL-based, or otherwise adaptive, is the principal lever for sample-efficient acquisition. We present evidence to the contrary in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), an atomic-resolution imaging modality whose every measurement deposits damaging electron dose. We introduce STEMGym, an open-source Gymnasium benchmark of 15 physics-simulated STEM worlds spanning five materials, three difficulty levels, and four characterisation tasks, scored by the Dose-Efficiency Curve area (DEC-AUC), a single scalar capturing the information-vs-dose Pareto frontier. Across 33 agent configurations under realistic dose budgets, the dominant determinant of dose efficiency is the analyst (perception) pipeline, not the navigator: pairing a trained CNN analyst with naïve raster scanning raises DEC-AUC by 5.5x over a CNN-free raster baseline (0.287 vs.\ 0.052), while substituting Bayesian or adaptive finite-state-machine navigation for raster yields no statistically significant further gain. Production-tier vision-language models further underperform task-specific CNNs by {\sim}13x on crystallographic defect analysis. By decoupling perception, navigation, and planning under a unified dose budget, STEMGym reframes where ML effort should be invested in autonomous electron microscopy and provides the measurement infrastructure to test it.

schema.problem: Answering research questions from scientific papers requires more than fluent generation: a reliable system must identify the relevant papers, locate concrete supporting evidence, and produce answers faithful to that evidence, but current scientific QA approaches are not evaluated on these connected capabilities.
schema.motivation: Scientific literature is increasingly used as a knowledge source for language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and research assistants, making verifiable literature-grounded QA essential.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark is constructed as a literature-grounded QA task: given a research question and a metadata pool of papers, a system returns canonical paper identifiers, supporting evidence locations, and answers in one or more requested formats (free-form text, multiple-choice, and structured tables). The benchmark targets evidence types common in scientific reading: tables, figures, text spans, equations or algorithms, and citation contexts. It includes a public development split of 55 examples (26 hidden-source single-paper and 29 multi-paper questions) with gold papers, evidence annotations, and answers for local validation, and a larger final annotation collection with 4,978 unique-question records over 4,859 unique gold papers.
schema.research_plan: The evidence for the benchmark's utility consists of a local validation split with gold papers, evidence annotations, and answers, and an analysis of a larger final annotation collection of 4,978 unique-question records over 4,859 unique gold papers. The design enables separate evaluation of paper retrieval, evidence grounding, and answer accuracy, which serves as the framework for assessing systems; no explicit failure conditions or baseline comparisons are described.

items.title: LitTraceQA: A Benchmark for Multi-Stage Grounding and Verification in Scientific Question Answering
items.abstract: Scientific literature is increasingly used as a knowledge source for language models, retrieval-augmented generation systems, and research assistants, but answering research questions from papers requires more than fluent generation. A reliable system must identify the relevant papers, locate the concrete evidence that supports the answer, and produce a response that is faithful to that evidence. We present LitTraceQA, a benchmark for literature-grounded question answering over scientific papers. Given a research question and a metadata pool of papers, a system must return three connected outputs: canonical paper identifiers, supporting evidence locations, and answers in one or more requested formats, including free-form text, multiple-choice answers, and structured tables. LitTraceQA targets evidence types common in scientific reading: tables, figures, text spans, equations or algorithms, and citation contexts. The public development split contains 55 examples, including 26 hidden-source single-paper questions and 29 multi-paper questions, and provides gold papers, evidence annotations, and answers for local validation. We also analyze a larger final annotation collection with 4,978 unique-question records over 4,859 unique gold papers. By evaluating paper retrieval, evidence grounding, and answer accuracy separately, LitTraceQA provides a testbed for scientific QA systems that produce verifiable answers rather than unsupported summaries.

schema.problem: Existing evaluations of LLM-generated research ideas mostly judge individual ideas by novelty, feasibility, or expert preference, leaving uncharacterized how far current LLM-generated ideas are from human researchers' ideas.
schema.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to brainstorm research ideas, understanding the distributional gap between LLM and human ideas is needed to interpret and improve their use in research ideation.
schema.proposed_approach: A large-scale evaluation framework is built from high-quality human research papers. For each paper, a small set of closely related prior works likely to have inspired its core idea is reverse-engineered; LLMs are then prompted to generate a new idea from the titles and summaries of that set. A two-axis taxonomy profiles each idea by its opportunity pattern and research paradigm and is used to quantify the divergence between human and LLM idea distributions.
schema.research_plan: The distributional-gap claim is tested by generating idea sets from different LLMs under the same reverse-engineered prior-work conditioning and comparing their taxonomy profiles with the human paper reference distribution.

items.title: Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas
items.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to brainstorm research ideas, but existing evaluations mostly judge individual ideas by novelty, feasibility, or expert preference. We instead ask: how far are current LLM-generated ideas from human researchers? To characterize this gap, we build a large-scale evaluation framework for ideation from high-quality human research papers. For each paper, we reverse-engineer a small set of closely related prior works that likely inspired its core idea. LLMs are then prompted to generate a new idea from the set of paper titles and summaries. We introduce a two-axis research-taste taxonomy to profile each idea by its opportunity pattern and research paradigm, and use it to quantify the divergence between human and LLM ideas. Across idea sets generated by different LLMs, we observe a consistent distributional gap: LLM ideas are disproportionately concentrated around bridge-like opportunities and synthesis methods, whereas the human paper reference distribution spreads more broadly across ways of framing gaps and constructing contributions. This result suggests that strong LLMs can produce a range of reasonable ideas, but that range remains narrower than, and systematically shifted relative to, human research taste.

schema.problem: Training scientific reasoning in large language models robustly and efficiently remains an open challenge; in instruction-based molecular optimization, answer-only supervised fine-tuning collapses multi-step reasoning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards suffers from sparse feedback, and reference-guided policy optimization is limited by reference quality, with weak or misaligned references imposing a performance ceiling.
schema.motivation: Removing the reference-quality ceiling would let reference guidance stay informative rather than restrictive throughout training, enabling more robust and efficient reasoning without discarding useful references or being capped by them.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach instantiates an active reasoning paradigm in which the policy chooses, per instance, whether to imitate a reference or reinforce its own discoveries. A first mechanism performs imitation learning while the reference still outperforms the policy's own candidates and shifts to reinforcement learning once the policy generates molecules that surpass the reference. A second mechanism continuously replaces the reference with the best policy-generated candidate discovered so far, raising the imitation target.
schema.research_plan: The claim of overcoming the reference-quality ceiling is supported by molecular optimization evaluation on TOMG-Bench MOLOPT: average SRxSim is compared under matched three-seed evaluation against GRPO and RePO, with statistical significance tested on LogP, MR, and QED. Implicitly, a failure condition is no improvement over those reference-guided baselines or no significant per-objective gains. The abstract does not describe ablations isolating the two mechanisms or robustness checks beyond the matched three-seed setting.

items.title: Active-GRPO: Adaptive Imitation and Self-Improving Reasoning for Molecular Optimization
items.abstract: Scientific reasoning is an increasingly important capability of large language models, yet improving the robustness and efficiency of training such reasoning remains a key open challenge. We study this problem in instruction-based molecular optimization, where answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses multi-step reasoning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) suffers from sparse feedback. Reference-guided Policy Optimization mitigates both by anchoring policy updates to dataset-provided references, but its effectiveness is tightly coupled to reference quality: weak or misaligned references impose a performance ceiling. To overcome this ceiling, we propose active reasoning, a paradigm in which the policy actively decides, on a per-instance basis, when to imitate a reference and when to reinforce its own discoveries, while continuously upgrading what it imitates. We instantiate this paradigm as Active Group Relative Policy Optimization (Active-GRPO), realized through two coupled mechanisms: active imitate-reinforce and active referencing. The former performs imitation learning when the reference still outperforms the policy's own candidates, and shifts to self-improvement via reinforcement learning once the policy has generated molecules that surpass the reference. The latter continuously upgrades the reference itself by replacing it with the best policy-generated candidate discovered so far, progressively raising the imitation target and ensuring that reference guidance remains informative-rather than restrictive-throughout training. Across TOMG-Bench MOLOPT, Active-GRPO improves average SRxSim from 0.0959 for GRPO and 0.1665 for RePO to 0.1773 under matched three-seed evaluation, with statistically significant gains on LogP, MR, and QED.

schema.problem: The field lacks a characterization of how maintaining relatively stable acceptance rates at top AI conferences despite exponentially growing submissions enables a structural vulnerability in which a malicious actor can exploit submission-volume inflation to manipulate publication probabilities without needing low-quality papers accepted.
schema.motivation: AI agents now make it cheap to generate superficially plausible low-quality papers at scale, and the stable-acceptance-rate equilibrium makes such volume attacks strategically worth addressing because they can overwhelm reviewing capacity and intensify reviewer burnout.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper characterizes the threat, analyzes its practical feasibility and broader consequences, proposes a range of mitigation strategies, and argues that durable protection requires system-level policy and incentive reforms rather than primarily technical detection.
schema.research_plan: (1) The threat mechanism and its feasibility are supported by analysis under the assumption of stable acceptance rates and scalable AI-generated submissions. (2) The proposed mitigation strategies are evaluated comparatively, with the argument holding that technical detection alone is inadequate and system-level reforms are necessary; the abstract does not specify evaluation criteria, baselines, or failure conditions.

items.title: Position: Academic Conferences are Potentially Facing Denominator Gaming Caused by Fully Automated Scientific Agents
items.abstract: The implicit policy of maintaining relatively stable acceptance rates at top AI conferences, despite exponentially growing submissions, introduces a critical structural vulnerability. This position paper characterizes a new systemic threat we term Agentic Denominator Gaming, in which a malicious actor deploys AI agents to generate and submit a large volume of superficially plausible but low-quality papers. Crucially, their objective is not the acceptance of low-quality papers, but rather to inflate the submission denominator and overwhelm reviewing capacity. Under a relatively stable acceptance rate, this dilution can systematically increase the publication probability of a small, targeted set of legitimate papers. We analyze the practical feasibility of this threat and its broader consequences, including intensified reviewer burnout, degraded review quality, and the emergence of industrialized automated agent mills. Finally, we propose and evaluate a range of mitigation strategies, and argue that durable protection will require system-level policy and incentive reforms, rather than relying primarily on technical detection alone.

schema.problem: World modeling is an unsettled field in which architectures, training objectives, and state representations interact in complex ways and no single recipe dominates across environments; current agent benchmarks evaluate engineering-to-spec tasks rather than open-ended research.
schema.motivation: World modeling's complexity makes it an ideal testbed for evaluating AI coding agents as autonomous researchers, and a unified structured-state representation that isolates dynamics from perception enables minutes-per-run iteration, making such open-ended evaluation practical.
schema.proposed_approach: A closed-loop benchmark is introduced in which frontier coding agents autonomously improve a provided base world model under a fixed compute budget. It spans eight game environments under a unified structured-state representation—ground-truth entity state extracted from each game and consumed through a shared tensor format—which isolates dynamics modeling from perception and enables minutes-per-run iteration.
schema.research_plan: (1) To support the claim that the benchmark isolates dynamics modeling from perception, the design uses a unified structured-state representation across eight game environments with ground-truth entity state. (2) To support the claim that the benchmark evaluates open-ended research, the evaluation runs 64 sessions with two frontier coding agents under a fixed compute budget, scoring edits on a held-out test split. Sessions are judged successful when the agent improves the held-out test split, and gains of at least +0.10 are considered substantial; winning edits are classified as substantive model or training changes versus hyperparameter tweaks.

items.title: AutoWorldModel-Bench: A State-Centric Benchmark for Automated World-Model Research
items.abstract: World modeling is an unsettled field: architectures, training objectives, and state representations interact in complex ways, and no single recipe dominates across environments. This makes it an ideal testbed for AI coding agents acting as autonomous researchers--a setting in which the improvement direction is not specified in advance, unlike the engineering-to-spec tasks that dominate current agent benchmarks. We introduce AutoWorldModel-Bench, a closed-loop benchmark in which frontier coding agents autonomously improve a provided base world model under a fixed compute budget. The benchmark spans eight game environments under a unified structured-state representation--ground-truth entity state extracted from each game and consumed through a shared tensor format--which isolates dynamics modeling from perception and enables minutes-per-run iteration. Across 64 sessions, Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 improve their base on a held-out test split in all but one session, with about half (33 of 64) a substantial gain ($Δ\geq +0.10$) and the remaining improvements smaller but positive; in 91% of sessions the winning edit is a substantive change to the model or training rather than a hyperparameter tweak. Our benchmark offers a setting in which frontier coding agents can be evaluated on open-ended research rather than engineering-to-spec problems.

schema.problem: Current approaches to modeling how genetic and chemical perturbations give rise to transcriptional responses remain expert-intensive, relying on iterative manual model design, training, and debugging over months.
schema.motivation: Autonomous construction of perturbation-response models would reduce development time and enable scalable, data-driven exploration of cellular systems for virtual cell world models and drug discovery.
schema.proposed_approach: The system combines an AI coding agent with multimodal biological foundation models to construct perturbation-response models. It explores large spaces of architectures and training pipelines with minimal human intervention, iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining candidate models.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the performance claim comes from evaluation across multiple perturbation-response benchmarks with comparison to expert-designed approaches and reported development time. The claim about non-obvious patterns is supported by analyzing architectural patterns found by the search. No explicit failure condition, ablation, or named baselines and metrics are stated in the abstract.

items.title: Harnessing AI to Build Virtual Cells
items.abstract: A virtual cell is a world model of a cell: a computational system that predicts, simulates and programs cellular processes across modalities and scales. An important path toward this goal is to model how genetic and chemical perturbations give rise to transcriptional responses, a core capability for disease understanding and drug discovery. However, current approaches remain expert-intensive, relying on iterative manual model design, training and debugging over months. Here we present VCHarness, an autonomous AI system that constructs perturbation-response models by combining an AI coding agent with multimodal biological foundation models. The system explores large spaces of architectures and training pipelines with minimal human intervention, iteratively generating, evaluating and refining candidate models. Across multiple perturbation-response benchmarks, VCHarness identifies architectures that outperform expert-designed approaches while reducing development time from months to days. It further uncovers non-obvious architectural patterns associated with improved performance, indicating that automated search can extend beyond conventional design strategies. These results suggest a shift from manually engineered models toward autonomous systems for constructing components of virtual cell world models, enabling scalable and data-driven exploration of cellular systems.

schema.problem: The exact value of the book Ramsey number R(B_8,B_10) was not known; a lower bound R(B_8,B_10) ≥ 37 was already available in the literature, but the matching upper bound, ruling out a 37-vertex counterexample, remained unproved.
schema.motivation: Newly available AI-assisted mathematical discovery makes finding the problem and proof tractable, and a Lean formalization provides a mechanically checkable upper-bound argument.
schema.proposed_approach: The proof rules out a 37-vertex graph whose edge set contains no B_8 and whose complement contains no B_10, using the known lower bound so that only this upper-bound case remains. The problem and proof were found with an AI-assisted mathematical discovery workflow developed by the first author. A Lean formalization of the upper-bound argument is available in the accompanying repository.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a mathematical proof of the upper-bound claim, excluding a 37-vertex counterexample as described. A Lean formalization of the upper-bound argument is available in the accompanying repository, supporting correctness by mechanical verification. The lower bound is cited from the literature rather than re-proven. No experimental baselines or metrics apply; the implicit failure condition would be a gap or error in the ruling-out argument.

items.title: An automated proof that R(B_8,B_10)=37
items.abstract: We present a short proof that the book Ramsey number $R(B_8,B_{10})$ equals 37. The lower bound $R(B_8,B_{10}) \ge 37$ is already available in the literature, so it is enough to rule out a 37-vertex graph containing neither a copy of $B_8$ nor a copy of $B_{10}$ in its complement. The problem as well as the proof were found with AutoMath, an AI-assisted mathematical discovery workflow developed by the first author. A Lean formalization of the upper-bound argument is available in the accompanying repository.

schema.problem: Parallel scaling approaches for deep research agents isolate subtask knowledge, preventing runtime adaptation of research plans and coherent synthesis for complex PhD-level report generation.
schema.motivation: Generating detailed research reports on complex doctoral-level topics requires search that remains coherent and adaptive without wasting effort in siloed parallel tasks.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture uses a sequential reflective process in which the agent keeps a centralized global research context, reviews current progress, reasons about the plan, and revises it at runtime. It deploys multiple LLM candidates with varied parameters to explore a larger search space, then synthesizes their findings into a unified final response. The final report is generated in one shot from that unified narrative. The system is powered by the Gemini 2.5 Pro model.
schema.research_plan: (1) The architecture is evaluated on the DeepResearch Bench, a benchmark of 100 doctoral-level research tasks. (2) It is compared against leading deep research agents: Claude Researcher, Nvidia AIQ Research Assistant, Perplexity Research, Kimi Researcher, and Grok Deeper Search, as well as the authors' previous static variant. (3) The benchmark comparison is used to support the claimed superiority over parallel self-consistency approaches; the abstract states no explicit failure condition or matched resource constraints.

items.title: Deep Researcher with Sequential Plan Reflection and Candidates Crossover (Deep Researcher Reflect Evolve)
items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel Deep Researcher architecture designed to generate detailed research reports on complex PhD level topics by addressing the inherent limitations of the Parallel Scaling paradigm. Our system utilizes two key innovations: Sequential Research Plan Refinement via Reflection and a Candidates Crossover algorithm. The sequential refinement process is demonstrated as an efficient method that allows the agent to maintain a centralized Global Research Context, enabling it to look back at current progress, reason about the research plan, and intelligently make changes at runtime. This dynamic adaptation contrasts with parallel approaches, which often suffer from siloed knowledge. The Candidates Crossover algorithm further enhances search efficiency by deploying multiple LLM candidates with varied parameters to explore a larger search space, with their findings synthesized to curate a comprehensive final research response. The process concludes with One Shot Report Generation, ensuring the final document is informed by a unified narrative and high fact density. Powered by the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, our Deep Researcher was evaluated on the DeepResearch Bench, a globally recognized benchmark of 100 doctoral level research tasks. Our architecture achieved an overall score of 46.21, demonstrating superior performance by surpassing leading deep research agents such as Claude Researcher, Nvidia AIQ Research Assistant, Perplexity Research, Kimi Researcher and Grok Deeper Search present on the DeepResearch Bench actively running leaderboard. This performance marginally exceeds our previous work, Static DRA, and reinforces the finding that sequential scaling consistently outperforms the parallel self consistency paradigm.

schema.problem: Amortized symbolic regression promises greater efficiency than genetic programming methods, but scaling to realistic scientific complexity is limited by the high computational cost of reducing equivalent expressions to a concise normalized form with general-purpose computer algebra systems.
schema.motivation: A fast normalization step would remove this bottleneck, enabling amortized symbolic regression to scale to larger training sets, use per-expression token budgets more efficiently, and systematically decontaminate training data against equivalent test expressions.
schema.proposed_approach: The work proposes a rule-based simplification engine for symbolic expressions that normalizes equivalent expressions quickly, replacing general-purpose computer algebra systems in amortized symbolic regression. This engine is integrated into an amortized symbolic regression framework, where it is used during training and inference to canonicalize expressions, enabling larger training sets, more efficient use of per-expression token budgets, and systematic removal of training examples equivalent to test expressions. The framework is evaluated on the FastSRB benchmark against amortized and direct optimization baselines.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is organized around three claims. (1) The simplification engine is benchmarked against SymPy; support requires faster runtime at comparable simplification quality. (2) The benefits of fast normalization for training-set size, token-budget efficiency, and decontamination are demonstrated within the proposed amortized symbolic regression framework. (3) The framework is compared with amortized baselines (NeSymReS, E2E) on the FastSRB benchmark and with direct optimization (PySR), with support requiring better accuracy than amortized baselines, parity with direct optimization, and increasing conciseness rather than complexity as inference budget grows.

items.title: Breaking the Simplification Bottleneck in Amortized Neural Symbolic Regression
items.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover interpretable analytical expressions that accurately describe observed data. Amortized SR promises to be much more efficient than the predominant genetic programming SR methods, but currently struggles to scale to realistic scientific complexity. We find that a key obstacle is the lack of a fast reduction of equivalent expressions to a concise normalized form. Amortized SR has addressed this with general-purpose Computer Algebra Systems (CAS) like SymPy, but the high computational cost severely limits training and inference speed. We propose SimpliPy, a rule-based simplification engine achieving a 100-fold speed-up over SymPy at comparable quality. This enables substantial improvements in amortized SR, including scalability to much larger training sets, more efficient use of the per-expression token budget, and systematic training set decontamination with respect to equivalent test expressions. We demonstrate these advantages in our Flash-ANSR framework, which achieves much better accuracy than amortized baselines (NeSymReS, E2E) on the FastSRB benchmark. Moreover, it performs on par with state-of-the-art direct optimization (PySR) while recovering more concise rather than more complex expressions with increasing inference budget.

schema.problem: The capability profile of frontier coding agents varies sharply across technical domains, but domain-specific evidence on whether and under what oversight they can contribute to specialised technical work is lacking; in computational phylogenetics, neighbour joining's constant-factor runtime is set by hand-tuned native implementations, and it is unknown whether a coding agent can advance that constant factor on a fixed benchmark.
schema.motivation: Because coding-agent capabilities are uneven, a domain-specific study can identify where they add value, and a positive result in performance-critical bioinformatics would make harness-guided optimisation a plausible route for tools whose runtime is otherwise manually tuned.
schema.proposed_approach: A current-generation coding agent is run under a correctness-gated optimisation harness with deterministic correctness gates calibrated against a QuickTree reference, producing an optimised neighbour-joining implementation. The implementation is compared with a locally rebuilt RapidNJ-native binary on a fixed benchmark of 59 matrices. Correctness is evaluated using shuffled inputs drawn from 16 small matrices of at most 2000 taxa, comparing tree topology to QuickTree via Robinson–Foulds distance.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is tested by comparing the optimised implementation with a locally rebuilt RapidNJ-native binary on the fixed 59-matrix corpus; support would be a runtime ratio below parity, while parity or worse would count against it. Claim (2) is tested on 400 shuffled inputs from 16 small matrices (n ≤ 2000), using Robinson–Foulds distance zero against QuickTree as the support condition and any nonzero distance as a correctness failure. The benchmark and correctness gates are held fixed for the trade-off claim, though the abstract does not describe parameter matching beyond the locally rebuilt baseline. No broader-domain or ablation evidence is reported, so the generalisation suggestion remains unestablished.

items.title: SwiftNJ: Fast Exact Neighbour Joining via Correctness-Gated Coding Agents
items.abstract: The capability profile of frontier coding agents in 2026 varies sharply across technical domains, motivating domain-specific empirical study of where, and under what oversight conditions, such systems can contribute to specialised technical work. This paper presents one such study in computational phylogenetics. Neighbour joining (NJ) is a widely used distance-based method for inferring evolutionary trees in microbial epidemiology, comparative genomics, and large-scale sequence clustering. Its constant-factor runtime is set by hand-tuned native implementations; RapidNJ is a widely-cited representative of that class and serves here as the comparison baseline. We ask whether a current-generation coding agent, operating under a correctness-gated optimisation harness with deterministic correctness gates calibrated against a QuickTree reference, can advance that constant factor on a fixed benchmark. The resulting implementation, SwiftNJ, achieves a geometric-mean runtime ratio of 0.565 against a locally-rebuilt RapidNJ-native binary across a 59-matrix corpus, sub-parity on 58 of 59 matrices. On 400 shuffled inputs drawn from 16 small matrices ( n ≤ 2000), SwiftNJ matched the QuickTree reference at Robinson–Foulds distance zero. In this domain, a correctness-gated coding agent meaningfully improved on a strong native baseline, suggesting that harness-guided optimisation holds promise for performance-critical bioinformatics tools; further work is needed to establish how broadly the approach generalises.

schema.problem: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation. Current world models for planning treat tactile information as an auxiliary prediction task rather than a first-class latent state variable.
schema.motivation: Explicitly representing contact state alongside scene geometry would enable model-based planning that respects contact constraints and supports tactile servoing trajectories.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach builds a world model with a shared latent dynamics space that unifies visual and tactile observations. The latent state explicitly represents contact state such as forces, slip, and pressure alongside scene geometry, and the model jointly predicts visual and tactile futures from that latent state for model-based planning that respects contact constraints and tactile servoing trajectories.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on contact-rich tasks including pushing, tool use, and in-hand manipulation compares the proposed model against visual-only and separate-modality baselines on sample efficiency, generalization to unseen objects, and task success. The explicit tactile latent state claim would fail if it did not outperform these baselines on those criteria.

items.title: Tactile-Aware Latent Dynamics World Models for Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet current world models for planning treat tactile information as an auxiliary prediction task rather than a first-class latent state variable. We propose Tactile-Aware Latent Dynamics (TALD), a world model that unifies visual and tactile observations into a shared latent dynamics space where contact state (forces, slip, pressure) is explicitly represented alongside scene geometry. Unlike prior work that learns separate visual and tactile representations or finetunes tactile prediction after visual alignment, TALD jointly predicts visual and tactile futures from a latent state that explicitly encodes contact dynamics. This enables model-based planning that respects contact constraints and tactile servoing trajectories. We validate TALD on contact-rich tasks (pushing, tool use, in-hand manipulation) and show that explicit tactile state in the latent dynamics improves sample efficiency, generalization to unseen objects, and task success compared to visual-only and separate-modality baselines.

schema.problem: Existing visual world models primarily capture appearance dynamics and overlook tactile states that govern contact-rich interactions, so they can produce imagined futures that appear visually plausible but violate physical dynamics.
