schema.motivation: Jointly modeling visual and tactile futures is needed for planning physical interactions, enabling imagined outcomes to respect contact-rich physical dynamics and supporting contact-aware planning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework jointly predicts future visual latents and three tactile states—contact state, a 3D tactile latent encoding force-related information, and slip state—using a shared latent dynamics model with explicit supervision. A contact-gated asymmetric attention mechanism maintains a visual-only prediction pathway before contact and enables joint visuo-tactile dynamics prediction during contact. Training uses autoregressive rollouts and context noise injection to improve robustness to compounding errors. The predicted contact and slip states support contact-aware planning.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates visual prediction quality via LPIPS at short and long autoregressive rollouts, comparing against a visual-only baseline, with longer rollouts testing robustness to compounding errors. It also assesses zero-shot planning success on chip grasping, fruit grasping, and USB insertion using contact-aware planning from predicted contact and slip states. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched compute/latency constraints.

items.title: FeelWorld: Visuo-Tactile World Model for Hierarchical Contact Prediction and Planning
items.abstract: Humans plan physical interactions by imagining the possible outcomes of candidate actions. However, existing visual world models primarily capture appearance dynamics while overlooking the tactile states that govern contact-rich interactions, potentially producing imagined futures that appear visually plausible but violate physical dynamics. We introduce FeelWorld, a hierarchical visuo-tactile world model that jointly predicts future visual latents and three tactile states. FeelWorld organizes these states hierarchically as contact state, a 3D tactile latent that encodes force-related information, and slip state. These states are jointly predicted by a shared latent dynamics model with explicit supervision. To prevent irrelevant tactile signals during free-space motion from degrading visual prediction, we introduce a contact-gated asymmetric attention mechanism that maintains a visual-only prediction pathway before contact and enables joint visuo-tactile dynamics prediction during contact. The model is further trained with autoregressive rollouts and context noise injection to improve robustness to compounding errors. The predicted contact and slip states also support contact-aware CEM planning. Experiments on chip grasping, fruit grasping, and USB insertion show that FeelWorld reduces 10-step LPIPS from 0.084 to 0.058 and maintains an LPIPS that is 61% lower than that of the visual baseline after an 80-step autoregressive rollout. FeelWorld also achieves an average zero-shot planning success rate of 81.7%, providing an effective approach for incorporating tactile sensing into world models.

schema.problem: Action-conditioned latent dynamics for planning with joint-embedding predictive architectures remain underdeveloped, despite their effectiveness for self-supervised visual representation learning from unlabeled video.
schema.motivation: Learning interpretable action directions in latent space would allow planning algorithms to operate in a geometry-aware representation where action effects are explicitly encoded.
schema.proposed_approach: The method augments JEPA by learning directional latent dynamics: action embeddings are trained to map to interpretable directions in the learned latent state space, with state transitions expected to follow predictable geodesic paths. A contrastive action embedding objective jointly optimizes state and action representations, yielding a geometry-aware latent space in which planning algorithms operate.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation compares the proposed method with standard action-conditioned world models on visual control tasks from robotics and simulated environments, using planning accuracy, sample efficiency, and zero-shot transfer as evidence for the claimed improvements. The abstract does not specify ablations isolating the directional latent dynamics or contrastive objective, matched compute or parameter controls, or explicit failure criteria.

items.title: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models with Directional Latent Dynamics
items.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have proven effective for self-supervised visual representation learning from unlabeled video, yet their integration with action-conditioned dynamics for planning remains underdeveloped. We propose a method that augments JEPA by learning directional latent dynamics, where action embeddings map to interpretable directions in the learned latent state space such that state transitions follow predictable geodesic paths. We introduce a contrastive action embedding objective that jointly optimizes state and action representations, enabling planning algorithms to operate in a geometry-aware latent space where action effects are explicitly encoded. We evaluate on visual control tasks from robotics and simulated environments, demonstrating improved planning accuracy, sample efficiency, and zero-shot transfer compared to standard action-conditioned world models.

schema.problem: Reconstruction-free joint-embedding world models can collapse to action-insensitive latent representations, leaving learned latent dynamics insufficiently sensitive to actions for rollout-based planning.
schema.motivation: Action-conditioned latent transitions are necessary for planning, so regularization that preserves action information in latent geometry would make reconstruction-free world models more reliable for rollout-based control.
schema.proposed_approach: An end-to-end reconstruction-free world model augments latent forward prediction with an action decoder. The decoder reconstructs the executed action from the latent displacement between consecutive observation embeddings, rather than from concatenated endpoint embeddings. Training uses only latent prediction and action reconstruction losses, with no pixel reconstruction or distribution-matching regularizer.
schema.research_plan: (1) The planning claim is evaluated on four visual continuous-control tasks against JEPA-based and representation-learning world model baselines; support requires the proposed framework to plan at least comparably to those baselines. (2) Ablations compare displacement-based action decoding with endpoint concatenation; support for the decoder-form claim requires displacement-based decoding to be at least as effective as endpoint concatenation. (3) Action-sensitivity analyses examine action-conditioned latent responses; support requires the representations to show action-conditioned structure.

items.title: Delta-JEPA: Learning Action-Sensitive World Models via Latent Difference Decoding
items.abstract: Learning visual world models for planning requires compact latent dynamics that remain sensitive to actions, yet reconstruction-free joint-embedding objectives can collapse to action-insensitive representations. We propose Delta-JEPA, an end-to-end reconstruction-free world model that augments latent forward prediction with a Latent Difference Action Decoder (LDAD). Unlike inverse decoders that infer actions from concatenated endpoint embeddings, LDAD reconstructs the executed action from the latent displacement between consecutive observations. This displacement-level supervision directly regularizes transition geometry: adjacent embeddings cannot collapse without losing action information, and different actions are encouraged to induce distinguishable latent changes for rollout-based planning. Delta-JEPA uses only latent prediction and action reconstruction, avoiding pixel reconstruction and distribution-matching regularizers. Across four visual continuous-control tasks, Delta-JEPA improves planning over JEPA-based and representation-learning world model baselines. Ablations show that displacement-based action decoding is consistently more effective than endpoint concatenation, and action-sensitivity analyses show clearer action-conditioned latent responses. These results indicate that supervising latent differences is a simple and effective mechanism for collapse-resistant and action-sensitive world model learning.

schema.problem: Model-based reinforcement learning and image-based world models such as Dreamer architectures excel at local control but suffer from compounding errors and drift during long-horizon latent rollouts.
schema.motivation: Recent retrieval-augmented mechanisms for LLM-based or video-generative world models rely on text tokens, large external video models, or heuristic memory structures that ignore the fine-grained metric geometry of visual latent spaces, leaving long-horizon correction unresolved.
schema.proposed_approach: A compact recurrent state-space model is coupled with a non-parametric visual-retrieval memory bank of past latent transition states. Historical encoder states are indexed in a learned metric space optimized via contrastive image retrieval objectives; during planning, the world model queries this memory and anchors its latent rollouts against verified past observations. Retrieved historical transitions are injected as corrective soft constraints into the latent transition model to mitigate compounding errors.
schema.research_plan: The proposal outlines implementation on standard visual control benchmarks and evaluates robustness against distribution shift and long-horizon trajectory divergence.

items.title: Retrieval-Augmented Latent Dynamics for Robust Image-Based World Models
items.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning and image-based world models (such as Dreamer architectures) excel at local control and predictive simulation, but suffer severely from compounding errors and drift during long-horizon latent rollouts. While recent advances introduce retrieval-augmented mechanisms to LLM-based or video-generative world models, these approaches typically rely on text tokens, large external video models, or heuristic memory structures that ignore the fine-grained metric geometry of visual latent spaces. In this proposal, we introduce Retrieval-Augmented Latent Dynamics (RALD), a framework that couples a compact recurrent state-space model with a non-parametric visual-retrieval memory bank of past latent transition states. RALD indexes historical encoder states using a learned metric space optimized via contrastive image retrieval objectives, allowing the world model to query and anchor its latent rollouts against verified past observations during planning. By injecting retrieved historical transitions as corrective soft constraints into the latent transition model, RALD mitigates error compounding over extended horizons. We outline an implementation on standard visual control benchmarks and evaluate its robustness against distribution shift and long-horizon trajectory divergence.

schema.problem: In long-horizon visual goal planning, existing JEPA-style world models learn only local transition consistency through next-step representation prediction; multi-step rollouts can remain locally plausible while drifting from goal-relevant trajectories, and locally similar future states can correspond to substantially different long-term progress.
schema.motivation: Accurate local prediction alone does not sustain progress toward a distant goal, and modeling the relative ordering of states by goal advancement, whose asymmetric coarse-to-fine structure suits hyperbolic geometry, makes it tractable to organize latent dynamics and guide planning.
schema.proposed_approach: The method builds a progress-aware hyperbolic visual world model. It uses a relative ordering of states by goal advancement to organize visual latent-space dynamics. Directional progress within trajectories is maintained through entailment learning in hyperbolic space, and progress ambiguity among locally similar future states is reduced through hyperbolic future discrimination. It also includes a planning objective that scores candidate rollouts by jointly considering proximity to the goal and sustained progress across intermediate states.
schema.research_plan: The claims are evaluated empirically on four visual goal-reaching tasks, comparing the proposed model against the LeWM baseline using success rate; all three claims rest on this comparison, and no ablations or matched-budget constraints are specified.

items.title: ProWorld: Progress-Aware Hyperbolic World Models for Long-Horizon Visual Goal Reaching
items.abstract: JEPA-style visual world models offer an effective paradigm for visual goal planning by predicting future latent representations. Existing methods typically learn local transition consistency through next-step representation prediction. However, in long-horizon tasks, accurate local prediction alone need not ensure sustained progress toward the goal. First, multi-step rollouts can remain locally plausible while drifting away from goal-relevant trajectories. Second, locally similar future states can correspond to substantially different long-term progress, making them difficult to distinguish in a latent space optimized mainly for local consistency. To address these challenges, we introduce goal-conditioned progress order, a relative ordering of states according to how they advance toward a given goal. This order exhibits an asymmetric, coarse-to-fine structure: early states retain broader future possibilities, while later states concentrate on more specific goal-relevant regions. Such a structure is well suited to hyperbolic geometry. Motivated by this observation, we propose ProWorld, a progress-aware hyperbolic visual world model. ProWorld leverages goal-conditioned progress order to organize visual latent-space dynamics, maintains directional progress within trajectories via hyperbolic entailment learning, and mitigates progress ambiguity among locally similar future states via hyperbolic future discrimination. Furthermore, we design a progress-aware planning objective that scores candidate rollouts by jointly considering proximity to the goal and sustained progress across intermediate states. Experiments on four visual goal-reaching tasks demonstrate that ProWorld achieves an average absolute success-rate gain of 9.67 over LeWM. The code will be released after the paper is accepted.

schema.problem: Current video-generative world models rely on multi-step diffusion or expensive autoregressive rollouts, causing severe computational bottlenecks and compounding errors over long horizons.
schema.motivation: World models for model-based reinforcement learning and interactive simulation require both high fidelity and real-time inference under action conditioning, and recent advances in adversarial post-training for image-to-video generation make fast single-step generation tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework transforms pre-trained video diffusion models into single-step latent world simulators by adding an action-conditioned latent transition network trained with student-forcing adversarial objectives. A spatiotemporal patch discriminator operates directly in latent space to enforce long-term consistency. The approach eliminates iterative denoising steps and is designed to reduce exposure bias and error accumulation during multi-step interactive rollouts.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of experimental evaluations across simulated robotic control and interactive video benchmarks, comparing the proposed single-step world simulator against slower multi-step diffusion world models on spatiotemporal coherence and real-time streaming frame generation. The abstract implies support requires real-time streaming generation with spatiotemporal coherence that matches or exceeds the slower baselines, while failure would be a loss of coherence or no real-time generation.

items.title: Adversarial Latent World Models: Real-Time Action-Conditioned Video Generation via Adversarial Post-Training
items.abstract: World models are foundational for model-based reinforcement learning and interactive simulation, requiring both high fidelity and real-time inference under action conditioning. However, current video-generative world models rely on multi-step diffusion or expensive autoregressive rollouts, leading to severe computational bottlenecks and compounding errors over long horizons. Inspired by recent advances in adversarial post-training for fast image-to-video generation, we propose Adversarial Latent World Models (ALWM), a framework that transforms pre-trained video diffusion models into efficient, action-conditioned, single-step latent world simulators. ALWM introduces an action-conditioned latent transition network trained via student-forcing adversarial objectives, leveraging a spatiotemporal patch discriminator operating directly in latent space to enforce long-term consistency. Our approach eliminates iterative denoising bottlenecks while mitigating exposure bias and error accumulation during multi-step interactive rollouts. Experimental evaluations across simulated robotic control and interactive video benchmarks demonstrate that ALWM achieves real-time streaming frame generation while matching or exceeding the spatiotemporal coherence of slower multi-step diffusion world models.

schema.problem: Autoregressive diffusion models for video generation suffer from error accumulation: in long-horizon video synthesis, minor prediction deviations compound over time, leading to generative drift, structural collapse, and severe visual degradation.
schema.motivation: Stable and temporally consistent long-horizon synthesis is necessary for autoregressive diffusion video generation, making a mechanism to control error drift valuable for minute-scale generation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework enforces strict temporal reversibility in both training and inference. During training, an efficient reverse-prediction model is integrated to implicitly embed causal constraints into the forward generator, compelling it to produce reversible sequences that adhere closely to the natural video manifold. At inference, the frozen reverse model is repurposed as a runtime corrector, and gradient-based cycle guidance iteratively refines generated latent representations to suppress accumulated errors before they are committed to historical context.
schema.research_plan: Evidence consists of a theoretical argument that a cycle-consistency objective bottlenecks forward generative drift, and experiments on the VBench benchmark assessing overall generation quality and long-horizon temporal consistency in 60-second synthesis. No explicit baselines, ablations, or failure conditions are described in the abstract.

items.title: Cycle-World: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Long-term Video World Models via Reverse-Prediction Cycle Consistency
items.abstract: Autoregressive diffusion models have enabled high-quality video generation, yet their sequential nature inherently suffers from error accumulation. In long-horizon video synthesis, minor prediction deviations compound over time, inevitably leading to unconstrained generative drift, structural collapse, and severe visual degradation. To address this, we propose Cycle-World, a novel framework designed for stable and temporally consistent long-video generation. Our approach tackles error drift by enforcing strict temporal reversibility across both the training and inference phases. Theoretically, we demonstrate that forward generative drift can be strictly bottlenecked by a cycle-consistency objective. During training, we integrate an efficient reverse-prediction model to implicitly embed causal constraints into the forward generator, compelling it to produce reversible sequences that tightly adhere to the natural video manifold. At inference time, we repurpose this frozen reverse model as a runtime corrector. Through gradient-based cycle guidance, it iteratively refines the generated latent representations, actively suppressing accumulated errors before they are committed to the historical context. Extensive experiments on the VBench benchmark demonstrate that Cycle-World's dual-phase synergy significantly mitigates error drift, achieving state-of-the-art overall generation quality and long-horizon temporal consistency in 60-second synthesis.

schema.problem: Current learned world models treat the sensor as a fixed exteroceptive input channel and reserve actions for the body; even multi-view world models integrate a given camera rig rather than choosing where to look next. The gap is the absence of a learned world model in which sensor configuration itself is the action space under a hard measurement budget.
schema.motivation: Optical sensing in robotics, metrology, and inspection is rarely passive and operates under hard measurement budgets, so treating sensing decisions as actions could reduce physical exposures and improve efficiency.
schema.proposed_approach: A decoder-free latent world model is trained with the sensor configuration as its action space. Given the current belief over a scene, it predicts the latent content and residual uncertainty of a hypothetical measurement from any candidate sensor setting. These predictions allow multi-step, non-myopic planning of sensing schedules directly in latent space, without pixel reconstruction. The setting includes simulated active-scanning and active-illumination inspection tasks.
schema.research_plan: (1) On simulated active-scanning and active-illumination inspection tasks, the number of physical exposures needed to reach a target reconstruction or classification accuracy is compared for the proposed planner against greedy one-step information-gain planners, model-free and imitation active-vision policies, and classical non-myopic POMDP view planners; the empirical claim fails if the proposed planner does not require fewer exposures than these baselines. (2) The framing claim is argued from this construction and is not given a separate empirical test in the abstract.

items.title: Dreaming the Next Measurement: Latent World Models for Multi-Step Active Optical Sensing
items.abstract: Optical sensors in robotics, metrology, and inspection are rarely passive: an agent decides where to point a camera, how long to expose it, what illumination to apply, and which spectral or temporal channel to record — all under a hard measurement budget. Yet almost all learned world models treat the sensor as a fixed exteroceptive input channel and reserve "actions" for the body , ; even multi-view world models integrate a given camera rig rather than choosing where to look next . I propose to close this gap by training a decoder-free latent world model in which the action space is the sensor configuration itself. The model learns to dream the next measurement: given the current belief over a scene, it predicts the latent content and residual uncertainty of a hypothetical measurement from any candidate sensor setting, enabling multi-step, non-myopic planning of sensing schedules directly in latent space without expensive pixel reconstruction. On simulated active-scanning and active-illumination inspection tasks I will test the falsifiable claim that planning over sequences of imagined measurements reduces the number of physical exposures needed to reach a target reconstruction or classification accuracy, relative to greedy one-step information-gain planners , , model-free and imitation active-vision policies , , and classical non-myopic POMDP view planners . This positions world-model-based planning as a method for deciding how to sense, rather than only how to act, with the sensor itself as an agent that predicts the consequences of its own observation process.

schema.problem: High-fidelity reconstruction of continuum physical fields remains challenging under sparse and constrained sensing, and conventional methods rely on fixed sensor layouts that cannot adapt to evolving physical states.
schema.motivation: Accurate field measurements are essential for scientific discovery and engineering design, and adaptive sensing could improve reconstruction under sparsity.
schema.proposed_approach: A unified closed-loop framework formulates active sensing as a partially observable Markov decision process. A continuum field latent world model captures underlying physical dynamics and generates intrinsic reward feedback, enabling a reinforcement learning policy to simulate hypothetical sensing scenarios in latent imagination space. Sensor movements are conditioned on predicted latent states to navigate toward potentially high-information regions beyond current observations.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports experiments across diverse continuum fields, comparing reconstruction quality under sparse sensing against static and offline-optimized sensing strategies; no metrics, ablations, or failure conditions are specified.

items.title: LASER: Learning Active Sensing for Continuum Field Reconstruction
items.abstract: High-fidelity measurements of continuum physical fields are essential for scientific discovery and engineering design but remain challenging under sparse and constrained sensing. Conventional reconstruction methods typically rely on fixed sensor layouts, which cannot adapt to evolving physical states. We propose LASER, a unified, closed-loop framework that formulates active sensing as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). At its core, LASER employs a continuum field latent world model that captures the underlying physical dynamics and provides intrinsic reward feedback. This enables a reinforcement learning policy to simulate ''what-if'' sensing scenarios within a latent imagination space. By conditioning sensor movements on predicted latent states, LASER navigates toward potentially high-information regions beyond current observations. Our experiments demonstrate that LASER consistently outperforms static and offline-optimized strategies, achieving high-fidelity reconstruction under sparsity across diverse continuum fields.

schema.problem: Vision-only latent-dynamics world models cannot represent or predict contact forces, slip onset, and incipient contact, which are the quantities that determine success in contact-rich manipulation.
schema.motivation: Giving a vision-only controller foresight over contact forces and slip would avoid the need for tactile sensing at deployment while improving contact-rich manipulation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a recurrent state-space world model trained with an asymmetric cross-modal predictive head that forecasts low-dimensional future contact-force and slip signals from the shared latent rollout; the tactile sensor is used only as a training-time oracle and is absent from perception, latent history, and policy input at deployment. The force-forecast loss acts as a regularizer that separates latent states with different physical consequences, reducing visual self-prediction ambiguity. At deployment, the vision-only controller plans over imagined force futures by scoring rollouts with predicted contact normal force or predicted slip.
schema.research_plan: The plan is comparative: (1) evaluate the proposed asymmetric cross-modal grounding against vision-only world models with matched-capacity same-modality auxiliary heads; (2) compare it against an oracle that retains real tactile sensing at deployment. Matched capacity is specified for the vision-only auxiliary-head baselines. The abstract does not name explicit metrics or quantitative failure conditions; the test is described as outperformance over the same-modality baselines and approaching the tactile-retaining oracle.

items.title: Tactile Imagination: Grounding Vision-Only Latent World Models in Contact Physics by Forecasting an Absent Modality
items.abstract: Latent-dynamics world models (Dreamer-style) predict future latent states from the observations the agent currently senses, so a vision-only robot has no way to represent — let alone predict — contact forces, slip onset, and incipient contact, which are precisely the quantities that determine success in contact-rich manipulation. We propose tactile imagination: a recurrent state-space world model trained with an asymmetric cross-modal predictive head that forecasts low-dimensional future contact-force and slip signals from the shared latent rollout, while the tactile sensor is used only as a training-time oracle and is never present in perception, latent history, or policy input at deployment. During training the force-forecast loss acts as a regularizer that forces latent states with different physical consequences apart, dissolving the visual self-prediction ambiguity that arises when many physically distinct states share a near-identical image. During deployment the robot plans over imagined force futures, e.g., scoring rollouts by predicted contact normal force or predicted slip, giving a vision-only controller contact foresight it never directly senses. We will test the claim that this asymmetric cross-modal grounding outperforms vision-only world models with matched-capacity same-modality auxiliary heads and approaches the performance of an oracle that retains real tactile sensing at deployment.

schema.problem: World action models inherit predictive capability but rely primarily on vision and often fail in contact-rich manipulation, where critical cues arise from physical interaction.
schema.motivation: Real-time contact-rich manipulation becomes possible if tactile cues are integrated into the predictive action-generation loop.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework jointly models actions, future visual observations, and tactile dynamics. It uses contact-gated visuotactile fusion to selectively integrate tactile signals and a contact-aware attention bias to regulate cross-modal interactions during manipulation. To support real-time deployment, the contact-aware bias is reformulated to preserve the fused attention path during training, and cache-based diffusion acceleration is used at inference.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation is conducted on six contact-rich manipulation tasks, using action accuracy to compare the proposed unified model against prior world action models; improvements in action accuracy count as support for the joint visuotactile modeling and the fusion/attention components. The acceleration strategy is assessed by measuring training and inference speed, with faster times counting as support for the dual-level reformulation and cache-based diffusion acceleration. Claims would be undermined if action accuracy does not improve over vision-only world action models or if the acceleration strategy fails to preserve the fused attention path while reducing training/inference time.

items.title: Dream-Tac: A Unified Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: World action models inherit the predictive capability of world models, enabling action generation to be guided by anticipated future observations. However, they rely primarily on vision and often fail in contact-rich manipulation, where critical cues arise from physical interaction. In this paper, we propose Dream-Tac, a unified Tactile-World Action Model that jointly models actions, future visual observations, and tactile dynamics. Specifically, Dream-Tac introduces (i) contact-gated visuotactile fusion to selectively integrate tactile signals and (ii) a contact-aware attention bias to better regulate cross-modal interactions during manipulation. To support real-time deployment, we further design a dual-level acceleration strategy, reformulating the contact-aware bias to preserve the fused attention path during training and introducing cache-based diffusion acceleration at inference, achieving up to 2.9$\times$ faster training and 1.8$\times$ faster inference. Across six contact-rich manipulation tasks, Dream-Tac improves action accuracy by 31.7\% on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of unified visuotactile world modeling.Code is available at https://github.com/LYFCLOUDFAN/Dream-Tac.

schema.problem: Existing driving world models are camera-centric: the latent state encodes the world exactly as the ego-camera sees it, and rollouts are only valid along training trajectories, so generating from novel camera paths requires exemplars or expensive reconstruction.
schema.motivation: Generating from novel camera paths is needed for data synthesis, simulator-in-the-loop planning, and multi-view perception.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed model consists of a factorized latent transition with a scene transition, a camera-motion transition, and a multi-modal residual; a self-supervised structure-from-motion pose head; and a VAE/VDM decoder conditioned on the scene and camera factors. The scene state evolves independently of the camera, and novel viewpoints are rendered by composing the learned camera model with the neural decoder.
schema.research_plan: The claims are evaluated on CARLA and nuScenes under seen, unseen, and held-out camera trajectories. Evidence for the claims comes from comparisons against camera-centric video world models and camera-conditioned view-synthesis pipelines using a newly introduced ratio metric for held-out camera paths and standard FID/FVD, SSIM, and closed-loop planning scores. The claim is treated as falsified if the factorization provides no benefit under trajectory augmentation.

items.title: EgoView-LM: A Camera-Aware Factorized Latent World Model for Viewpoint-Invariant Video Rollout and Closed-Loop Planning in Driving
items.abstract: Driving world models today are camera-centric: the latent state encodes the world exactly as the ego-camera sees it, and rollouts are only valid along training trajectories, so generating from novel camera paths — a requirement for data synthesis, simulator-in-the-loop planning, and multi-view perception — requires exemplars or expensive reconstruction. We hypothesize that explicitly factorizing the world model into a camera-invariant scene state and a learnable camera model yields a generative model closer to the true joint distribution over scenes and camera trajectories: the scene state rolls forward independently of the camera, and novel viewpoints are rendered by composing the camera model with a neural decoder. We introduce EgoView-LM, a video world model with a factorized latent transition (scene transition + camera-motion transition + multi-modal residual), a self-supervised structure-from-motion pose head, and a VAE/VDM decoder conditioned on both factors. We evaluate on CARLA and nuScenes under seen, unseen, and held-out camera trajectories, with a new metric, the novel-view rollout ratio (NVR²), alongside standard FID/FVD, SSIM, and closed-loop planning scores. Against camera-centric video world models and camera-conditioned view-synthesis pipelines , we predict large NVR² gains on held-out trajectories while matching ego-view quality — a result that is directly falsifiable if factorization buys nothing under trajectory augmentation.

schema.problem: Existing video generation models entangle the dynamic content of a scene and the camera motion through which it is observed, so the two factors cannot be controlled independently.
schema.motivation: Disentangling these dimensions would allow video generation from arbitrary pairings of camera and content conditions, greatly expanding creative control.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework explicitly separates dynamic scene content and camera motion, allowing arbitrary combinations of camera and content conditions for video generation. It is trained with a hybrid dataset that combines curated real-world videos and synthetic data to provide diverse paired examples. Training uses a two-level curriculum: at the condition level, control modalities are introduced progressively by difficulty; at the data level, the model is first trained for precise control on synthetic data and then adapted to real data for photorealism.
schema.research_plan: (1) Independent control is evaluated through generated pairings of camera and content conditions, including complex camera movements. (2) Visual quality is compared against existing generation models. The abstract names no metrics, baselines, or failure conditions for the dataset and curriculum components.

items.title: OmniCamera: A Unified Framework for Multi-task Video Generation with Arbitrary Camera Control
items.abstract: Video fundamentally intertwines two crucial axes: the dynamic content of a scene and the camera motion through which it is observed. However, existing generation models often entangle these factors, limiting independent control. In this work, we introduce OmniCamera, a unified framework designed to explicitly disentangle and command these two dimensions. This compositional approach enables flexible video generation by allowing arbitrary pairings of camera and content conditions, unlocking unprecedented creative control. To overcome the fundamental challenges of modality conflict and data scarcity inherent in such a system, we present two key innovations. First, we construct OmniCAM, a novel hybrid dataset combining curated real-world videos with synthetic data that provides diverse paired examples for robust multi-task learning. Second, we propose a Dual-level Curriculum Co-Training strategy that mitigates modality interference and synergistically learns from diverse data sources. This strategy operates on two levels: first, it progressively introduces control modalities by difficulties (condition-level), and second, trains for precise control on synthetic data before adapting to real data for photorealism (data-level). As a result, OmniCamera achieves state-of-the-art performance, enabling flexible control for complex camera movements while maintaining superior visual quality.

schema.problem: Model-based RL from pixels is caught between two failure modes: decoding architectures share a representation between control and reconstruction, producing latent drift and unstable policy learning under multi-object interaction, while zero-shot reward-transfer methods sidestep reconstruction but rely on task encoders, functional reward encodings, or stationary behavioral datasets rather than reusing one visual world model closed-loop.
schema.motivation: Separating planning from reconstruction in a structurally enforced way could provide grounded generalization and closed-loop controllability, and a free deployment-time audit of what states are controllable, while avoiding the instability of sharing a pixel-grounded representation.
schema.proposed_approach: The planning latent is trained with zero reconstruction gradient, using only a contrastive InfoMax objective plus action-grounding losses in the form of inverse dynamics and a bisimulation-style h-divergence, theoretically anchored in reward- and model-feature abstraction. An explicit amortized rendering tower is trained to render a family of views with randomized cameras, textures, and lighting. A conditional normalizing-flow bridge maps the planning latent to a renderable latent, and its KL to a prior over renderable states plus a decayed h-divergence against the encoded image is the sole channel through which pixel-level plausibility constrains the planner. The actor-critic is optimized entirely in the planning latent under imagined rollouts whose states are pushed through the bridge and re-rendered by the tower, providing a zero-cost-at-deployment audit of controllability.
schema.research_plan: (1) Closed-loop task success on DMControl and a standardized action API provides evidence for grounded generalization of the planning latent. (2) Rendering-shift transfer and change-of-reward transfer against TD-JEPA, DiSPOs, and FRE baselines test whether the contract generalizes across visual and reward changes. (3) Pre-registered falsifiers are: zero-reconstruction latents failing under rendering shift would falsify the claim; and ablating the tower and bridge, if it does not degrade grounding while restoring object vanishing, would indicate the contract rather than the framing is wrong.

items.title: RenderBridge: A Reconstruction-Free Planning Latent Grounded by a Contracted Stochastic Rendering Tower for Closed-Loop Control and Change-of-Reward Transfer
items.abstract: Model-based RL from pixels is caught between two failure modes, and the literature I retrieved leaves a clear structural gap. Decoding architectures (Dreamer-family VAEs) ground planning latents in pixels, but control and reconstruction then share one representation, which the object-centric world-model literature shows produces latent drift under multi-object interaction and unstable policy learning ; zero-shot reward-transfer methods (TD-JEPA, DiSPOs, FRE) sidestep reconstruction but rely on task encoders, functional reward encodings, or stationary behavioral datasets rather than reusing one visual world model closed-loop . I propose RenderBridge, a world-model architecture enforced by one strict structural contract: (i) a planning latent z^p that receives zero reconstruction gradient, trained only by a contrastive InfoMax objective plus action-grounding losses (inverse dynamics and a bisimulation-style h-divergence, theoretically anchored in reward-/model-feature abstraction ); (ii) an explicit amortized rendering tower trained to render a family of views (randomized cameras, textures, lighting); and (iii) a conditional-normalizing-flow bridge B(z^p) → z^r whose KL to a prior over renderable states, plus a decayed h-divergence against the encoder image, is the sole channel through which pixel-level plausibility may ever constrain the planner. The actor-critic is optimized entirely inside z^p under imagined rollouts whose states are additionally pushed through B and re-rendered by the tower, giving closed-loop control a free, zero-cost-at-deployment audit of controllability-to-what. Unlike Dreamer-style VAEs, unlike decoder-free Dreaming/DreamingV2 , and unlike isometric controllable/noncontrollable splits , RenderBridge makes the absence of pixel pressure on z^p an explicit, enforceable contract rather than a side effect of architecture. I evaluate the hypothesis that the contract — not the presence or absence of a decoder — is what buys grounded generalization, via closed-loop task success on DMControl and a World-in-World-style standardized action API , plus two transfer protocols no retrieved work performs jointly: rendering-shift transfer and change-of-reward transfer against TD-JEPA/DiSPOs/FRE as baselines. Falsifiers are pre-registered: if zero-reconstruction latents fail under rendering shift, or if ablating the tower and bridge does not degrade grounding while restoring object vanishing, the contract — not the framing — is wrong.

schema.problem: In model-based reinforcement learning with high-dimensional observations, world models typically learn representations through reconstruction objectives, which can make representations sensitive to task-irrelevant details; reconstruction-free alternatives so far underperform reconstruction-based methods on the Crafter benchmark.
schema.motivation: Removing reconstruction objectives may yield representations better suited to planning and control, and making reconstruction-free model-based RL competitive on a standard benchmark makes this alternative viable.
schema.proposed_approach: The method learns a world model with continuous, deterministic representations and trains a JEPA-style predictor over those representations, replacing observation-space reconstruction. It is applied within a model-based RL agent and evaluated on the Crafter environment.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is an empirical comparison on Crafter against Dreamer and recent reconstruction-free alternatives using auxiliary action prediction heads or view augmentation. Support consists of matching Dreamer's performance while using no reconstruction objective; the implied failure condition is failing to close the performance gap to Dreamer. No evaluation metric is specified.

items.title: Dreamer-CDP: Improving Reconstruction-free World Models Via Continuous Deterministic Representation Prediction
items.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) agents operating in high-dimensional observation spaces, such as Dreamer, rely on learning abstract representations for effective planning and control. Existing approaches typically employ reconstruction-based objectives in the observation space, which can render representations sensitive to task-irrelevant details. Recent alternatives trade reconstruction for auxiliary action prediction heads or view augmentation strategies, but perform worse in the Crafter environment than reconstruction-based methods. We close this gap between Dreamer and reconstruction-free models by introducing a JEPA-style predictor defined on continuous, deterministic representations. Our method matches Dreamer's performance on Crafter, demonstrating effective world model learning on this benchmark without reconstruction objectives.

schema.problem: Model-based reinforcement learning for complex robotic control currently struggles with sample efficiency and long-horizon planning.
schema.motivation: Improving sample efficiency and long-horizon planning would make complex robotic control tasks, such as multi-step manipulation and navigation, more tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: Develop a hierarchical latent dynamics world model that represents environment dynamics at multiple levels of abstraction and across different timescales; integrate this model with an actor-critic architecture for model-based reinforcement learning; evaluate on long-horizon robotic control tasks including multi-step manipulation and navigation.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an empirical evaluation of the integrated hierarchical model and actor-critic model-based reinforcement learning system on long-horizon robotic control tasks, including multi-step manipulation and navigation, with comparison against existing methods. No named baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions are specified.

items.title: Hierarchical Latent Dynamics World Models for Long-Horizon Robotic Control
items.abstract: We propose a novel hierarchical latent dynamics world model designed to enhance the sample efficiency and long-horizon planning capabilities of model-based reinforcement learning (MB-RL) in complex robotic control tasks. Our model represents environment dynamics at multiple levels of abstraction and across different timescales, enabling more efficient learning of long-horizon tasks by capturing both short-term and long-term dependencies in the environment. We will develop this hierarchical model, integrate it with an actor-critic architecture for MB-RL, and evaluate its performance on long-horizon robotic control tasks such as multi-step manipulation and navigation. Our expected contribution is a hierarchical latent dynamics world model that improves the efficiency and effectiveness of MB-RL, along with empirical evidence demonstrating its advantages over existing methods.

schema.problem: Existing world model planners struggle on long-horizon, multi-stage tasks because prediction errors compound and naive search is exponential in the planning horizon; prior hierarchical approaches either amortize control into task-specific policies or assume low-dimensional states and known dynamics.
schema.motivation: Hierarchy can decompose long-horizon tasks into shorter, tractable subproblems, making zero-shot planning with learned visual world models applicable to manipulation and navigation.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework learns world models at multiple temporal scales in a shared latent space, trained only by next-latent prediction. Long-horizon model predictions serve as subgoals for the short-horizon model through latent matching. An action encoder compresses primitive action chunks into latent macro-actions, which keeps long-horizon search tractable. The resulting hierarchical MPC operates directly on visual observations and requires no task-specific rewards, skills, or hierarchical policies.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes real-world Franka manipulation on pick-and-place from a single goal image, compared against single-level planning, and simulated push manipulation and maze navigation, measuring long-horizon task success and planning compute. The comparison isolates the effect of hierarchical planning over single-level planning, with support expected as higher success and lower compute and failure as no better than the single-level baseline.

items.title: Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models
items.abstract: World models are a promising path to zero-shot embodied control through planning. However, existing world model planners struggle on long-horizon, multi-stage tasks: prediction errors compound and naive search is exponential in the planning horizon. Hierarchy mitigates both by decomposing tasks into shorter, tractable subproblems; yet prior hierarchical approaches either amortize control into task-specific policies (hierarchical RL) or assume low-dimensional states and known dynamics (classical hierarchical MPC). We present Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models (HWM), an architecture and planning paradigm for hierarchical model predictive control (MPC) directly on visual world models trained solely via next-latent prediction. HWM learns world models at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, so predictions from the long-horizon model serve as subgoals for the short-horizon model via latent matching, without task-specific rewards, skill learning, or hierarchical policies. To keep long-horizon search tractable, HWM learns an action encoder that compresses primitive action chunks into latent macro-actions. On real-world Franka manipulation, HWM solves pick-and-place from a single goal image at 70% success vs. 0% for single-level planning. Across simulated push manipulation and maze navigation, HWM consistently improves performance on long-horizon tasks while requiring up to 3x less planning compute.

schema.problem: World models for video generation currently struggle to maintain scene consistency during revisits and tend to forget previously generated environments.
schema.motivation: This is worth solving because it is expected to improve the quality, consistency, and context length of generated videos.
schema.proposed_approach: A geometry-grounded long-term spatial memory mechanism is introduced into world models to retain spatial information over long horizons and support revisits. The mechanism is integrated into state-of-the-art world models.
schema.research_plan: The claimed improvement is assessed by integrating the memory mechanism into state-of-the-art world models and evaluating on the Memory Maze and Minecraft datasets; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, or failure conditions.

items.title: Enhancing Temporal Consistency in Video Generation with Geometry-Grounded Long-term Spatial Memory
items.abstract: We propose a novel approach to enhance temporal consistency in video generation by introducing a geometry-grounded long-term spatial memory mechanism into world models. Our method addresses the challenges of maintaining scene consistency during revisits and forgetting previously generated environments. We integrate our memory mechanism into state-of-the-art world models and evaluate its effectiveness using Memory Maze and Minecraft datasets. Our approach is expected to improve the quality, consistency, and context length of generated videos.

schema.problem: Existing video generation for interactive worlds does not jointly provide the four required capabilities of interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response.
schema.motivation: Instant generation of customized, explorable, continuously evolving virtual worlds from text, image, or video would replace labor-intensive game-development production pipelines.
schema.proposed_approach: Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, the framework generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts, producing 24-fps video at 540p and 720p. Its bounded visual context combines a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. Long-term drift is reduced by training with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from the model's own roll-outs. A discrete autoregressive distillation formulation combines distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation to enable low-step sampling per chunk.
schema.research_plan: The model is evaluated on iWorld-Bench for long-horizon generation, which serves as evidence for the capability and stability claims. The efficiency claim is supported by comparing per-chunk sampling-step counts, though the abstract does not state what quality constraints or matched compute conditions were enforced. No ablations or failure thresholds for the bounded-context or corrective-training components are described.

items.title: AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling -- Full Technical Report
items.abstract: Unlike conventional video game development, which relies on labor-intensive pipelines for asset production, animation, physics, and programming, video world models generate interactive environments from user inputs instantly. It enable us to create customized, explorable, and continuously evolving virtual world from text, an image, or video. Realizing this vision requires four tightly coupled capabilities: interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response. We present AlayaWorld, an interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24-fps video at 540p and 720p. Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, AlayaWorld generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. Its bounded visual context combines a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. To reduce long-term drift, the model is trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from its own roll-outs. We further introduce a discrete autoregressive distillation formulation that combines distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation, reducing inference from approximately 30 sampling steps to four steps per chunk. On iWorld-Bench, AlayaWorld achieves the best performance over long-horizon generation. Conceived as a full-stack, open-source, and long-term project, AlayaWorld is intended to provide an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

schema.problem: Interactive video world models for games represent the environment entirely in pixel space or learned pixel-derived latents, and their dominant, repeatedly reported failure mode is long-horizon drift: compounding generation error, forgotten objects, and silently violated game rules. In games the engine's structured state—entity slots, positions, inventory, score, timers, rule flags—is directly observable from the engine but is left unused by this literature.
schema.motivation: Modern automated data pipelines make instrumented engine-state data cheap to collect at scale, and anchoring generation to low-dimensional, exactly checkable state offers a way to curb the dominant long-horizon drift in a regime-specific way rather than correcting it in pixel space.
schema.proposed_approach: Learn a compact structured state predictor supervised by ground-truth engine exports (privileged distillation); advance that state with a cheap, rule-constrained dynamics head in state space; and condition an autoregressive generative backbone on the predicted state, so state error lives in a low-dimensional, exactly checkable space rather than pixel space, with no engine access at inference. The mechanism is paired with a dual-run benchmark that executes the same action traces in the real engine and in the model and automatically scores rule-level state fidelity against ground truth.
schema.research_plan: (1) For C1, evaluate the proposed method at matched backbone size and pixel quality against three conditioning baselines: pixel-only autoregression, extended pixel-history conditioning, and visual-retrieval conditioning. Use the dual-run benchmark to measure rule-level state fidelity—permanence, conservation, loop consistency, rule compliance; C1 is supported if predicted-state conditioning materially lowers long-horizon state drift under those matched constraints and is falsified if the baselines match it. (2) For C2, evaluate models with both pixel-level metrics (FVD/LPIPS, playability checks, physics-judgment benchmarks) and the dual-run benchmark; C2 is supported if the benchmark separates models that pixel-level metrics rank as equivalent and is falsified if the rankings coincide.

items.title: State-Anchored Interactive Game World Models: Engine-Grounded Structured State as a Low-Dimensional Scaffold for Long-Horizon Generative Simulation
items.abstract: Interactive video world models for games — Genie, GameGen-X, GameFactory, Hunyuan-GameCraft, MineWorld, DIAMOND — represent the environment entirely in pixel space or learned pixel-derived latents, and their dominant, repeatedly reported failure mode is long-horizon drift: compounding generation error, forgotten objects, and silently violated game rules. We exploit a regime-specific advantage this literature leaves unused: in games, the environment's structured state — entity slots with positions, inventory, score, timers, rule flags — is directly observable from the engine, and modern automated data pipelines make such instrumented data cheap to collect at scale. We propose State-Anchored World Models (SAWM), which (i) learn a compact Structured State Predictor supervised by ground-truth engine exports (privileged distillation), (ii) advance that state with a cheap, rule-constrained dynamics head in state space, and (iii) condition an autoregressive generative backbone on the predicted state, so state error lives in a low-dimensional, exactly checkable space rather than pixel space; at inference the model never touches the engine. We pair the mechanism with SFBench, a dual-run benchmark that executes the same action traces in the real engine and in the model and automatically scores rule-level state fidelity — permanence, conservation, loop consistency, rule compliance — against ground truth, a quantity that FVD/LPIPS, playability checks, and physics-judgment benchmarks do not measure. Our falsifiable core claims: (C1) at matched backbone size and pixel quality, conditioning on predicted structured state reduces long-horizon state drift by a large factor versus pixel-only autoregression, extended pixel-history conditioning, and visual-retrieval conditioning; and (C2) SFBench separates models that pixel-level metrics rank as equivalent. Together these would establish explicit engine-supervised state as the missing scaffold for generative game engines.

schema.problem: Existing game world models generate visually realistic, action-conditioned environments but do not model the explicit state-dependent mechanics—such as health points, skill meters, and timers—that govern gameplay, so their rollouts can violate underlying game rules.
schema.motivation: Because games are defined by mechanics as well as pixels, modeling internal state dynamics is necessary to move beyond pixel-level realism toward complete and mechanically faithful game generation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework jointly predicts visual frames and game states for action-conditioned game rollouts. It adopts a mixture-of-transformers-style architecture with specialized visual and state branches that preserve modality-specific representations while enabling cross-modal interaction, so predicted states can guide frame generation. Each branch is optimized with a distinct objective suited to its modality.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation has two parts: (1) state-prediction accuracy is measured by average normalized L1 distance, and (2) mechanics fidelity of generated rollouts is compared against game world models without explicit state modeling. Support is indicated by low state-prediction error and higher mechanics fidelity relative to the baseline; the abstract does not state a formal pre-specified failure condition.

items.title: StatePlay: State-Aware Game World Models for Mechanics-Consistent Generation
items.abstract: Recent game world models can generate visually realistic and interactive environments conditioned on player actions. However, games are not defined by pixels alone; they are governed by explicit mechanics, namely state-dependent rules that control health reduction, skill activation, and game termination. These mechanics depend on precise internal states, such as health points, skill meters, and timers, which are tightly coupled with visual observations and determine how gameplay evolves. Without modeling these state dynamics, existing game world models may generate visually plausible rollouts but violate the underlying game rules. In this paper, we propose StatePlay, a novel state-aware game world model that jointly predicts visual content and game states to promote mechanics-consistent generation. StatePlay adopts a mixture-of-transformers (MoT)-style architecture that preserves specialized visual and state representations while enabling cross-modal interaction, allowing predicted states to guide frame generation. Each branch is further optimized with a distinct objective suited to its modality. Experiments show that StatePlay achieves an average normalized L1 distance below 0.06 for state prediction. Furthermore, compared with models without explicit state modeling, our method improves mechanics fidelity in generated game rollouts by 18.6%. Overall, our work highlights the importance of state-aware game world modeling and advances beyond pixel-level realism toward complete and mechanically faithful game generation.

schema.problem: Video world models are trained by frame or latent reconstruction and scored by visual fidelity, yet they are deployed for closed-loop planning where fidelity is a weak proxy; prior work has shown that task success decouples from visual quality and that controllability matters more, but no training criterion for controllability or cheap test of which model, checkpoint, or rollout will be useful inside the loop exists.
schema.motivation: A training criterion and environment-query-free diagnostic for controllability would make closed-loop usefulness a first-class objective, avoiding costly environment queries and the selection of models or checkpoints that look photorealistic but plan poorly.
schema.proposed_approach: The work proposes two coupled components. A training regularizer takes counterfactual latent rollouts from the same observed state under different actions and pushes predicted latent futures apart when the actions are outcome-differentiating while compressing them when they are action- or nuisance-invariant; it uses inverse-dynamics or latent-action estimates as a self-supervised proxy when ground-truth outcomes are unavailable. An environment-query-free open-loop diagnostic measures how well a linear probe on predicted latent deltas identifies which of k candidate actions was rolled out and predicts which candidate yields the better task outcome.
schema.research_plan: Evidence is organized by claim: (1) the proposed diagnostic is compared with FID/FVD/JEDi for correlation with closed-loop planning success across world-model architectures on closed-loop manipulation/navigation suites following the World-in-World protocol; (2) the proposed regularizer is compared against single-term ablations and PLSM, empowerment, and motion-reinforced loss on the closed-loop success–FVD Pareto frontier at fixed visual fidelity; (3) nuisance-compression attribution is tested through distractor-robustness and half-regularizer ablations. Evaluations cover latent-predictor models in the DINO-world line, latent-action baselines PlaySlot, CoLA-World, and DWS, and driving on nuScenes/NAVSIM against Epona and DriveLaW style pipelines. The proposal fails if FID/FVD correlate at least as well as the proposed diagnostic with closed-loop success, or if the regularizer does not beat its own halves.

items.title: Action-Contrastive State Sufficiency: A Training Regularizer and a Cheap Open-Loop Predictor of Closed-Loop Planning Utility for Video World Models
items.abstract: Video world models are trained by frame/latent reconstruction and scored by visual fidelity (FID/FVD), yet deployed for closed-loop planning where fidelity is a demonstrably weak proxy: World-in-World showed that task success decouples from visual quality and that "controllability matters more," and Target-Bench found the best off-the-shelf video world model scores only 0.341 on semantic planning despite photorealistic rollouts — but neither work provides a training criterion for controllability, nor a cheap test of which model, checkpoint, or rollout will actually be useful inside the loop. We propose Action-Contrastive State Sufficiency (ACSS) with two coupled components: (i) an ACSS-Reg training regularizer that, over counterfactual latent rollouts from the same observed state under different actions, pushes predicted latent futures apart when the actions are outcome-differentiating and compresses them when they are action- or nuisance-invariant, using inverse-dynamics/latent-action estimates (à la PlaySlot and PreLAR ) as a self-supervised proxy when ground-truth outcomes are unavailable; and (ii) the Action-Contrast Score (ACS), an environment-query-free open-loop diagnostic that measures how well a linear probe on predicted latent deltas (a) identifies which of k candidate actions was rolled out and (b) predicts which candidate yields the better task outcome. We make three falsifiable claims: (H1) ACS correlates with closed-loop planning success across world-model architectures far better than FID/FVD/JEDi; (H2) ACSS-Reg moves the closed-loop success–FVD Pareto frontier upward at fixed visual fidelity, beating single-term ablations and the closest regularizers (PLSM , empowerment , motion-reinforced loss ); (H3) the gain is attributable to nuisance compression rather than better fidelity, as shown by distractor-robustness and half-regularizer ablations. We test these on closed-loop manipulation/navigation suites following the World-in-World protocol , on latent-predictor models in the DINO-world line , on latent-action baselines (PlaySlot , CoLA-World , DWS ), and on driving (nuScenes/NAVSIM) against Epona and DriveLaW style pipelines. If FID/FVD correlate at least as well as ACS with closed-loop success, or the regularizer does not beat its own halves, the proposal fails.

schema.problem: Action-conditioned world models can exploit visual inertia and recurring motion patterns as statistical shortcuts, so different actions may produce similar futures and motion may persist even under zero action without meaningful action-dependent dynamics.
schema.motivation: Enforcing consistency under counterfactual changes to actions and observations, rather than merely injecting action features, is needed to make visible dynamics depend on action and improve action controllability.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework uses two complementary counterfactual consistency constraints: multi-step counterfactual consistency constrains reference, inverse-action, and zero-action rollouts, while action-spatial counterfactual consistency enforces consistent predictions under mirrored scenes and transformed actions. These constraints reduce reliance on statistical shortcuts. It also introduces action controllability metrics and a same-state multi-action counterfactual evaluation setting.
schema.research_plan: The evidence bears on the two claims: (1) the reduction in shortcut reliance and action controllability is assessed on same-state multi-action counterfactual evaluation using the introduced action controllability metrics against a baseline; (2) visual planning success is evaluated on VP2 against state-of-the-art models, and preservation of video prediction quality and transfer are evaluated on BAIR and RoboNet. Support is indicated by improved controllability and planning without loss of prediction quality; failure would be a trade-off between controllability gains and prediction quality or failure to transfer across model settings.

items.title: Overcoming Statistical Bias in Action-Controllable World Models
items.abstract: Action-conditioned world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve under an agent's actions. Yet future frames are often highly predictable from visual inertia and recurring motion patterns alone. This creates a shortcut: models can fit the data by exploiting statistical biases without making their visible dynamics meaningfully depend on the action. As a result, different actions may produce similar futures, while motion may persist even under zero action. The key question is how to reduce reliance on statistical shortcuts from dominating action-conditioned prediction. We argue that action control requires more than injecting action features; it requires enforcing consistency under counterfactual changes to actions and observations. Based on this insight, we introduce CoCo, a Counterfactual Consistency framework to enhance action controllability through two complementary constraints. Multi-step counterfactual consistency constrains reference, inverse-action, and zero-action rollouts, while action-spatial counterfactual consistency enforces consistent predictions under mirrored scenes and transformed actions. Together, they reduce reliance on statistical shortcuts from substituting for action-dependent dynamics. We further introduce Action Response Consistency (ARC) and Drift Energy (DE) to assess action controllability, together with Mini-SSMB for same-state, multi-action counterfactual evaluation. On Mini-SSMB, our full model achieved ARC_inv of 0.412 and ARC_ref of 0.483, while reducing DE by 17.07% relative to the baseline. On VP2 visual planning, it achieves the highest average success rate among SOTA models, at 73.1%. Experiments on BAIR and RoboNet further show that these gains preserve video prediction quality and transfer across model settings.

schema.problem: Current world models represent actions either as monolithic latent vectors or through latent discovery from dynamics, which prevents compositional generalization to novel objects and novel action-object combinations.
schema.motivation: A compositional action representation would allow agents to transfer action semantics to new object classes and predict unseen action-object interactions without exhaustive training.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method factorizes action effects into reusable primitive operations and learns their per-object applicability structure. It decomposes actions into independent primitive action components—such as force direction, magnitude, and friction mode—and learns masks indicating which primitives apply to which objects.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation uses multi-object manipulation benchmarks and compares the proposed method against monolithic latent-action baselines on few-shot generalization to novel objects and systematic compositional generalization; support for the improvement claim requires favorable comparison to those baselines.

items.title: Compositional Action Effect Grammars for Structured World Models
items.abstract: Current world models learn actions either as monolithic latent vectors or through latent discovery from dynamics, losing opportunities for compositional generalization to novel objects and action-object combinations. We propose Learning Compositional Action Effect Grammars (LCAEG), a method that factorizes action effects into reusable primitive operations and learns their per-object applicability structure. Unlike latent-action approaches that treat actions as indivisible embeddings, LCAEG explicitly decomposes actions into independent effect primitives (e.g., force direction, magnitude, friction mode) with learned masks indicating which primitives apply to which objects. This structure enables transfer of action semantics to novel object classes and compositional zero-shot prediction of unseen action-object interactions. We evaluate LCAEG on multi-object manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating improved few-shot generalization to novel objects and systematic compositional generalization compared to monolithic latent-action baselines.

schema.problem: World models trained in one domain typically fail to support planning in visually or morphologically different domains, despite the underlying physics remaining identical.
schema.motivation: A transferable causal model would allow a planner trained in one domain to be reused across domains with only a small amount of new visual grounding, avoiding retraining from scratch.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework jointly learns a sparse causal graph representing what causes what, modular dynamics components tied to causal edges, and lightweight domain-specific adapters that map visual observations into a shared causal state space. It is trained on a primary domain; then the learned causal graph is transferred with minimal modification to new domains, with only the adapters requiring new visual grounding data. The design separates domain-invariant causal structure from domain-specific visual and morphological realization.
schema.research_plan: (1) The domain-invariance claim is evidenced by training the architecture on a primary domain and assessing whether the causal graph transfers to new domains with only adapter-level visual grounding. (2) The transfer/planning claim is evaluated across three substantially different domains—simulated manipulation, real robot manipulation, and autonomous driving—by comparing planning performance and the amount of retraining data required against baselines trained from scratch. The abstract does not state an explicit failure condition or specify matched model capacity and compute.

items.title: Causal Skeleton Transfer: Learning Domain-Invariant World Model Components for Cross-Domain Planning
items.abstract: World models trained in one domain typically fail to support planning in visually or morphologically different domains, despite the underlying physics remaining identical. We propose Causal Skeleton Transfer (CST), a framework that explicitly disentangles the causal structure of environment dynamics from domain-specific visual embeddings and parameter-bearing dynamics modules. The core insight is that causal relationships—which objects/agents affect which, under what conditions—are largely domain-invariant, while the realization of those relationships in sensors, pixels, and embodiment is domain-specific. CST jointly learns a sparse causal graph representing "what causes what" and modular dynamics components tied to causal edges, along with lightweight domain-specific adapters that map visual observations into a shared causal state space. We train this architecture on a primary domain and demonstrate that the learned causal graph transfers with minimal modification to new domains, enabling effective planning with only a small amount of new visual grounding data. We evaluate on three substantially different domains—simulated manipulation, real robot manipulation, and autonomous driving—showing that CST achieves >85% of single-domain planning performance while using <10% of the retraining data required by baselines trained from scratch.

schema.problem: Existing search-guided visual planners for long-horizon robotic planning score rollout trajectories only with task reward signals or action samplers, leaving them vulnerable to visual hallucinations and epistemic uncertainty where the world model drifts from physical reality.
schema.motivation: As video-generative world models with Monte Carlo Tree Search are increasingly used for long-horizon planning, keeping lookahead search away from unverified states is necessary to make generated plans reliable in physical execution.
schema.proposed_approach: A tree-search planning framework couples a calibrated video world model with subpatch-level uncertainty quantification; the resulting dense epistemic uncertainty estimates are added to MCTS selection and evaluation objectives so that high-variance or high-hallucination branches are penalized during lookahead search, steering planned actions away from unverified or out-of-distribution states.
schema.research_plan: Experimental evaluation on challenging long-horizon manipulation benchmarks compares the proposed framework against reward-only visual planning baselines, using catastrophic task failures as the central metric. The main claim is supported if the framework reduces catastrophic task failures and outperforms those baselines; it would be weakened if adding the uncertainty penalty does not improve over reward-only scoring.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Search-Guided Generative World Models for Safe Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Video-generative world models combined with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) have recently emerged as powerful frameworks for long-horizon robotic planning. However, existing search-guided visual planners rely exclusively on task reward signals or action samplers to score rollout trajectories, making them vulnerable to visual hallucinations and epistemic uncertainty where the world model drifts from physical reality. In this work, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Tree Search (UATS), a novel planning framework that integrates dense, calibrated epistemic uncertainty estimates directly into the MCTS selection and evaluation objectives. By coupling a calibrated video world model with subpatch-level uncertainty quantification, UATS penalizes high-variance or high-hallucination branches during lookahead search, actively steering the robot away from unverified or out-of-distribution states. Experiments on challenging long-horizon manipulation benchmarks will demonstrate that UATS significantly reduces catastrophic task failures and outperforms reward-only visual planning baselines.

schema.problem: Existing end-to-end spoken dialogue agents lack a unified internal world model that learns continuous latent dynamics over acoustic-prosodic states and conversational intentions for model-based reinforcement learning.
schema.motivation: Such a world model would allow learning proactive turn-taking, prosodic adaptation, and goal-directed dialogue strategies without costly live human interactions.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework casts spoken dialogue interaction as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process over latent acoustic-semantic embeddings. It learns a joint latent dynamics world model of continuous speech streams and user turn-taking behavior, predicting future user audio reactions, backchannels, and user state transitions. Policy optimization is performed through imagination in the learned latent space, targeting proactive turn-taking, prosodic adaptation, and goal-directed strategies.
