schema.research_plan: The planned experiments compare the framework with cascaded and model-free end-to-end baselines on sample efficiency, turn-taking latency, and task completion. These evaluations are intended to support the comparative claim; failure would occur if the framework does not show superior performance on these metrics. No matching of compute, parameters, or latency is specified.

items.title: Spoken-Dreamer: End-to-End Spoken Dialogue World Models with Continuous Latent Dynamics for Anticipatory Turn-Taking and Policy Planning
items.abstract: Modern spoken dialogue systems (SDS) predominantly rely on either cascaded pipelines (speech recognition, text LLM, text-to-speech) or end-to-end speech-language models that treat dialogue interaction as a black-box sequence generation task. While recent work has introduced text-based dialogue world models and modular speech reasoning frameworks, end-to-end spoken dialogue agents still lack a unified internal world model capable of learning continuous latent dynamics over acoustic-prosodic states and conversational intentions for model-based reinforcement learning. In this proposal, we introduce Spoken-Dreamer, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for end-to-end spoken dialogue systems that learns a joint latent dynamics world model of continuous speech streams and user turn-taking behavior. By casting spoken dialogue interaction as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) over latent acoustic-semantic embeddings, Spoken-Dreamer predicts future user audio reactions, backchannels, and user state transitions. Through imagination-based policy optimization in the latent space, our agent learns proactive turn-taking, appropriate prosodic adaptation, and goal-directed dialogue strategies without requiring costly live human interactions. Experiments and evaluations will demonstrate superior sample efficiency, latency reduction in turn-taking, and improved task completion compared to existing cascaded and model-free end-to-end baselines.

schema.problem: Repeated 3D surveys of heritage monuments are sparse and irregularly spaced, often years apart, while conservation decisions must be made now for damage that will accrue over decades; existing 3D world-model work targets dense, fast streams and built-heritage digital-twin work is reactive or static rather than predictive.
schema.motivation: A predictive ability to forecast surface deterioration and rank conservation interventions would directly support conservation decisions that must be taken now for damage accruing over decades.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a continuous-time latent world model whose latent state evolves between sparsely surveyed epochs of a monument surface. The dynamics are driven by exogenous climate series and reset by discrete conservation interventions, and an implicit neural representation decodes the state into spatially continuous displacement fields at any future time.
schema.research_plan: The three claims are evaluated on a ground-truth synthetic deterioration benchmark. (1) Forecast accuracy is tested on holdout epochs 1–5 years ahead against persistence, temporal interpolation, discrete-step recurrent forecasters, and a DINo-style continuous baseline. (2) The role of cross-site amortized dynamics is isolated by comparing with per-site models. (3) Predictive uncertainty is checked for calibration and counterfactual rankings of conservation interventions are compared with the simulated ground truth.

items.title: PATINA: A Continuous-Time, Intervention-Conditioned Point-Surface World Model for Forecasting Geometric Decay of Heritage Monuments from Sparse Surveys
items.abstract: Repeated 3D survey campaigns of heritage monuments are sparse and irregularly spaced — often years apart — yet conservation decisions (shelter, clean, consolidate, or do nothing) must be made now for damage that will accrue over decades. The 3D world-model literature retrieved here forecasts dense, fast streams — ego-vehicle point clouds over milliseconds , robot scenes over seconds , PDE fields over dense simulated grids — while the built-heritage digital-twin work is reactive (anomaly detection, model updating) or static (segmentation) . We propose PATINA, a continuous-time latent world model whose state evolves between sparsely surveyed epochs of a monument surface, driven by exogenous climate series and reset by discrete conservation interventions, and decoded by an implicit neural representation into spatially continuous displacement fields at any future time. We claim that on a ground-truth synthetic deterioration benchmark (i) PATINA forecasts holdout epochs 1–5 years ahead more accurately than persistence, temporal interpolation, discrete-step recurrent forecasters, and a DINo-style continuous baseline ; (ii) cross-site amortized dynamics are what make few-epoch learning feasible, so per-site models collapse; and (iii) PATINA yields calibrated predictive uncertainty and a counterfactual ranking of conservation interventions that matches the simulated ground truth. This frames conservation forecasting as a world-modeling problem — a formulation absent from both the world-model and heritage literatures we retrieved.

schema.problem: A world model trained in one regime silently becomes unreliable when dynamics shift, and standard trust heuristics such as ensemble disagreement measure internal model doubt rather than the error an agent will actually incur by acting on an imagined trajectory.
schema.motivation: Model-based agents need to know when imagined rollouts diverge from reality under distribution shift; cheap audits from already executed transitions provide dense supervision that makes a direct error forecaster tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: A metacognitive forecaster learns, from the imagined trajectory available at planning time, to predict the per-lead divergence between a plan's fantasies and the states that would actually be realized. It is trained by replaying real transitions already executed by the agent through the world model, synthesizing corresponding imagined rollouts and dense supervised labels for every lead time. During planning, the forecast truncates or discards high-imagined-return plans whose predicted hallucination crosses a calibrated threshold, replaces a globally tuned rollout horizon with a predicted per-plan trust horizon, and triggers early re-planning when the forecast indicates even short dreams are unreliable.
schema.research_plan: The method is evaluated on continuous-control benchmarks with sudden dynamics shifts and novelties against uncertainty-gated and fixed-horizon baselines. Evidence is assessed through return, horizon-level calibration, and detection of large one-step surprises before they occur. The central assumption is falsified by comparing a forecaster trained on internal ensemble disagreement with one trained on realized divergence: if the two perform identically, then the exploited reality signal is not the bottleneck and the proposal's central assumption is wrong.

items.title: Where Imagination Ends: Supervised Reality-Gap Forecasting for Trust-Aware Model-Based Planning
items.abstract: Model-based agents act on imagined rollouts, but a world model trained in one regime silently stops being reliable when dynamics shift, and the standard remedy — replacing "when to trust your model" with uncertainty estimates such as ensemble disagreement — is a proxy: it measures the model's internal doubt, not the error the agent will actually incur by acting on an imagined trajectory. We propose Reality-Gap Forecasting (RGF), a metacognitive module that learns to predict, from the imagined trajectory available at planning time, the per-lead divergence between a plan's fantasies and the states that would actually be realized. The forecaster is trained on cheap "audits": real transitions already executed by the agent are replayed through the world model to synthesize the corresponding imagined rollouts, yielding dense supervised labels for every lead time that current methods discard. During planning the forecast (i) truncates or discards high-imagined-return plans whose predicted hallucination crosses a calibrated threshold, (ii) replaces a globally tuned rollout horizon with a predicted per-plan trust horizon, and (iii) triggers early re-planning when the forecast says even short dreams are unreliable. On continuous-control benchmarks with sudden dynamics shifts and novelties, we hypothesize RGF will match or beat uncertainty-gated and fixed-horizon baselines in return while being substantially better calibrated at the horizon level and catching more large one-step surprises before they happen. The claim is falsifiable: if a forecaster trained on internal ensemble disagreement performs identically to one trained on realized divergence, then the reality signal we exploit is not the bottleneck, and the proposal's central assumption is wrong.

schema.problem: Surveillance multi-object tracking at scale is blocked by two bottlenecks that prior work treats in isolation: the supervision cost of per-frame identity labels, and the brittleness of appearance-based data association during long occlusions, which dominate real camera footage.
schema.motivation: Removing identity supervision makes tracking deployable on raw unlabeled video at scale, while predictive association during long occlusions targets the dominant failure regime of real surveillance footage and additionally supports trajectory forecasting and anomaly flagging.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system reformulates tracking as inverse inference over a self-supervised object-centric world model: entities persist as latent slots, a temporally-difference-trained latent dynamics model predicts entity states several frames ahead, and candidate matches are rolled forward under the learned dynamics and scored by predicted multi-step future-state agreement rather than instantaneous appearance. The model is trained from raw unlabeled video only, with no detection supervision and no identity labels. The same rollouts additionally produce multi-modal trajectory forecasts and zero-shot anomaly flagging from prediction surprise.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a pre-registered evaluation on the occlusion-heavy MOT20 benchmark. Claim (1) is tested by comparing the predictive association against the model's own single-step ablation on ID switches. Claim (2) is tested by comparing the fully self-supervised model against the best label-free baseline on tracking performance. The rejection condition is a flat horizon sweep. Auxiliary outputs are evaluated through multi-modal trajectory forecasting and zero-shot anomaly flagging from prediction surprise.

items.title: TrackRollout: Label-Free Surveillance Multi-Object Tracking by Predictive Latent Imagination
items.abstract: Surveillance multi-object tracking at scale is blocked by two bottlenecks that prior work treats in isolation: the supervision cost of per-frame identity labels, and the brittleness of appearance-based data association during long occlusions — the regime that dominates real camera footage. We propose TrackRollout, a system in which tracking is reformulated as inverse inference over a self-supervised object-centric world model: entities persist as latent slots, a temporally-difference-trained latent dynamics model predicts entity states several frames ahead, and data association is performed by imagination — candidate matches are rolled forward under the learned dynamics and scored by predicted multi-step future-state agreement rather than by instantaneous appearance. The model is trained from raw unlabeled video only: no detection supervision and no ID labels. We hypothesize that this predictive association reduces ID switches by at least 30% relative to the model's own single-step ablation on the occlusion-heavy MOT20 benchmark, and that the fully self-supervised model stays within 8 points of the best label-free baseline. These claims are pre-registered with a flat horizon sweep as the rejection condition. The same rollouts additionally yield multi-modal trajectory forecasts and zero-shot anomaly flagging from prediction surprise, addressing surveillance operations needs beyond association.

schema.problem: Existing learned 3D world models for robot manipulation predict the next raw point cloud, particle set, Gaussian scene, or per-object latent code, and thereby discard the structure that physics and planning most need: an explicit geometric correspondence between the object's current state and a canonical shape.
schema.motivation: Prior work identifies latent geometry, not the dynamics network, as the bottleneck of long-horizon world models, so designing correspondence directly into the state avoids a post-hoc contrastive regularizer and yields a geometry-aware differentiable state from which learned SDF functionals can optimize manipulation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed world model parameterizes state as a shared, category-level canonical template plus a dense, bijective deformation field predicted lazily in a low-dimensional latent container. State transitions are displacements of this deformation flow, which composes diffeomorphically across time, guaranteeing correspondence by construction rather than estimating it per step. The deformed template is decoded as a signed-distance field by a template-deformation network, giving a geometry-aware, differentiable state from which learned SDF functionals can optimize manipulation directly.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is validation on cloth flattening, rope coiling, and clay reshaping in simulation and on real robots, comparing against RobotD-based latent models, point-cloud world models, and graph models; the abstract does not state metrics, ablations, held-matched conditions, or failure criteria.

items.title: ShapeAnchor: A Canonical-Template, Bijective-Deformation World Model for Long-Horizon 3D Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Learned 3D world models for robot manipulation predict the next raw point cloud, particle set, Gaussian scene, or per-object latent code, and all of them discard the one structure that physics and planning most need: an explicit geometric correspondence between the object's current state and a canonical shape. We propose ShapeAnchor, a world model whose state is parameterized as a shared, category-level canonical template plus a dense, bijective deformation field predicted lazily in a low-dimensional latent container. State transitions are displacements of this deformation flow, which composes diffeomorphically across time, so correspondence is guaranteed by construction rather than estimated per-step. The deformed template is decoded as a signed-distance field via a template-deformation network, yielding a geometry-aware, differentiable state from which learned SDF functionals can optimize manipulation directly. Prior work identifies latent geometry—not the dynamics network—as the bottleneck of long-horizon world models (Cloning Deterministic Worlds); ShapeAnchor answers that call architecturally, by designing geometry into the state rather than adding a post-hoc contrastive regularizer. We validate on cloth flattening, rope coiling, and clay reshaping in simulation and real robots, comparing against RobotD-based latent models, point-cloud world models, and graph models.

schema.problem: NLP applications often lack interpretability, and world models and topic modeling have not been combined into a unified framework for explaining text data.
schema.motivation: Providing more transparent and explainable NLP systems is needed for applications such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and summarization, and integrating complementary techniques can support that interpretability.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework consists of three modules: a world-model learner that captures the dynamics and semantics of text data, a topic-modeling component that identifies and interprets underlying topics, and an integration mechanism through which the world model enhances the interpretability of the topic-modeling process.
schema.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on benchmark datasets for text classification, sentiment analysis, and document summarization, using metrics for interpretability, accuracy, and efficiency. The abstract does not specify baselines, ablations, or failure conditions, so no controlled comparison or falsification threshold is given.

items.title: Integrating World Models with Topic Modeling for Enhanced Interpretability in NLP
items.abstract: This proposal aims to develop a systematic framework that integrates world models with topic modeling to enhance interpretability in natural language processing (NLP) applications. The goal is to create a unified approach that leverages the strengths of both world models and topic modeling to provide more transparent and explainable NLP systems. Our framework will include a module for learning world models that capture the dynamics and semantics of text data, a topic modeling component that identifies and interprets the underlying topics in the text data, and an integration mechanism that ensures the world model enhances the interpretability of the topic modeling process. We will evaluate our framework on benchmark datasets for NLP tasks such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and document summarization using metrics for interpretability, accuracy, and efficiency.

schema.problem: Simulating and predicting complex environments is limited in efficiency and accuracy, particularly in capturing long-term dependencies and handling uncertainty.
schema.motivation: Efficiently capturing long-term dependencies and handling uncertainty would improve simulation and prediction in complex environments.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed approach is a multi-scale hierarchical world model that incorporates learned temporal abstractions; it combines recent hierarchical world model designs with temporal abstraction concepts.
schema.research_plan: The model will be evaluated on complex simulation tasks and compared with state-of-the-art methods; the abstract specifies no named baselines, metrics, or criteria for support versus failure.

items.title: Hierarchical World Models with Temporal Abstractions for Efficient Simulation and Prediction
items.abstract: This proposal aims to develop a multi-scale, hierarchical world model that incorporates temporal abstractions to improve efficiency and accuracy in simulating and predicting complex environments. By integrating learned temporal abstractions into a hierarchical world model, we can efficiently capture long-term dependencies and handle uncertainty in complex environments. Our approach combines the strengths of recent works on hierarchical world models with the concept of temporal abstractions. We will evaluate our model on complex simulation tasks and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.

schema.problem: Compact latent world models make closed-loop planning fast, but their rollouts become unreliable beyond a model- and state-dependent horizon. Adaptive-horizon methods that source trust from the same model's internal signals can be miscalibrated under distribution shift.
schema.motivation: Trustworthy horizon calibration would let compact planners retain their speed while maintaining reliable rollouts under distribution shift, rather than either trusting miscalibrated internal signals or paying for costly simulator use.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach freezes the compact world model and uses an external high-fidelity action-conditioned video or latent simulator only as a runtime verifier. Candidate action sequences are scored by both the compact planner and the external simulator on decision-relevant quantities such as predicted success probability, goal-embedding approach, and expected reward. Their disagreement is calibrated against ground-truth rollout failure to produce a state-dependent reliable horizon h*(s). During MPC, compact-model rollouts are truncated, trust-weighted, or re-verified beyond that horizon.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation is on VP² and DROID-derived manipulation tasks under fixed computational budgets for the external simulator. The evidence compares the proposed calibration against internal-uncertainty horizon adaptation on horizon-prediction AUC and planning success. The proposal is treated as falsified if internal-uncertainty adaptation reaches the same horizon-prediction AUC and planning success without external queries, or if the external simulator must be queried more often than the budget to matter.

items.title: Verifying the Verifier: External Decision-Relevant Calibration of Reliable Planning Horizons in Compact Latent World Models
items.abstract: Compact latent world models make closed-loop planning fast, but their rollouts become unreliable beyond a model- and state-dependent horizon. Adaptive-horizon methods retrieved in this area typically source trust from the same model's internal signals—variance, reconstruction error, value confidence, or self-reported uncertainty—which can be miscalibrated under distribution shift. We propose Externally Verified Horizon Calibration (EVHC), which uses a high-fidelity action-conditioned video or latent simulator as a sparse runtime verifier rather than as a data generator or weight teacher. Candidate action sequences are scored by both the compact planner and the external simulator on decision-relevant quantities such as predicted success probability, goal-embedding approach, and expected reward; their disagreement is calibrated against ground-truth rollout failure to produce a state-dependent reliable horizon h*(s). During MPC, the compact model plans cheaply but its rollouts are truncated, trust-weighted, or re-verified beyond h*(s), while its weights remain frozen. We evaluate on VP² and DROID-derived manipulation tasks with fixed computational budgets for the external simulator. The proposal is falsified if internal-uncertainty horizon adaptation reaches the same horizon-prediction AUC and planning success without external queries, or if the external simulator must be queried more often than the budget to matter.

schema.problem: Decision-time planning with learned world models is confined to three mechanism families: proposal-resampling, backpropagation through a fixed differentiable pipeline, and offline policy/prior learning; no planner is framed as stochastic-gradient MCMC over action sequences.
schema.motivation: A sampling-based planner could give a nearly valid sampler over a reward-tilted target under stochastic, multimodal, and partially non-differentiable world models, improving robustness to model mismatch at matched budgets.
schema.proposed_approach: The planner performs Langevin/MALA-style updates on candidate action sequences using minibatched world-model rollouts. The update drift is the clean-data score of a diffusion action prior plus a variance-reduced minibatched estimate of the world-model return. It employs common random numbers, trajectory-wise control variates, adaptive covariance, and an optional Metropolis correction.
schema.research_plan: (1) The primary diagnostic is a synthetic multimodal benchmark with known ground-truth posteriors, testing whether the planner targets the reward-tilted multimodal posterior. (2) Latent continuous-control world models (D4RL) and action-conditioned video/scenario world models test return and robustness to model mismatch. (3) Comparisons run against Diffuser, D-the proposed method, MPDiffuser, Diffusion-ES, DIAL-the proposed method, CEM-GD, MPPI, and gradient-the proposed method at matched world-model-rollout and wall-clock budgets. (4) The specified support/failure pattern is: largest gains where the planning posterior is multimodal or dynamics are stochastic, and on deterministic single-mode tasks the planner should match, not beat, cheaper planners.

items.title: Score-Langevin World-Model MPC (SLWM): Stochastic-Gradient MCMC for Action-Sequence Planning with Diffusion World Models
items.abstract: Learned world models increasingly support planning by proposing, filtering, or denoising candidate action sequences, yet decision-time planning with them is still performed by one of three mechanisms: proposal-resampling (CEM/MPPI), backpropagation through a fixed differentiable pipeline, or offline policy/prior learning. We propose Score-Langevin World-Model MPC (SLWM), which instead treats planning as stochastic-gradient MCMC over action sequences, with drift given by the clean-data score of a diffusion action prior plus a variance-reduced minibatched estimate of the world-model return. The planner performs Langevin/MALA-style updates on candidate actions using minibatched world-model rollouts, common random numbers, trajectory-wise control variates, adaptive covariance, and an optional Metropolis correction, so it remains a (nearly) valid sampler over a reward-tilted target even under stochastic, multimodal, and partially non-differentiable world models. Our falsifiable core claim: at matched world-model-rollout and wall-clock budgets, SLWM improves return and robustness to model mismatch over proposal-resample, denoising, and backprop planners, with the largest gains exactly where the planning posterior is multimodal or the dynamics are stochastic — and on deterministic single-mode tasks it should match (not beat) cheaper planners. We test this on a synthetic multimodal benchmark with known ground-truth posteriors (primary diagnostic), latent continuous-control world models (D4RL), and action-conditioned video/scenario world models, against Diffuser, D-MPC, MPDiffuser, Diffusion-ES, DIAL-MPC, CEM-GD, MPPI, and gradient-MPC baselines at matched budgets.

schema.problem: UAV-based active object detection research lacks high-quality datasets and benchmarks for algorithm development and evaluation, while existing AOD policies relying on deep reinforcement learning suffer from poor generalization.
schema.motivation: A large-scale real-world dataset and benchmark would enable construction of diverse training and testing environments for UAV agent interaction and active observation policy learning, advancing research on occlusion and target pixel scarcity in UAV object detection.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a large-scale real-world UAV-Ground Active Object Detection dataset containing 121,000 multi-view panoramic multi-target aerial images and 1.21 million local single-target slices, covering 10 vehicle targets across 40 scenarios. On this dataset, it builds a benchmark for active object detection policy learning methods. For the policy, it leverages the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture to construct a world model and incorporates AOD-specific prior knowledge into state representation learning. The dataset and code are made publicly available.
schema.research_plan: The dataset's scale and coverage are reported to support construction of diverse training and testing environments. Existing AOD policy learning methods, primarily DRL-based, are evaluated on the proposed benchmark, with training and testing performance compared to characterize generalization. The proposed method is evaluated on the same benchmark and compared against existing AOD policies, with improvements in benchmark performance treated as support for effectiveness and superiority. No explicit failure conditions or matched compute/latency constraints are stated.

items.title: Toward Active Object Detection for UAVs in the Wild: A Large-Scale Dataset, Benchmark and Method
items.abstract: Object detection is a fundamental component in numerous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) applications, yet it has long been plagued by hindrances like occlusion or target pixel scarcity. Active Object Detection (AOD) provides a novel paradigm to address these challenges via active vision, while UAV-based AOD research remains scarce due to the lack of high-quality datasets and benchmarks for algorithm development and evaluation. To fill this gap, this paper presents ATRNet-LUDO, the first large-scale real-world dataset for UAV-Ground Active Object Detection (UGAOD). It contains 121,000 multi-view panoramic multi-target aerial images and 1.21 million local single-target slices, covering 10 vehicle targets across 40 scenarios. It enables the construction of diverse training and testing environments for UAV agent interaction and active observation policy learning. Based on this dataset, we establish a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for AOD policy learning methods. Most existing AOD policies rely on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) but suffer from poor generalization. Evaluations on our benchmark reveal a significant generalization gap between training and testing performance, highlighting an urgent need for solutions. To this end, we leverage the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to construct a world model that enhances state representation learning, and propose AOD-JEPA by incorporating AOD-specific prior knowledge. Extensive experiments validate its effectiveness and superiority. We hope ATRNet-LUDO and the benchmark will advance research in the UGAOD field. The dataset and code are soon available at https://github.com/Leo000ooo/LUDO_dataset.

schema.problem: Learning-based driving agents are predominantly evaluated against rule-following pedestrians, leaving their behavior under non-compliant or adversarial pedestrian interactions poorly understood.
schema.motivation: Adversarial pedestrian interaction is a central safety challenge for autonomous driving, so worst-case evaluation is needed to avoid overconfidence from rule-following benchmarks.
schema.proposed_approach: A configurable benchmark in CARLA defines three adversarial pedestrian archetypes: one intruding into the road, one crossing indecisively, and one moving slowly in protest. A DreamerV3 agent is trained with sparse rewards where the only pedestrian-specific signal is a terminal collision penalty. Evaluation uses a frozen-policy protocol with explicit train-test separation, and safety behavior is decomposed into endpoint outcomes, evasion dynamics, and efficiency costs.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation compares nominal and adversarial pedestrian conditions; nominal conditions test route completion and generalization to an unseen town, while adversarial conditions examine evasion dynamics for each archetype and compare collision rates to establish difficulty order. Safety behavior is scored via endpoint outcomes, evasion dynamics, and efficiency costs, with the frozen-policy protocol and train-test separation controlling for memorization. The evidence bears on the claim that a terminal penalty suffices and is bounded by pedestrian-persistence prediction.

items.title: Emergent Pedestrian Safety in a World-Model Driving Agent Under Adversarial Interaction Without Explicit Safety Rewards
items.abstract: Pedestrian interaction remains a central safety challenge for autonomous driving, particularly under non-compliant or adversarial pedestrian behavior. Existing research and evaluations predominantly test against rule-following pedestrians, leaving a gap in understanding how learning-based agents handle worst-case interactions. We introduce the Jaywalkers Library, a novel configurable benchmark in CARLA with three adversarial pedestrian archetypes (Intruder, Indecisive Crosser, and Protester). We evaluate a DreamerV3 agent trained with sparse rewards, where the only pedestrian-specific signal is a terminal collision penalty. Evaluation employs a frozen-policy protocol with explicit train–test separation. Safety behavior is decomposed into endpoint outcomes, evasion dynamics, and efficiency costs. Under nominal conditions, the agent achieves high route completion and generalizes to an unseen town, whereas under adversarial exposure, an archetype-sensitive evasion strategy emerges. The agent swerves at speed against dynamic pedestrians but decelerates against the slow-moving Protester. Collision rates reveal a counterintuitive difficulty ordering in which the Protester is the hardest, followed by the Intruder, with the Indecisive Crosser as the most survivable. These findings show that a sparse terminal penalty suffices for emergent pedestrian avoidance in a world-model agent, but that effectiveness is bounded by the world model’s ability to predict pedestrian persistence.

schema.problem: Most hierarchical vision-language-action models make each high-level decision with a single forward pass, leaving no mechanism to allocate additional computation to difficult or consequential choices.
schema.motivation: Long-horizon manipulation requires coherent subtask sequencing, so improving high-level decisions has direct downstream impact on closed-loop success.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed hierarchical robot foundation model formulates high-level subtask generation as a compute-scalable inference problem through world-model-guided test-time computation. At each inference step, the high-level policy uses execution memory to generate a subtask and, when needed, searches over alternatives before committing to its output. A low-level policy then executes the generated subtask across multiple robot embodiments. The policy is trained on 40,115 hours of heterogeneous real-world data with multimodal co-training.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is evaluated by next-subtask prediction accuracy with additional test-time computation across in-domain and distribution-shifted settings; claim (2) is evaluated by closed-loop success on long-horizon robot manipulation tasks. The abstract does not name baselines, metrics, held-matched resources, or failure conditions.

items.title: $τ_0$-VLA: a Hierarchical Robot Foundation Model with World-Model-Guided Test-Time Computation
items.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to both execute individual skills reliably and sequence them coherently over extended tasks. Most hierarchical vision-language-action (VLA) models make each such decision with a single forward pass, leaving no mechanism to allocate additional computation to difficult or consequential choices. We introduce $τ_0$-VLA, a hierarchical robot foundation model that formulates high-level subtask generation as a compute-scalable inference problem through world-model-guided test-time computation. At each inference step, the high-level policy uses execution memory to generate a subtask and, when needed, searches over alternatives before committing to its output. A low-level policy then executes the generated subtask across multiple robot embodiments. The policy is trained on 40,115 hours of heterogeneous real-world data with multimodal co-training. Across in-domain and distribution-shifted settings, allocating additional test-time computation substantially improves next-subtask prediction accuracy, and these gains translate into higher closed-loop success on long-horizon robot manipulation tasks.

schema.problem: Optimizing GPU kernels is critical for efficient modern machine learning systems but remains challenging due to the complex interplay of design factors and rapid hardware evolution; existing automated approaches treat LLMs as stochastic code generators inside heuristic-guided evolutionary loops and struggle with complex kernels that require coordinated multi-step structural transformations because they lack explicit planning and discard promising strategies when intermediate implementations are inefficient or incorrect.
schema.motivation: The difficulty of manually optimizing complex kernels and the availability of LLMs with prior domain knowledge create an opportunity for automated search that can plan multi-step transformations and tolerate imperfect intermediate implementations.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework builds on a co-evolving world model that replaces static search heuristics, using the LLM's prior domain knowledge to guide search and actively explore the optimization space. It explicitly decouples high-level algorithmic planning from low-level program instantiation, so the search can navigate non-monotonic optimization paths while remaining resilient to temporary implementation defects. The approach is applied to GPU kernel optimization and evaluated on complex kernels from FlashInfer, including GQA, MLA, and MoE kernels, as well as the GPUMode TriMul task.
schema.research_plan: The work evaluates the proposed framework on diverse complex kernels from FlashInfer (GQA, MLA, and MoE kernels), comparing against state-of-the-art evolutionary search methods to support the claimed performance improvement. It further tests the approach on the GPUMode TriMul task on H100 against prior evolution and human-designed solutions. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions, controlled matching of compute or parameters, or precise metrics beyond the reported latency on TriMul.

items.title: K-Search: LLM Kernel Generation via Co-Evolving Intrinsic World Model
items.abstract: Optimizing GPU kernels is critical for efficient modern machine learning systems yet remains challenging due to the complex interplay of design factors and rapid hardware evolution. Existing automated approaches typically treat Large Language Models (LLMs) merely as stochastic code generators within heuristic-guided evolutionary loops. These methods often struggle with complex kernels requiring coordinated, multi-step structural transformations, as they lack explicit planning capabilities and frequently discard promising strategies due to inefficient or incorrect intermediate implementations. To address this, we propose Search via Co-Evolving World Model and build K-Search based on this method. By replacing static search heuristics with a co-evolving world model, our framework leverages LLMs' prior domain knowledge to guide the search, actively exploring the optimization space. This approach explicitly decouples high-level algorithmic planning from low-level program instantiation, enabling the system to navigate non-monotonic optimization paths while remaining resilient to temporary implementation defects. We evaluate K-Search on diverse, complex kernels from FlashInfer, including GQA, MLA, and MoE kernels. Our results show that K-Search significantly outperforms state-of-the-art evolutionary search methods, achieving an average 2.10x improvement and up to a 14.3x gain on complex MoE kernels. On the GPUMode TriMul task, K-Search achieves state-of-the-art performance on H100, reaching 1030us and surpassing both prior evolution and human-designed solutions.

schema.problem: Joint-embedding predictive energy functions and quasimetric value functions for goal-conditioned control are studied separately, and it is unclear how the scalar compatibility energies in JEPA relate to the directed distance values used in quasimetric reinforcement learning.
schema.motivation: Connecting the two viewpoints makes explicit when representation energies must be asymmetric for one-way reachability and allows principles from one framework to be applied to the other.
schema.proposed_approach: The article restricts JEPA energy functions to a least-action class defined as infima of accumulated local effort over admissible trajectories between two states. It analyzes these energy functions under mild closure and additivity assumptions on local effort, relating them to quasimetric properties. It then maps optimal goal-reaching cost-to-go functions and JEPA-learned energies into this same class, and compares symmetric finite energies with the requirements of one-way reachability.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is formal: (1) a derivation that least-action energies under closure and additivity assumptions are quasimetrics; (2) a derivation mapping optimal cost-to-go functions to least-action form and JEPA-learned energies to the quasimetric value class; (3) a structural argument that symmetric finite energies cannot match one-way reachability. No experimental evaluation or explicit failure condition is stated.

items.title: Intrinsic-Energy Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures Induce Quasimetric Spaces
items.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) aim to learn representations by predicting target embeddings from context embeddings, inducing a scalar compatibility energy in a latent space. In contrast, Quasimetric Reinforcement Learning (QRL) studies goal-conditioned control through directed distance values (cost-to-go) that support reaching goals under asymmetric dynamics. In this short article, we connect these viewpoints by restricting attention to a principled class of JEPA energy functions : intrinsic (least-action) energies, defined as infima of accumulated local effort over admissible trajectories between two states. Under mild closure and additivity assumptions, any intrinsic energy is a quasimetric. In goal-reaching control, optimal cost-to-go functions admit exactly this intrinsic form ; inversely, JEPAs trained to model intrinsic energies lie in the quasimetric value class targeted by QRL. Moreover, we observe why symmetric finite energies are structurally mismatched with one-way reachability, motivating asymmetric (quasimetric) energies when directionality matters.

schema.problem: In language, the interface between continuous representation and symbolic operations is given by tokens, but for speech and audio it must be learned. Existing audio tokenizers use local quantization, clustering, or reconstruction, leaving sequence consistency, compactness, length control, termination, and edit geometry only indirectly optimized.
schema.motivation: A compact learned symbolic interface for speech and audio would make comparison, retrieval, memory, alignment, and reasoning more natural and reduce archive storage, analogous to tokens in language.
schema.proposed_approach: An encoder maps speech to a condition, and an autoregressive decoder emits tokens from BOS to EOS, so tokenization is treated as conditional sequence generation that learns identity, order, length, and termination. Given two content-preserving views, each token string is trained to be likely under the other's representation while unrelated examples provide competing sequences, yielding a surrogate for edit-distance preservation and discouraging collapse. Starting from a VQ tokenizer, the framework extends a frame-synchronous prior into an autoregressive tokenizer using VQ-derived and EMA-teacher targets, cross-paired teacher forcing, anti-bypass regularization, likelihood contrast, length control, and timing recovery.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation covers 3-second speech: cross-view consistency of the learned token strings, and retrieval performance against a VQ tokenizer baseline using token rate and archive token reduction while preserving edit-distance search. Dense geometric and SSL tokenizers are used to characterize the compactness–locality trade-off rather than to compete on every local metric. No explicit failure thresholds are stated beyond the trade-off positioning.

items.title: PairAlign: A Framework for Sequence Tokenization via Self-Alignment with Applications to Audio Tokenization
items.abstract: Modern learning systems represent perceptual signals with continuous vectors, but comparison, retrieval, memory, alignment, and reasoning are often naturally symbolic. In language, this interface is given by tokens; for speech and audio, it must be learned. Existing audio tokenizers use local quantization, clustering, or reconstruction, leaving sequence consistency, compactness, length control, termination, and edit geometry indirectly optimized. We introduce PairAlign, a framework for compact audio tokenization through sequence-level self-alignment. PairAlign treats tokenization as conditional sequence generation: an encoder maps speech to a condition, and an autoregressive decoder emits tokens from BOS to EOS, learning identity, order, length, and termination. Given two content-preserving views, each token string is trained to be likely under the other's representation, while unrelated examples provide competing sequences. This yields a surrogate for edit-distance preservation while discouraging collapse. Starting from a VQ tokenizer, PairAlign extends a frame-synchronous prior into an autoregressive tokenizer using VQ-derived and EMA-teacher targets, cross-paired teacher forcing, anti-bypass regularization, likelihood contrast, length control, and timing recovery. On 3 s speech, PairAlign learns compact token strings with strong cross-view consistency. In retrieval, it operates at 12.71 tokens/s and reduces archive tokens by 55% versus VQ while preserving edit-distance search. The results expose a compactness--locality trade-off: PairAlign does not aim to dominate dense geometric or SSL tokenizers on every local metric, but provides a lower-rate symbolic interface for comparison, retrieval, and analysis. More broadly, PairAlign is a sequence-symbolic analogue of JEPA-style predictive learning, predicting a learned variable-length symbolic sequence rather than a continuous latent.

schema.problem: It is unclear which latent space should be used in action-conditioned latent diffusion world models for robot control; the status quo relies on reconstruction-oriented autoencoding latents, and visual fidelity alone may not capture policy-relevant quality.
schema.motivation: World model-based policy evaluation is a practical proxy for real-world robot control, and as these models increasingly adopt latent diffusion, the choice of latent space has become critical; recent pretrained encoders with representation-aligned semantic latent spaces make a systematic comparison timely.
schema.proposed_approach: The study trains action-conditioned latent diffusion world models using six encoders—reconstruction-oriented encoders such as VAE and Cosmos and semantic encoders such as V-JEPA 2.1, Web-DINO, and SigLIP 2—under a fixed protocol on the BridgeV2 dataset. It evaluates the trained variants along three axes: visual fidelity, planning and downstream policy performance, and latent representation quality, including high-dimensional representation spaces with and without dimension compression.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim that effective world model training is possible in high-dimensional representation spaces is tested by training action-conditioned LDM variants with six encoders, both with and without dimension compression, under a fixed protocol on BridgeV2. (2) The claim that visual fidelity alone is insufficient is tested by comparing visual fidelity rankings against planning and downstream policy performance and latent representation quality; support requires visual fidelity rankings to diverge from policy-relevant rankings. (3) The claim that semantic latent spaces are stronger for policy-relevant world models is tested by comparing reconstruction-oriented encoders (VAE, Cosmos) with semantic encoders (V-JEPA 2.1, Web-DINO, SigLIP 2) across all model scales, holding dataset and protocol fixed.

items.title: Reconstruction or Semantics? What Makes a Latent Space Useful for Robotic World Models
items.abstract: World model-based policy evaluation is a practical proxy for testing real-world robot control by rolling out candidate actions in action-conditioned video diffusion models. As these models increasingly adopt latent diffusion modeling (LDM), choosing the right latent space becomes critical. While the status quo uses autoencoding latent spaces like VAEs that are primarily trained for pixel reconstruction, recent work suggests benefits from pretrained encoders with representation-aligned semantic latent spaces. We systematically evaluate these latent spaces for action-conditioned LDM by comparing six reconstruction and semantic encoders to train world model variants under a fixed protocol on BridgeV2 dataset, and show effective world model training in high-dimensional representation spaces with and without dimension compression. We then propose three axes to assess robotic world model performance: visual fidelity, planning and downstream policy performance, and latent representation quality. Our results show visual fidelity alone is insufficient for world model selection. While reconstruction encoders like VAE and Cosmos achieve strong pixel-level scores, semantic encoders such as V-JEPA 2.1 (strongest overall on policy), Web-DINO, and SigLIP 2 generally excel across the other two axes at all model scales. Our study advocates semantic latent space as stronger foundation for policy-relevant robotics diffusion world models.

schema.problem: Long-form fiction writers need memory that answers multi-hop questions about evolving story state—who knows a secret and when they learned it, whether an event preceded the narration that revealed it, whether a setup paid off, and how a relationship shifted—but general-purpose retrieval and agent-memory systems represent entities and facts, not the narratological structure those questions turn on, so they surface the wrong evidence or none at all.
schema.motivation: Reliable narratological memory would let long-form fiction writers query evolving story state directly instead of reconstructing it by hand across chapters, and would avoid evidence retrieval that is irrelevant to narrative structure.
schema.proposed_approach: The system represents story state as a graph whose typed temporal states encode narratological structure—such as event ordering, knowledge state and timing, setup/payoff relations, and relationship trajectories—rather than only entities and facts. Retrieval is conditioned on the query and combines multiple retrieval modes, returning chapter-safe evidence that a fixed reader then consumes. The system is evaluated as a memory component over a public fiction corpus and a validated multi-hop narratological benchmark.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed system and comparison systems on a public corpus and a validated multi-hop narratological benchmark. Each system supplies chapter-safe evidence to a single held-constant Opus 4.8 reader, so the reader is not a variable. The proposed system is compared against Graphiti/Zep as the strongest temporal-knowledge-graph agent-memory framework, and against GraphRAG and flat retrieval. To test the representational claim, the Graphiti/Zep baseline is rebuilt with the proposed system's extractor; if the proposed system's advantage disappears under that condition, the representational claim would fail. To isolate the source of advantage, the paper traces whether performance follows narratology-grounded structure and retrieval design while holding graph size and extractor quality as alternative explanations; if advantage traces to graph size or extractor quality instead, the attribution to representation would fail.

items.title: Narrative World Model: Narratology-Grounded Writer Memory for Long-Form Fiction
items.abstract: Long-form fiction writers need memory that answers multi-hop questions about evolving story state: who knows a secret and when they learned it, whether an event preceded the narration that revealed it, whether a setup paid off, and how a relationship shifted. General-purpose retrieval and agent-memory systems represent entities and facts but not the narratological structure these questions turn on, so they surface the wrong evidence or none at all. We introduce the Narrative World Model (NWM), a writer-memory system that pairs a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval. To measure memory rather than the answerer, we read every system through a single held-constant Opus 4.8 reader over only that system's chapter-safe evidence, on a reproducible public corpus and a validated multi-hop benchmark, and we compare against the strongest existing temporal-knowledge-graph agent-memory framework, Graphiti/Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025). NWM substantially and significantly outperforms this baseline on multi-hop narratological QA across both corpora, and far exceeds GraphRAG and flat retrieval. The advantage is representational rather than an artifact of extraction: it survives rebuilding the baseline with NWM's own extractor, and traces to its narratology-grounded structure and query-conditioned retrieval, not to graph size or extractor quality.

schema.problem: GUI agents trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning lack action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics.
schema.motivation: A pretraining stage on visual state transitions offers a new scalable axis for improving GUI agents across desktop and mobile scenarios.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach adds a pretraining stage before task fine-tuning. During this stage, a unified multimodal model is continually pretrained on visual state transitions with two joint objectives: predicting actions from state changes (inverse dynamics) and predicting next states from current states and actions (forward dynamics). The resulting model is then fine-tuned on trajectories with task instructions.
schema.research_plan: Evidence consists of fine-tuning the pretrained model on task-instruction trajectories and evaluating on desktop and mobile GUI agent benchmarks (AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey) against direct trajectory fine-tuning baselines. Further empirical studies compare joint dynamics optimization against single-objective training and vary the volume of transition data to assess scaling.

items.title: Scaling GUI Agents with Visual State Transitions
items.abstract: We introduce State Transition Pretraining (STP) as a new scaling axis for GUI agents. During the STP stage, we continually pretrain a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions by jointly optimizing inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes) and forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions). This optimization equips the model with better action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics. When subsequently fine-tuned on trajectories with task instructions, our STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning across agent benchmarks in both desktop and mobile GUI scenarios (AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey). Further empirical studies show that joint dynamics optimization yields stable improvements over single-objective training, and downstream performance scales steadily with the volume of transition data.

schema.problem: In unsupervised reinforcement learning, traditional world models are prone to single-step errors that produce distributional shifts, limiting robust environmental modeling.
schema.motivation: Improving environmental modeling would allow agents to explore more effectively and adapt rapidly to task-specific environments.
schema.proposed_approach: A diffusion model serves as the environmental model in unsupervised reinforcement learning. During pre-training, it generates future observations conditioned on current observations and actions; these generated observations are used to define an intrinsic reward that incentivizes exploration of diverse and high-uncertainty states. In fine-tuning, the model performs data augmentation by producing synthetic data to expand the training dataset for downstream tasks.
schema.research_plan: The approach is evaluated on the URLB benchmark across three domains and twelve downstream tasks, comparing exploration and adaptability against existing methods. The abstract does not specify named baselines, metrics, ablations, held-matched conditions, or failure criteria.

items.title: Diffusion Dynamic Model for Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) enables agents to adapt efficiently to novel tasks but relies on robust environmental modeling. Traditional world models enhance exploration but are prone to single-step errors, leading to distributional shifts. To address this challenge, we introduce the Diffusion Dynamic Model (DDM), incorporating diffusion models into the environmental modeling component of unsupervised reinforcement learning. During pre-training, DDM generates future observations conditioned on current observations and actions. These generated observations are used to design an intrinsic reward function that incentivizes the agent to explore diverse and high-uncertainty states. In the fine-tuning phase, DDM leverages its generative capabilities to perform data augmentation. By producing diverse, high-quality synthetic data, DDM expands the training dataset, enabling the agent to generalize better and adapt more rapidly to task-specific environments. Our approach is validated across three domains and twelve downstream tasks in the URLB benchmark, demonstrating superior exploration and adaptability compared to existing methods.

schema.problem: Most available world-model implementations remain publication-specific, which limits their reusability, increases the risk of bugs, and reduces evaluation standardization.
schema.motivation: A shared, standardized research ecosystem could make world-model work easier to reuse and compare, and environments with controllable factors could support robustness and continual learning research.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work is a modular, tested, and documented world-model research ecosystem. It integrates efficient data-collection tools, standardized environments, planning algorithms, and baseline implementations. Each environment provides controllable factors of variation, including visual and physical properties, to support robustness and continual learning research. The ecosystem is then used to study zero-shot robustness in DINO-WM.
schema.research_plan: The paper supports the utility of the ecosystem through a demonstration in which it is used to study zero-shot robustness in DINO-WM. The abstract does not specify metrics, baselines, or failure conditions for that demonstration.

items.title: stable-worldmodel-v1: Reproducible World Modeling Research and Evaluation
items.abstract: World Models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning compact, predictive representations of environment dynamics, enabling agents to reason, plan, and generalize beyond direct experience. Despite recent interest in World Models, most available implementations remain publication-specific, severely limiting their reusability, increasing the risk of bugs, and reducing evaluation standardization. To mitigate these issues, we introduce stable-worldmodel (SWM), a modular, tested, and documented world-model research ecosystem that provides efficient data-collection tools, standardized environments, planning algorithms, and baseline implementations. In addition, each environment in SWM enables controllable factors of variation, including visual and physical properties, to support robustness and continual learning research. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of SWM by using it to study zero-shot robustness in DINO-WM.

schema.problem: Existing world-model-based autonomous driving approaches typically predict future scenes first and plan afterward, so imagined futures are generated in an open loop and may drift from the actual decision process.
schema.motivation: Tightly interleaving future prediction and planning could enable more adaptive decision-making in dynamic traffic and is positioned as a promising direction for scalable vision-language-action driving systems.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a unified vision-language-action model that alternates between predicting future frames and ego actions step by step. Each planning step is conditioned on the imagined future observation generated by the previous prediction step, forming a closed loop between world modeling and control; monocular depth information is incorporated into frames for geometric world-modeling cues.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark evaluate closed-loop planning performance and future frame prediction fidelity. These results are offered as support for the claims that interleaving prediction and planning yields competitive planning and high-fidelity frames and that the approach is promising for scalable driving systems. The abstract does not specify a failure condition, ablation design, or matched compute/latency comparison.

items.title: Uni-World VLA: Interleaved World Modeling and Planning for Autonomous Driving
items.abstract: Autonomous driving requires reasoning about how the environment evolves and planning actions accordingly. Existing world-model-based approaches typically predict future scenes first and plan afterwards, resulting in open-loop imagination that may drift from the actual decision process. In this paper, we present Uni-World VLA, a unified vision-language-action (VLA) model that tightly interleaves future frame prediction and trajectory planning. Instead of generating a full world rollout before planning, our model alternates between predicting future frames and ego actions step by step, allowing planning decisions to be continuously conditioned on the imagined future observations. This interleaved generation forms a closed-loop interaction between world modeling and control, enabling more adaptive decision-making in dynamic traffic scenarios. In addition, we incorporate monocular depth information into frames to provide stronger geometric cues for world modeling, improving long-horizon scene prediction. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark show that our approach achieves competitive closed-loop planning performance while producing high-fidelity future frame predictions. These results demonstrate that tightly coupling world prediction and planning is a promising direction for scalable VLA driving systems.

schema.problem: Large language models frequently struggle to generate correct code when natural language specifications are ambiguous or incomplete, and current approaches usually react by iteratively fixing code after generation rather than preventing specification misalignment.
schema.motivation: Explicitly validating and refining specifications before code generation can serve as a grounding intermediate step, avoiding the costly iterative repair that arises from specification misalignment.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system automatically extracts structured specifications from natural language, validates their clarity, and interactively resolves detected ambiguities through multi-turn clarification dialogue before code generation begins. It is implemented by combining neuro-symbolic specification extraction with the clarification dialogue.
schema.research_plan: The approach is evaluated on HumanEval, MBPP+, and a newly introduced ambiguity benchmark by comparing downstream code generation accuracy against approaches that skip the specification validation/refinement step. Support for the core claim would be higher accuracy with the proposed pre-generation validation than without it; failure would be no such improvement.

items.title: Specification Validation for Reliable Code Generation: Detecting and Resolving Ambiguity Before Generation
items.abstract: Large language models demonstrate impressive code generation capabilities, yet they frequently struggle when natural language specifications are ambiguous or incomplete. Rather than iteratively fixing code after generation, we propose a proactive approach: automatically extracting structured specifications from natural language, validating their clarity, and interactively resolving detected ambiguities before code generation begins. Our core insight is that explicit specification validation and refinement can serve as a critical intermediate step to ground code generation, reducing the specification misalignment that plagues current LLM-based approaches. We introduce SpecValidator, a system that combines neuro-symbolic specification extraction with multi-turn clarification dialogue to resolve specification ambiguities. Our evaluation on HumanEval, MBPP+, and a new ambiguity benchmark demonstrates that specification validation significantly improves downstream code generation accuracy compared to approaches that skip this step.

schema.problem: Text-to-CAD systems that synthesize parametric CAD programs from natural-language prompts often receive under-specified or internally inconsistent geometric descriptions, with missing critical dimensions or conflicting constraints, and existing fine-tuned models reactively follow instructions and hallucinate dimensions when the text is ambiguous.
schema.motivation: Resolving specification issues before code synthesis would make text-to-CAD more robust to ambiguous prompts and reduce invalid programs, while keeping the interaction burden of clarification low.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework pairs a proactive clarifying agent with a CAD coding agent. The clarifying agent audits the prompt and asks targeted clarification questions only when necessary, producing a self-consistent specification; the coding agent then translates this specification into an executable CadQuery program. The coding agent is fine-tuned on a curated high-quality text-to-CadQuery dataset, and the clarifying agent is trained via supervised fine-tuning on clarification trajectories. Code and datasets are released publicly.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes experiments comparing the proposed framework to frontier closed-source models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 on mean Chamfer distance and invalidity ratio, with additional measurement of interaction overhead for ambiguous prompts. The abstract does not specify held-matched conditions, ablations, or failure thresholds.

items.title: Clarify Before You Draw: Proactive Agents for Robust Text-to-CAD Generation
items.abstract: Large language models have recently enabled text-to-CAD systems that synthesize parametric CAD programs (e.g., CadQuery) from natural-language prompts. In practice, however, geometric descriptions can be under-specified or internally inconsistent: critical dimensions may be missing and constraints may conflict. However, existing fine-tuned models tend to reactively follow the user instructions and hallucinate dimensions when the text is ambiguous. To address this, we propose a proactive agentic framework for text-to-CadQuery generation, named as ProCAD, that resolves specification issues before code synthesis. Our framework pairs a proactive clarifying agent, which audits the prompt and asks targeted clarification questions only when necessary to produce a self-consistent specification, with a CAD coding agent that translates the specification into an executable CadQuery program. We fine-tune the coding agent based on a curated high-quality text-to-CadQuery dataset and train the clarifying agent via agentic SFT on clarification trajectories. Experiments show that proactive clarification significantly improves robustness to ambiguous prompts while keeping interaction overhead low. ProCAD outperforms frontier closed-source models, including Claude Sonnet 4.5, reducing the mean Chamfer distance by 79.9% and lowering the invalidity ratio from 4.8% to 0.9%. Our code and datasets are made publicly available on https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/Pro-CAD.

schema.problem: Current multi-agent code generation frameworks validate generated code through test oracles, simulation, or external debuggers, all assuming executable specifications are available; real-world software requirements, however, are predominantly expressed in natural language and lack clear executable ground truth.
schema.motivation: Without executable specifications, existing code generation frameworks cannot validate code in the way they were designed to, so addressing this gap would make multi-agent code generation applicable to real-world requirement documents and reduce dependence on test oracles.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework extracts formal and semi-formal constraints from natural-language requirement documents and generates code with embedded requirement-to-implementation traceability. It validates generated code through progressive multi-level verification: logical consistency of extracted constraints, architectural conformance of code structure to requirements, and functional behavior against extracted constraints. When verification fails, specialized agents receive requirement-grounded feedback, rather than only test failures, to guide repair.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on a new benchmark of application-level code generation tasks derived from real requirement documents, comparing the proposed framework with test-oracle-only approaches on correctness and on the maintainability and traceability of generated code. The abstract does not name specific metrics, baselines beyond the test-oracle-only comparison, ablations, or matched compute/latency conditions. An implied failure condition is that requirement-aligned validation fails to show higher correctness or better maintainability and traceability than test-oracle-only approaches.

items.title: Requirement-Aligned Code Verification: Progressive Validation of LLM-Generated Code Against Natural-Language Requirements
items.abstract: Current multi-agent code generation frameworks validate generated code through test oracles, simulation, or external debuggers—all assuming executable specifications are available. However, real-world software requirements are predominantly specified in natural language, without clear executable ground truth. We propose ReqAlign, a framework that extracts formal and semi-formal constraints from natural-language requirements, generates code with embedded requirement-to-implementation traceability, and validates code through progressive multi-level verification: logical consistency (do constraints contradict?), architectural conformance (does code structure match requirements?), and functional behavior (does code satisfy extracted constraints?). When verification fails, specialized agents receive requirement-grounded feedback (not just test failures) to guide repair. We will evaluate this on a new benchmark of application-level code generation tasks derived from real requirement documents, showing that requirement-aligned validation achieves higher correctness and produces more maintainable, traceable code than test-oracle-only approaches.

schema.problem: Formal verification requires specifications, but real-world codebases frequently lack them, and writing high-quality specifications is expensive and expertise-intensive.
schema.motivation: Automating specification synthesis would reduce the cost and expertise required for formal verification and make correctness guarantees achievable for increasingly prevalent LLM-generated code.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework decomposes a natural-language specification task into atomic requirements. It then generates requirement-targeted tests with explicit traceability maps to validate generated Lean specifications. When validation fails, the traceability maps attribute failures to specific requirements, enabling targeted clause-level repairs. The framework also generates 343K training examples from its refinement trajectories.
schema.research_plan: To support the synthesis-quality claim, the paper evaluates the framework on the VERINA SpecGen task using Claude Opus 4.5 as the underlying model and compares against baselines across different model families and scales, using accuracy on the benchmark as the success metric; no explicit failure threshold or matched-compute statement is given. To support the training-data claim, it generates 343K training examples from refinement trajectories, trains models on them, and measures relative improvement in specification synthesis and transfer to general reasoning abilities, again without an explicit failure condition.

items.title: Intent-aligned Formal Specification Synthesis via Traceable Refinement
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate code from natural language, but ensuring correctness remains challenging. Formal verification offers a principled way to obtain such guarantees by proving that a program satisfies a formal specification. However, specifications are frequently missing in real-world codebases, and writing high-quality specifications remains expensive and expertise-intensive. We present VeriSpecGen, a traceable refinement framework that synthesizes intent-aligned specifications in Lean through requirement-level attribution and localized repair. VeriSpecGen decomposes natural language into atomic requirements and generates requirement-targeted tests with explicit traceability maps to validate generated specifications. When validation fails, traceability maps attribute failures to specific requirements, enabling targeted clause-level repairs. VeriSpecGen achieve 86.6% on VERINA SpecGen task using Claude Opus 4.5, improving over baselines by up to 31.8 points across different model families and scales. Beyond inference-time gains, we generate 343K training examples from VeriSpecGen refinement trajectories and demonstrate that training on these trajectories substantially improves specification synthesis by 62-106% relative and transfers gains to general reasoning abilities.

schema.problem: Repository-level code generation still struggles with complex cross-file dependencies, and recent software engineering agents and retrieval-augmented generation frameworks rely on static code graphs and the current repository snapshot, ignoring how files, APIs, and configurations historically co-evolve across commits.
schema.motivation: Version control histories contain evidence of how features and bug fixes have spanned multiple files over time, so mining that historical co-change signal could make complex feature additions and refactorings more tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed multi-agent repository-level code generation framework mines version control histories to build historical dependency edges between software entities such as files, APIs, and configurations, capturing how features and bug fixes have spanned multiple files across commits. This historical co-change information is then fed into a multi-agent planning and retrieval loop so the generated plans account for non-local modifications likely needed in feature additions and refactorings.
schema.research_plan: Evaluations on repository-level benchmarks compare the proposed framework against purely static graph-guided agents, using generation accuracy and localization as evidence. Support would be better accuracy and localization; failure would be no improvement over the static baseline. The abstract does not specify named benchmarks, additional metrics, or matched compute controls.

items.title: HAM-RepoGen: History-Aware Multi-Agent Repository-Level Code Generation via Co-Evolution Graph Mining
items.abstract: Repository-level code generation requires models to understand complex cross-file dependencies, global semantics, and project structures. While recent software engineering agents and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks achieve notable progress, they rely predominantly on static code graphs and the current snapshot of the repository, ignoring how files, APIs, and configurations historically co-evolve across commits. To bridge this gap, we propose HAM-RepoGen, a novel multi-agent repository-level code generation framework driven by a dynamic commit-history co-evolution graph. HAM-RepoGen mines past version control histories to construct historical dependency edges between software entities, capturing patterns of how features and bug fixes have traditionally spanned multiple files. By injecting this historical co-change intelligence into a multi-agent planning and retrieval loop, HAM-RepoGen effectively anticipates non-local modifications required for complex feature additions and refactorings. Extensive evaluations on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate that incorporating historical co-evolution significantly improves generation accuracy and localization over purely static graph-guided agents.

schema.problem: In asynchronous collaborative software development, a single change often requires synchronized updates across multiple files, and current code-generation approaches neglect the implicit collaborative knowledge embedded in a project’s evolutionary history.
schema.motivation: Making this implicit coordination explicit can enable LLMs to generate coherent cross-file modifications and to understand not only code but also collaboration.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework builds a weighted evolutionary coupling graph that acts as a dynamic knowledge base for cross-file modification. It introduces a time-weighted mutual information metric that combines commit recency, focus, and statistical independence to model co-evolution robustly. This knowledge base is then used to guide LLMs in generating coherent cross-file modifications.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on six open-source and industrial projects evaluate coupling effectiveness across projects with different commit-pattern distributions to test the contingency claim (1), and compare LLMs guided by the proposed coupling graph against baselines lacking evolutionary context, including static tools, to test the generation-quality claim (2). The abstract does not state an explicit failure condition or what is held matched across comparisons.

items.title: EvoCoGen: Collaborative Code Generation Guided by Evolutionary Coupling
items.abstract: In asynchronous software development, a single change often requires synchronized updates across multiple files, posing a significant challenge for collaborative code generation. Current approaches often overlook the implicit collaborative knowledge embedded in the project’s evolutionary history. To bridge this gap, we propose EvoCoGen, a framework that leverages a Weighted Evolutionary Coupling Graph (WECG). Unlike static analysis, which misses implicit dependencies, and traditional frequency-based methods prone to noise, we introduce Time-Weighted Mutual Information (TWMI). This metric integrates commit recency, focus, and statistical independence to robustly model co-evolution. WECG serves as a dynamic knowledge base, guiding Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate coherent cross-file modifications. Experiments on six open-source and industrial projects reveal that coupling effectiveness is contingent on "commit culture": TWMI excels in projects with skewed/heavy-tailed distributions via its denoising capability, while traditional methods suit stable environments. Moreover, WECG-guided LLMs consistently equal or outperform baselines lacking evolutionary context, particularly excelling in capturing implicit dependencies invisible to static tools. This work offers a socio-technical perspective: by making implicit coordination explicit, LLMs are empowered to not only "understand code" but also "understand collaboration".

schema.problem: Current LLM-based automated program repair and software engineering agents produce a significant fraction of overfitted patches that pass sparse test suites but fail to capture true developer intent or break unseen edge cases; existing test-generation and repair approaches either decouple test generation from the repair loop or rely solely on static test augmentation after patch generation.
