schema.motivation: Overfitted patches undermine the reliability of LLM-based program repair, and embedding counterexample synthesis directly into the repair loop could constrain patch generation and improve semantic correctness for real-world issues.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework treats automated program repair as a rigorous test-driven synthesis game. The agent dynamically synthesizes falsifying unit tests based on execution traces and bug localization feedback, uses these counterexamples to constrain and refine patch generation, and iteratively co-evolves tests and patches until semantic convergence. The implementation plan uses the SWE-bench benchmark and a detailed evaluation strategy against state-of-the-art baselines.
schema.research_plan: The plan is to implement the framework on SWE-bench and evaluate it against state-of-the-art baselines, measuring the reduction in overfitted patches and the improvement in semantic correctness. These metrics would bear directly on the claim that active counterexample synthesis improves repairs over decoupled or post-hoc test generation. The abstract does not specify failure thresholds, named baselines, or what is held matched between comparisons.

items.title: Counterexample-Guided Test-Driven Agentic Repair for Real-World Software Issues
items.abstract: Automated program repair (APR) and software engineering agents have achieved remarkable success in resolving real-world GitHub issues using Large Language Models. However, recent empirical audits reveal a critical vulnerability: a significant fraction of generated patches are overfitted, passing existing sparse test suites while failing to capture the true developer intent or breaking unseen edge cases. Existing test-generation and repair approaches either decouple test generation from the repair loop or rely solely on static test augmentation after patch generation. In this proposal, we introduce CETAR (Counterexample-Guided Test-Driven Agentic Repair), a novel framework that embeds active counterexample synthesis directly into the agent's iterative repair loop. Unlike existing methods that generate tests from issues once or validate patches post-hoc, CETAR treats repair as a rigorous test-driven synthesis game: the agent dynamically synthesizes falsifying unit tests based on execution traces and bug localization feedback, uses these counterexamples to constrain and refine patch generation, and iteratively co-evolves both tests and patches until semantic convergence. We outline an implementation plan using SWE-bench and a detailed evaluation strategy to measure reduction in overfitted patches and improvement in semantic correctness compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

schema.problem: It remains unclear whether bug reproduction tests can also help the more central stage of patch generation, and direct use of advanced BRT generators to guide patch generation is not beneficial because fail-to-pass BRTs may cover only one manifestation of an issue while fail-to-fail BRTs are unreliable as direct patch-generation targets.
schema.motivation: BRTs are already important for patch validation and issue reports state multiple behavioral requirements, so deriving runtime-grounded diagnoses from multi-faceted BRT executions may guide patch generation and reduce partial patches.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed agent is a software issue resolution agent that first generates multi-faceted bug reproduction tests for the different behavioral requirements stated in an issue report. It then executes and debugs these tests to construct runtime-grounded diagnosis records. The diagnoses are used together with localization information inferred during BRT generation to guide patch generation and reduce partial patches.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the preliminary finding, the evidence is an analysis of direct use of advanced BRT generators, separating fail-to-pass and fail-to-fail BRTs and examining their effects on patch generation. (2) For the proposed agent claim, the evaluation uses Python bug-fixing issues from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro across five LLM backends, comparing the proposed agent against existing agents on resolution rates. Support is consistent improvement across the LLM-benchmark combinations; no explicit failure condition or matched compute/latency is stated.

items.title: SWE-Doctor: Guiding Software Engineering Agents with Runtime Diagnosis from Multi-Faceted Bug Reproduction Tests
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based software engineering agents are increasingly developed to resolve software issues by generating patches from issue reports and code repositories. Bug reproduction tests (BRTs) are an important building block for such agents and have been shown useful for patch validation. However, it remains unclear whether BRTs can also help the more central stage of patch generation. We first conduct a preliminary study and find that directly using advanced BRT generators to guide patch generation is not beneficial: fail-to-fail BRTs can mislead agents, while even fail-to-pass BRTs bring limited or negative gains. Our analysis reveals two reasons: fail-to-pass BRTs may cover only one manifestation of the reported issue, leading to partial patches, whereas fail-to-fail BRTs are unreliable as direct patch-generation targets. Motivated by these insights, we propose SWE-Doctor, a software issue resolution agent that guides patch generation with runtime diagnoses derived from multi-faceted BRT executions. SWE-Doctor first generates multi-faceted BRTs for different behavioral requirements stated in the issue, then executes and debugs these BRTs to construct runtime-grounded diagnosis records, and finally uses the diagnoses together with localization information inferred during BRT generation to guide patch generation and reduce partial patches. We evaluate SWE-Doctor on Python bug-fixing issues from the widely adopted SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro across five LLM backends. SWE-Doctor consistently outperforms existing agents across all 10 LLM-benchmark combinations, achieving average resolution rates of 75.7% on SWE-bench Verified and 59.4% on SWE-bench Pro. In particular, on the more challenging SWE-bench Pro, SWE-Doctor improves the average resolution rate by 8.0-8.9 percentage points over the baseline agents.

schema.problem: Widely used retrieval selectors for code LLMs retrieve exemplars by whole-specification similarity (token, embedding, or pseudocode-plan), but real specifications are composite—activating several functional concerns—so top-k similarity retrieves redundant exemplars that showcase one dominant concern.
schema.motivation: Composite specifications are common in competition-level and API-heavy requests, so correcting exemplar selection to cover all activated functional concerns may remove a bottleneck in retrieval-augmented code generation.
schema.proposed_approach: The method treats the exemplar bank and the target specification as mixtures over latent functional topics of code, where each topic clusters (problem, accepted-solution) pairs that perform the same algorithmic computation. A code-aware topicizer is built over natural-language–code pairs, the target specification's sparse topic-activation vector is inferred, and the few-shot budget is allocated across activated topics using a greedy coverage objective. Two allocation variants are used: a quota variant and a topic-restricted determinantal-point-process variant, with exemplar ordering applied only after selection.
schema.research_plan: (1) The comparative claim is evaluated on composite-specification slices of competition benchmarks that include per-problem algorithm tags, using execution-based Pass@1 and a new skill-recall diagnostic against nearest-neighbour and diversity-only baselines. (2) Support requires coverage-based selection to outperform baselines on multi-topic problems while matching them on single-topic problems; if topic coverage is irrelevant, the method should degenerate to nearest-neighbour retrieval. (3) The abstract does not state whether compute, parameters, or other conditions are held matched across comparisons.

items.title: Covering the Functional Topics of a Specification: Latent Topic Mixtures for Demonstration Selection in Few-Shot Code Generation
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting is the main practical recipe for improving code LLMs, yet the most widely used selectors retrieve the most similar exemplars by whole-specification similarity (token, embedding, or pseudocode-plan). We observe that real specifications are composite: a competition-level or API-heavy request activates several functional concerns (string parsing plus modular arithmetic; a suffix-array step plus a Fenwick-tree update), and top-k similarity retrieves k redundant exemplars that all showcase one dominant concern. We propose to treat both the exemplar bank and the target specification as mixtures over latent functional topics of code — clusters of (problem, accepted-solution) pairs sharing the algorithmic computation they perform — and to select the in-context demonstration set by covering the query's topic mixture rather than matching its surface. Concretely, we build a code-aware topicizer over NL–code pairs, infer the target's sparse topic-activation vector, and allocate the few-shot budget across activated topics with a greedy coverage objective (a quota variant and a topic-restricted DPP variant), applying order only after selection. We evaluate on composite-specification slices of competition benchmarks that carry per-problem algorithm tags, measuring execution-based Pass@1 and a new SkillRecall diagnostic. The core falsifiable claim: coverage-based topic-aware selection beats every nearest-neighbour and diversity-only baseline on multi-topic problems while tying them on single-topic problems, establishing that the bottleneck on composite problems is topic coverage, not within-topic similarity. If topic coverage is irrelevant, the method degenerates to nearest-neighbour retrieval, so the design cleanly separates the two explanations of retrieval success.

schema.problem: Existing in-context learning exemplar selection for CAD code generation mainly uses similarity or point-wise diversity, which overlooks the compositional nature of design specifications; selected exemplars can be individually relevant but collectively redundant, leaving complex multi-requirement design queries insufficiently covered.
schema.motivation: Domain-specific CAD code generation is constrained by scarce high-quality training data, and better exemplar selection could make training-free in-context learning more effective for such tasks without additional fine-tuning.
schema.proposed_approach: The method decomposes a target CAD design specification into multi-granular components and selects a compact set of exemplars by maximizing the proportion of query components covered by the selected examples, using a surrogate tiling ratio. The resulting coverage objective is formulated as submodular maximization, and a polynomial-time greedy algorithm is used for selection with a (1−1/e) approximation guarantee.
schema.research_plan: The empirical claim (1) is evaluated through experiments across multiple LLMs, comparing the proposed selection method with existing ICL exemplar selection strategies on CAD code generation quality. The theoretical claim (2) is supported by a submodularity formulation of the coverage objective and analysis of the greedy algorithm's approximation guarantee; no explicit failure condition or matched-resource control is stated for the empirical evaluation.

items.title: Design-Specification Tiling for ICL-based CAD Code Generation
items.abstract: Large language models~(LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in code generation, yet their performance remains limited on domain-specific tasks such as Computer-Aided Design~(CAD) code generation, largely due to the scarcity of high-quality training data. In-Context Learning~(ICL) provides a training-free alternative by prompting LLMs with task-specific exemplars, but its effectiveness critically depends on how exemplars are selected. Existing selection strategies mainly rely on similarity or point-wise diversity, often overlooking the compositional nature of CAD design specifications, where a query may involve multiple functional requirements, geometric constraints, and design primitives. As a result, selected exemplars can be individually relevant but collectively redundant, providing insufficient coverage for complex design requirements. In this work, we propose \emph{knowledge sufficiency} as a principled objective for exemplar selection, aiming to select a compact set of exemplars that maximally satisfies the requirements contained in a target design specification. To instantiate this objective, we introduce \emph{Design-Specification Tiling~(DST)}, which estimates knowledge sufficiency through a surrogate tiling ratio by decomposing design specifications into multi-granular components and measuring the proportion of query components covered by selected exemplars. We further show that optimizing this objective can be formulated as a submodular maximization problem, and develop a polynomial-time greedy algorithm tailored to this setting with a $(1-1/e)$-approximation guarantee. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that DST substantially improves CAD code generation quality and consistently outperforms existing ICL exemplar selection strategies, highlighting the importance of requirement-level knowledge coverage for domain-specific code generation.

schema.problem: Automated program repair and LLM-based issue-solving agents are validated by incomplete test suites, so patches that pass all tests may nonetheless be incorrect. Existing patch-correctness-assessment techniques either learn from previously labeled patches, rank patches by static or dynamic similarity, or generate more tests whose oracles are derived from the implemented behaviour of the patched program—exactly the behaviour LLMs tend to encode.
schema.motivation: Using the pre-patch buggy program as an oracle offers a way to specify which behaviours must change and which must be preserved without depending on labelled patches or on the patched program’s own behaviour, enabling machine-checkable evidence of incorrectness.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a buggy program, a bug report, and a patch, an LLM infers an explicit executable two-clause specification: one clause is a predicate over inputs that characterises the bug-triggering region and the behaviour that must change there, and the other clause is a predicate over inputs on which the patched and pre-patch programs must behave identically. A differential executor searches for inputs inside the must-differ region and outside it (must-equal), and an iterative falsification loop feeds discrepancies back to the LLM. Any out-of-frame behavioural divergence is reported as a machine-checkable counterexample certificate naming the violated clause, the input, and the two outputs.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation compares the proposed method against RGT, Poracle, Shibboleth, FixCheck, LLM4PatchCorrect, and a random-selection baseline on curated overfitting corpora and on SWE-bench-Verified-style issue-solving patches; the fraction of patches undecidable from the bug report alone is reported as a first-class result. No explicit failure condition or held-matched quantities are stated for the comparative claims.

items.title: FRAMECHECK: Contract-Guided Differential Patch Validation from Bug Reports
items.abstract: Automated program repair (APR) and LLM-based issue-solving agents are validated by test suites that are incomplete, so patches that pass all tests may nonetheless be incorrect. Existing patch-correctness-assessment techniques either learn from previously labeled patches, rank patches by static or dynamic similarity, or generate more tests whose oracles are derived from the implemented behaviour of the patched program — exactly the behaviour LLMs tend to encode. FRAMECHECK makes the opposite move: it uses the pre-patch (buggy) program as an oracle. Given a buggy program, a bug report, and a patch, an LLM infers a change frame: an explicit, executable two-clause specification consisting of (i) an obligation clause, a predicate over inputs that characterises the bug-triggering region and the behaviour that must change there, and (ii) a preservation clause, a predicate over inputs on which the patched and pre-patch programs must behave identically. A differential executor then searches for inputs inside the frame (must-differ) and outside it (must-equal), and an iterative falsification loop feeds discrepancies back to the LLM. Any out-of-frame behavioural divergence is reported as a machine-checkable counterexample certificate naming the violated clause, the input, and the two outputs. I evaluate FRAMECHECK against RGT, Poracle, Shibboleth, FixCheck, LLM4PatchCorrect, and the random-selection baseline on curated overfitting corpora and on SWE-bench-Verified-style issue-solving patches, reporting as a first-class result the fraction of patches that are undecidable from the bug report alone.

schema.problem: Software patches may unintentionally alter program behavior, and validating a patch against its intended semantics is difficult because regression tests are incomplete and natural-language descriptions of patch intent are informal and non-executable.
schema.motivation: Making patch intent executable would enable automated validation and provide documentation, complementing code review and regression testing; large language models now make it feasible to extract intent from natural-language artifacts.
schema.proposed_approach: Given a pull request, the proposed technique uses large language models to extract developer intent from natural-language artifacts and synthesizes executable patch specifications expressed as runtime assertions in comparison programs that integrate pre- and post-patch versions. The specifications focus on patch-relevant behaviors and support cross-version properties. The technique iteratively refines inferred specifications by comparing pre- and post-patch behaviors, identifies violations, filters inconsistencies via self-review, and generates bug reports.
schema.research_plan: (1) The specification-inference ability is evaluated on 400 recent pull requests from four widely used open-source Python projects, with precision measured against developer-confirmed true positives. (2) The practical usefulness is evaluated by whether reported warnings correspond to confirmed bugs and subsequent fixes, and by per-pull-request time and monetary cost. (3) The technique is compared with the state-of-the-art technique Testora.

items.title: PatchGuru: Patch Oracle Inference from Natural Language Artifacts
items.abstract: As software systems evolve, patches may unintentionally alter program behavior. Validating patches against their intended semantics is difficult due to incomplete regression tests and informal, non-executable natural language (NL) descriptions of patch intent. We present PatchGuru, the first automated technique that infers executable patch specifications from real-world pull requests (PRs). Given a PR, PatchGuru uses large language models (LLMs) to extract developer intent from NL artifacts and synthesizes patch oracles: under-approximate yet practical specifications expressed as runtime assertions in comparison programs that integrate pre- and post-patch versions. Patch oracles focus on patch-relevant behaviors, enable automated validation, and support cross-version properties. PatchGuru iteratively refines inferred oracles by comparing pre- and post-patch behaviors, identifies violations, filters inconsistencies via self-review, and generates bug reports. We evaluate PatchGuru on 400 recent PRs from four widely used open-source Python projects. PatchGuru reports 39 warnings with a precision of 0.62, yielding 24 confirmed true positives, including 12 previously unknown bugs, 11 of which were subsequently fixed by developers. Compared to the state-of-the-art technique Testora, PatchGuru detects 17 more bugs (24 vs. 7) while improving precision from 0.32 to 0.62. PatchGuru incurs an average cost of 8.9 minutes and USD 0.07 per PR. These results suggest that PatchGuru complements code review and regression testing by providing executable documentation and automated validation of patch intent.

schema.problem: There is no cheap per-sample signal that tells a developer whether a specific generated program is correct before execution-based certification, and existing likelihood-based execution-free heuristics are known to mis-rank.
schema.motivation: A reliable execution-free per-sample correctness signal would give developers immediate feedback and avoid reliance on expensive hidden-test execution; LLM rewriting now makes semantically equivalent requirement paraphrases available to construct such a signal.
schema.proposed_approach: For a single coding instance, the proposal generates several semantically equivalent paraphrases of the same requirement using LLM rewriting plus a semantic-equivalence filter following prior work, then generates code under each paraphrase under a fixed sample budget. It measures agreement among the resulting programs at textual, AST-level structural, and identifier/role-level. The construction also includes the paraphrase/equivalence filter and an abstention study comparing against selective generation with unit-test validation.
schema.research_plan: The proposal tests the main hypothesis with a sign test comparing the per-instance paraphrase-agreement signal against likelihood baselines and other execution-free signals for Pass@1, under a fixed sample budget that isolates paraphrase agreement from sampling noise. Paraphrase-quality ablations diagnose failure modes if agreement under remote-but-equivalent paraphrases fails to separate correct from incorrect code; an abstention study evaluates the signal against selective generation with unit-test validation.

items.title: SpecPar-Con: Per-Instance Specification-Paraphrase Consistency as an Execution-Free Predictor of Functional Correctness in LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: Code generation benchmarks rely on executing hidden tests to certify functional correctness, but no cheap per-sample signal tells a developer whether a specific generated program is right before that certificate is available, and likelihood-based heuristics are known to mis-rank , . We propose specification-paraphrase consistency (SpecPar): for a single coding instance, generate code under several semantically equivalent paraphrases of the same requirement (produced with LLM rewriting plus a semantic-equivalence filter following ) and measure agreement between the resulting programs — textual, AST-level structural, and identifier/role-level. Our falsifiable hypothesis is that per-instance SpecPar agreement out-predicts existing execution-free signals (max-likelihood, mean log-prob, internal correctness representations, uncertainty estimates, LLM-as-judge scores) for that instance's Pass@1, because correct code must anchor deterministically to the requirement across independently worded specs, whereas wrong code follows spurious surface cues , . The proposal includes the exact construction of the paraphrase/equivalence filter, a fixed sample budget that isolates paraphrase agreement from sampling noise, a careful sign test against likelihood baselines, and an abstention study against selective generation with unit-test validation . If agreement under remote-but-equivalent paraphrases fails to separate correct from incorrect code, the hypothesis is refuted and the failure modes are precisely diagnosed by our paraphrase-quality ablations.

schema.problem: LLM-generated code quality is still questionable, and code validation remains a challenging problem.
schema.motivation: The observation that correct code pieces exhibit intrinsic consistency while flawed code pieces may not provides a signal by which flaws can be detected.
schema.proposed_approach: The method varies a given prompt into multiple paraphrased prompts and asks an LLM to generate multiple versions of code. It then cross-validates whether the semantic relations still hold among the acquired code versions, treating inconsistencies as signals of flaws.
schema.research_plan: The method is initially evaluated on the HumanEval benchmark using erroneous programs generated by GPT-4o, with detection of erroneous programs and false positive rate as the quality measures; no explicit failure threshold or baseline comparisons are stated.

items.title: Automatic Validation of LLM-Generated Code with Prompt Paraphrasing
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used for code generation. However, the quality of generated code is still questionable, and code validation remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a novel solution called paraphrase prompt testing. Our intuitive observation is that intrinsic consistency always exists among correct code pieces but may not exist among flawed code pieces, so we can detect flaws in the code by detecting inconsistencies. Therefore, we can vary a given prompt to multiple prompts with paraphrasing, and to ask the LLM to acquire multiple versions of generated code, so that we can validate whether the semantic relations still hold in the acquired code through cross-validation. Our initial evaluation on HumanEval shows that paraphrase prompt testing is able to detect 70.6% of the erroneous programs generated by GPT-4o, with a false positive rate of 6.1%.

schema.problem: Code LLMs routinely emit APIs that cannot resolve in the target project—non-existent packages, attributes absent from the pinned dependency version, and signatures from the wrong library version—and existing remedies (retrieved documentation, statically mined project structure, post-generation repair) do not restrict the generator's vocabulary against the API surface actually resolvable in the repository's declared dependency environment.
schema.motivation: Decode-time grounding against the exact API surface could avoid a large class of dependency- and version-induced code errors before generation, rather than relying on retrieval or repair, and matters especially where documentation-derived retrieval systematically misleads on version-mismatched symbols.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework builds an exact API-surface manifest for a repository by introspecting the pinned dependency set: resolving lock files into an ephemeral environment, then enumerating modules, attributes, and signatures. It constrains decoding so that API-identifier positions—imports, dotted heads, member accesses—are restricted to symbols in the manifest, with version-qualified variants. It also scores every generation with a verifiability protocol consisting of import resolution, compilation, and execution against the pinned environment plus repository test-suite pass rates.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the core claims comes from multi-file, repository-level generation tasks across Python and JavaScript ecosystems. Generated code is produced with vanilla prompting, RAG-style grounding, static-dependency constrained decoding, compiler-feedback repair, and the proposed framework. Hallucination-free rates are decomposed into package/module/attribute/version categories, with pass rates against pinned-environment compile and tests and latency overhead. The primary removal and low-overhead claim is assessed through hallucination-free and pass-rate comparisons across conditions; the version-mismatch superiority claim is assessed through the version-category decomposition. No explicit numerical failure thresholds are stated in the abstract.

items.title: Environment-Grounded Decode-Time API-Surface Constraint for Hallucination-Free Code Generation
items.abstract: Code LLMs routinely emit APIs that cannot resolve in the target project: non-existent packages, attributes absent from the pinned dependency version, and signatures from the wrong library version. Existing remedies either inject retrieved documentation into the prompt, restrict decoding with statically mined project structure, or repair code after generation; none restricts the generator's vocabulary against the API surface that is actually resolvable in the repository's declared dependency environment. We propose EnvGround, a decode-time grounding framework that (1) builds an exact API-surface manifest for a repository by introspecting the dependency set it pins—lock-file resolution into an ephemeral environment, then module/attribute/signature enumeration; (2) constrains decoding so that API-identifier positions (imports, dotted heads, member accesses) are restricted to symbols in that manifest, with version-qualified variants; and (3) scores every generation with a verifiability protocol: import resolution, compilation, and execution against the pinned environment plus repository test-suite pass rates. The falsifiable core claim is that environment-grounded decoding removes the large majority of API-availability hallucination at small latency cost, and outperforms equivalent-context retrieval-augmented grounding and static-dependency constrained decoding—specifically on version-mismatched symbols where documentation-derived retrieval systematically misleads the model. We will evaluate on multi-file, repository-level generation tasks across Python and JavaScript ecosystems, against vanilla prompting, RAG-style grounding, static-dependency constrained decoding, and compiler-feedback repair, measuring hallucination-free rates decomposed into package/module/attribute/version categories, pass rates against pinned-environment compile and tests, and overhead.

schema.problem: Even under grammar-constrained decoding, models generating code for low-resource programming surfaces such as domain-specific languages, custom library APIs, and command-line tools can still produce references invalid in the current environment, including undeclared buffers, absent schema columns, functions the library does not provide, and unsupported CLI options.
schema.motivation: As large language models increasingly generate code inside agents and serving systems that compile, execute, or dispatch it without line-by-line review, semantic invalidity on such low-resource surfaces has direct operational cost and needs to be prevented rather than only syntactically constrained.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach instantiates grammar fragments during generation from a runtime environment. A region-specific policy selects a fragment for each hole, and a tightening operator replaces open reference positions with environment-typed slots whose candidates are exactly the names, fields, APIs, or options available at that point. Newly generated declarations enter the environment before later regions are decoded, so the constraining grammar can depend on the prefix already generated. The formal setting treats grammar fragments as environment-indexed grammars ordered by refinement; the implementation uses offline grammar induction and online policy resolution.
schema.research_plan: The semantic-correctness claim is supported by formal proofs: a soundness guarantee for environment-typed fragments, preservation of that guarantee under refinement, and characterization of the boundary of token-mask-enforceable properties. The practical claim is evaluated by an implementation with offline grammar induction and online policy resolution, tested across TileLang, SQL, and P4 with models from 0.6B to 236B parameters, comparing against standard constrained decoding on invalid-reference rate and decoding overhead.

items.title: Decode-Time Grammars: Constrained LLM Generation over a Refinement Order of Grammar Fragments
items.abstract: Large language models now write a growing share of the world's code, increasingly inside agents and serving systems that compile, execute, or dispatch generated code without line-by-line review. This works well for mainstream languages but remains brittle for low-resource programming surfaces such as domain-specific languages, custom library APIs, and command-line tools. Even under grammar-constrained decoding, a model can still produce references invalid in the current environment: a buffer never declared, a column absent from the schema, a function the library does not provide, or an unsupported CLI option. This paper introduces decode-time grammars: grammar fragments instantiated during generation from a runtime environment Gamma. A region-specific policy selects a fragment for each hole, and a tightening operator replaces open reference positions with Gamma-typed slots whose candidates are exactly the names, fields, APIs, or options available at that point. Newly generated declarations enter Gamma before later regions are decoded, so the constraining grammar can depend on the prefix already generated. This ensures not only grammatical correctness but also semantic correctness, by preventing references to undefined symbols. We formalize grammar fragments as environment-indexed grammars ordered by refinement, prove No-Ghost soundness for Gamma-slotted fragments, show that refinement preserves this support-set guarantee, and characterize the boundary of mask-enforceable properties. We implement the approach in gproj with offline grammar induction and online policy resolution. Across TileLang, SQL, and P4, with models from 0.6B to 236B parameters, gproj eliminates ghost references by construction at moderate overhead over standard constrained decoding.

schema.problem: Code LLMs do not reliably handle ambiguous specifications.
schema.motivation: Improving handling of ambiguous requirements would make generated code more accurate and reliable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system integrates code LLMs with component-based synthesis and uses a feedback loop to clarify ambiguous requirements before code generation, aiming to improve accuracy and reliability.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is evaluation on multiple benchmarks, including HumanEvalComm, SpecEval, and VERINA, against existing baselines; support for claim (1) is outperforming those baselines on accuracy and reliability, while failure is not outperforming; no ablation, matched-compute, metric, or robustness protocol is described.

items.title: Enhancing Code LLMs for Ambiguous Specifications via Feedback Loop
items.abstract: This proposal presents a novel approach to enhancing code Large Language Models (LLMs) for handling ambiguous specifications via a feedback loop. The proposed system integrates LLMs with component-based synthesis and employs a feedback loop to clarify ambiguous requirements, improving code generation accuracy and reliability. We evaluate our approach on multiple benchmarks, including HumanEvalComm, SpecEval, and VERINA, and demonstrate its effectiveness in outperforming existing benchmarks and baselines.

schema.problem: Natural-language requirements for program synthesis are often incomplete or ambiguous, yet large language models are commonly expected to generate code in a single pass; existing clarification-based methods use fixed clarify-on-disagreement policies that can overuse clarification and overtrust weak behavioral agreement.
schema.motivation: Selective clarification can avoid unnecessary token costs and reallocate computation to harder cases while preserving accuracy, making clarification feasible even when ambiguity is observed only indirectly through candidate behavior.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework augments a ClarifyGPT-style pipeline with execution-driven confidence estimation, semantic difference analysis, and bounded candidate expansion. At inference time it treats clarification as a control decision and chooses among direct generation, additional evidence gathering, and clarification. Clarification is triggered selectively based on execution evidence and semantic disagreement rather than a fixed clarify-on-disagreement policy.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation compares the framework with single-pass baselines and fixed-policy clarification on MBPP, HumanEval, and extended-test variants using GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-5.4 mini. Claim (1) about improved pass@1 accuracy is tested against single-pass baselines; claim (2) about preserving accuracy, reducing token usage, and reallocating computation is tested against fixed-policy clarification using accuracy, token usage, and computation allocation measures. Claim (3) is supported by the same evaluation through accuracy and token-usage comparisons across models and the framework's selective triggering from execution evidence and semantic disagreement.

items.title: Toward Reliable LLM Code Generation: Adaptive Routing Framework for Ambiguous Requirements
items.abstract: Natural-language requirements for program synthesis are often incomplete or ambiguous, yet large language models are commonly expected to generate code in a single pass. Prior clarification-based methods address this issue by asking follow-up questions when sampled candidate programs disagree, but fixed clarify-on-disagreement policies can overuse clarification and can also overtrust weak behavioral agreement. We present an adaptive routing framework for LLM-based program synthesis that treats clarification as an inference-time control decision. The framework augments a ClarifyGPT-style pipeline with execution-driven confidence estimation, semanticdifference analysis, and bounded candidate expansion, allowing the system to choose among direct generation, additional evidence gathering, and clarification. We evaluate the framework on MBPP, HumanEval, and extended-test variants using GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-5.4 mini. Adaptive routing improves pass@1 accuracy by up to 7.60 percentage points over single-pass baselines. Compared with fixed-policy clarification, it preserves accuracy while reducing token usage by up to 57.2% for GPT-4.1 mini, and reallocates computation toward harder cases for Claude Haiku 4.5. These results suggest that clarification is most useful when triggered selectively based on execution evidence and semantic disagreement, even when ambiguity is observed indirectly through candidate behavior rather than through explicitly annotated ambiguous requirements.

schema.problem: Ambiguous or incomplete natural language descriptions pose a challenge for domain-specific code generation, making generated code less robust and accurate.
schema.motivation: Improving robustness and accuracy in code generation from natural language is valuable for real-world domain-specific programming tasks; large language models and domain-specific knowledge now make this tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach leverages large language models and integrates domain-specific knowledge. It disambiguates natural language descriptions through a combination of retrieval-augmented generation, contrastive learning, and specialized prompt engineering, then generates domain-specific code.
schema.research_plan: The approach will be evaluated against state-of-the-art methods using comprehensive benchmarks. Its applications and limitations will be investigated in real-world domain-specific programming tasks. No explicit failure condition or matched-budget criteria are stated.

items.title: Domain-Specific Code Generation with Enhanced Robustness to Ambiguous Natural Language Descriptions
items.abstract: This proposal seeks to address the challenge of handling ambiguous or incomplete natural language descriptions in domain-specific code generation. We aim to develop a novel approach that leverages large language models (LLMs) and integrates domain-specific knowledge to improve the robustness and accuracy of code generation. Our method will focus on disambiguating natural language descriptions through a combination of retrieval-augmented generation, contrastive learning, and specialized prompt engineering. We will evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods using comprehensive benchmarks and investigate its applications and limitations in real-world domain-specific programming tasks.

schema.problem: Current code generation models implicitly assume task descriptions are sufficiently detailed and well-formed, but in practice users provide defective descriptions that can strongly affect code correctness.
schema.motivation: Automatically detecting such defects before generation could reduce correctness failures and make LLM-based code generation more reliable in real-world settings.
schema.proposed_approach: The authors build a lightweight classifier by parameter-efficiently finetuning a small model to detect defects in task descriptions. The classifier targets three defect types: lexical vagueness, under-specification, and syntax-formatting. It is evaluated on three benchmarks with task descriptions of varying structure and complexity.
schema.research_plan: (1) The detection claim is tested by measuring F1 and MCC for the proposed classifier across the three defect types and three benchmarks and comparing them with two general-purpose LLM baselines; high scores support detection, and low scores would fail it. (2) The generalization claim is tested on unseen issues and on unknown under-specification defects in the original descriptions of the benchmarks. (3) The robustness claims are tested by analyzing LLM performance across defect types and benchmarks, including LiveCodeBench, to see whether robustness tracks defect type and contextual grounding rather than model capacity.

items.title: Defective Task Descriptions in LLM-Based Code Generation: Detection and Analysis
items.abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, yet they rely on an implicit assumption that the task descriptions are sufficiently detailed and well-formed. However, in practice, users may provide defective descriptions, which can have a strong effect on code correctness. To address this issue, we develop SpecValidator, a lightweight classifier based on a small model that has been parameter-efficiently finetuned, to automatically detect task description defects. We evaluate SpecValidator on three types of defects, Lexical Vagueness, Under-Specification and Syntax-Formatting on 3 benchmarks with task descriptions of varying structure and complexity. Our results show that SpecValidator achieves defect detection of F1 = 0.804 and MCC = 0.745, significantly outperforming GPT-5-mini (F1 = 0.469 and MCC = 0.281) and Claude Sonnet 4 (F1 = 0.518 and MCC = 0.359). Perhaps more importantly, our analysis indicates that SpecValidator can generalize to unseen issues and detect unknown Under-Specification defects in the original (real) descriptions of the benchmarks used. Our results also show that the robustness of LLMs in task description defects depends primarily on the type of defect and the characteristics of the task description, rather than the capacity of the model, with Under-Specification defects being the most severe. We further found that benchmarks with richer contextual grounding, such as LiveCodeBench, exhibit substantially greater resilience, highlighting the importance of structured task descriptions for reliable LLM-based code generation.

schema.problem: Execution-based code-generation benchmarks judge LLM-generated code by hidden unit tests, but the validity of those tests with respect to the natural-language specification is rarely audited; test suites can be under-constrained, accepting programs that violate the specification, or over-constrained, rejecting programs that satisfy it because a test encodes implementation-specific behavior.
schema.motivation: Making oracle validity an auditable property rather than an assumption prevents benchmark scores and model rankings from being misleading due to invalid hidden tests.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed audit converts each task's natural-language description into a checklist of behavioral constraints, then generates two LLM-based mutant pools: spec-consistent mutants, which are plausible alternative correct programs, and spec-violating mutants that target named specification behaviors. Hidden tests are run against both pools; over-constrained tests are flagged with witnessing mutants, and under-constrained specification behaviors are measured. From this audit a validity-adjusted scoring protocol is derived that removes over-constrained tests and reports results alongside raw and EvalPlus pass@k.
schema.research_plan: (1) Over-constrained tests are flagged by running hidden tests against spec-consistent and spec-violating mutant pools; support is found if such flags occur at material rates across the audited benchmarks. (2) The proposed validity-adjusted scoring protocol is compared with raw and EvalPlus pass@k on correlation with human-judged correctness; support requires higher correlation. (3) Pairwise model rankings under the proposed protocol and baseline metrics are compared on standard benchmarks; support requires at least one ranking change.

items.title: SpecCheck: Auditing Benchmark Test Oracles for Over- and Under-Constrained Tests in Code Generation Evaluation
items.abstract: Execution-based code-generation benchmarks judge LLM-generated code by hidden unit tests, but the validity of those tests with respect to the natural-language specification is rarely audited. A test suite can be under-constrained, accepting programs that violate the specification, or over-constrained, rejecting programs that satisfy it because a test encodes implementation-specific behavior. We propose SpecCheck, a white-box audit that converts each task's natural-language description into a checklist of behavioral constraints and generates two LLM-based mutant pools: spec-consistent mutants that are plausible alternative correct programs, and spec-violating mutants that target named specification behaviors. By running hidden tests against these pools, SpecCheck flags over-constrained tests with witnessing mutants and measures under-constrained specification behaviors. From the audit we derive pass@k^v, a validity-adjusted scoring protocol that removes over-constrained tests and reports results alongside raw and EvalPlus pass@k. Our falsifiable claim is that over-constrained hidden tests occur at material rates, that pass@k^v correlates better with human-judged correctness than raw or EvalPlus pass@k, and that at least one pairwise model ranking on standard benchmarks shifts under pass@k^v. This work turns oracle validity from an assumption into an auditable property of code-generation benchmarks.

schema.problem: Test-based code generation benchmarks often rely on references and tests whose reliability is not audited, and test-based correctness captures only part of the observable properties of generated code, so the validity of current LLM code evaluation is uncertain.
schema.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for code generation, trustworthy and reproducible evaluation is needed to compare models and guide AI-augmented software development.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark comprises 185 Python tasks across ten software-engineering categories. Its construction combines audited ground-truth references, public tests for generation and repair, hidden tests for grading, mutation-based validation of the test suites, and selected code-property measures. The evaluation covers seven proprietary LLMs under standard and security-focused prompts and includes regrading fixed model outputs after ground-truth auditing to assess label changes.
schema.research_plan: The benchmark's references are audited and fixed model outputs are regraded to test whether ground-truth errors change correctness labels and model separation; mutation testing validates the complete and hidden test suites. Model correctness is compared across seven proprietary LLMs under standard prompts, with pairwise comparisons among models, and code properties are compared on the tasks solved by all model-prompt configurations to test whether any model dominates across all properties. A security-focused prompt is compared with the standard prompt on correctness, selected static-analysis findings, program length, and cyclomatic complexity to test whether the prompt changes correctness or code properties. These analyses bear on the claims that reliable evaluation requires audited ground truth and protected tests and that observable code properties require multiple measures.

items.title: CodeAssay: A Multi-Metric Benchmark with Audited Ground Truth for LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly evaluated for code generation using test-based benchmarks. The validity of such evaluations depends on the reliability of their references and tests, while test-based correctness captures only part of the observable properties of generated code. We present CodeAssay, a taxonomy-first benchmark of 185 Python tasks across ten software-engineering categories. It combines audited ground truth, public tests for generation and repair, hidden tests for grading, mutation-based test-suite validation, and selected code-property measures. Regrading fixed model outputs after the audit changed 170 of 1,890 correctness labels (9.0%) and increased the measured best-to-worst model spread from 11.9 to 23.7 percentage points, although aggregate correctness remained nearly unchanged. The complete and hidden test suites achieved mutation scores of 82.6% and 74.8%, respectively. Across seven proprietary LLMs, standard-prompt correctness ranged from 77.3% to 98.9%, with significant differences in 12 of 21 model pairs. On the 120 tasks solved by all 14 model-prompt configurations, no model performed best across all selected code properties. A security-focused prompt produced no significant change in correctness or consistent reduction in the selected static-analysis findings, while increasing program length and cyclomatic complexity across all models. These findings show that reliable evaluation of LLM-generated code requires validated ground truth, protected tests, and multiple explicitly interpreted measures. CodeAssay provides a reproducible basis for evidence-based model evaluation in AI-augmented software development.

schema.problem: Large language models generate code from natural-language specifications, but on long, multi-requirement specifications they often silently omit requirements that the available tests do not exercise.
schema.motivation: Detecting test-uncovered omissions requires evaluating whether generated code covers the specification even when tests do not exercise it; the authors argue that natural-language programming specifications contain a learnable shared latent structure that can make such guidance and coverage evaluation tractable.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework learns a class-based topic model over a corpus of natural-language programming requirements, then decomposes a target specification into evidence-linked requirement facets. Generation is grounded in these facets using checklist prompting or a per-facet generate-then-compose procedure. The proposed requirement-coverage metric projects natural-language artifacts of generated code into the same learned facet space and measures whether the code covers the specification's facets, adapting topic-coverage machinery from topic-model evaluation. The work also constructs a benchmark for diagnosing which requirement facets LLMs drop.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from multi-requirement code-generation and text-to-SQL benchmarks. (1) Facet-grounded generation is compared with monolithic prompting and LLM-ad-hoc decomposition on pass@1; support requires higher pass@1, and failure would show no improvement or worse. (2) The proposed coverage metric is evaluated by correlation with human requirement-satisfaction judgments, compared with LLM-as-judge and pass@k for detecting test-uncovered requirements; support requires correlation at least as high as LLM-as-judge and better than pass@k, and failure would show weaker alignment or detection. (3) The contribution of the learned shared facet space is isolated by contrasting it with ad-hoc decomposition; support requires the learned space to account for gains, and failure would show ad-hoc decomposition performs comparably.

items.title: TopicLens: Learning Latent Requirement Facets for Grounded NL2Code Generation and Explainable Spec-Coverage Evaluation
items.abstract: Large language models generate code from natural-language specifications, but on long, multi-requirement specifications they often silently omit requirements that the available tests do not exercise. We argue that natural-language programming specifications contain a learnable shared latent structure that can be used both to guide generation and to evaluate whether generated code covers the specification. We propose TopicLens, a framework that learns a class-based topic model over a corpus of NL programming requirements, decomposes a target specification into evidence-linked requirement facets, and performs facet-grounded generation through checklist prompting or per-facet generate-then-compose. We also introduce FacetCover, an executable-agnostic requirement-coverage metric that projects natural-language artifacts of generated code into the same learned facet space and measures whether the code covers the specification's facets, adapting topic-coverage machinery from topic-model evaluation. Across multi-requirement code-generation and text-to-SQL benchmarks, we test three falsifiable hypotheses: facet-grounded generation improves pass@1 over monolithic prompting and LLM-ad-hoc decomposition; FacetCover correlates with human requirement-satisfaction judgments at least as well as LLM-as-judge and better than pass@k at detecting test-uncovered requirements; and the learned shared facet space, rather than ad-hoc decomposition, is responsible for the gains. The expected contribution is a learned requirement-facet space, a grounded generation protocol, an explainable spec-coverage metric, and a benchmark for diagnosing which requirement facets LLMs drop.

schema.problem: LLMs translating natural language into code degrade on large-scale, multi-modal requirement documents containing hundreds of scenarios, producing incorrect implementations or missing critical constraints.
schema.motivation: Accurately compiling DSL-based requirement documents would allow runnable systems to be generated from rich specifications without manual correction, including by users with limited programming experience.
schema.proposed_approach: Given DSL-based requirement documents, the framework compiles them into runnable software systems and automatically generates modular software architecture, comprehensive test suites, and traceability across requirements, design, and code. It uses a bidirectional test-driven agentic workflow that combines a top-down architecture design phase with a bottom-up implementation phase, using synthesized tests to check that generated code satisfies the requirements.
schema.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on six runnable web system benchmarks and the AppForge benchmark of 101 mobile app generation tasks, across three independent trials, against state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines, using GUI tests passed, compilation success rate, and test pass rate as metrics. A user study with 21 participants examines whether users with limited programming experience can write DSL-based requirement documents to generate maintainable runnable systems, including a real-world ticket-booking application of approximately 10K lines of code.

items.title: Compiling Large Multi-Modal Requirement Documents into Runnable Software Systems: From an Agentic Test-Driven Perspective
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved programming efficiency by translating natural language into code, yet their performance deteriorates when handling large-scale, multi-modal requirement documents containing hundreds of scenarios, often producing incorrect implementations or missing critical constraints. To address this challenge, we propose ARC (Agentic Requirement Compilation), a framework that compiles DSL-based requirement documents into runnable software systems while automatically generating modular software architecture, comprehensive test suites, and traceability across requirements, design, and code. ARC adopts a bidirectional test-driven agentic workflow, combining a top-down architecture design phase with a bottom-up implementation phase to ensure that generated code satisfies synthesized tests. We evaluate ARC on six runnable web system benchmarks and the AppForge benchmark of 101 mobile app generation tasks. Across three independent trials, ARC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines, achieving 50.6% more GUI tests passed on average for web systems, a 100% compilation success rate, and a 68.3% test pass rate on AppForge. A user study with 21 participants further shows that users with limited programming experience can write DSL-based requirement documents containing up to 174 scenarios within an average of 5.6 hours to generate maintainable runnable systems, including a real-world ticket-booking application of approximately 10K lines of code.

schema.problem: We lack a mechanistic understanding of how code idioms spread through developer communities and become culturally established.
schema.motivation: Understanding idiom dynamics would improve code generation systems by predicting which generated patterns developers will adopt, identify social barriers to idiom uptake, and inform better design of refactoring tools and LLM-based code assistants.
schema.proposed_approach: The study reconstructs idiom adoption trajectories in 500+ open-source communities using repository histories from 2020–2025. It measures diffusion rates and identifies early adopters with survival analysis, then tests mechanistic models linking network position, cognitive biases, and learning barriers to adoption likelihood. Findings are validated through developer interviews.
schema.research_plan: (1) Repository histories from 500+ open-source communities (2020–2025) are used to reconstruct idiom adoption trajectories; (2) survival analysis measures diffusion rates and identifies early adopters; (3) mechanistic models test links between network position, cognitive biases, learning barriers, and adoption likelihood; (4) developer interviews validate the findings. All four components bear on the hypothesis that adoption follows predictable patterns shaped by those factors.

items.title: Idiom Adoption Dynamics: Modeling Code Culture Evolution Through Developer Communities
items.abstract: Code idioms—language-specific patterns and conventions—are core to software quality and maintainability, yet we lack a mechanistic understanding of how idioms spread through developer communities and become culturally established. This proposal models code idiom adoption as a cultural transmission phenomenon, drawing parallels to linguistic evolution. We hypothesize that idiom adoption follows predictable patterns shaped by network structure, cognitive biases, and transmission bottlenecks (peer review, social platforms). Our empirical approach will: (1) reconstruct idiom adoption trajectories in 500+ open-source communities using repository histories (2020–2025); (2) measure diffusion rates and identify early adopters using survival analysis; (3) test mechanistic models linking network position, cognitive biases, and learning barriers to adoption likelihood; and (4) validate findings through developer interviews. Understanding idiom dynamics will improve code generation systems by predicting which generated patterns developers will adopt and identifying social barriers to idiom uptake, thereby informing better design of refactoring tools and LLM-based code assistants.

schema.problem: Code generation evaluation focuses on functional correctness and systematically underemphasizes robustness—whether generated code validates inputs, handles errors, and tolerates edge cases.
schema.motivation: Code that passes functional tests can still fail in real-world use due to missing input validation and error handling, and state-of-the-art models show a gap between implicit awareness of needed defensive constructs and actually emitting them, making robustness a pressing reliability concern.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework iteratively generates code and combines a defensiveness validator that detects missing input validation and error handling via static analysis and LLM critique with targeted feedback asking the model to add defensive constructs. It evaluates code using a dual-metric protocol that measures both functional correctness and defensiveness, and is assessed on HumanEval+, MBPP+, and a new robustness-focused benchmark.
schema.research_plan: The approach is evaluated on HumanEval+, MBPP+, and a new robustness-focused benchmark; the evidence consists of changes in defensiveness and functional correctness, plus comparisons against single-turn prompting and decoding-time logit adjustment to isolate the benefit of iterative defensiveness feedback. A claim is supported if defensiveness improves while correctness is maintained and if the multi-turn refinement condition outperforms the alternatives.

items.title: Bridging Robustness and Correctness: Iterative Code Generation with Defensiveness-Aware Validation
items.abstract: Current code generation evaluation focuses on functional correctness (pass/fail on test cases) but systematically underemphasizes robustness—whether generated code validates inputs, handles errors, and tolerates edge cases. We find that 35.2% of code from state-of-the-art LLMs lacks defensive programming constructs despite implicit awareness (if-tokens rank top-3 in 63% of cases where conditionals are needed but absent). We propose DefenseIter, an iterative code generation framework that combines (1) a defensiveness validator that detects missing input validation and error handling via static analysis and LLM critique, (2) targeted feedback asking the model to add defensive constructs, and (3) a dual-metric evaluation protocol (correctness + defensiveness) that reveals real-world reliability gaps. Evaluated on HumanEval+, MBPP+, and a new robustness-focused benchmark, DefenseIter improves defensiveness by 18–22% while maintaining functional correctness, and demonstrates that multi-turn refinement with defensiveness signals is more effective than single-turn prompting or decoding-time logit adjustment alone.

schema.problem: In repository-level code generation and autonomous software engineering, multi-agent frameworks and tree search agents suffer from context staleness and structural drift across long-horizon, multi-step edits; without real-time synchronization between runtime execution feedback and code graph topology, agents repeatedly query outdated code chunks, miss newly introduced dependencies, and fail to track the cascading impact of intermediate patches.
schema.motivation: Making retrieval-augmented code generation and multi-agent reasoning operate over a provably consistent, freshly aligned structural memory during agentic development could reduce patch failures and structural localization errors.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework couples multi-agent software engineering workflows with an incrementally updated, execution-validated dependency graph. It intercepts compiler/test feedback and parses intermediate AST diffs during agentic development cycles to dynamically mutate graph edges and node representations. Retrieval-augmented code generation and multi-agent reasoning engines then operate over this structural memory.
schema.research_plan: The proposed framework will be evaluated on repository-level benchmarks, including SWEBench and NL2Repo-Bench, against static and purely heuristic graph retrieval baselines, using patch failure rates and structural localization errors as the measured evidence for the comparative claim.

items.title: Execution-Guided Dynamic Code Graphs for Repository-Level Multi-Agent Software Engineering
items.abstract: Repository-level code generation and autonomous software engineering agents must navigate massive codebases with complex, interdependent files. While recent multi-agent frameworks and tree search agents have advanced task execution, they suffer from context staleness and structural drift as agents perform multi-step edits across long horizons. Without real-time synchronization between runtime execution feedback and code graph topology, agents repeatedly query outdated code chunks, miss newly introduced dependencies, and fail to track the cascading impact of their intermediate patches. We propose EG-DCG (Execution-Guided Dynamic Code Graph), a framework that couples multi-agent software engineering workflows with an incrementally updated, execution-validated dependency graph. By intercepting compiler/test feedback and parsing intermediate abstract syntax tree (AST) diffs during agentic development cycles, EG-DCG dynamically mutates graph edges and node representations. This ensures that retrieval-augmented code generation and multi-agent reasoning engines operate over a provably consistent, freshly aligned structural memory. Experiments on repository-level benchmarks such as SWEBench and NL2Repo-Bench will demonstrate that execution-guided graph adaptation significantly reduces patch failure rates and structural localization errors compared to static or purely heuristic graph retrieval baselines.

schema.problem: Large language models for code generation remain bottlenecked by specification ambiguities and brittle handling of edge cases; existing agentic code generation and test-driven development frameworks rely on static test suites or fixed initial metamorphic relations that fail to evolve when iterative code repairs expose unforeseen logical flaws.
schema.motivation: Practical deployment of code generation demands more robust handling of edge cases and specifications, and dynamic test evolution during debugging could improve semantic robustness, functional correctness, and code coverage.
schema.proposed_approach: An agentic framework dynamically co-evolves metamorphic test relations and concrete test inputs within a multi-turn code generation and refinement loop. It continuously synthesizes, mutates, and verifies metamorphic relations based on runtime execution anomalies and coverage gaps during the agentic debugging cycle.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on HumanEval-Pro and MBPP-Pro compares the proposed framework against standard static feedback loops and baseline agentic systems, measuring semantic robustness, functional correctness, and code coverage. No explicit failure condition or matched-resource control is stated.

items.title: MetaCoAgent: Metamorphic Test-Driven Agentic Code Generation with Dynamic Test Evolution
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed code generation, yet their practical deployment is persistently bottlenecked by specification ambiguities and brittle handling of edge cases. While recent agentic code generation and test-driven development (TDD) frameworks incorporate execution feedback or upfront metamorphic specification mutation to guide synthesis, they rely on static test suites or fixed initial metamorphic relations that fail to evolve when iterative code repairs expose unforeseen logical flaws. To bridge this gap, we propose MetaCoAgent, an agentic framework that dynamically co-evolves metamorphic test relations and concrete test inputs within a multi-turn code generation and refinement loop. Unlike existing methods that treat metamorphic testing solely as a pre-processing specification modifier or a post-hoc validation oracle, MetaCoAgent continuously synthesizes, mutates, and verifies metamorphic relations based on runtime execution anomalies and coverage gaps during the agentic debugging cycle. We evaluate our approach on complex benchmarks like HumanEval-Pro and MBPP-Pro, demonstrating that adaptive metamorphic test evolution significantly enhances semantic robustness, functional correctness, and code coverage over standard static feedback loops and baseline agentic systems.

schema.problem: In LLM-based code self-repair, the tests that drive the repair loop are usually the same tests used to grade the outcome, and per-round gains are read as correctness gains even though repairing against weak test oracles can produce plausible-but-wrong patches; it is not known whether iterative self-repair improves genuine specification conformance or only its visible feedback scores.
schema.motivation: If visible-test repair gains do not reflect correctness, the code community's standard reading of iterative self-repair results is unjustified; determining this would show whether repair actually improves correctness or merely inflates a reward proxy.
schema.proposed_approach: A measurement framework re-scores every repair round against two oracles: the visible feedback tests the model sees, and an independent EvalPlus-style mutation-and-model-amplified hidden oracle the model never sees. It also includes a cheap regression-veto mitigation that accepts a candidate only if it also passes an independent anchor-test subset, and measures how many legitimate repairs the mitigation discards.
schema.research_plan: (1) For C1, re-score every repair round against both visible feedback tests and the independent hidden oracle to test whether the visible-hidden gap widens across rounds. (2) For C2, compare same-model code-and-test generation against independent cross-model test generation to measure shared-misconception coupling. (3) For C3, re-audit published one-shot generation gains under amplified tests using strengthened per-round scoring, and assess whether iterative self-repair gains survive. The regression-veto mitigation is evaluated by measuring how many legitimate repairs it discards.

items.title: RepairDrift: Do Self-Repair Loops Make Code Better, or Merely Better-Tested? Per-Round Dual-Oracle Measurement of Overfitting in LLM Self-Debugging
items.abstract: Iterative self-repair — generate code, execute visible tests, feed failures back, regenerate — is now a standard component of LLM-based code generation, and benchmarks report that a few repair rounds raise pass rates substantially. Yet in nearly all such evaluations, the tests that drive the loop are the same tests used to grade the outcome, and every round is scored only against that fixed oracle. The classical program-repair literature established that repairing against weak test oracles yields plausible-but-wrong patches , and the adjacent non-code literature has shown that iterative self-refinement where a model both generates and evaluates can exhibit reward hacking ; no retrieved work transfers either lesson to code self-repair at the per-round level. We propose RepairDrift, a measurement framework that re-scores every repair round against two oracles: the visible feedback tests the model sees, and an independent EvalPlus-style mutation-and-model-amplified hidden oracle the model never sees . Our falsifiable claims are (C1) the visible–hidden gap widens across repair rounds — repair improves the reward proxy faster than genuine specification conformance; (C2) this "repair drift" is largest when the same model generates both the code and the feedback tests (shared-misconception coupling) and shrinks with independent cross-model test generation; and (C3) re-auditing published one-shot generation gains under amplified tests , at least some reported iterative self-repair gains do not survive strengthened per-round scoring. We also propose SpecAnchor, a cheap regression-veto mitigation that accepts a candidate only if it also passes an independent anchor-test subset, and we measure how many legitimate repairs it discards. Either outcome — drift confirmed or refuted — is consequential: the code community currently reads visible-test repair gains as correctness gains, and the framework tells us whether that reading is justified.

schema.problem: Current evaluations of LLM self-repair measure only the net outcome of the loop—final pass rate over visible tests, sometimes re-checked against held-out tests—so they cannot distinguish a repair that fixes a problem from one that trades one correct behavior for another.
schema.motivation: LLM self-repair is increasingly promoted as a way to turn flawed generations into correct solutions; detecting behavioral regressions is needed to avoid overestimating repair quality and to determine how far classic automated program repair overfitting findings transfer to LLM self-debugging.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach conducts a per-test behavioral study: it defines metrics that compare each repaired program's behavior against its own pre-repair version over a complete behavioral oracle, capturing regressed behaviors, regression frequency, and repairs that pass visible tests while regressing held-out behaviors. A benchmark protocol is built from standard code-generation benchmark problems by splitting full test suites into visible and held-out sets. The work also proposes a repair protocol that, for each candidate repair, gates acceptance on differential preservation checks over input neighborhoods where the pre-repair version's behavior is considered safe.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the regression-prevalence and depth-growth claims, the study uses the benchmark protocol built from standard code-generation problems, splitting each full test suite into visible and held-out sets, and measures the defined behavioral regression metrics for self-repairs that pass visible tests; a low regression share at scale would count against the first hypothesis and limit transfer of classic automated program repair overfitting findings, while an increasing share with repair depth is sought for the second. (2) For the gating protocol, the evaluation compares candidate repairs gated on differential preservation checks over input neighborhoods where the pre-repair version's behavior is considered safe against standard self-repair at a matched test-execution budget, with held-out correctness as the metric; support is a lift in held-out correctness and failure is no lift at matched budget.

items.title: RegressLess: Quantifying and Preventing Behavioral Regressions in LLM Self-Repair of Generated Code
items.abstract: LLM self-repair — running a generated program against tests, feeding failures back to the model, and revising the code — is increasingly promoted as a way to turn flawed generations into correct solutions. Yet the evaluations we retrieved measure only the net outcome of the loop: final pass rate over the visible test suite, sometimes re-checked against held-out tests. That aggregate cannot distinguish a repair that fixes a problem from one that trades one correct behavior for another. We propose RegressLess, the first per-test, behavioral-level study that treats LLM self-repair as a potential source of regression rather than only missed fixes. We define regression-aware metrics — regression set, regression rate, and deceptive-repair counts — that trace how each repaired program's behavior changes relative to its own pre-repair version over a complete behavioral oracle, and we present RegBench, a protocol built from standard code-generation benchmark problems whose full test suites are split into visible and held-out sets. We hypothesize that a substantial share of plausible self-repairs (those passing all visible tests) regress at least one previously-correct held-out behavior, and that this share grows with repair depth. We further propose and empirically test RegGuard, a repair protocol that gates each candidate repair on differential preservation checks over safe input neighborhoods of the pre-repair version, and ask whether such gating lifts held-out correctness at matched test-execution budget. If, contrary to our hypothesis, self-repair regressions are rare at scale, that is an equally informative result that would limit how far classic APR overfitting findings transfer to LLM self-debugging.

schema.problem: Agent-based program repair systems are evaluated purely behaviorally—patches pass held-out or regression tests or match a ground-truth fix—but the agent's own stated rationale, its claimed root cause and implicated code locations, has never been graded for causal grounding.
schema.motivation: As APR agents now generate patches at scale, unchecked rationales mean successful repairs may be unexplained; grading causal grounding would reveal whether passing patches can explain the failures they fix.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed evaluation protocol takes the lines a repair rationale implicates and requires (a) that they are exercised by the original failure signal (fault coverage) and (b) that they are counterfactually necessary for the repair: reverting implicated lines reinstates the failure while reverting non-implicated lines does not. It comes with a dataset of agent-repair trajectories whose gold rationale anchors are developer-verified and delta-debugged, and a metric that scores self-reported root causes on this protocol. The work applies the grader to three state-of-the-art agents to test whether passing patches carry ungrounded or partially grounded rationales.
schema.research_plan: The central hypothesis is tested by applying the proposed grader to self-reported rationales from three state-of-the-art agents across the delivered trajectories and measuring the fraction of passing patches whose rationales are ungrounded or partially grounded. The proposed protocol's fault-coverage and counterfactual-necessity rules serve as the grading evidence, while developer-verified, delta-debugged gold rationale anchors provide reference annotations. The hypothesis is falsifiable: if it fails, the metric and benchmark are delivered as an evaluation harness regardless; if behavioral metrics already suffice, the metric is published as an analysis-only diagnostic.

items.title: GroundedPatch: Counterfactual Verification of Stated Root Causes in Agentic Program Repair
items.abstract: Agent-based program repair (APR) systems now generate patches at scale, but their evaluation remains purely behavioral — a patch passes held-out or regression tests, or matches a ground-truth fix. What has never been graded is the agent's own stated rationale: the root cause it claims and the code locations it says caused the failure. This proposal introduces GroundedPatch, the first evaluation protocol and benchmark that scores an APR agent's self-reported root cause for causal grounding using mutation-style machinery repurposed as a rationale grader: the lines the rationale implicates must (a) be exercised by the original failure signal (fault coverage) and (b) be counterfactually necessary for the repair — reverting them reinstates the failure while reverting non-implicated lines does not. We contribute RationalEval, a dataset of agent-repair trajectories with developer-verified, delta-debugged gold rationale anchors, and the Causal Rationale Score (CRS).
