We test a falsifiable hypothesis: across three state-of-the-art agents, a large fraction of passing patches will ship ungrounded or partially grounded rationales, meaning today's "successful" runs often cannot explain the failures they fix. If the hypothesis fails, we deliver the metric and benchmark as an evaluation harness regardless; if a rival claim holds that behavioral metrics already suffice, CRS is published as an analysis-only diagnostic.

schema.problem: Feedback-driven code repair with large language models is limited less by how a model uses feedback than by which feedback channel is requested next and when the loop stops, yet current pipelines fix the feedback channel upstream of the loop, leaving per-instance modality choice and stopping unaddressed.
schema.motivation: Optimizing per-instance feedback-modality choice and stop/restart decisions could reduce wasted token expenditure and improve repair efficiency, and making token cost a measured first-class dimension is necessary because current evaluation hides the cost of feedback requests.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed selector is a black-box sequential policy that, per instance, prices each available feedback modality (compiler message, failing test, model review, mixed channel, execution trace) in tokens, predicts from the running repair state that modality's marginal probability of turning the current failing state into a passing patch, and requests the modality with the maximum expected repair credit per token; it stops when no channel's predicted gain exceeds its price. A learned restart head converts global debugging-decay scheduling into a per-instance refactor/restart action, and a token-ledger protocol makes repair cost a first-class measured dimension. The controller is trained on randomized-modality exploration trajectories from a multi-channel feedback benchmark with importance-weighted corrections for exploration/deployment mismatch, and the work releases token ledgers and selection traces.
schema.research_plan: (1) The selection and stopping claims are tested by comparing the adaptive policy against the best static modality, fixed-depth mixed-feedback loops, token-frugality budgeting, agreement-based early stopping, and oracle modality selection on cost-normalized repair rate and token-to-first-success. (2) The restart head's contribution is assessed through fixed-depth loop and agreement-based stopping comparisons, which isolate stop/restart decisions. (3) A lineage-free ablation serves as a falsification control: if running repair state carries no signal beyond channel priors, the adaptive policy must collapse to a constant and the headline hypotheses should fail. (4) The benchmark harness with released token ledgers and selection traces supports cost-normalized audit; the policy would be unsupported if it does not improve cost-normalized repair rate or token-to-first-success over baselines or does not collapse under the lineage-free ablation.

items.title: AdaptFeed: A Value-of-Information Policy for Feedback Modality Selection and Budgeting in LLM Code Repair
items.abstract: Feedback-driven code repair with large language models is gated less by how a model uses feedback than by which feedback channel is requested next and when the loop stops, yet current pipelines fix the channel upstream of the loop. We propose AdaptFeed, a black-box sequential policy that treats feedback-modality choice in LLM repair as a priced value-of-information problem: a per-instance controller prices each available modality (compiler message, failing test, model review, mixed channel, execution trace) in tokens, predicts its marginal probability of turning the current failing state into a passing patch from the running repair state, requests the modality maximizing expected repair credit per token, and stops when no channel's predicted gain exceeds its price. A learned restart head converts prior work's global debugging-decay scheduling into a per-instance "refactor now" action. A token-ledger protocol makes cost a first-class, measured dimension of repair evaluation. We train the controller on randomized-modality exploration trajectories built on the multi-channel FeedbackEval benchmark, with importance-weighted corrections for the mismatch between the random exploration policy and the deployed policy, and evaluate against the best static modality, fixed-depth mixed-feedback loops, token-frugality budgeting, agreement-based early stopping, and oracle modality selection, using cost-normalized repair rate and token-to-first-success. A lineage-free ablation serves as an explicit falsification control: if repair state carries no signal beyond channel priors, the adaptive policy must collapse to a constant and the headline hypotheses should fail. Contributions: the formal framing of modality selection as a priced sequential decision problem, a generator-agnostic black-box selector with priced stop/restart, a cost-normalized benchmark harness with released token ledgers and selection traces, and the first quantitative characterization of when per-instance feedback selection pays for its modeling overhead.

schema.problem: Large language models currently have difficulty generating accurate and relevant legal content in legal document drafting.
schema.motivation: LLMs have shown significant potential in legal document drafting, so improving their accuracy and relevance could make automated legal drafting more usable.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed work fine-tunes code LLMs on legal document datasets and evaluates the fine-tuned models on existing legal drafting benchmarks and metrics. It also characterizes the challenges these models face in generating accurate and relevant legal content.
schema.research_plan: The planned evaluation uses existing benchmarks and metrics to assess performance, and the work will analyze the challenges these models face; no specific baseline or failure condition is stated.

items.title: Enhancing Code Generation Models for Legal Document Drafting through Fine-Tuning and Evaluation
items.abstract: The application of large language models (LLMs) in legal document drafting has shown significant potential, but faces challenges in generating accurate and relevant legal content. This proposal aims to investigate the fine-tuning of code LLMs on legal document datasets to improve their performance in legal document drafting. We will explore the challenges faced by these models, evaluate their performance using existing benchmarks and metrics, and develop a comprehensive understanding of the current state of code generation models in legal document drafting.

schema.problem: Repository-level code generation still faces unresolved challenges in scalability, context understanding, and efficiency despite progress in large language models and retrieval-augmented generation.
schema.motivation: Repository-level code generation is a crucial task in software development automation.
schema.proposed_approach: A framework that integrates hierarchical retrieval with static code analysis for repository-level code generation.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on repository-level code generation benchmarks MRG-Bench and FEA-Bench, comparing against state-of-the-art methods RepoCoder and CatCoder, with claims assessed on accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.

items.title: Repository-Level Code Generation with Hierarchical Retrieval and Static Code Analysis
items.abstract: Repository-level code generation is a crucial task in software development automation. Despite the progress made by large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation methods, challenges such as scalability, context understanding, and efficiency remain unresolved. This proposal introduces a novel framework that integrates hierarchical retrieval with static code analysis to address these challenges. The proposed approach aims to improve the performance of code generation models in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. We plan to evaluate our framework using benchmarks like MRG-Bench and FEA-Bench, and compare it with state-of-the-art methods such as RepoCoder and CatCoder.

schema.problem: Code LLMs are increasingly asked to generate end-to-end machine-learning pipelines from natural-language specifications over real EHR data, but existing code-generation and self-repair machinery verifies such code only through execution and tests. This certifies that a pipeline runs and reports a number, not that the number is methodologically valid; a likely bug class is leakage from future features, train/test subject overlap, or target/label dependence that inflates reported AUC and is invisible to existing repair loops because the code works.
schema.motivation: Undetected leakage can produce overoptimistic clinical prediction pipelines that pass existing execution checks, and the growing use of code LLMs on real EHR data makes this an urgent failure mode to measure and repair.
schema.proposed_approach: The work constructs a benchmark of natural-language clinical prediction task specifications over MIMIC-IV and eICU, with ground truth enforced by executable behavioral oracles. These include a probe that scrambles all records after the prediction time and requires valid predictions to be invariant, a probe that randomizes labels and requires AUC to collapse to chance, and a probe that instruments subject identity to detect any train/test subject overlap. On top of this benchmark, the work adds a repair loop that converts failures of these probes into executable-form feedback so standard self-repair machinery (self-reflection, test-driven multi-agent repair, debugger control) can be applied to a bug class for which no test can fail.
schema.research_plan: Claims are evaluated as follows. (1) For the high-baseline-leakage claim, the benchmark probes measure leakage incidence among executable pipelines produced by current code LLMs across the task specifications. (2) For the claim that execution/test-feedback-only self-repair does not reduce leakage, leakage is measured after applying existing execution/test-oriented self-repair loops and compared with the baseline incidence. (3) For the audit-feedback claim, leakage incidence and reported AUC after probe-failure feedback repair are compared with a leak-free gold reference. The abstract states the claims are falsifiable: the first fails if observed leakage is not high, the second fails if execution/test-only repair reduces leakage, and the third fails if probe-failure feedback does not substantially reduce leakage or does not recover AUC near the leak-free reference.

items.title: ClinLeak-Bench: Auditing and Repairing Methodological Leakage in LLM-Generated Clinical ML Pipelines
items.abstract: Code LLMs are increasingly asked to generate end-to-end machine-learning pipelines — not just snippets — from natural-language specifications over real EHR data. Existing code-generation and self-repair machinery verifies such code only through execution and tests, which certifies that a pipeline runs and reports a number, not that the number is methodologically valid. We hypothesize that a large fraction of executable, test-passing clinical prediction pipelines generated by strong code LLMs contain methodological leakage — features drawn from after the prediction time, subject overlap across train/test splits, or target/label dependence — that inflates reported AUC and is invisible to every existing repair loop, because the buggy code "works." We propose ClinLeak-Bench, a benchmark of natural-language clinical prediction task specifications over real EHR data (MIMIC-IV, eICU) whose ground truth is enforced by programmatic leakage audit probes: executable behavioral oracles, e.g., a future-scrambling probe (a valid pipeline's predictions must be invariant to scrambling all records after the prediction time), a label-shuffle probe (valid AUC must collapse to chance), and an instrumented subject-isolation probe (no train/test subject overlap). On top of the benchmark we propose an audit-feedback repair loop that converts probe failures into executable-form feedback so that standard self-repair machinery (self-reflection, test-driven multi-agent repair, debugger control) can be applied to a bug class for which no test can fail. The core claims are falsifiable: (H1) baseline leakage incidence among executable pipelines of current code LLMs is high (predicted ≥40%); (H2) execution/test-feedback-only self-repair does not reduce leakage; (H3) audit feedback reduces leakage incidence by at least 2× and recovers AUC within a few points of a leak-free gold reference. Contributions: the first leakage-auditable clinical code-generation benchmark, the first measurement of execution-feedback blindness to methodological bugs, and a repair method for "working-but-invalid" code.

schema.problem: Execution-based code benchmarks are known to ship underspecified test suites with high statement coverage but low branch coverage and mutation score, yet no study has asked what that underspecification means at the level of individual specification requirements, or whether code LLMs fail on the same untested requirements.
schema.motivation: Understanding the per-requirement structure of underspecification would make benchmark evaluation more faithful to the natural-language spec and enable targeted feedback to reduce shared, systematic failures across code LLMs.
schema.proposed_approach: The work decomposes natural-language problem statements into atomic specification-derived behavioral requirements (boundary, empty/degenerate input, off-by-one, error/exception, return-value, side-effect/mutation, type coercion, complexity) and synthesizes execution-validated probe tests for each requirement. It runs a cross-model evaluation measuring per-requirement satisfaction rates, per-requirement pass@k saturation, and a chance-corrected inter-model failure correlation. It also tests an intervention that re-prompts the generator with feedback from failing probe tests. The release includes a benchmark of requirements and gold-validated probes for HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, an evaluation harness, and per-model maps of failure blind spots.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation anchors four falsifiable predictions: (1) more than 30% of specification-derived requirements are unexercised by original tests; (2) inter-model requirement-failure correlation significantly exceeds an independent-error null; (3) pass@1 model rankings shift materially under requirement-weighted scoring; (4) pass@k and self-consistency do not close systematic requirement failures, while requirement-targeted re-prompting does and generic test augmentation does not as well. Supporting evidence comes from the decomposed, execution-validated probe tests, cross-model measurements of per-requirement satisfaction and pass@k saturation, and the re-prompting versus generic augmentation comparison. For the correlation claim, the independent-error null is the falsification threshold; for the intervention comparisons, pass@k/self-consistency and generic test augmentation serve as matched baselines. The abstract does not state model selection, sample budgets, or what is held matched for model comparisons.

items.title: SpecBlind: Obligation-Level Probing of Silent Specification Violations in LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: Execution-based code benchmarks are known to ship underspecified test suites (very high statement coverage but low branch coverage and mutation score), yet no study has asked what that underspecification means at the level of individual specification obligations, or whether code LLMs fail on the same untested obligations. We hypothesize that benchmark-passing LLM solutions contain "silent specification violations" — behaviors that contradict the natural-language spec but are never exercised — and, more strongly, that these failures are correlated across models, reflecting shared inductive biases rather than independent random errors. We propose a three-part program: (1) a method that decomposes NL problem statements into atomic, spec-entailed obligations (boundary, empty/degenerate input, off-by-one, error/exception, return-value, side-effect/mutation, type coercion, complexity) and synthesizes execution-validated probe tests for each; (2) a cross-model evaluation measuring obligation-satisfaction rates, per-obligation pass@k saturation, and chance-corrected inter-model failure correlation; and (3) an intervention that re-prompts the generator with obligation-targeted probe feedback. Four falsifiable predictions anchor the work: P1, a large fraction (>30%) of obligations are unexercised by the original tests; P2, inter-model obligation-failure correlation significantly exceeds an independent-error null; P3, pass@1 model rankings shift materially under obligation-weighted scoring; P4, pass@k and self-consistency do not close systematic obligation failures, while obligation-targeted re-prompting does and generic test augmentation does not as well. We will release OblibBench (obligations + gold-validated probes for HumanEval/MBPP/LiveCodeBench), an evaluation harness, and per-model blind-spot atlases.

schema.problem: It is not understood why more elaborate harnesses for LLM agents—those with more task decomposition or more guided execution—sometimes improve execution but sometimes reduce final task success.
schema.motivation: Harness engineering is an important inference-time technique for long-term LLM agent performance, so understanding when elaboration helps or hurts can guide harness design and avoid costly failure modes.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper formalizes harness design by viewing it as aligning the agent's inference-time trajectory, separating harnesses into two mechanisms: structuring tasks into sub-goals and reshaping local action distributions during execution. Using this separation, it analyzes how workflow granularity, retry budgets, and guidance-induced action reweighting determine performance limits and produce failure modes, then uses the resulting characterization to construct partial harnesses that specify only initial steps.
schema.research_plan: The paper validates its theoretical predictions through controlled synthetic experiments and real terminal agent benchmarks. The abstract does not name baselines, metrics, matched settings, or explicit failure conditions, but the design indicates that the quantified influence of granularity, retry budgets, and action reweighting is tested in controlled settings and the predicted failure modes and partial-harness advantage are tested on terminal-agent tasks.

items.title: Harnesses for Inference-Time Alignment over Execution Trajectories
items.abstract: Harness engineering has emerged as an important inference-time technique for large language model (LLM) agents, aiming to improve long-term performance through task decomposition and guided execution. However, more elaborate harnesses are not uniformly better: increasing decomposition or guidance can sometimes improve execution, but can also reduce final task success. We study harness design through the lens of inference-time trajectory alignment. This perspective separates harness into two mechanisms: task decomposition, which structures a task into sub-goals, and guided execution, which reshapes local action distributions during execution. This decomposition allows us to quantify how workflow granularity, retry budgets, and guidance-induced action reweighting shape the performance limits of harness design. It further reveals concrete failure modes, including over-decomposition, over-pruning, and hallucinated execution. We validate these predictions through controlled synthetic experiments and real terminal agent benchmarks. Inspired by the theory, we further show that effective harnesses can be partial: specifying only the initial steps and leaving the remaining execution to agent can achieve higher pass rate than fully structured workflows.

schema.problem: Large language models still struggle with generating SystemVerilog Assertions from natural language because formal verification training data are limited and formal verification operators are intrinsically complex, making correct SVA operator selection a central unsolved challenge.
schema.motivation: Formal verification remains highly labor-intensive, and recent LLM reasoning and code generation capabilities make it timely to automate NL-to-SVA translation and reduce manual assertion-writing effort.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework models SystemVerilog Assertion generation as structured, interpretable reasoning. In the training phase, it constructs an operator reasoning tree that decomposes natural-language-to-SVA alignment into fine-grained, operator-aware questions and combines reasoning paths that lead to correct assertions. In the testing phase, it performs operator-aligned retrieval to fetch relevant reasoning traces from the learned tree and generate new operator-level rules for unseen specifications. Source code and a benchmark are released.
schema.research_plan: (1) The framework is compared against a state-of-the-art baseline on syntax correctness and functional correctness for NL-to-SVA generation; support requires higher correctness on average. (2) A functional taxonomy analysis across operator categories tests whether SVA functional failures are reduced; support requires reductions across categories. (3) Generalization is tested by applying the learned operator tree to generate operator-level rules for unseen NL-to-SVA tasks.

items.title: FVRuleLearner: Operator-Level Reasoning Tree (Op-Tree)-Based Rules Learning for Formal Verification
items.abstract: The remarkable reasoning and code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have recently motivated increasing interest in automating formal verification (FV), a process that ensures hardware correctness through mathematically precise assertions but remains highly labor-intensive, particularly through the translation of natural language into SystemVerilog Assertions (NL-to-SVA). However, LLMs still struggle with SVA generation due to limited training data and the intrinsic complexity of FV operators. Consequently, a more efficient and robust methodology for ensuring correct SVA operator selection is essential for producing functionally correct assertions. To address these challenges, we introduce FVRuleLearner, an Operator-Level Rule (Op-Rule) learning framework built on a novel Operator Reasoning Tree (Op-Tree), which models SVA generation as structured, interpretable reasoning. FVRuleLearner operates in two complementary phases: (1) Training: it constructs Op-Tree that decomposes NL-to-SVA alignment into fine-grained, operator-aware questions, combining reasoning paths that lead to correct assertions; and (2) Testing: it performs operatoraligned retrieval to fetch relevant reasoning traces from the learned Op-Tree and generate new rules for unseen specifications. In the comprehensive studies, the proposed FVRuleLearner outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline by $3.95 \%$ in syntax correctness and by $31.17 \%$ in functional correctness on average. Moreover, FVRuleLearner successfully reduces an average of 70.33 % of SVA functional failures across diverse operator categories through a functional taxonomy analysis, showing the effectiveness of applying learned Op-Tree to the OpRule generations for unseen NL-to-SVA tasks. These results establish FVRuleLearner as a new paradigm for domain-specific reasoning and rule learning in formal verification. The source code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/NVlabs/FVRuleLearner.

schema.problem: There is no systematic way to evaluate the reliability of LLM-based misbehavior monitors across diverse tasks and failure modes.
schema.motivation: Monitors can fail either by missing misbehavior or by false-alarming on benign behavior, so systematic measurement of both failure modes is needed to achieve safe and useful deployment.
schema.proposed_approach: The work builds a benchmark of 3,010 carefully annotated test samples spanning question answering, code generation, and reasoning, with paired misbehavior and benign instances. Monitors are evaluated using two complementary metrics: miss rate, capturing failures to detect misbehavior, and false alarm rate, capturing oversensitivity to benign behavior. It evaluates 12 proprietary and 10 open-source LLM-based monitors. To probe training effects, it constructs a training corpus of 153,581 samples and fine-tunes Qwen3-4B-Instruction on known, relatively easy-to-construct misbehavior datasets.
schema.research_plan: The benchmark's systematic coverage is supported by its 3,010 annotated paired samples across three tasks, and its use to evaluate 12 proprietary and 10 open-source monitors with miss rate and false alarm rate supports the coverage claim (1). The variability and trade-off claim (2) is assessed by comparing the two metrics across the 22 evaluated monitors. A separate fine-tuning experiment trains Qwen3-4B-Instruction on 153,581 known misbehavior samples and evaluates it on unseen, more implicit misbehaviors to test transfer to harder monitoring cases. The abstract does not specify explicit success thresholds or matched conditions for the trade-off.

items.title: AutoMonitor-Bench: Evaluating the Reliability of LLM-Based Misbehavior Monitor
items.abstract: We introduce AutoMonitor-Bench, the first benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the reliability of LLM-based misbehavior monitors across diverse tasks and failure modes. AutoMonitor-Bench consists of 3,010 carefully annotated test samples spanning question answering, code generation, and reasoning, with paired misbehavior and benign instances. We evaluate monitors using two complementary metrics: Miss Rate (MR) and False Alarm Rate (FAR), capturing failures to detect misbehavior and oversensitivity to benign behavior, respectively. Evaluating 12 proprietary and 10 open-source LLMs, we observe substantial variability in monitoring performance and a consistent trade-off between MR and FAR, revealing an inherent safety-utility tension. To further explore the limits of monitor reliability, we construct a large-scale training corpus of 153,581 samples and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Instruction to investigate whether training on known, relatively easy-to-construct misbehavior datasets improves monitoring performance on unseen and more implicit misbehaviors. Our results highlight the challenges of reliable, scalable misbehavior monitoring and motivate future work on task-aware designing and training strategies for LLM-based monitors.

schema.problem: Existing automated patch correctness assessment methods have notable limitations: learning-based state-of-the-art methods require large, high-quality patch datasets; they typically give only binary predictions with little interpretability to support manual review; and they often fail to fully use rich contextual information within and beyond the patched program or to incorporate expert knowledge about patch correctness assessment.
schema.motivation: Large language models offer a promising way to address these limitations because they are trained on vast corpora, generalize across tasks, can learn from experience, and can provide interpretable explanations in a manner analogous to human reasoning.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed multi-agent framework formulates automated patch correctness assessment as a reasoning task. It employs a pretrained retriever and four specialized agents: one analyzes developer intent from failing tests and bug reports, one analyzes code semantics from the function-level patch, one analyzes potential degradations from the patch context, and a final agent synthesizes the candidate patch, failing tests, bug reports, intermediate reasoning reports from the other agents, retrieved similar patches, and instructive empirical tips derived from prior APCA studies to determine patch correctness. The framework is designed to be used with popular large language models.
schema.research_plan: (1) Correctness assessment claim: evaluate the proposed framework on the public CACHE-small benchmark against state-of-the-art APCA baselines using Accuracy and F1; support is outperforming those baselines. (2) Reasoning quality claim: apply a new evaluation scheme that rates generated explanations on factual consistency, logical clarity, and readability and compares them with state-of-the-art baselines. (3) Generalization claim: test the framework on a newly constructed dataset, with competitive patch-correctness performance as the support criterion.

items.title: FURINA: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Patch Correctness Assessment
items.abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) has made substantial advancements in fixing real-world defects. However, the overfitting problem, namely the phenomenon where APR-generated patches pass the given test suite but fail to correctly fix the underlying defects, remains a major challenge. To mitigate this problem, numerous Automated Patch Correctness Assessment (APCA) methods have been proposed. Among them, learning-based APCA methods currently represent the state-of-the-art (SOTA). However, these methods require training on large, high-quality patch datasets. Moreover, their lack of interpretability, as they often produce only simple binary predictions, provides little support for subsequent manual review. Finally, existing APCA methods often fail to fully leverage the rich contextual information both within and beyond the patched program, and they struggle to incorporate expert knowledge about patch correctness assessment. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising path to address these limitations. Trained on vast corpora, they demonstrate strong generalization across tasks and an ability to learn from experience, allowing them to provide interpretable explanations in a manner analogous to human reasoning. In this paper, we propose a multi-agent framework FURINA, which formulates APCA as a reasoning task. The framework employs a pre-trained retriever and four specialized agents to analyze a candidate patch from multiple perspectives: a Profiler to analyze developer intent from failing tests and bug reports; an Interpreter to analyze code semantics according to the function-level patch; a Critic to analyze potential degradations from the patch context; and a final Judge to synthesize the patches, failing tests, bug reports, intermediate reasoning reports generated by other agents, the retrieved similar patches, along with instructive empirical tips derived from prior APCA studies to determine patch correctness. Evaluation results on the public benchmark CACHE-small demonstrate that FURINA, when equipped with popular LLMs, outperforms SOTA APCA baselines, achieving improvements of at least 5.58% in \(Accuracy\) and 5.93% in \(F1\) . To further assess its reasoning quality, we design a new evaluation scheme that considers three dimensions: factual consistency, logical clarity, and readability. The results show that FURINA achieves a score of at least 4.8 out of 5, demonstrating superior reasoning quality compared with SOTA baselines. Finally, based on our constructed dataset, FURINA still achieves competitive performance, indicating strong generalization ability.

schema.problem: Most agent benchmarks rely on synthetic sandboxes, short-horizon tasks, mock-service APIs, and final-answer checks, so it remains unclear whether agents can complete realistic long-horizon work in the runtimes where they are deployed.
schema.motivation: Agents increasingly act on a user's behalf through command-line interface harnesses, making realistic native-runtime evaluation necessary to assess whether such agents can perform sustained work outside synthetic environments.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark consists of 60 human-authored, bilingual, multimodal tasks across six thematic categories; tasks average roughly 8 minutes of wall-clock time and over 20 tool calls. Each task runs inside a reproducible Docker container hosting an actual CLI agent harness—OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes Agent—with access to real tools rather than mock services. Grading is hybrid: deterministic rule-based checks, environment-state auditing of side effects, and an LLM/VLM judge for semantic verification. Tasks, code, and containerized tooling are released to support reproducible evaluation.
schema.research_plan: The benchmark-adequacy claim is supported by the construction and release protocol: 60 human-authored, bilingual, multimodal tasks across six categories, run in a reproducible Docker container with real tools. The grading-validity claim is supported by the hybrid grading design using deterministic rules, environment-state auditing, and an LLM/VLM judge, though no explicit grading-agreement failure condition is stated. The unresolved-status and harness-sensitivity claims are tested by evaluating 19 frontier models under the benchmark and comparing performance across the supported harnesses. The abstract does not state held-matched compute or an explicit success threshold.

items.title: WildClawBench: A Benchmark for Real-World, Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
items.abstract: Large language and vision-language models increasingly power agents that act on a user's behalf through command-line interface (CLI) harnesses. However, most agent benchmarks still rely on synthetic sandboxes, short-horizon tasks, mock-service APIs, and final-answer checks, leaving open whether agents can complete realistic long-horizon work in the runtimes where they are deployed. This work presents WildClawBench, a native-runtime benchmark of 60 human-authored, bilingual, multimodal tasks spanning six thematic categories. Each task averages roughly 8 minutes of wall-clock time and over 20 tool calls, and runs inside a reproducible Docker container hosting an actual CLI agent harness (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes Agent) with access to real tools rather than mock services. Grading is hybrid, combining deterministic rule-based checks, environment-state auditing of side effects, and an LLM/VLM judge for semantic verification. Across 19 frontier models, the best, Claude Opus 4.7, reaches only 62.2% overall under OpenClaw, while every other model stays below 60%, and switching harness alone shifts a single model by up to 18 points. These results show that long-horizon, native-runtime agent evaluation remains a far-from-resolved task for current frontier models. We release the tasks, code, and containerized tooling to support reproducible evaluation.

schema.problem: There is uncertainty about the characteristics of code and comments likely generated by LLMs in real repositories, how these differ between company- and community-maintained projects, and whether LLM-detected code is associated with bugs.
schema.motivation: As LLM-assisted software development becomes common, concerns about debugging burden and unnatural comments make empirical characterization of generated code and comments in real repositories timely.
schema.proposed_approach: The study analyzes code and comments likely generated by LLMs in active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025, using various tools and techniques that detect LLM-generated code and comments. It examines repository location such as test cases, code clones, grammatical correctness of comments, differences by repository maintenance type, and attribution of human-labelled bugs to detected LLM-generated code.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from automated detection across active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025. Temporal trends and code location analysis bear on the first claim; clone and grammaticality analyses bear on the second claim; repository-type comparison and human-labelled bug attribution bear on the third claim. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched controls.

items.title: An exploratory study on LLM-generated code and comments in code repositories
items.abstract: The use of LLMs in software development has become increasingly widespread on tasks such as code generation and summarization. Reports from large technology companies showed that around 20% to 30% of their code are generated by LLMs. However, there remains skepticism about the practical usage of LLM-generated code and comments, such as concerns on more time for debugging the generated code and the unnaturalness of the generated comments. In this paper, we study the code and comments that were likely to be generated by LLMs and their characteristics, the differences between company- and community-maintained repositories, and how likely bugs are introduced by LLMs. We conduct extensive experiments on active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025 using various tools and techniques that detect code and comments generated by LLMs. We observed code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs decreased over time and was primarily in test cases, while that of comments, the proportion remains relatively similar over the years. We also observed code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs have code clones within their own repository, while comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs show a low percentage of grammatically correct sentences. Furthermore, the company-maintained repositories show a higher percentage of code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs, and only a small percentage of the human-labelled bugs found in the repositories are detected as introduced by LLMs.

schema.problem: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can elicit strong multi-step reasoning but often encourages overly verbose traces, and naive length penalties in group-relative optimization can severely hurt accuracy.
schema.motivation: Decoupling efficiency optimization from correctness and adapting penalty strength to problem difficulty could reduce token use without sacrificing reasoning quality.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method decouples efficiency optimization from correctness. It computes length advantages conditionally within the correct-response cluster so that incorrect responses with zero length reward do not dilute the baseline. It dynamically scales penalty strength using the group pass rate as a proxy for problem difficulty, applying weaker penalties on hard instances and stronger on easy ones. The method is evaluated on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, and AIME25.
schema.research_plan: Experiments on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, and AIME25 evaluate efficiency-accuracy trade-off and token reduction relative to adaptive baselines. Support for the method's claim is shown by improved trade-off while maintaining or improving accuracy; a failure condition would be lower accuracy or no efficiency gain relative to baselines. The diagnosis about baseline dilution and difficulty-penalty mismatch is supported by comparing the proposed conditional estimation and dynamic scaling against naive group-relative length penalties.

items.title: Think Dense, Not Long: Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage for Efficient Reasoning
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can elicit strong multi-step reasoning, yet it often encourages overly verbose traces. Moreover, naive length penalties in group-relative optimization can severely hurt accuracy. We attribute this failure to two structural issues: (i) Dilution of Length Baseline, where incorrect responses (with zero length reward) depress the group baseline and over-penalize correct solutions; and (ii) Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch, where a static penalty cannot adapt to problem difficulty, suppressing necessary reasoning on hard instances while leaving redundancy on easy ones. We propose Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage (DDCA) to decouple efficiency optimization from correctness. DDCA computes length advantages conditionally within the correct-response cluster to eliminate baseline dilution, and dynamically scales the penalty strength using the group pass rate as a proxy for difficulty. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, and AIME25 show that DDCA consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off relative to adaptive baselines, reducing generated tokens by approximately 60% on simpler tasks (e.g., GSM8K) versus over 20% on harder benchmarks (e.g., AIME25), thereby maintaining or improving accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/alphadl/DDCA.

schema.problem: Current natural language-to-Bash agents primarily rely on proprietary cloud-based models, which raise privacy and data confidentiality concerns, and the performance of locally hosted open-source LLMs on these tasks remains unclear.
schema.motivation: Locally hosted open-source LLMs offer a promising privacy-preserving alternative, but their task performance must be established before adoption in real-world environments.
schema.proposed_approach: The study evaluates 22 open-source language models ranging from 1B to 32B parameters on natural language-to-Bash translation tasks. It uses an improved scoring system for task success and analyzes model performance under 10 distinct prompting techniques, including role-play, Chain-of-Thought, and retrieval-augmented generation.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a systematic empirical evaluation: 22 open-source LLMs (1B–32B) are assessed on natural language-to-Bash translation tasks using the improved scoring system, with performance compared under 10 prompting techniques. This design supports the claims about model-family performance, the benefit of role-play prompting, and the potentially negative effects of Chain-of-Thought and retrieval-augmented generation. The abstract does not state an explicit failure condition or which factors are held matched across models.

items.title: Local LLMs for NL2Bash: A Large-Scale Open-Source Model Evaluation for Bash Command
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as autonomous agents in domains such as cybersecurity and system administration.The performance of these agents depends heavily on their ability to interact effectively with operating systems, often through Bash commands.Current implementations primarily rely on proprietary cloud-based models, which raise privacy and data confidentiality concerns when deployed in real-world environments.Locally hosted open-source LLMs offer a promising alternative, but their performance for such tasks remains unclear.This paper presents an empirical evaluation of 22 opensource language models (ranging from 1B to 32B parameters) on Natural Language-to-Bash translation tasks.We introduce an improved scoring system for assessing task success and analyze performance under 10 distinct prompting techniques.Our findings show that Qwen3 models achieve strong results in NL2Bash tasks, that role-play prompting significantly benefits most models, and Chain-of-Thought and RAG can surprisingly hurt local model performance if not carefully designed.We further observe that the impact of prompting strategies varies with model size.

schema.problem: Creating and maintaining Page Objects for automated end-to-end web tests is largely manual and labor-intensive; existing automated solutions have seen limited practical adoption, and the potential of LLMs for these tasks is largely unexplored.
schema.motivation: Reducing manual Page Object creation and maintenance could improve the maintainability and scalability of automated web testing.
schema.proposed_approach: The study uses two LLMs, GPT-4o and DeepSeek Coder, to automatically generate Page Objects for web testing; the generated artifacts are evaluated on an existing benchmark of five web applications with manually written Page Objects.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation of LLM-generated Page Objects against manually written Page Objects on an existing benchmark of five web applications, reporting accuracy and element recognition; the abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched baselines.

items.title: Towards Automated Page Object Generation for Web Testing using Large Language Models
items.abstract: Page Objects (POs) are a widely adopted design pattern for improving the maintainability and scalability of automated end-to-end web tests. However, creating and maintaining POs is still largely a manual, labor-intensive activity, while automated solutions have seen limited practical adoption. In this context, the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for these tasks has remained largely unexplored. This paper presents an empirical study on the feasibility of using LLMs, specifically GPT-4o and DeepSeek Coder, to automatically generate POs for web testing. We evaluate the generated artifacts on an existing benchmark of five web applications for which manually written POs are available. Our results show that LLMs can generate syntactically correct and functionally useful POs with accuracy values ranging from 32.6% to 54.0% and element recognition rate exceeding 70% in most cases. Our study contributes the first systematic evaluation of LLMs strengths and open challenges for automated PO generation, and provides directions for further research on integrating LLMs into practical testing workflows.

schema.problem: Existing LLM-based robot task planning methods are often closed-source or computationally intensive, limiting deployment on real-world physical systems. There is also no universally accepted plug-and-play representation for robotic task generation.
schema.motivation: An open-source lightweight model and a standardized representation and benchmark would make LLM-based task planning reproducible, comparable, and deployable on resource-constrained robots.
schema.proposed_approach: The work builds a 1B-parameter open-source small language model that takes natural language task descriptions and a list of robot action primitives and outputs executable behavior trees in XML, with support for zero-shot generation and error recovery at inference and runtime. It also constructs a standardized benchmark covering 52 navigation and manipulation tasks in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the model on the introduced benchmark using functional and non-functional metrics, comparing against GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, larger open-source models, and the previous model. Evidence for the capability claim comes from zero-shot and one-shot success rates on the benchmark; evidence for efficiency comes from inference speed comparisons; evidence for the benchmark's adequacy comes from its coverage of navigation and manipulation tasks.

items.title: BTGenBot-2: Efficient Behavior Tree Generation with Small Language Models
items.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning increasingly rely on LLM-based task planning, leveraging their ability to bridge natural language with executable actions. While prior works showcased great performances, the widespread adoption of these models in robotics has been challenging as 1) existing methods are often closed-source or computationally intensive, neglecting the actual deployment on real-world physical systems, and 2) there is no universally accepted, plug-and-play representation for robotic task generation. Addressing these challenges, we propose BTGenBot-2, a 1B-parameter open-source small language model that directly converts natural language task descriptions and a list of robot action primitives into executable behavior trees in XML. Unlike prior approaches, BTGenBot-2 enables zero-shot BT generation, error recovery at inference and runtime, while remaining lightweight enough for resource-constrained robots. We further introduce the first standardized benchmark for LLM-based BT generation, covering 52 navigation and manipulation tasks in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that BTGenBot-2 consistently outperforms GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and larger open-source models across both functional and non-functional metrics, achieving average success rates of 90.38% in zero-shot and 98.07% in one-shot, while delivering up to 16x faster inference compared to the previous BTGenBot.

schema.problem: Translating LLM-driven agentic discovery to multi-system data backends is harder than benchmark settings because the search space is heterogeneous, the verifier is whether a deployed stack actually runs, and composition knowledge is unevenly captured in pretraining; unbounded agentic discovery fails to converge consistently on a working stack even with iteration and explicit composition knowledge.
schema.motivation: Real-world multi-system data backends demand compositions that actually run, and the deployed-stack verifier is a stronger target than benchmark conditions; if structured search can converge there, agentic discovery becomes usable for production data services.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture takes declarative user intent and owns four typed contracts at successive layers for intent, operator DAG, per-system skills, and runtime attribution. These contracts decompose the global search into bounded sub-searches, with separate sub-agents searching each typed space. The framework supplies channels by which knowledge flows forward as inline skill citations and errors route backward as typed signals, so runtime failures can become skill patches cited by later deployments.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports a proof-of-life evaluation on a trading-backend workload as evidence for the convergence claim. To support claim (1), the proposed structured discovery is compared with unbounded agentic discovery on reaching a working deployed stack; support requires the proposed system to converge under conditions where unbounded search does not. To support claim (2), the paper examines whether runtime failures from one deployment become skill patches that the next deployment cites inline. The workload is a real-world data-system composition setting; no separate ablation beyond the bounded/typed decomposition is described.

items.title: Declarative Data Services: Structured Agentic Discovery for Composing Data Systems
items.abstract: Agentic discovery has shown that LLM-driven search can find novel algorithms, designs, and code under benchmark conditions. Translating the paradigm to multi-system data backends surfaces a harder problem: the search space is heterogeneous, the verifier is whether a deployed stack actually runs, and composition knowledge is unevenly captured in pretraining. Unbounded agentic discovery, a coding agent iterating on failure-log feedback, fails to converge consistently on a working stack even when iteration and explicit composition knowledge are added. We propose Declarative Data Services (DDS), an architecture for structured agentic discovery of data-system compositions from declarative user intent. The framework owns four typed contracts at successive layers (intent, operator DAG, per-system skills, runtime attribution) that decompose the global search into bounded sub-searches; sub-agents search each typed space, while the framework provides the channels by which knowledge flows forward as inline skill citations and errors route backward as typed signals. As a proof of life on a trading-backend workload, DDS converges where unbounded discovery does not; runtime failures become skill patches that the next deployment cites inline. We position this as an early prototype reporting lessons from real-world data-system composition.

schema.problem: Existing multi-token prediction training frameworks use a fixed-length prediction horizon, ignoring the non-uniform information density of natural language and code; forcing auxiliary heads to predict across high-entropy semantic boundaries injects noisy, conflicting gradients that interfere with the shared backbone's core capabilities.
schema.motivation: Aligning the prediction horizon with sequence predictability would reduce harmful gradient interference while retaining multi-token prediction's richer supervision and inference acceleration.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed adaptive training paradigm dynamically aligns the prediction horizon with the intrinsic predictability of the sequence. An entropy-based segmentation algorithm uses the base model to detect sudden increases in uncertainty as semantic boundaries and partitions sequences into variable-length groups. Each token is assigned an adaptive prediction depth, and a dynamically masked multi-token prediction objective suppresses loss for predictions that cross these boundaries, attenuating noisy gradients.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the claim by comparing the proposed adaptive paradigm against standard multi-token prediction on task performance and inference speedup, across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general benchmarks using Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-3-12B. The abstract does not specify failure conditions, ablation structure, or matched compute/parameter budgets.

items.title: AdaMTP: An Adaptive Training Paradigm for Multi-Token Prediction
items.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) has emerged as an effective paradigm that augments a shared Large Language Model backbone with auxiliary heads, training the model to predict several future tokens in parallel to enrich its supervision signal and accelerate inference. However, existing training frameworks adopt a rigid, fixed-length prediction horizon, disregarding the highly non-uniform information density of natural language and code. Forcing the auxiliary heads to predict across high-entropy semantic boundaries injects noisy, conflicting training signals; because these heads share the backbone's latent representations, the resulting gradients backpropagate and interfere with the model's core capabilities. We propose AdaMTP, an adaptive training paradigm that dynamically aligns the prediction horizon with the intrinsic predictability of the sequence. At its core, an entropy-based segmentation algorithm leverages the base model to detect sudden surges in uncertainty as semantic boundaries, partitioning sequences into variable-length groups. Each token is assigned an adaptive prediction depth, and a dynamically masked MTP objective suppresses the loss for predictions that cross these boundaries, attenuating the noisy gradients that degrade the backbone. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general benchmarks on three backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-12B), AdaMTP consistently outperforms standard MTP in both task performance and inference speedup.

schema.problem: Speculative decoding drafters become bottlenecked by their output projection once vocabularies exceed 100k tokens, and existing static vocabulary-subset or static-cluster restrictions ignore that different token types have fundamentally different prediction entropy.
schema.motivation: Dynamic vocabulary restriction could reduce drafter computation for easy-to-predict tokens while retaining full-vocabulary verification by the target model, making speculative decoding more practical for long-context and domain-specific workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method estimates per-token prediction entropy with a lightweight online classifier and uses it to route tokens: low-entropy tokens are restricted to a small vocabulary in the drafter, while the target model verifies against the full vocabulary. This dynamic selection reduces the drafter's output projection cost while preserving target-side full-vocabulary verification.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates on long-context and domain-specific benchmarks against fixed-vocabulary baselines, measuring throughput and acceptance rates. (1) The throughput improvement claim is tested by comparing the entropy-guided restriction against fixed-vocabulary baselines. (2) The acceptance-rate claim is tested by measuring how many drafter proposals the full-vocabulary target accepts; the approach would fail if throughput gains required lower acceptance rates.

items.title: Entropy-Guided Vocabulary Restriction in Speculative Decoding (EntroSpec)
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using a fast drafter to propose multiple tokens, which a large target model verifies. As vocabularies exceed 100k tokens, the drafter's output projection becomes a computational bottleneck. Existing approaches restrict the drafter to static vocabulary subsets (e.g., frequency-ranked) or learn static clusters, but these ignore the observation that different token types have fundamentally different prediction entropy—function words and common tokens are highly predictable from context, while rare and domain-specific tokens require broader attention and deeper reasoning. We propose EntroSpec, an entropy-guided vocabulary restriction mechanism that dynamically selects which tokens the drafter should predict based on per-token entropy metrics. By restricting low-entropy (high-confidence, easy-to-predict) tokens to a small vocabulary in the drafter while allowing the target model to verify the full vocabulary, EntroSpec reduces drafter computation while maintaining high acceptance rates. We implement entropy routing via a lightweight online classifier and evaluate on long-context and domain-specific benchmarks, demonstrating 2.1–2.4× throughput improvements over fixed-vocabulary baselines.

schema.problem: State-of-the-art speculative decoding draft models are bottlenecked by the output embedding matrix; recent work reduces the draft vocabulary, which improves throughput but compromises speculation effectiveness when the target token is out-of-vocabulary.
schema.motivation: The output embedding matrix dominates drafting time in latest language models, so a draft model that keeps target-token coverage while reducing per-step output computation would remove a key accelerator bottleneck.
schema.proposed_approach: The method selects a vocabulary subset per decoding step for a speculative decoding draft model, replacing the use of a fixed reduced vocabulary so that the output embedding lookup is limited at each step while the target token can remain in the selected subset.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is an empirical comparison across a variety of tasks, measuring acceptance length and average throughput against EAGLE-3 as the state-of-the-art speculative decoding baseline. The abstract does not state ablations, matched compute settings, or failure conditions.

items.title: Speculative Decoding with a Speculative Vocabulary
items.abstract: Speculative decoding has rapidly emerged as a leading approach for accelerating language model (LM) inference, as it offers substantial speedups while yielding identical outputs. This relies upon a small draft model, tasked with predicting the outputs of the target model. State-of-the-art speculative decoding methods use a draft model comprising a single decoder layer and output embedding matrix, with the latter dominating drafting time for the latest LMs. Recent work has sought to address this output distribution bottleneck by reducing the vocabulary of the draft model. While this can improve throughput, it compromises speculation effectiveness when the target token is out-of-vocabulary. In this paper, we argue for vocabulary speculation as an alternative to a reduced vocabulary. We propose SpecVocab, an efficient and effective method that selects a vocabulary subset per decoding step. Across a variety of tasks, we show that SpecVocab can achieve a higher acceptance length than state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, EAGLE-3. Notably, this yields up to an 8.1% increase in average throughput over EAGLE-3.

schema.problem: Speech dialogue systems, whether cascaded or end-to-end, wait for the user's utterance to complete before starting language model inference, creating a fundamental latency bottleneck.
schema.motivation: Lower latency would make streaming speech dialogue more responsive, and the paper targets achieving this without sacrificing response quality.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework speculatively starts language model decoding on incomplete ASR hypotheses while a lightweight end-turn classifier predicts likely utterance boundaries, so detection and generation run concurrently. As the ASR stream refines or extends hypotheses, an incremental key-value cache management strategy reuses cached intermediate computations to limit recomputation. The design is intended to be agnostic to the underlying ASR, language model, and TTS components and compatible with both modular pipelines and end-to-end systems.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim of latency reduction without quality sacrifice is tested by comparing the proposed framework against fixed-latency baselines (waiting for ASR completion) and full-recompute speculative schemes in streaming speech dialogue, measuring latency and response quality. (2) A failure condition would be no latency reduction or degraded response quality.

items.title: Adaptive End-Turn Aware Streaming LLM Inference for Low-Latency Speech Dialogue
items.abstract: Speech dialogue systems face a fundamental latency bottleneck: whether cascaded (ASR → LLM → TTS) or end-to-end, the system must wait for the user's utterance to complete before starting language model inference. We propose AdaptiveStream, a novel framework that speculatively initiates LLM decoding on incomplete (partial) ASR hypotheses, guided by end-turn prediction signals. The key insight is that end-turn detection and LLM inference can proceed in parallel, with a lightweight end-turn classifier predicting likely utterance boundaries while the main LLM speculatively generates responses based on evolving ASR. When the ASR stream refines (correcting or extending the hypothesis), we employ an incremental KV-cache management strategy that reuses cached intermediate computations, minimizing recomputation overhead. We validate this approach against fixed-latency baselines (waiting for ASR completion) and full-recompute speculative schemes, demonstrating up to 40% latency reduction in streaming speech dialogue without sacrificing quality. Our framework is agnostic to the underlying ASR, LLM, and TTS, making it compatible with both modular pipelines and end-to-end systems.

schema.problem: Current large language models reason reactively, beginning to think only after receiving a user input, which introduces latency and degrades conversational fluidity; they do not exploit conversational pauses to anticipate or plan upcoming responses as human speakers do.
schema.motivation: Making models anticipate and plan during conversational downtime would reduce interaction latency and move toward more seamless, real-time conversational AI.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework enables models to pre-compute potential response elements during conversational downtime instead of waiting for the next input. A training-free baseline anticipates likely future states by speculatively generating possible future content in a continual manner, trading off efficiency and quality. To evaluate the approach in practice, three benchmarks of varying complexity are adapted into time-aware environments that simulate real-time conversational flow.
schema.research_plan: The evaluation adapts three benchmarks of varying complexity into time-aware environments and measures whether the proposed anticipatory approach improves interaction efficiency without compromising performance in simulated real-time conversation; the abstract does not name specific metrics, baselines, or an explicit failure condition, so the plan records only this high-level evidence design.

items.title: Don't Wait to Reply: Towards Responsive yet Thoughtful Dialogue through Proactive Thinking
items.abstract: Thinking has emerged as a critical capability for Large Language Models (LLMs) tackling complex tasks. However, its reactive nature, where reasoning is passively triggered only upon receiving a user response, inevitably introduces latency that compromises conversational fluidity. This stands in sharp contrast to human dialogue, where speakers proactively anticipate and plan future content during natural pauses to ensure seamless interaction. To bridge this gap, we propose Proactive Thinking, a framework that empowers models to pre-compute potential response elements during conversational downtime instead of waiting idly for the next input. We then introduce a training-free baseline that can think ahead by anticipating future states, balancing efficiency and quality through speculative continual thinking. To evaluate this approach in practice, we adapt three benchmarks of varying complexity into time-aware environments that simulate real-time conversational flow. We demonstrate that proactive thinking effectively improves interaction efficiency without compromising performance. Ultimately, this work advocates for a fundamental shift toward more intelligent, anticipatory, and real-time conversational AI.

schema.problem: Existing multi-tenant LoRA serving frameworks are architected for single-adapter isolation, with disjoint adapter loading and static routing; when a single generation request dynamically combines multiple adapters, these systems suffer memory fragmentation, combinatorial cache thrashing, and inefficient kernel dispatch.
schema.motivation: Few-shot domain adaptation and multi-task pipelines increasingly rely on composable LoRA inference, so serving engines must handle dynamic combinations of adapters efficiently to avoid these overheads and meet strict service-level objectives.
schema.proposed_approach: The system comprises a dynamic weight-fusion operator that coalesces multiple active LoRA ranks on-the-fly during prefill and decoding. It also includes a joint memory manager that unifies adapter weight caching with token-level composition graph tracking, and a composition-aware batching scheduler that groups requests with overlapping sub-adapters to maximize arithmetic intensity and satisfy strict service-level objectives.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the claimed latency and memory reduction is empirical: the proposed system is compared against naive multi-adapter serving baselines on serving latency and memory footprint. The abstract does not state failure conditions, ablations, or what is held matched across comparisons.

items.title: Composition-Aware Serving and Scheduling for Multi-Adapter LLM Inference
items.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the de facto standard for customizing large language models (LLMs), giving rise to multi-tenant serving engines that manage thousands of adapters concurrently. However, emerging few-shot domain adaptation and multi-task pipelines increasingly rely on composable LoRA inference—where a single generation request dynamically combines multiple adapters (e.g., domain specialization combined with task-specific reasoning or stylistic tuning) rather than utilizing a single isolated adapter. Existing multi-tenant LoRA serving frameworks are fundamentally architected for single-adapter isolation, assuming disjoint adapter loading and static routing. Consequently, serving composable adapters leads to severe memory fragmentation, combinatorial cache thrashing, and inefficient kernel dispatch. In this work, we propose CompoServe, a composition-aware serving and scheduling system for multi-adapter LLM inference. CompoServe introduces a dynamic weight-fusion operator that coalesces multiple active LoRA ranks on-the-fly during prefill and decoding stages, a joint memory manager that unifies adapter weight caching with token-level composition graph tracking, and a composition-aware batching scheduler that groups requests with overlapping sub-adapters to maximize arithmetic intensity and satisfy strict service-level objectives (SLOs). Extensive evaluations demonstrate that CompoServe significantly reduces serving latency and memory footprint compared to naive multi-adapter baselines.

schema.problem: Existing multi-tenant inference systems are primarily architected for a one-to-one mapping between requests and single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, limiting their efficiency when serving requests that require compositions of multiple LoRA adapters.
schema.motivation: Serving multi-tenant LLM requests with composed LoRA adapters efficiently would improve inference throughput, latency, and GPU memory usage under high-throughput and diverse workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: The system dynamically fuses corresponding LoRA adapters on the GPU for multi-tenant requests with LoRA compositions. It is built from three components: a manager for efficient GPU memory management of individual basic adapters, a composition-aware greedy scheduler that forms batches, and a mapping-based matrix-vector multiplication kernel for adapter fusion with high computational throughput.
schema.research_plan: Experimental evaluations are conducted on multiple setups, comparing the proposed system with state-of-the-art methods on inference throughput, time-to-first-token, and GPU memory consumption across diverse workload conditions. Support would be observed improvements on these metrics, though the abstract does not specify matched compute or parameter conditions.

items.title: DyMerge-LoRA: On-GPU Post-Merge Fusion for High-Throughput Multi-Tenant Composite LoRA Serving
items.abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of efficiently serving multi-tenant requests for large language models (LLMs) equipped with compositions of multiple Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, aiming to optimize inference throughput, latency, and GPU memory usage. Existing multi-tenant inference systems are primarily architected for a one-to-one mapping between requests and single adapters, limiting their efficiency in handling compositions of multiple LoRA adapters. To address these issues, we propose DyMerge-LoRA, a novel inference serving system specifically designed for high-throughput multi-tenant scenarios by dynamically fusing corresponding LoRA adapters on the GPU. DyMerge-LoRA introduces a Base Adapter Manager (BAM) for efficient GPU memory management of individual basic adapters, a LoRA-Aware Greedy Scheduler (LAG) for batching, and a Mapping-based Adapter Fusion Matrix-Vector Multiplication (MAF-MVM) kernel for high computational throughput. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple setups demonstrate that DyMerge-LoRA achieves up to 1.1-4× improvement in inference throughput compared to state-of-the-art methods, significantly reduces TTFT, and effectively mitigates GPU memory consumption, validating its effectiveness and performance advantages under diverse workload conditions.

schema.problem: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the massive memory footprint and high communication latency of the KV cache across GPU HBM, host CPU DRAM, and remote storage tiers; existing systems decouple cache management from speculative decoding execution, causing redundant data movement, suboptimal cache utilization, and frequent pipeline stalls during multi-step speculative rollouts.
schema.motivation: As long-context inference stretches the KV cache across hierarchical memory tiers, decoupled reactive offloading and single-step prefetching become costly, so coordinating admission and prefetching with speculative decoding is needed to reduce time-to-first-token and time-between-tokens.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework analyzes draft token generation paths from speculative decoding to predict future attention targets across GPU HBM, host CPU DRAM, and remote storage tiers. It asynchronously prefetches required KV blocks before verification and concurrently filters low-utility KV states via lightweight admission gating. Token utility admission and multi-step trajectory-aware prefetching are integrated in a single multi-tier KV-cache management framework.
schema.research_plan: The paper uses comparative evaluation on long-context benchmarks, measuring time-to-first-token and time-between-tokens against state-of-the-art offloading and speculative caching baselines; the abstract does not specify ablations that isolate admission gating from trajectory-aware prefetching.

items.title: Speculative Multi-Tier KV-Cache Orchestration for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is severely bottlenecked by the massive memory footprint and high communication latency of the key-value (KV) cache across GPU HBM, host CPU DRAM, and remote storage tiers. While existing systems employ reactive offloading, KV admission control, or single-step speculative prefetching, they treat cache management and speculative decoding execution as decoupled modules. This leads to redundant data movement, suboptimal cache utilization, and frequent pipeline stalls during multi-step speculative rollouts. In this paper, we propose Chronos-KV, a co-designed multi-tier KV-cache management framework that integrates token utility admission with multi-step speculative trajectory-aware prefetching. By analyzing draft token generation paths from speculative decoding, Chronos-KV predicts future attention targets across hierarchical memory tiers and prefetches required KV blocks asynchronously before verification, while concurrently filtering out low-utility states via lightweight admission gating. Evaluations on long-context benchmarks demonstrate significant reductions in time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT) compared to state-of-the-art offloading and speculative caching baselines.

schema.problem: Long-context LLM decoding requires large KV caches whose memory demands challenge GPU budgets. Existing offloading systems keep the full cache in host memory and fetch critical entries during decoding, but their sparsity cannot be increased without degrading accuracy, so KV transfer volume grows with context length and batch size and dominates decoding latency.
schema.motivation: Sustaining high-throughput inference under tight GPU budgets and scaling long-context inference beyond GPU and DRAM limits requires removing the data-movement bottleneck rather than further increasing sparsity.
schema.proposed_approach: A holistic multi-tier KV cache management system spanning GPU memory, host DRAM, and SSD. The system jointly orchestrates cache placement, pipeline scheduling, and cross-tier coordination; it adapts cache management to attention behavior to maximize reuse and minimize redundant data movement, and it restructures the decoding pipeline to overlap I/O- and CPU/GPU compute-bound stages. It is implemented as a fully functional prototype.
schema.research_plan: The paper implements and evaluates a fully functional prototype. Evidence for the throughput and accuracy claim is a comparison with state-of-the-art works on long-context benchmarks using popular LLMs, measuring throughput while preserving accuracy. The abstract does not name baselines, benchmarks, or metrics, and does not state failure conditions or matched budgets for the trade-off claim.

items.title: KVD rive: A Holistic Multi-Tier KV Cache Management System for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: Supporting long-context LLMs is challenging due to the substantial memory demands of the key–value (KV) cache. Existing offloading systems store the full cache in host memory and selectively fetch critical entries during decoding, but this strategy quickly hits a ceiling: sparsity cannot be pushed further without degrading accuracy. As a result, when context length and batch size grow, the volume of KV transfers rises sharply and becomes the dominant source of decoding latency. We present KVD rive, a holistic multi-tier KV cache management system spanning GPU memory, host DRAM, and SSD. Unlike prior work that pursues greater sparsity through algorithmic refinements, KVD rive tackles the problem from a systems perspective—jointly orchestrating cache placement, pipeline scheduling, and cross-tier coordination to sustain high-throughput inference under tight GPU budgets. KVD rive advances three fundamental capabilities: it adapts cache management to attention behavior to maximize reuse and minimize redundant data movement; it restructures the decoding pipeline to overlap I/O- and CPU/GPU compute-bound stages, eliminating stalls across heterogeneous resources; and it harmonizes data movement across memory tiers to unlock scalable long-context inference far beyond GPU and DRAM limits. We have implemented a fully functional prototype of KVD rive and evaluated it on long-context benchmarks with popular LLMs. The system achieves up to 1.74× higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art works while preserving accuracy.

schema.problem: Heterogeneous GPU pools force LLM serving systems to decide how to partition model layers across devices with different compute-to-bandwidth ratios; because prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, the optimal partition depends on the prefill/decode mix, but existing systems compute one partition from a single workload snapshot and that partition becomes stale as the mix drifts.
schema.motivation: Real serving workloads drift in prefill/decode mix over hours, so a one-shot partition periodically degrades throughput and SLO attainment; online re-partitioning could maintain performance under drift on heterogeneous pools.
schema.proposed_approach: A control layer treats the pipeline partition as online state. It measures a sliding-window estimate of the prefill/decode mix, models each device's calibrated prefill and decode capacity separately, and periodically re-solves a polynomial dynamic program that re-cuts layer boundaries to equalize stage service times under the measured mix. When a candidate re-cut clears an explicit migration-cost gate, the control layer executes it with state-preserving, KV-cache-aware transfer so in-flight requests drain on the old layout while new work flows through the new one.
schema.research_plan: The central claim is tested on drifted workloads by comparing the proposed control layer against the best static partition and a zero-cost, phase-synchronized oracle; support requires recovering more than half of the throughput gap, spending less than 5% of cumulative GPU time on migration, and preserving SLO attainment. Failure of any threshold would refute the claim. The abstract does not specify ablations, benchmarks, or what is held matched across conditions.

items.title: EbbFlow: Closed-Loop, Phase-Mix-Driven Layer Repartitioning for Heterogeneous-GPU LLM Serving
items.abstract: Heterogeneous GPU pools force LLM serving systems to answer a placement question: how should the model's layers be divided across devices that differ in compute-versus-bandwidth ratio? Because prefill is compute-bound while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, the answer is itself a function of the prefill/decode mix φ — yet existing systems solve it once, from one workload snapshot. Real serving workloads drift in φ over hours (diurnal demand, bursts of long prompts, changing output-length distributions), so a one-shot partition is periodically stale. We present EbbFlow, a control layer that treats the pipeline partition as online state: it measures a sliding-window estimate of the phase mix, models each device's calibrated prefill and decode capacity separately, and periodically re-solves a polynomial dynamic program that re-cuts layer boundaries to equalize stage service times under the measured mix.
