When a candidate re-cut clears an explicit migration-cost gate, EbbFlow executes it with state-preserving, KV-cache-aware transfer so in-flight requests drain on the old layout while new work flows through the new one. Our central falsifiable claim is that on drifted workloads EbbFlow recovers more than half of the throughput gap between the best static partition and a zero-cost, phase-synchronized oracle, while spending less than 5% of cumulative GPU time on migration and preserving SLO attainment.

schema.problem: Efficiently serving LLM inference under limited GPU resources is difficult; in serverless settings, workloads are highly diverse and GPU clusters heterogeneous, so deployment configurations must be adjusted online, but online reconfiguration is hard because LLM inference is stateful and model parameters are massive.
schema.motivation: Serverless computing paradigms are increasingly used for LLM serving to maximize resource utilization, and their elastic, dynamic nature makes online reconfiguration necessary for adapting to diverse workloads and heterogeneous hardware.
schema.proposed_approach: The work develops a dynamic pipeline reconfiguration mechanism for LLM serving that can adjust the pipeline layout at runtime. The system selects an optimal pipeline configuration when the workload changes and migrates the running inference service between configurations while aiming to limit downtime and performance degradation. The approach is deployed and tested on heterogeneous GPU platforms including NVIDIA A100 and L40s.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation on heterogeneous GPU platforms including NVIDIA A100 and L40s measures service downtime during migration and the overhead on time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token; low downtime and low overhead are the implied support criteria. The abstract names no explicit baselines or matched conditions beyond the heterogeneous hardware setting.

items.title: LLM-Driven Intent-Based Privacy-Aware Orchestration Across the Cloud-Edge Continuum
items.abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), efficiently serving LLM inference under limited GPU resources has become a critical challenge. Recently, an increasing number of studies have explored applying serverless computing paradigms to LLM serving in order to maximize resource utilization. However, LLM inference workloads are highly diverse, and modern GPU clusters are inherently heterogeneous, making it necessary to dynamically adjust deployment configurations online to better adapt to the elastic and dynamic nature of serverless environments. At the same time, enabling such online reconfiguration is particularly challenging due to the stateful nature of LLM inference and the massive size of model parameters. In this paper, we propose a dynamic pipeline reconfiguration approach that enables online adjustment of pipeline configurations while minimizing service downtime and performance degradation. Our method allows the system to select the optimal pipeline configuration in response to changing workloads. Experimental results on heterogeneous GPU platforms, including NVIDIA A100 and L40s, demonstrate that our migration mechanism incurs less than 50 ms of service downtime, while introducing under 10% overhead on both time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT).

schema.problem: Speculative decoding for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs is unreliable because draft tokens from a separate drafter collectively route to a scattered expert union, which inflates verification traffic and often makes speculation slower than autoregressive decoding. Existing systems mitigate this with trained drafters or adapters, gating a static drafter, or architecture redesign, but none change where the proposal distribution comes from.
schema.motivation: A zero-parameter, lossless, on-the-fly alternative would make speculative decoding viable on off-the-shelf Mixture-of-Experts checkpoints and convert the dominant verification cost into a predictable, budget-controllable quantity.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a zero-parameter, lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding method in which the Mixture-of-Experts target is its own drafter. The draft pass is the full transformer with each layer's Mixture-of-Experts block executing only the router-selected top-k′ (where k′<k) experts, while the unmodified top-k model verifies the speculative block in parallel under standard rejection sampling. Because proposals come from the target's own router over its own hidden states, the draft trajectory is also an exact lookahead of the expert sets the verifier will need. This predictability lets a budget controller adapt k′ and the draft length.
schema.research_plan: (1) The speedup and distribution-preservation claim is to be evaluated in the memory-bound decode regime against the strongest separate-drafter Mixture-of-Experts speculative decoding baselines at equal memory footprint, using wall-clock speedup and exact output-distribution preservation as the criteria. (2) The proposed framework's viability on off-the-shelf checkpoints is checked through acceptance of expert-marginal proposals; if those proposals are accepted too rarely to amortize their own cost, that outcome is treated as a negative result corroborating architectural pessimism rather than as a success.

items.title: EM-SSD: Zero-Parameter Expert-Marginal Self-Speculative Decoding for Memory-Bound Mixture-of-Experts Inference
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) is unreliable for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs because batches of draft tokens produced by a separate drafter collectively route to a scattered expert union, inflating verification traffic 2–3× and often making speculation slower than autoregressive decoding , . Existing systems fix this by adding trained drafters or adapters, gating a static drafter on and off , or redesigning the MoE architecture for chunk-level sparsity ; none change where the proposal distribution comes from. We present EM-SSD (Expert-Marginal Self-Speculative Decoding), a zero-parameter, lossless, on-the-fly framework in which the MoE target is its own drafter: the draft pass is the full transformer whose per-layer MoE blocks execute only the router-selected top-k′ (k′<k) experts, and the unmodified top-k model verifies the speculative block in parallel under standard rejection sampling. Because proposals are produced by the target's own router over the target's own hidden states, the draft trajectory is also an exact lookahead of the expert sets the verifier will need — converting MoE speculation's dominant cost , into a predictable quantity that our budget controller uses to adapt k′ and the draft length γ. We claim that in the memory-bound decode regime EM-SSD yields >20% median wall-clock speedup over the strongest separate-drafter MoE-SD baselines at equal memory footprint, while exactly preserving the output distribution; if expert-marginal proposals are accepted too rarely to amortize their own cost on off-the-shelf checkpoints, that negative result would corroborate the architectural pessimism of .

schema.problem: In latency-critical single-user MoE inference with expert offloading, existing self-speculative decoding faces a bottleneck: using a larger draft expert set improves draft accuracy but requires loading additional experts, while small-footprint drafts have low acceptance; verifying a multi-token block activates the union of target experts rather than remaining close to a single target step.
schema.motivation: End-device MoE deployment is attractive because only a small subset of experts is active per token, but routed expert weights often exceed accelerator memory; removing the drafting and expert-loading bottleneck would make speculative decoding practical for low-latency single-user settings.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method is a self-speculative decoding framework for expert-offloaded MoE inference in latency-critical single-user settings. It trains one lightweight accelerator-resident draft expert per layer by self-distilling residual, logit/token, and router-agreement signals from the frozen target MoE. At inference time it uses a fixed-footprint drafter combining shared, top-1, and the learned draft expert, with confidence-expansion truncation and target-expert prefetching; final tokens are still exactly verified by the target model.
schema.research_plan: (1) The throughput claim is supported by measured decode throughput on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B across CPU-GPU and Flash-NPU offload. (2) The acceptance and prefetch claims are supported by measured draft acceptance and prefetch hit rates in the same settings. The abstract does not specify a named baseline, ablation design, or explicit failure condition.

items.title: DraftExpert: Expansion-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for End-Device MoE Inference
items.abstract: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models are attractive for end-device deployment because only a small subset of experts is active per token, but their routed expert weights often exceed accelerator memory. We target latency-critical single-user settings where routed experts are staged on demand from CPU memory to a GPU or from Flash to a mobile NPU. In this setting, self-speculative decoding faces a new bottleneck: increasing the draft expert set improves accuracy but triggers extra expert loading, while cheap small-footprint drafts have low acceptance; moreover, verifying a multi-token block activates the union of target experts and is no longer close to one target step. We propose DraftExpert, an expansion-aware self-speculative decoding framework for expert-offloaded MoE inference. DraftExpert trains one lightweight accelerator-resident draft expert per layer by self-distilling residual, logit/token, and router-agreement signals from the frozen target MoE. At inference time, it uses a fixed-footprint shared+top-1+draft-expert drafter together with confidence--expansion truncation and target-expert prefetching, while final tokens are still exactly verified by the target model. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B across CPU-GPU and Flash-NPU offload, DraftExpert improves decode throughput by 1.45x on average, raises draft acceptance to 84~87%, and achieves 86~88% prefetch hit rates.

schema.problem: In paged KV-cache serving, token-level relevance signals can only be acted on at fixed-size page granularity; partially evicted pages remain fully resident, wasting memory and reducing throughput under memory pressure.
schema.motivation: Accurate token-level signals make sub-page savings actionable; converting them into memory savings could improve serving goodput under latency SLOs.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed KV-cache manager adds compact per-block metadata—a slot-validity bitmap and a slot-to-position remap table—so pages whose evicted tokens are not a union of whole blocks can be repacked in place, keeping live tokens dense in surviving blocks. Batch compaction of repacked pages runs between decode steps and at quiescent scheduling boundaries so the decode path is never blocked. An admission/quality controller co-designed with the compaction budget decides per sequence how much to compact, trading marginal accuracy against decode and repack overhead while optimizing serving goodput under latency SLOs. The attention kernel requires only batch metadata append and a remap-table indirection read, with no per-token gather math.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes evaluation against block-wise eviction [2], whole-context compression/eviction [3], attention-aggregated token eviction without layout exploitation [5], token retrieval without paging [4], and scheduler co-design baselines [6,8]. (1) Sub-page compaction is tested for measurable memory and goodput gains over page-granular accounting; failure is no measurable gain. (2) The remap-table indirection is tested for under 2% per-token decode cost; failure is exceeding that overhead. (3) Joint compaction and admission control is tested against memory-only policies under pressure; failure is no advantage over memory-only policies. The abstract does not specify held-matched controls for these comparisons.

items.title: TokenRoster: Token-Level KV-Cache Compaction Coupled with Admission Control for Paged LLM Serving
items.abstract: PagedAttention-style serving allocates KV cache in fixed-size blocks, so token-level relevance signals—however accurate they are—can only be monetized at page granularity: when only some tokens of a page should be retained, the partially evicted page remains fully resident, wasting memory and starving throughput under memory pressure. Existing work either evicts or compresses at whole-context granularity or block granularity , or scores tokens for retrieval without touching the memory layout , leaving the sub-page savings unharvested. We propose TokenRoster, a KV-cache manager that makes token-level eviction payoff inside a paged allocator: (i) each allocated block carries a compact token roster—a slot-validity bitmap and a slot→position remap table—so a page whose evicted tokens are not a union of whole blocks can be repacked in place, keeping live tokens dense in the surviving blocks; (ii) batch compaction of repacked pages runs between decode steps and at quiescent scheduling boundaries so the decode path is never blocked; (iii) an admission/quality controller co-designed with the compaction budget decides per sequence how much to compact, trading marginal accuracy against decode and repack overhead, optimizing serving goodput under latency SLOs rather than isolated cache-budget accuracy. TokenRoster requires only batch metadata append plus a remap-table indirection read in the existing attention kernel—no per-token gather math—so the claimed decode overhead is bounded by two extra loads per head per token. We evaluate against block-wise eviction , whole-context compression/eviction , attention-aggregated token eviction without layout exploitation , token retrieval without paging , and scheduler co-design baselines , testing the falsifiable claims that sub-page compaction recovers measurable memory and goodput gains over page-granular accounting, that roster indirection adds under 2% per-token decode cost, and that jointly optimizing compaction with admission control beats memory-only policies under pressure.

schema.problem: LLM serving faces a memory bottleneck because the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention manages KV cache in fixed-size blocks, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at token granularity, causing intra-block fragmentation and leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable.
schema.motivation: Reclaiming this fragmented memory is important because serving is memory-bound and better KV reclamation can improve throughput and concurrency for long sequences and large batches.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach inserts a lightweight token-level virtualization layer over PagedAttention-managed KV cache. It maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and reclaims physical memory by asynchronously repacking live tokens from fragmented blocks. The design preserves existing PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. The layer is implemented in vLLM and evaluated with token-level eviction policies including H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models.
schema.research_plan: (1) The retained-KV-block claim is assessed by comparing the proposed layer against a paired Naive-Evict baseline across token-level eviction policies including H2O, Random, and Scissorhands and across models. (2) The SLA-constrained throughput and maximum feasible concurrency claims are assessed under constrained active-KV budgets in vLLM. (3) The integration-effort claim is assessed by per-policy integration footprint. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched-resource controls for the comparisons.

items.title: vToken: Token-Level Virtualization for Reclaimable KV Caches
items.abstract: Large language model serving faces a critical memory bottleneck: the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention uses fixed-size memory blocks to reduce allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at a token granularity finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable. We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. We implement vToken in vLLM and evaluate it with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models. Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.

schema.problem: Shared KV-cache memory in multi-tenant LLM inference is efficient but exposes an honest-but-curious serving host to observables—page ownership, eviction/promotion events, and reuse orderings—that enable end-to-end recovery of prompts and responses through timing side channels and colliding reuse histories. Existing defenses either sacrifice sharing efficiency through per-user cache partitions, incur ORAM-style access overhead that cannot scale, or flag only a sensitive subset of blocks and leave the residual reuse policy and execution timing visible.
schema.motivation: Efficient multi-tenant inference depends on this shared paged KV cache, and black-box attacks have now demonstrated end-to-end recovery of victim prompts and responses, making it urgent to preserve the efficiency of global sharing while preventing the host-visible observables from leaking request content.
schema.proposed_approach: The system separates layout execution from reuse-policy attestation. A TEE-resident oracle replaces raw radix-tree keys with keyed, pseudonymous page identities, holds per-page reuse-contribution commitments and gated eviction decisions inside a CPU-side private enclave, and exposes only a quantized, padded paged layout advisory plus heartbeat-smoothed deallocation events to the untrusted host. It composes with existing paged serving stacks, requires no model or operator changes, and avoids end-to-end encryption of per-token traffic; only per-page identities and release cues are handled.
schema.research_plan: (1) The security claim is tested under honest-but-curious host semantics by measuring an adversary's reconstruction recall over victim request tokens from the released interface against budget-K public-token-prior guessing and against recall from unprotected timing channels. (2) The performance claim is tested by comparing TTFT, inter-token latency, and steady-state throughput against full global sharing and per-user isolation, with the serving stack and batch sizes matched. (3) The auditability claim is tested by verifying that reuse decisions satisfy a reusability-diversity invariant from only the enclave commitments; failure would occur if reconstruction recall exceeds the stated tolerance, latency overhead exceeds the stated bound, throughput recovery falls below the stated share, or the audit cannot be completed from the commitments.

items.title: CacheCommit: Bounded-Leakage, High-Reuse Multi-Tenant LLM Serving via TEE-Resident Page Contributions and Oblivious Paged Layout
items.abstract: Shared KV-cache memory — global paged allocation, prefix reuse, and cross-request page sharing — is the backbone of efficient multi-tenant LLM inference, but it exposes an honest-but-curious serving host to three privacy-relevant observables: which request owns which page, when pages are evicted or promoted, and long-run reuse orderings. These suffice to recover victim prompts and responses through timing side channels and colliding reuse histories, as black-box attacks have now demonstrated end to end . Prior responses fall into three postures: ban sharing with per-user cache partitions and sacrifice the efficiency that motivates paging ; make the whole access path oblivious with ORAM-style machinery that cannot scale to token-rate KV traffic ; or detect-and-isolate a flagged subset of sensitive blocks inside the serving runtime, leaving the residual reuse policy and its execution timing visible to the host . We propose CacheCommit, a system-level separation of layout execution from reuse-policy attestation: a TEE-resident oracle substitutes keyed, pseudonymous page identities for raw radix-tree keys, holds per-page reuse-contribution commitments and gated eviction decisions inside a CPU-side private enclave, and exposes only a quantized, padded "paged layout advisory" plus heartbeat-smoothed deallocation events to the untrusted host. Our falsifiable hypotheses: (H1) under honest-but-curious host semantics, an adversary's best reconstruction recall@K over victim request tokens from the released interface stays within ε≈0.2 of budget-K public-token-prior guessing, versus the ~0.6-class recall of unprotected timing channels ; (H2) TTFT and inter-token latency incur ≤20% overhead versus full global sharing, and steady-state throughput recovers ≥70% of the full-sharing–versus–isolation gap; (H3) reuse decisions can be publicly audited against an RDR-style reusability-diversity invariant using only the enclave commitments . The design composes with existing paged serving stacks, adds no model or operator changes (unlike content-level masking defenses ), and scales to production batch sizes because per-token traffic is never encrypted end-to-end — only per-page identities and release cues are.

schema.problem: Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) introduces timing side channels in multi-tenant LLM serving systems, allowing attackers to infer other users' request content from cache hit/miss latency differences, while existing defenses prevent this only by disabling cache sharing and losing efficiency.
schema.motivation: Multi-tenant LLM serving relies on APC for throughput and latency, so a security defense that preserves cache reuse for regular users would avoid the efficiency loss imposed by current isolation-based defenses.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system monitors cache reuse across users, flags suspicious sharing patterns, and selectively isolates prefixes, restricting their reuse only when necessary. It is designed as a lightweight addition to multi-tenant LLM serving systems.
schema.research_plan: The paper reports an evaluation comparing the proposed system with existing defenses that isolate users, measuring cache reuse and inference latency; no formal security evaluation methodology or failure condition is stated.

items.title: PrefixWall: Mitigating Prefix Caching Side Channels in Shared LLM Systems
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on optimizations like Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) to accelerate inference. APC works by reusing previously computed states for the beginning part of a request (prefix), when another request starts with the same text. While APC improves throughput, it introduces timing side channels: cache hits are faster than misses, creating observable latency differences. In multi-tenant systems, attackers can exploit these differences to infer sensitive information, e.g., by incrementally reconstructing another user's request by observing hit/miss patterns. Current defenses take a sledgehammer approach: they disable APC and cache sharing, isolating users, and sacrificing efficiency for regular users. This paper presents PrefixWall, a system that secures multi-tenant LLM serving systems against APC side channels without sacrificing performance and efficiency. PrefixWall monitors cache reuse across users, flags suspicious sharing, and selectively isolates prefixes, restricting their reuse only when necessary. Evaluation shows that PrefixWall enables up to 70% higher cache reuse and 30% lower inference latency compared to existing defenses that isolate users. PrefixWall's lightweight design demonstrates how security in LLM serving does not have to come at the cost of unnecessarily reduced performance or unbearable overheads.

schema.problem: Large language model deployment is challenged by high computational and memory demands.
schema.motivation: Improving LLM inference efficiency can reduce deployment costs and make LLMs more practical across applications.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method is a hardware-software co-optimization for LLM inference systems that combines dynamic memory allocation and scheduling by integrating and extending existing methods for token-level simulation, hardware-based heterogeneous memory management, and online scheduling under KV cache constraints.
schema.research_plan: The efficiency claim is to be supported through extensive experiments on real-world datasets and comparison against state-of-the-art baselines; no metrics, failure conditions, or matched-compute specifications are stated.

items.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation and Scheduling for Large Language Model Inference Systems: A Hardware-Software Co-Optimization Approach
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become integral to various applications, but their deployment is challenged by high computational and memory demands. This proposal presents a novel hardware-software co-optimization approach for LLM inference systems, focusing on dynamic memory allocation and scheduling. By integrating and extending existing works like TokenSim [D2c96f2bcfd2f], Hardware-based Heterogeneous Memory Management [D2ea8f320029e], and Online Scheduling for LLM Inference with KV Cache Constraints [D57c881d23c03], we aim to significantly improve the efficiency of LLM inference. Our approach will be evaluated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets and compared against state-of-the-art baselines.

schema.problem: LLM inference is computationally and energy intensive, and current deployment practices may not exploit hardware-aware software-stack optimizations to reduce those costs.
schema.motivation: Widespread LLM adoption across education and scientific research makes inference energy and runtime efficiency important, and a portable software-stack optimization methodology would reduce costs without modifying neural models.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed pipeline operates at the software-stack level. It formulates LLM inference engine optimization as a combinatorial optimization problem and solves it with a cellular genetic algorithm that evolves variable-length sequences of code optimizations. The algorithm incorporates a mutation operator that uses density information and a crossover operator that recombines sequences via longest common subsequences, aiming to find hardware-optimized inference configurations without modifying the neural model.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the energy and runtime reduction claim, the pipeline is evaluated on a Mac Mini with Apple Silicon M4 using llama.cpp, with two Llama 3.2 variants (1B and 3B parameters) quantized to 4-bit; the optimized engine is compared to the non-optimized baseline and to the aggressive -O3 compilation flag using total energy consumption and runtime as metrics. (2) For the cross-quantization generalization claim, the optimized engines are evaluated on 8-bit quantized versions of the same models and compared to the non-optimized baseline with the same metrics. The abstract does not state explicit failure thresholds or ablation controls isolating individual operators.

items.title: Energy-efficient large language models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become widely used tools across domains such as education and scientific research, following recent progress in computing infrastructure, data availability, and training techniques. However, their increasing deployment raises significant concerns about their high computational and energy demands at inference time. This work tackles the problem from a software-stack perspective, presenting an automatic optimization pipeline for LLM inference engines. This task is formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem and addressed using a cellular genetic algorithm that evolves variable-length sequences of code optimizations. The algorithm proposes a novel density-guided mutation and a longest common subsequence crossover operator. Experiments conducted on a Mac Mini with Apple Silicon M4 using llama.cpp demonstrate that, for two Llama 3.2 variants (with 1 and 3 billion parameters) quantized to 4-bit precision, the optimized engine reduces total energy consumption by 13.5% and runtime by 19.5% for the 1-billion-parameter model, compared to the non-optimized version, while the corresponding reductions for the 3-billion-parameter model were 5.3% in energy and time. If we compare against the aggressive -O3 compilation optimization flag, 4.4% and 2.7% energy savings are achieved for the two optimized engines, respectively, with comparable runtimes. It was also studied how the optimized engines generalize to their 8-bit versions, and their improvements over the non-optimized baseline were around 12% in energy consumption and 11.5% in runtime. These results demonstrate cross-quantization generalization and confirm that hardware-aware optimizations can deliver energy savings without modifying the neural model, offering a portable optimization methodology toward greener LLM deployment.

schema.problem: Attention mechanisms in transformer-based architectures have high computational complexity, limiting the efficiency and scalability of language models.
schema.motivation: Reducing attention complexity would make transformer-based language models more efficient and scalable.
schema.proposed_approach: The approach integrates topic modeling into the attention mechanism to enable more focused processing of input sequences. The proposal will investigate various topic modeling techniques, such as embedded topic models, and evaluate their impact on attention efficiency.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of evaluating various topic modeling techniques, such as embedded topic models, for their impact on attention efficiency; no baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified.

items.title: Efficient Topic Modeling for Attention Mechanisms in Transformer-Based Architectures
items.abstract: This proposal aims to explore the application of topic modeling techniques to improve the efficiency of attention mechanisms in transformer-based architectures. By leveraging topic modeling, we can potentially reduce the computational complexity of attention mechanisms, leading to more efficient and scalable language models. Our approach involves integrating topic modeling into the attention mechanism, allowing for more focused and efficient processing of input sequences. We will investigate the use of various topic modeling techniques, such as embedded topic models [Df86de9a36590], and evaluate their impact on attention mechanism efficiency.

schema.problem: Vanilla self-attention behaves as an N-width fast-weight MLP and becomes unscalable for very long sequences. Existing efficient attention mechanisms scale fast weights through routing or compression, but routing-based Mixture-of-Experts attention uses rigid block experts and top-k attention uses query-specific sets, limiting flexibility and reusability.
schema.motivation: Long-context vision tasks need attention mechanisms that remain scalable without losing the expressiveness of the fast-weight MLP view; the fast-weight perspective makes it possible to unify and improve routing- and compression-based efficiency.
schema.proposed_approach: The work elevates the fast-weight view of attention into a framework that organizes efficient attention mechanisms along five dimensions according to whether they scale fast weights by routing or compression. It then proposes an attention method that uses a small set of landmark queries to gather top-k attended key-value pairs as query-aware, deformable routed experts, while compressing the original N-width fast-weight MLP into a narrower shared expert. A code implementation is released.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is a set of vision-task experiments comparing the proposed attention to existing efficient attention mechanisms on effectiveness and efficiency, with qualitative investigation of the claimed token-pruning effect and initialization from standard attention. The abstract does not identify datasets, baselines, metrics, ablations, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: Mixture-of-Top-k Attention: Efficient Attention via Scalable Fast Weights
items.abstract: The vanilla self-attention mechanism in Transformers can be viewed as a two-layer fast-weight MLP, whose weights are dynamically induced by inputs and whose hidden dimension is equal to the sequence length $N$. As the context extends, the expressive capacity of such an $N$-width MLP increases, but it becomes unscalable for extremely long sequences. Recently, this fast-weight perspective has motivated the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) attention mechanism, which partitions the sequence into rigid blocks, treats them as fast-weight experts, and sparsely routes the tokens to them. In this paper, we elevate this perspective to a unifying framework for efficient attention mechanisms, interpreting them as making fast weights scalable through either routing or compression, and organizing them into a five-dimensional taxonomy. Then, we propose Mixture-of-Top-$k$ Attention (MiTA), which employs a small set of landmark queries to gather top-$k$ attended key-value pairs as query-aware and deformable routed experts, while compressing the $N$-width MLP into a narrower shared expert. Consequently, our MiTA improves the flexibility of prior MoE attention from rigid to deformable fast-weight experts, as well as the scalability of prior top-$k$ attention from query-specific set to reusable top-$k$ set. We conduct extensive experiments on vision tasks showing the superior effectiveness and efficiency of our MiTA, and also uncovering intriguing properties such as an emergent token-pruning effect and easy generalization from standard attention. Code is available at https://github.com/QishuaiWen/MiTA.

schema.problem: Existing speculative-decoding cost models for mixture-of-experts LLMs omit that verification cost depends on the union of experts activated across a draft tree's candidate tokens, not on token count, and it is not known how to shape that union at draft time without modifying the target model.
schema.motivation: In mixture-of-experts models, speculative decoding verification is bottlenecked by expert reads, so controlling the expert union at draft time could reduce verification traffic and improve throughput on open checkpoints without retraining or new hardware.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework is a training-free, router-aware speculative decoding system. A profiler learns per-layer expert co-activation statistics and predicts each draft token's target-router top-k expert set. A tree-building policy constructs draft trees under a budgeted marginal expert-union cost while keeping the standard rejection-sampling acceptance rule, so outputs remain exactly target-distributed, and a verifier orders and tile-packs verification positions by expert set so each expert is read once per step. A roofline-based cost model sets the cost-weight parameter online from measured speculation utility; all work is inference-time on open checkpoints and open serving stacks with no retraining and no new hardware.
schema.research_plan: (1) The latency-prediction claim is tested on Mixtral 8x7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B by comparing predicted expert-union bytes against measured verification latency; failure occurs if prediction error is not within the claimed tolerance. (2) The traffic and throughput claims are evaluated at batch sizes 1–16 against EAGLE-style and utility-driven K-tuning baselines, holding acceptance length matched by evaluating at a near-maximal acceptance length, with expert traffic and tokens per second as metrics; failure occurs if the proposed method does not reduce expert traffic or improve throughput at matched acceptance. (3) The offloaded-expert claim is evaluated by using the predicted union as a prefetch list and composing it with existing speculative-decoding-aware offloaders; failure occurs if it does not yield a tighter prefetch list or does not compose. The roofline-based cost model is set online from measured speculation utility.

items.title: ECSpec: Expert-Coherent Draft Trees for Lossless Speculative Decoding of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) is well-understood for dense LLMs, where verifying K extra tokens adds almost no weight traffic. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models — the de facto architecture for scaling — every speculative position can route to a different subset of experts, so a draft tree's verification cost is governed by the union of experts activated across its candidate tokens, not by token count. We argue this expert-union size is the missing term in MoE SD cost models, and that it can be shaped at draft time without touching the target model. We propose ECSpec, a training-free, router-aware SD framework with three components: (1) an expert-affinity profiler that learns per-layer expert co-activation statistics and a cheap prediction of each draft token's target-router top-k set; (2) an expert-coherent tree policy that builds the draft tree under a budgeted marginal-union cost, keeping the standard rejection-sampling acceptance rule so outputs remain exactly target-distributed (lossless); and (3) an expert-grouped verifier that orders and tile-packs verification positions by expert set so each expert is read once per step. A roofline-based cost model sets the cost weight λ online from measured speculation utility. We claim: (C1) per-step expert-union bytes predict MoE SD verification latency within ±15% on Mixtral 8x7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B; (C2) at ≥95% of the acceptance length of an acceptance-maximizing tree, ECSpec cuts expert traffic 15–40% and improves tokens/s by 20–50% over EAGLE-style and utility-driven K-tuning baselines at batch 1–16; and (C3) the predicted union yields a tighter prefetch list for offloaded-expert deployments, composing with existing SD-aware offloaders. All work is inference-time on open checkpoints and open serving stacks; no retraining, no new hardware.

schema.problem: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts inference efficiency depends strongly on expert activation patterns, but existing speculative decoding draft selection primarily optimizes acceptance likelihood; in large-scale MoE models this can produce expert scattering, where high-probability draft tokens route to disjoint experts, increasing expert-weight memory traffic and reducing the speedup from speculation.
schema.motivation: Large sparse MoE models are a key scaling path for LLMs, and their inference cost depends on activated experts, so making speculative decoding cost-aware may reduce expert-weight memory traffic and improve end-to-end decoding speed.
schema.proposed_approach: A cost-aware speculative decoding framework that incorporates predicted marginal expert activation cost into draft-tree selection. It uses a lightweight expert predictor and a dynamic expert buffer to favor draft paths that preserve high acceptance likelihood while reusing experts already covered by the current verification set. The target-model verification rule is left unmodified. The framework is evaluated on three large-scale MoE models across reasoning, coding, question-answering, and dialogue benchmarks.
schema.research_plan: Evaluation uses three large-scale MoE models, DeepSeek-V3.1 (671B), Qwen3-235B-A22B, and GPT-OSS-120B, across reasoning, coding, question-answering, and dialogue benchmarks. The design measures active expert footprints and end-to-end decoding speed, with the target-model verification rule held unchanged, to assess the cost-aware draft selection relative to confidence-driven speculative decoding. No explicit failure condition is stated in the abstract.

items.title: Less Experts, Faster Decoding: Cost-Aware Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts
items.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs), but their inference efficiency depends strongly on expert activation patterns. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel, yet existing draft selection strategies primarily optimize acceptance likelihood. In large-scale MoE models, however, selecting draft tokens also determines the union of experts activated during verification. We observe that confidence-driven SD can introduce \textit{expert scattering}: high-probability draft tokens may route to disjoint experts, increasing expert-weight memory traffic and reducing the speedup from speculation. Motivated by this observation, we revisit draft-tree selection under the non-uniform memory-cost structure of MoE inference. We propose \textsc{EcoSpec}, a cost-aware speculative decoding framework that incorporates predicted marginal expert activation cost into draft selection. With a lightweight expert predictor and a dynamic expert buffer, \textsc{EcoSpec} favors draft paths that preserve high acceptance likelihood while reusing experts already covered by the current verification set, without modifying the target-model verification rule. We evaluate \textsc{EcoSpec} on three large-scale MoE models, including DeepSeek-V3.1 (671B), Qwen3-235B-A22B, and GPT-OSS-120B, across reasoning, coding, question-answering, and dialogue benchmarks. \textsc{EcoSpec} consistently reduces active expert footprints and improves end-to-end decoding speed, achieving up to $1.62\times$ speedup. These results show that accounting for expert activation cost is important for efficient speculative decoding in large-scale MoE models.

schema.problem: Long-context LLM inference is memory-bound on the KV cache, and the dominant flat token-importance eviction strategy (keeping top-k attention scores plus sink/recent tokens) can silently drop entire semantic topics when each topic's tokens are only moderately scored. At tight budgets of ≤8% of the full cache, loss of topic coverage rather than raw per-token importance may be the binding constraint behind the accuracy collapse documented by oracle studies.
schema.motivation: At tight KV budgets, preserving semantic topic coverage is necessary to avoid collapsing long-context accuracy, and a training-free allocation method that does so would be practical without iterative inference.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method is a training-free KV-cache budget allocator that treats the prompt as a small set of semantic topics in key-embedding space. After prefill, it performs a one-time GPU k-means over the prompt's key vectors and measures each topic's attention demand from an observation window of queries. It then allocates the KV budget across topics by a water-filling rule proportional to measured demand with a per-topic floor so no topic is fully evicted, and retains the highest-attention tokens within each topic. Online reallocation during generation is done via a single matrix product, avoiding iterative inference.
schema.research_plan: (1) The method is evaluated on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-128K, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B at 256–4096-token budgets, using replayed attention mass and long-context accuracy as metrics, and compared against flat importance eviction (H2O, SAGE-KV, NACL), head-budget allocation (BaKlaVa, Ada-KV, LAVa), and centroid clustering (CentroidKV, ClusterKV, ClusterAttn) at matched memory. (2) A diagnostic auditing semantic topic coverage and a KV-footprint sweep are contributed as additional evidence. (3) The causal role of the per-topic floor is tested through ablation and the coverage audit; failure to show a causal effect is treated as a first-class negative result against the tight-budget oracle bounds.

items.title: TopicKV: Topic-Proportional KV-Cache Budget Allocation with Coverage Floors for Long-Context LLM Inference
items.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is memory-bound on the KV cache, and the dominant remedy — flat token-importance eviction (keep the top-k attention scores plus a few sink/recent tokens) — silently amputates entire semantic topics of a prompt whenever a topic's individual tokens are each only moderately scored. We hypothesize that at tight budgets (≤ 8% of the full cache) this loss of topic coverage, rather than raw per-token importance, is the binding constraint behind the accuracy collapse documented by oracle studies. We propose TopicKV, a training-free budget allocator that treats the prompt as a small set of semantic topics in the key-embedding space: (i) a one-time GPU k-means over the prompt's key vectors after prefill, (ii) measuring each topic's attention demand from an observation window of queries, (iii) allocating the KV budget across topics by a water-filling rule proportional to measured demand with a per-topic coverage floor so no topic is fully evicted, (iv) keeping the highest-attention tokens within each topic, and (v) online reallocation via a single matrix product as generation proceeds (the single-pass inference trick from streaming topic models, not iterative inference). On LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-128K, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B at 256–4096-token budgets, we predict TopicKV retains strictly more replayed attention mass and outperforms flat importance eviction (H2O, SAGE-KV, NACL), head-budget allocation (BaKlaVa, Ada-KV, LAVa), and centroid clustering (CentroidKV, ClusterKV, ClusterAttn) by 2–5 absolute points at matched memory, and we contribute a topic-coverage audit diagnostic plus a KV-footprint sweep. If the floor ablation and coverage audit show no causal effect, the hypothesis is falsified — which we treat as a first-class negative result against the tight-budget oracle bounds.

schema.problem: KV cache memory grows linearly with input length, limiting long-context deployment of transformer inference. Existing token eviction methods reduce memory by discarding tokens, which amounts to a coarse dimensionality reduction that assigns each token either zero or full cache dimension.
schema.motivation: Finer-grained allocation of cache dimensions could reduce long-context KV cache memory while retaining token-level information that whole-token eviction discards, making long-context deployment more practical.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method compresses KV caches by assigning dimensions to tokens at a finer granularity than token eviction, rather than retaining or discarding whole tokens. A variant incorporates head-level importance information into this allocation.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the claim of superiority over methods without head-level profiling, long-context benchmark comparisons are run against prior KV cache compression methods. (2) For the claim against HeadKV, the head-level variant is compared with HeadKV under the same head-level importance information. (3) For the full-attention comparability claim, the method is evaluated on LongBench at a small fixed KV-cache budget and checked for comparable performance to full attention. (4) For the long-context retrieval claim, Needle-in-a-Haystack is run at 50K context length with an extremely small cache budget. Support requires the method to outperform the specified baselines and preserve benchmark/retrieval performance; failure would be non-superiority or marked loss in these evaluations.

items.title: Beyond Token Eviction: Mixed-Dimension Budget Allocation for Efficient KV Cache Compression
items.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is widely used to accelerate transformer inference, but its memory cost grows linearly with input length, limiting long-context deployment. Existing token eviction methods reduce memory by discarding less important tokens, which can be viewed as a coarse form of dimensionality reduction that assigns each token either zero or full dimension. We propose MixedDimKV, a mixed-dimension KV cache compression method that allocates dimensions to tokens at a more granular level, and MixedDimKV-H, which further integrates head-level importance information. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MixedDimKV outperforms prior KV cache compression methods that do not rely on head-level importance profiling. When equipped with the same head-level importance information, MixedDimKV-H consistently outperforms HeadKV. Notably, our approach achieves comparable performance to full attention on LongBench with only 6.25% of the KV cache. Furthermore, in the Needle-in-a-Haystack test, our solution maintains 100% accuracy at a 50K context length while using as little as 0.26% of the cache.

schema.problem: Modern LLM inference systems allocate KV-cache resources uniformly at prefill time based on worst-case assumptions, despite high heterogeneity in request output length and attention patterns.
schema.motivation: Heterogeneous workloads make uniform allocation inefficient; dynamic per-request allocation could enable larger batch sizes and reduce memory pressure.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is implemented as lightweight middleware in existing inference frameworks and requires no model training. During prefill it predicts per-request token-generation characteristics, including attention sparsity and generation length, from prompt features and model signals; during decode it dynamically adjusts each request's KV-cache budget using these predictions and runtime observations.
schema.research_plan: The evidence consists of a comparison against state-of-the-art baselines on heterogeneous workloads, reporting system throughput, memory pressure, and batch size; the abstract gives no named baselines, ablations, or explicit failure conditions.

items.title: Adaptive KV-Cache Budget Allocation for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Serving
items.abstract: Modern LLM inference systems face a fundamental challenge: requests exhibit high heterogeneity in output length and attention patterns, yet current systems allocate KV-cache resources uniformly at prefill time based on worst-case assumptions. We propose AdaptiKV, a system that predicts per-request token-generation characteristics early (during prefill, from prompt features and model signals) and dynamically adjusts per-request KV-cache budget during decode. By coupling KV-cache allocation to runtime observations and predictions of attention sparsity and generation length, AdaptiKV enables larger batch sizes, reduces memory pressure, and improves system throughput by 15-25% on heterogeneous workloads compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The system is implemented as a lightweight middleware in existing inference frameworks and requires no model training.

schema.problem: In batched LLM serving with speculative decoding, the target model's verification phase computes and discards KV caches that may be reusable by subsequent draft proposals, causing redundant KV computation.
schema.motivation: Reusing these otherwise discarded target-model KV caches across draft-verification rounds and request batches can reduce redundant computation and improve throughput in batched serving.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system maintains a time-indexed, request-aware KV cache pool and matches draft attention patterns to previously computed verification contexts. It reuses target-model KV caches across draft-verification rounds and across request batches to reduce redundant KV computation. Correctness is preserved through position-aware cache invalidation and compatibility checking. The system is implemented on top of a speculative decoding framework.
schema.research_plan: The work evaluates the proposed system on standard LLM benchmarks, comparing throughput against baseline speculative decoding in batched scenarios with moderate to high request overlap. The throughput claim is assessed by the throughput comparison, while the correctness claim is supported by the described position-aware cache invalidation and compatibility checking, though no empirical correctness evaluation is described. No explicit failure condition is given.

items.title: Temporal KV-Cache Reuse for Batched Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using lightweight draft models to propose tokens that are then verified in parallel by the target model. However, in batched serving where multiple requests interleave, the target model's verification phase computes and discards KV caches that may be reusable by subsequent draft proposals in the same or different requests. We propose TemporalSpec, a system that enables temporal reuse of target-model KV caches across draft-verification rounds and across request batches. By maintaining a time-indexed, request-aware KV cache pool and matching draft attention patterns to previously-computed verification contexts, TemporalSpec reduces redundant KV computation while preserving correctness through position-aware cache invalidation and compatibility checking. We implement TemporalSpec on top of a speculative decoding framework and evaluate it on standard LLM benchmarks; we expect to demonstrate 15–30% additional throughput improvements over baseline speculative decoding in batched scenarios with moderate to high request overlap.

schema.problem: Tree-based speculative decoding verification under long-context settings requires a massive KV cache for both the prefix and the speculative branches, causing severe GPU memory and I/O bottlenecks. Existing systems either optimize KV cache offloading/caching independently of speculative branches or optimize tree attention without considering hierarchical memory tiers.
schema.motivation: Addressing this gap can reduce memory bottlenecks and end-to-end latency in long-context tree-based speculative decoding.
schema.proposed_approach: The framework co-designs KV cache management and verification scheduling for tree-based speculative decoding. It uses a tree-aware hierarchical prefetching engine that coordinates with the speculative verification schedule and pre-fetches required KV blocks from CPU memory or lower-tier storage into GPU VRAM along the candidate paths of the verification tree. Prefix-aware memory allocation is used to avoid redundant I/O for shared prefixes across speculative paths.
schema.research_plan: (1) The main reduction claim is evaluated on long-context benchmarks against decoupled baseline systems using memory bottleneck and end-to-end latency measures. (2) The prefix-aware allocation claim is not separately evaluated in the abstract; no ablation, held-matched compute settings, or failure condition is stated.

items.title: SpecTree-Cache: Co-designed Hierarchical KV Cache Management and Verification Scheduling for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by generating multiple candidate tokens in a tree structure and verifying them in a single target model forward pass. However, executing these verification trees under long-context settings introduces severe GPU memory and I/O bottlenecks due to the massive Key-Value (KV) cache required for both the prefix and the speculative branches. Existing systems either optimize KV cache offloading and caching independently of speculative branches (e.g., SpeCache) or optimize tree attention without considering hierarchical memory tiers (e.g., DeFT, TriForce). In this paper, we propose SpecTree-Cache, a co-designed KV cache management and verification scheduling framework tailored for tree-based speculative decoding. SpecTree-Cache integrates a tree-aware hierarchical prefetching engine that coordinates with the speculative verification schedule, pre-fetching required KV blocks from CPU memory or lower-tier storage into GPU VRAM precisely aligned with the candidate paths of the verification tree. Furthermore, it incorporates prefix-aware memory allocation to eliminate redundant I/O for shared prefixes across speculative paths. Evaluations on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that SpecTree-Cache significantly reduces memory bottlenecks and end-to-end latency compared to decoupled baseline systems.

schema.problem: Speculative decoding generates token candidate trees verified in a single parallel forward pass, but tree-structured attention over branching candidate paths requires non-linear KV cache structures; existing memory managers such as PagedAttention are designed for linear request sequences and cause memory fragmentation, redundant block allocations for overlapping prefix branches, and high latency when recycling rejected candidate branches.
schema.motivation: Efficient memory management for speculative candidate trees is necessary to avoid wasted memory and latency, and to realize throughput gains from speculative decoding in large language model inference.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a tree-aware KV cache memory manager. It maps speculative tree structures directly onto virtual memory blocks with zero-copy shared prefix references, uses predictive copy-on-write block allocation to reserve physical memory based on draft model token acceptance probabilities, and recycles rejected candidate branches with confidence-weighted priority.
schema.research_plan: Evaluations across diverse speculative decoding benchmarks compare the proposed memory manager with existing approaches; the relevant outcomes are fragmentation overhead, peak KV cache memory consumption, and end-to-end generation throughput. The abstract does not name the specific benchmarks, baselines beyond PagedAttention, or matched compute/latency budgets, so the exact conditions of comparison are not stated. A failure condition implied by the claims is that the system would fail if it did not reduce these overheads relative to existing managers.

items.title: TreeVary: Predictive Copy-on-Write and Branch-Aware Memory Management for Tree-Structured Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive large language model inference by generating token candidate trees that are verified in a single parallel forward pass. However, executing tree-structured attention over branching candidate paths requires maintaining complex, non-linear key-value (KV) cache structures. Existing memory managers, such as PagedAttention, are designed for linear request sequences and struggle with tree topologies, resulting in severe memory fragmentation, redundant block allocations for overlapping prefix branches, and high latency when recycling rejected candidate branches. In this paper, we propose TreeVary, a tree-aware KV cache memory management system featuring predictive copy-on-write (CoW) block allocation and confidence-weighted branch recycling. TreeVary maps speculative tree structures directly onto virtual memory blocks with zero-copy shared prefix references, while dynamically prioritizing physical memory reservation based on the draft model's token acceptance probabilities. Evaluations across diverse speculative decoding benchmarks demonstrate that TreeVary eliminates fragmentation overhead, reduces peak KV cache memory consumption, and significantly boosts end-to-end generation throughput.

schema.problem: High-content microscopy produces long time-lapse streams and z-stacks in which consecutive frames are nearly identical, yet dense-prediction vision transformers re-encode every frame from scratch and pay full attention cost per layer even though only a small support set changes.
schema.motivation: Avoiding full recomputation could substantially reduce serving cost for live-cell time-lapse and z-stack analysis, and controlling accumulated approximation error matters because downstream segmentation and tracking are sensitive to accuracy loss.
schema.proposed_approach: The runtime caches per-row numerator and denominator accumulator state and, when keys and values change only on a support set, reconstructs each unchanged query's attention output as a rank-structured correction whose dimension is bounded by the support size; elementwise MLP changes propagate exactly on the same support. It adds a computable per-token, per-layer error bound and promotes tokens whose bound exceeds a threshold to full recompute. It also includes an empirical procedure for tracking growth of the changed-token set across layers.
schema.research_plan: (1) The exact recovery, subspace-dimension, cost, and MLP delta-propagation claims are supported by the derivation and complexity analysis. (2) The controlled-accuracy and throughput claim is tested on live-cell segmentation with downstream tracking metrics, using throughput, Dice, and tracking thresholds as success/failure criteria. (3) Ablations against DeltaCNN-style truncation, token skipping, and adaptive patching isolate the proposed mechanism. (4) Viability is tested by measuring how the set of changed activations grows with depth.

items.title: RankDelta: Error-Controlled Rank-Structured Attention Deltas for Streaming Dense Cell Segmentation
items.abstract: High-content microscopy produces long time-lapse streams and z-stacks in which consecutive frames are nearly identical — cells move a few micrometres, background and non-motile cells are unchanged — yet every frame is re-encoded from scratch by a dense-prediction vision transformer. I propose RankDelta, a serving runtime that computes a new frame as an exact, rank-structured correction to the previous frame's cached attention state rather than a full forward pass. The key derivation: when keys and values change only on a support set C, the new attention output of an unchanged query is exactly recoverable from cached per-row numerator/denominator accumulators, and the per-row correction lies in a subspace of dimension at most |C|+1, so per-layer cost drops from O(N²d) to O(N|C|d); elementwise MLP layers propagate deltas exactly on the same support. I add a computable per-token, per-layer error bound that promotes a token to a full recompute whenever its bound exceeds ε, making accuracy loss a controlled knob instead of a heuristic, and I characterize empirically how the "dirty set" grows with depth — the single measurement that decides whether the idea works at all. The experiments target ≥3× end-to-end throughput at <0.2 Dice change on live-cell segmentation and unchanged downstream tracking metrics, with ablations against DeltaCNN-style truncation, token skipping, and adaptive patching.

schema.problem: Production LLM serving workloads drift non-stationarily in arrival rates, prompt/output-length distributions, and request mixes over diurnal and bursty timescales, while existing batching, admission, and prefill/decode control loops are static, reactive, or rely on performance models profiled offline and refreshed infrequently.
schema.motivation: Maintaining SLO-attaining throughput under such drift is necessary to avoid wasted compute and to keep tail-latency SLOs satisfied, and online bandit feedback makes continual adaptation feasible where offline models become stale.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed controller treats per-epoch configuration selection for a single LLM inference engine as a constrained, non-stationary bandit. Each epoch it chooses one discrete operating point from a small set of scheduler configurations, observes goodput and SLO-violation feedback, and updates sliding-window estimates that explicitly forget stale workload statistics; a slower-timescale Lagrangian dual updates a price on violations to steer exploration toward configurations predicted to respect a tail-latency SLO budget, while a switching-aware penalty discourages oscillation between configurations that would preempt in-flight requests and waste KV-cache state.
schema.research_plan: The drift-adaptation claim is evaluated under piecewise-stationary and real production traces against static, reactive, and periodically-refreshed offline-model baselines, using SLO-attaining throughput and SLO violation feedback; the claim would be falsified if SLO-attaining throughput fails to stay above the baselines or if the advantage does not grow monotonically with drift rate.

items.title: ServeTune: SLO-Constrained Non-Stationary Bandit Control of LLM Serving Configurations under Workload Drift
items.abstract: Production LLM serving workloads are fundamentally non-stationary: arrival rates, prompt/output-length distributions, and request mixes drift over diurnal and bursty timescales, yet the control loops that pick batching, admission, and prefill/decode configurations are either static, reactive, or dependent on performance models profiled offline and refreshed infrequently. We propose ServeTune, an online controller that treats per-epoch configuration selection for a single LLM inference engine as a constrained, non-stationary bandit problem. Each control epoch, ServeTune chooses one discrete operating point from a small set of scheduler configurations, receives feedback on goodput (SLO-attaining throughput) and SLO violations, and updates sliding-window estimates that explicitly forget stale workload statistics. A slower-timescale Lagrangian dual updates a price on violations, so exploration is steered only toward configurations predicted to respect a tail-latency SLO budget; a switching-aware penalty discourages oscillation between configurations that would preempt in-flight requests and waste KV-cache state. We make the drift-adaptation benefit falsifiable: under piecewise-stationary and real production traces, ServeTune's SLO-attaining throughput must remain above that of static, reactive, and periodically-refreshed offline-model baselines, with a gap that grows monotonically with drift rate.

schema.problem: Multi-SLO LLM serving is memory-bound: the KV cache caps the number of resident requests, and existing mitigations are either lossy (evicting or compressing individual tokens with documented quality degradation) or coarse (preempting an entire request to free its KV cache even when only a few blocks are missing).
schema.motivation: A sub-request granularity release mechanism with a hard quality guarantee can reclaim only the memory actually needed while keeping output correct, avoiding both quality degradation and unnecessary request-level preemption.
schema.proposed_approach: Under memory pressure, the mechanism deletes individual PagedAttention blocks (16-128 tokens) from running requests, but only from owners that retain enough deadline slack (residual SLO budget, measured against high-probability output-length bounds) to cover the block's worst-case exact recompute cost. Released blocks are re-prefilled bit-exactly on next use or during slack windows, so output is bit-identical to an un-evicted run. It is implemented as a vLLM plug-in reusing the paged block manager and a fused partial-prefill path, without attention-kernel changes.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is comparative: the mechanism is evaluated for SLO-constrained goodput at matched tail TTFT/TBT attainment against request-level preemption systems (FastSwitch, Ascendra) and tier/utility KV managers (EVICPRESS, MCaM). The design also isolates an explicit negative regime with uniform tight deadlines, in which whole-request preemption is expected to win, to characterize where block granularity pays off. The bit-identical output and leakage-immunity properties are supported by the exact re-prefill design; failure would be failing to outperform the named baselines at matched tail attainment or failing to preserve bit-identical output.

items.title: SLACKKV: Deadline-Slack-Gated, Lossless Block-Granular Partial Preemption of KV Caches in Multi-SLO LLM Serving
items.abstract: Multi-SLO LLM serving is today memory-bound: the KV cache caps the number of resident requests, and every mitigation on the table is either lossy — evict or compress individual tokens with documented quality degradation — or coarse — preempt an entire request to free its KV cache , even when only a few blocks of memory are actually missing. We propose SLACKKV, the first KV-cache release mechanism that operates at sub-request granularity with a hard quality guarantee. Under memory pressure, SLACKKV deletes individual PagedAttention blocks (e.g., 16–128 tokens) from running requests — but only from blocks whose owner retains enough deadline slack (residual SLO budget, measured against CacheOPT-style high-probability output-length bounds ) to cover the block's worst-case exact recompute cost. Released blocks are re-prefilled bit-exactly on next use or during slack windows, so output is bit-identical to an un-evicted run and immune to the multi-instruction and system-prompt leakage failures that lossy compression exhibits . SLACKKV is implemented as a vLLM plug-in reusing the paged block manager and a fused partial-prefill path, without attention-kernel changes . The falsifiable headline claim is ≥1.20× SLO-constrained goodput at matched tail TTFT/TBT attainment versus request-level preemption systems (FastSwitch, Ascendra) and tier/utility KV managers (EVICPRESS, MCaM); we additionally isolate and measure an explicit negative regime (uniform tight deadlines), where whole-request preemption wins, characterizing precisely where block granularity pays off.

schema.problem: Speculative decoding and memory-aware KV-cache management are designed in isolation: existing speculative decoding systems assume memory is free, while existing KV-cache managers schedule and manage caches as if speculation did not exist.
schema.motivation: Long-context and multi-tenant serving creates simultaneous latency and KV-cache memory pressure, so a joint treatment could avoid speculation becoming SLO-harmful under cache saturation and enable memory-aware speculation decisions.
schema.proposed_approach: Builds a memory-priced speculation layer with three components: (i) a PagedAttention-style block manager that accounts for draft and target KV caches jointly; (ii) a real-time memory-pressure index computed from soft vs. hard memory watermark occupancy; and (iii) a per-step speculation decision that maps the memory-pressure index, per-request SLO headroom, and draft acceptance rate to one of expanding the verification tree, speculating at a fixed budget, shrinking to greedy drafting with K=1..2, gating the request to plain autoregressive decoding for that step, or swapping/compressing the draft KV to a 4-bit snapshot for one verification round. The design is implemented in a vLLM-based prototype and evaluated under long-context and multi-tenant workloads.
schema.research_plan: (1) C1 is evaluated at ≥90% KV-cache fill by comparing fixed-scheme speculative decoding against non-speculated serving on p99 time-between-tokens; support requires at least 20% degradation. (2) C2 evaluates the proposed memory-priced speculation layer on effective throughput, requiring at least 1.2× SLO-attained requests/time at ≤1% output-quality delta. (3) C3 evaluates whether the memory-pressure index signal, rather than acceptance rate alone, predicts when gating helps and thereby isolates memory from the quality dimension. Evaluation uses a vLLM-based prototype under long-context and multi-tenant workloads. If C1 fails, the mechanism degrades to a memory-pressure-index-aware adaptive-K policy and the novelty claim narrows accordingly.

items.title: SpecuMem: Memory-Priced Speculative Decoding for SLO-Critical LLM Serving
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) is by now a standard latency accelerator for LLM serving, and memory-aware KV-cache management is a standard remedy for long-context serving pressure—but the two are always designed in isolation. SD must maintain two KV caches (a draft/target pair or a self-speculative stack), yet every SD system we retrieved assumes memory is free, while every KV-cache manager we retrieved (EVICPRESS, MCaM, Apt-Serve, TokenCake, KVShare) schedules and manages caches as if speculation did not exist. This proposal establishes a joint negative result and a positive mechanism. First, we hypothesize that under KV-cache-saturated serving, naive speculative decoding is not merely unhelpful but SLO-harmful: draft KV allocation inflates GPU memory residency and paged-attention block pressure, and forces target-KV evictions that serialize decoding—the opposite of the parallelism SD promises. Second, we build SpecuMem, a memory-priced speculation layer that (i) accounts for draft and target KV cache jointly in a PagedAttention-style block manager, (ii) computes a real-time memory-pressure index (MPI) from soft vs. hard memory watermark occupancy, and (iii) maps (MPI, per-request SLO headroom, draft acceptance rate) to a per-step speculation decision: expand the verification tree, speculate at fixed budget, shrink to K=1..2 greedy drafting, gate the request to plain autoregressive decoding for that step, or swap/compress the draft KV to a 4-bit snapshot for one verification round. We evaluate in a vLLM-based prototype under long-context and multi-tenant workloads. The proposal is falsifiable on three counts: (C1) at ≥90% KV-cache fill, fixed-scheme SD raises p99 time-between-tokens by ≥20% versus non-speculated serving; (C2) SpecuMem recovers and exceeds that gap to deliver ≥1.2× effective throughput (SLO-attained requests/time) at ≤1% output-quality delta; (C3) the MPI signal—not acceptance rate alone—predicts when gating helps, isolating memory from the quality dimension. If C1 fails, the mechanism degrades gracefully to an MPI-aware adaptive-K policy and the novelty claim narrows accordingly.

schema.problem: Deploying ML and LLM models in real-time game applications is challenging, particularly with respect to inference latency and adaptability.
schema.motivation: ML and LLMs show promise for enhancing game AI, but real-time game deployments require resolving latency and adaptability constraints to become usable.
schema.proposed_approach: The work will investigate applying ML system optimizations—efficient model serving, scheduling, and quantization—to ML/LLM models in game environments, and explore the associated challenges, benefits, and trade-offs.
schema.research_plan: The evidence will consist of exploring the challenges, benefits, and trade-offs of these optimizations in game AI applications; the abstract does not specify experimental design, baselines, metrics, ablations, or failure conditions.

items.title: Efficient ML/LLM Model Serving and Scheduling for Real-Time Game AI Applications
items.abstract: The integration of Machine Learning (ML) and Large Language Models (LLMs) in game environments has shown great promise for enhancing game AI. However, deploying these models in real-time game applications poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of inference latency and adaptability. This proposal aims to investigate the application of ML system optimizations, such as efficient model serving, scheduling, and quantization, to improve the real-time inference and adaptability of ML/LLM models in game environments. We will explore the challenges, benefits, and trade-offs of these optimizations in game AI applications.

schema.problem: Machine learning models currently lack efficient and accurate integration of ontological information, and there is no general, scalable method for building the taxonomic backbone of an ontology from scratch.
schema.motivation: Large language models make ontology learning and enrichment newly tractable, and improving ontology integration would benefit applications such as protein-protein interaction explanation and mathematical knowledge graphs.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed method uses large language models to perform ontology learning and enrichment and to construct the taxonomic backbone of an ontology from scratch. The design coordinates interactions between ontology learning subtasks and incorporates mechanisms to reduce overfitting on high-frequency concepts. It also defines new metrics for evaluating the quality of generated ontologies.
schema.research_plan: The method is to be applied to protein-protein interaction explanation and mathematical knowledge graphs, with the generated ontology evaluated using the proposed new quality metrics. The abstract does not specify baselines, ablations, matched-compute constraints, or failure conditions for any claim.

items.title: Efficient Ontology-Based Machine Learning with Large Language Models
items.abstract: This proposal aims to improve the efficiency and accuracy of machine learning (ML) models by integrating ontological information using large language models (LLMs). We focus on developing a general and scalable method for building the taxonomic backbone of an ontology from scratch, leveraging LLMs for ontology learning and enrichment. Our approach will address the interactions between subtasks of ontology learning, reducing overfitting on high-frequency concepts, and introducing novel metrics for evaluating the quality of the generated ontology. We will apply our method to various domains, including protein-protein interaction explanation and mathematical knowledge graphs.

schema.problem: Gigascale 3D Gaussian Splatting captures (city blocks, campuses, digital twins) contain 40M–100M+ Gaussians that exceed a single large GPU's HBM; once rasterization is optimized and the scene file is compressed, the dominant remaining serving cost is unaddressed: memory-hierarchy management of which spatial tiles at which LOD reside in HBM vs DRAM vs NVMe, when they are fetched, and how they are shared and evicted across concurrent clients.
schema.motivation: Making photorealistic real-time 3D serving of gigascale scenes to concurrent VR/AR users possible requires managing this multi-tier memory hierarchy under multi-client load, not just accelerating rasterization or compression.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed serving runtime treats a 3DGS scene as a large, spatially structured parameter set served from a unified 3-level cache: an LOD octree of quantized Gaussian tiles with graceful coarse-level degradation on a miss; asynchronous NVMe→DRAM and DRAM→HBM pipelines built on GPU-Direct-Storage-style transfers and multipath host-GPU movement; and a per-client camera-trajectory predictor that drives geometry-aware prefetch over an adaptive lookahead window. It also uses cost-aware eviction with cross-client refcounting to keep shared viewpoints resident and a per-client SLO scheduler over frame deadlines, residency, and bandwidth. It builds on the FlashGS rasterizer and Octree-GS/H-3DGS tiles.
schema.research_plan: Evidence includes a first-of-kind bandwidth feasibility study for the NVMe tier and ablations isolating each lever (prediction, lookahead, tiering depth, sharing, scheduling).
