The falsifiable test is the stated claim: under scenes 10–20× HBM and 1–16 concurrent clients, support requires sustaining the 90 FPS @ 1080p deadline with near-zero miss-induced frame drops and sub-linear HBM residency growth; failure would show one or more baselines match or the scaling/deadline conditions are not met. Baselines are resident, synchronous-LOD, cache-centric single-scene, and naive-LRU streaming.

items.title: SplatServe: Trajectory-Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management and Multi-Client Serving for Gigascale 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
items.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the dominant format for photorealistic real-time 3D, but gigascale captures — city blocks, campuses, digital twins — contain 40M–100M+ Gaussians that exceed the HBM of a single large GPU. We argue that once the rasterizer is optimized (order-of-magnitude speedups are already demonstrated) and the scene file is compressed, the dominant remaining cost in serving such scenes is memory-hierarchy management under a multi-client workload: which spatial tiles, at which level of detail, reside in GPU HBM vs. host DRAM vs. NVMe, when they are fetched, and how they are shared and evicted across concurrent VR/AR users. We present SplatServe, a serving runtime that treats a 3DGS scene as a large, spatially structured parameter set served from a unified 3-level cache: an LOD octree of quantized Gaussian tiles with graceful coarse-level degradation on a miss; asynchronous NVMe→DRAM and DRAM→HBM pipelines built on GPU-Direct-Storage-style transfers and multipath host-GPU movement; a per-client camera-trajectory predictor that drives geometry-aware prefetch over an adaptive lookahead window; cost-aware eviction with cross-client refcounting that keeps shared viewpoints resident; and a per-client SLO scheduler over frame deadlines, residency, and bandwidth. Our falsifiable claim: on scenes 10–20× HBM with 1–16 concurrent clients, SplatServe sustains a 90 FPS @ 1080p frame deadline with near-zero miss-induced frame drops and sub-linear growth of total HBM residency in client count — which resident, synchronous-LOD, cache-centric single-scene, and naive-LRU streaming baselines cannot. We build on the FlashGS rasterizer and Octree-GS/H-3DGS tiles, and evaluate with a first-of-kind bandwidth feasibility study for the NVMe tier plus ablations isolating each lever (prediction, lookahead, tiering depth, sharing, scheduling).

schema.problem: Tiled diffusion image super-resolution at production resolutions incurs two avoidable serving costs: every tile recomputes the same overlap halo that its neighbors also compute, and every tile consumes the full uniform denoising-step budget even though flat regions converge in far fewer steps than textured or heavily degraded regions.
schema.motivation: Serving diffusion-based super-resolution at production resolutions with state-of-the-art quality is inefficient in latency and SLO goodput; removing redundant halo compute and uniform step budgets would reduce p95 latency and improve throughput without quality loss.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed serving system for tiled diffusion image enhancement allocates per-tile denoising-step budgets using a cheap region-difficulty estimator gated by a bounded-difference probe. It reuses cached halo features across tiles under a per-operator reuse-legality policy: exact for global-grid-aligned local-attention backbones and verification-gated for tile-relative global attention. To reconcile seams from heterogeneous step counts, it recomputes only the overlap strips for the extra steps, relying on cached interior features and displaced previous-step context. These components are wrapped in an SLO-aware continuous-batching tile scheduler with a bounded-VRAM halo feature store.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the system on tiled diffusion image enhancement at production resolutions, comparing p95 latency, SLO goodput, and boundary-band PSNR against full-step tiling at iso-quality. It also measures the fraction of tiled FLOPs removed by halo reuse and checks whether seam reconciliation closes heterogeneous-step seams. The core claim is treated as falsified if per-tile step heterogeneity produces seams that strip-wide reconciliation cannot close, or if halo reuse removes less than the stated threshold of tiled FLOPs.

items.title: HaloServe: Per-Tile Denoising-Step Budgets and Overlap-Strip Reconciliation for SLO-Optimized Diffusion Super-Resolution Serving
items.abstract: Diffusion-based image super-resolution (SR) achieves state-of-the-art enhancement quality, but at production resolutions (2K→4K, 4K→8K) it must be served with tiling, and tiled diffusion serving today pays two avoidable costs: every tile re-computes the same overlap halo that its neighbors also compute, and every tile consumes the full uniform denoising-step budget even though flat regions converge in a fraction of the steps that textured or heavily degraded regions need. We propose HaloServe, a serving system for tiled diffusion image enhancement that (i) allocates a per-tile denoising-step budget from a cheap region-difficulty estimator gated by a bounded-difference probe, (ii) reuses cached halo features across tiles under a per-operator reuse-legality policy (exact for global-grid-aligned local-attention backbones, verification-gated for tile-relative global attention), and (iii) reconciles the seams that heterogeneous step counts create by recomputing only the overlap strips for the extra steps, using cached interior features and displaced previous-step context. Wrapped in an SLO-aware, continuous-batching tile scheduler with a bounded-VRAM halo feature store, HaloServe targets ≥30% p95 latency reduction and ≥1.5× SLO goodput at iso-quality, with boundary-band ΔPSNR ≤ 0.2 dB versus full-step tiling. The core claim is falsifiable: if per-tile step heterogeneity produces seams that O(strip)-wide reconciliation cannot close, or if halo reuse removes <10% of tiled FLOPs, the contribution does not hold. To our knowledge, no retrieved system combines spatially-localized step-budget allocation, seam reconciliation, and SLO-aware scheduling for image-enhancement serving [1–21].

schema.problem: Standard matrix multiplication has cubic time complexity, which creates computational challenges for large-scale matrix computations such as deep learning.
schema.motivation: Reducing the number of multiplicative operations would lower computational cost across applications in physics, electronics, and artificial intelligence.
schema.proposed_approach: A lightweight neural network is trained to discover matrix multiplication algorithms by minimizing the number of multiplicative operations. Training uses a combination of mean squared error and a regularization function that constrains weights to 0, 1, or −1. The model is applied to 2×2 and 3×3 matrix multiplication.
schema.research_plan: (1) The model's ability to discover multiplication algorithms is tested on 2×2 and 3×3 matrices, with discovery as the success condition. (2) The regularization's contribution is assessed through its effect on the number of iterations needed to find algorithms. No explicit failure condition or matched-resource comparison is stated.

items.title: ProdNet: A Lightweight Network for Fast Discovery of Matrix Multiplication Algorithms
items.abstract: Matrix multiplication is a fundamental operation with significant applications across diverse fields, such as physics, electronics, and artificial intelligence. Traditional implementations of this operation exhibit cubic time complexity, which presents computational challenges, particularly in deep learning scenarios that necessitate large-scale matrix computations. In this study, we introduce ProdNet , a lightweight neural network model designed to autonomously discover efficient matrix multiplication algorithms without the need for extensive computational resources or prior knowledge of existing methods. Our approach seeks to alleviate complexity by minimizing the number of multiplicative operations involved. To achieve this, we utilize a combination of Mean Squared Error (MSE) and a regularization function, targeting weight values to be constrained to 0, 1, or –1 . We emphasize the effectiveness of our regularization techniques in accelerating the algorithm discovery process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ProdNet successfully identifies multiplication algorithms for 2 $$\times $$ × 2 and 3 $$\times $$ × 3 matrices, achieving this in a limited number of iterations (starting from 500 iterations for $$2 \times 2$$ 2 × 2 and 8800 iterations for $$3 \times 3$$ 3 × 3 )

schema.problem: Published KV-cache quantization methods take different routes to reducing cache memory, but their trade-offs along criteria such as bit budget, calibration requirement, and decode-time key reconstruction are not obvious.
schema.motivation: With a four-billion-parameter model accumulating several gigabytes of KV cache at 32K tokens, often exceeding model weights, choosing among quantization methods matters when calibration prompts are unstable or unavailable or when one compressed cache must span multiple model variants.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper selects an uncompressed bf16 reference and five published KV-cache quantization methods, KIVI, KVQuant, QuaRot, QJL, and Turbo Quant, for comparison. It evaluates them along five criteria including bit budget, calibration requirement, and decode-time key reconstruction. All numerical figures are taken from the corresponding source publications.
schema.research_plan: Claim (1) is supported by compiling each method's reported compression ratio and comparing it with its nominal bit budget. Claim (2) is supported by examining each method's documented calibration-data requirement and whether attention requires key reconstruction. The comparison relies on figures reported in source publications rather than new measurements.

items.title: A Comparative Study of KV-Cache Quantisation Methods for Large Language Model Inference
items.abstract: A four-billion-parameter language model accumulates several gigabytes of key–value (KV) cache at a context of 32K tokens, often exceeding the size of the model weights. Quantising this cache reduces the memory footprint, but five published methods take different routes to that goal, with non-obvious trade-offs between them. This paper compares six KV-cache representations an uncompressed bf16 reference, KIVI, KVQuant, QuaRot, QJL, and Turbo Quant along five criteria including bit budget, calibration requirement, and decode-time key reconstruction. All numerical figures are taken from the corresponding source publications. Two findings follow. Reported compression ratios range from 2.6× (KIVI at 2-bit) to 6.4× (KVQuant at 2-bit non-uniform), and the gap between nominal bit budget and reported ratio reflects the cost of per-block metadata. QJL and TurboQuant share two properties absent from KIVI, KVQuant, and QuaRot: they require no calibration data, and they compute attention without reconstructing keys. This combination is most valuable in deployments where calibration prompts are unstable or unavailable, or where the same compressed cache spans multiple model variants.

schema.problem: Profiling tools for GPU-GPU communication in NCCL-based distributed deep learning are still at an early stage of development, and existing profilers may not reliably capture all collective-operation events or accurate timing.
schema.motivation: Distributed deep learning is central to modern HPC and depends on continuous GPU-GPU data exchange via NCCL, so accurate profilers are needed to diagnose communication behavior in AI workloads.
schema.proposed_approach: Presents the latest version of a GPU-GPU communication profiler and evaluates it against NVIDIA Inspector and Google CoMMA. The evaluation uses micro-benchmarks and a real distributed training workload, DenseNet121 with PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel. Experiments run on two nodes of the Leonardo supercomputer, each with four NVIDIA A100 GPUs connected via NVLink, with 200 Gbit/s InfiniBand between nodes.
schema.research_plan: Evidence comes from micro-benchmark runs and a real DenseNet121 DDP training run on a two-node A100 system. For claim (1), complete event capture is assessed by comparing profiler traces against micro-benchmark collective-operation sets, with any missing events counting against the profiler. For claim (2), timing accuracy is assessed by comparing the proposed profiler's timings to communication times reported by the micro-benchmarks. Practical AI workload fitness is assessed through the DenseNet121 DDP training run.

items.title: To ncclsee, or Not to ncclsee: That is the Profiling Question
items.abstract: Distributed deep learning has become the backbone of modern HPC systems, in which multiple accelerators (typically GPUs) continuously exchange data during model training and inference. For such tasks, NCCL (and related libraries such as RCCL, OneCCL, etc.) is the most widely used library for GPU-GPU communication. Despite NCCL being a well-established technology, profiling tools are still in an early stage of development. In this work, we present the latest version of ncclsee and compare it against two other profilers, NVIDIA Inspector and Google CoMMA. We evaluate the three profilers using micro-benchmarks and a real-world DDL application, training a DenseNet121 model using PyTorch and Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). We run our experiments on two nodes of the Leonardo supercomputer, each equipped with 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs interconnected via NVLink, and the nodes are connected via 200 Gbit/s InfiniBand. In our experiments with micro-benchmarks, we find that Inspector and CoMMA miss collective-operation events, while ncclsee records them all (Fig. 1). Therefore, ncclsee provides more accurate timing information that closely matches the communication time reported by the micro-benchmarks (Fig. 2); and thus, allows us to get accurate profiling information of AI workloads.

schema.problem: Scaling distributed GPU training to more nodes is widely assumed to yield predictable performance gains, but real deployments often show diminishing returns and unstable behavior well before theoretical limits. The causes of these failures, especially network and fabric effects, are not well understood and are often overlooked by higher-level training frameworks.
schema.motivation: Misattributing scaling failures to framework or model inefficiencies wastes resources and leaves scaling limits unpredictable; recognizing fabric-level causes can improve predictability and reduce the cost of large-scale distributed training.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper conducts an empirical study of distributed GPU training performance across multiple production-scale clusters. It treats network and fabric factors—topology, congestion dynamics, collective synchronization behavior, and GPU locality—as the primary explanatory variables for end-to-end performance beyond small node counts. It examines cases in which identical models and software stacks exhibit different scaling depending on fabric design and runtime communication patterns, and identifies recurring failure modes in the transition from single-node to multi-node execution. It then codifies the observed failure patterns into diagnostic principles for system builders.
schema.research_plan: (1) The claim that fabric effects dominate scaling is supported by observational performance data across multiple production-scale clusters as node counts grow. (2) The claim that identical models and software stacks can scale differently is examined through observed cases where those are identical while fabric design and runtime communication patterns vary. (3) The failure-mode claim is derived from recurring patterns in this cross-cluster data, including cases where standard profiling tools did not reveal the effects. The diagnostic principles are presented as derived guidance and are not separately evaluated; the abstract names no quantitative metrics or baselines.

items.title: When Scaling Fails: Network and Fabric Effects on Distributed GPU Training Performance
items.abstract: Scaling distributed GPU training is commonly assumed to yield predictable performance gains as additional nodes are added. In practice, many large-scale deployments encounter diminishing returns and unstable behavior well before theoretical limits are reached. This paper examines why scaling fails in real systems, with a focus on the role of network and fabric effects that are often overlooked by higher-level training frameworks. We present an empirical study of distributed GPU training performance across multiple production-scale clusters. Our results show that network topology, congestion dynamics, collective synchronization behavior, and GPU locality frequently dominate end-to-end training performance once workloads move beyond a small number of nodes. Identical models and software stacks can exhibit sharply different scaling characteristics depending on fabric design and runtime communication patterns. We identify recurring failure modes that emerge as training transitions from single-node to multi-node execution, including synchronization amplification, topology-induced contention, and locality-driven performance variance. These effects are often invisible to standard profiling tools and are therefore misdiagnosed as framework or model-level inefficiencies. Based on these findings, we outline practical diagnostic principles that system builders can apply to understand scaling limits, improve predictability, and reduce the cost of large-scale distributed training.

schema.problem: Most Federated Learning frameworks presume uninterrupted participation from selected clients, but edge devices frequently have low battery, high CPU or memory load, limited bandwidth, and unstable connectivity, causing latency, client dropout, and reduced training performance.
schema.motivation: Predicting client participation from real-time resource conditions would allow Federated Learning to avoid wasted computation on unreliable devices, reduce dropout, speed up convergence, and keep client selection modular and scalable across architectures.
schema.proposed_approach: A lightweight participation prediction model based on a HistGradientBoosting Classifier is trained solely on device-level resource indicators such as battery level, CPU or memory load, bandwidth, and connectivity. A synthetic dataset reflecting realistic resource variability is constructed using weighted logistic scoring combined with probabilistic Bernoulli sampling. The trained predictor is intended to serve as a modular scheduling component that informs real-time resource-aware client selection and is compatible with a wide range of Federated Learning architectures.
schema.research_plan: (1) The participation predictor is evaluated on the synthetic dataset using standard classification metrics, including AUC, as evidence of its predictive capability. (2) The Federated Learning efficiency, dropout reduction, and convergence speed benefits are asserted from the results, though the abstract does not specify a separate controlled experiment or named baselines isolating the client selection mechanism.

items.title: Resource-Aware Client Participation Prediction in Federated Learning Using Probabilistic Labeling and HGBM
items.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving distributed training by avoiding centralized data collection. However, most FL frameworks presume uninterrupted participation from selected clients, which is impractical in edge environments with fluctuating resources. Devices often experience low battery, high CPU or memory load, limited bandwidth, and unstable connectivity, resulting in latency, client dropout, and reduced training performance. To address this issue, we introduce a lightweight, resource-aware participation prediction model based on a HistGradientBoosting Classifier (HGBC), trained solely on device-level resource indicators. A synthetic dataset is constructed through weighted logistic scoring combined with probabilistic Bernoulli sampling to reflect realistic resource variability. Evaluation using standard classification metrics shows strong predictive capability, including a high AUC value. Overall, the results highlight that incorporating an intelligent client selection mechanism aware of real-time resource conditions can significantly improve FL efficiency. It reduces unnecessary computation, lowers the chances of client dropout, and speeds up convergence, all while maintaining scalability and compatibility with a wide range of FL architectures as a modular scheduling component.

schema.problem: Cross-regional data sharing among heterogeneous regional governance nodes lacks a federated learning approach that jointly handles contribution estimation, privacy protection, communication load, and compliance constraints; conventional frameworks deploy privacy protection, encryption, compression, and access control separately.
schema.motivation: Coupling these mechanisms in one adaptive training process would allow the global model to adjust aggregation weights, privacy intensity, and transmission frequency according to node heterogeneity, data sensitivity, and governance authorization status, supporting secure collaboration.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed governance-constrained federated learning model couples node contribution estimation, privacy-risk-aware perturbation, communication-load scheduling, and compliance decision constraints within one adaptive training process. It adjusts aggregation weights, privacy intensity, and transmission frequency based on node heterogeneity, data sensitivity, and governance authorization status.
schema.research_plan: The model is evaluated experimentally on multiple datasets and distributed training environments against FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedNova, DP-FedAvg, and QSGD-FedAvg, using accuracy, F1 score, RMSE, privacy leakage risk, communication volume, total training time, stability, and compliance rate. No failure conditions or matched training constraints are stated.

items.title: A federated learning model enables secure data sharing across regions in digital governance
items.abstract: To support secure collaboration among heterogeneous regional governance nodes, this study develops a governance-constrained federated learning model for cross-regional data sharing. Different from conventional federated learning security frameworks that separately deploy privacy protection, encryption, compression, and access control, the proposed model couples node contribution estimation, privacy-risk-aware perturbation, communication-load scheduling, and compliance decision constraints within one adaptive training process. This design enables the global model to adjust aggregation weights, privacy intensity, and transmission frequency according to node heterogeneity, data sensitivity, and governance authorization status. Experimental evaluation was conducted using multiple datasets and distributed training environments, and the proposed model was compared with FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedNova, DP-FedAvg, and QSGD-FedAvg. The improved model achieved an accuracy of 92.6%, an F1 score of 91.8%, and an RMSE of 0.109. The privacy leakage risk decreased to 0.087, the communication volume was reduced to 1.5 MB, the total training time was 131 s, the stability metric reached 0.95, and the compliance rate increased to 96.8%.

schema.problem: The cost of large language model inference is heavily tied to the memory capacity required for model parameters, a challenge worsened when parameters are replicated across servers. No existing simulator supports LLM inference systems that use a CXL memory pool to share parameters across servers.
schema.motivation: Sharing parameters via a CXL memory pool may reduce memory-capacity pressure, and a validated simulator is needed to evaluate design choices such as emerging optical interconnects without requiring physical hardware.
schema.proposed_approach: The work builds a simulator by extending LLMServingSim and integrating it with NS-3 to model the CXL switch and with Mess to model the memory modules in the CXL memory pool. The simulator models LLM inference systems in which model parameters are stored in and shared through a CXL memory pool across multiple servers, while activations and KV-caches remain in each server's local memory. It is validated against a system connecting an industry CXL memory pool to two servers running two instances of the same LLM, with separate evaluations for OPT-1.6B and OPT-6.7B.
schema.research_plan: (1) The simulator-accuracy claim is evaluated by comparing simulated inference latency against a real system connecting an industry CXL memory pool to two servers running two instances of the same LLM, separately for OPT-1.6B and OPT-6.7B; a small latency error counts as support. (2) The sensitivity and optical-interconnect claims are evaluated with the simulator by varying the CXL memory pool interconnect bandwidth and comparing an emerging optical interconnect against the traditional electrical counterpart for OPT-1.6B and OPT-6.7B, with the electrical interconnect as the baseline and latency changes as the evidence.

items.title: A Simulator for LLM Inference Systems Exploiting CXL Memory Pools
items.abstract: The cost of large language model (LLM) inference is heavily tied to the immense memory capacity required to store model parameters—a challenge exacerbated by current systems that replicate these parameters across multiple servers to scale. To tackle this challenge, we may consider LLM inference systems exploiting a CXL memory pool to store and share model parameters across multiple servers, while keeping server-specific activations and KV-caches within each server’s local memory. Motivated by the lack of existing simulators for such systems, we first develop a simulator that extends LLMServingSim and integrates it with NS-3 and Mess to accurately model the CXL switch and the memory modules within the CXL pool, respectively. Second, we validate this simulator against a system connecting an industry CXL memory pool to two servers running two instances of the same LLM; across separate evaluations for OPT-1.6B and OPT-6.7B, the simulator demonstrates a$\approx$3% error in inference latency. Lastly, using our simulator, we uncover a significant sensitivity between inference latency and the interconnect bandwidth of the CXL memory pool, demonstrating that adopting an emerging optical interconnect over the traditional electrical counterpart reduces inference latency by 67.9% and 64.4% for OPT-1.6B and OPT-6.7B, respectively.

schema.problem: Existing block diffusion language models are mostly trained under teacher forcing, where the model observes only one noisy block conditioned on a clean prefix. Recent diffusion forcing introduces visibility among multiple noisy blocks, but its training states still differ from inference that decodes a bounded running set of consecutive blocks with heterogeneous slot-wise noise patterns.
schema.motivation: Extending these models to concurrent decoding of a running set of consecutive blocks would increase inter-block parallelism and practical efficiency; making that inference mode executable requires closing the gap between training states and the heterogeneous noise conditions of multi-block decoding.
schema.proposed_approach: Existing block diffusion language models are post-trained with a teacher-forcing-style objective that operates on bounded groups of consecutive noisy blocks conditioned on clean prefixes, using randomized noise schedulers to approximate the heterogeneous slot-wise noise patterns of concurrent multi-block decoding. This objective gives the model visibility within the noisy group while retaining a clean prefix. To execute the resulting concurrent decoding, an optimized decoding algorithm uses a buffer mechanism that maintains a bounded running set of consecutive blocks, preserves prefix-cache reuse, and keeps input shapes static across steps. The post-trained models are evaluated on math and code benchmarks, including a variant combined with DMax for additional parallelism.
schema.research_plan: (1) For the claim that training matches multi-block inference, the evidence is a comparison of average tokens per forward pass and average accuracy on math and code benchmarks between single-block and the proposed multi-block decoding. (2) For the claim that the buffer-based decoding algorithm preserves cache reuse and static shapes, the evidence is its use in those decoding runs and the resulting wall-clock acceleration relative to single-block decoding. (3) The variant combined with DMax is compared on the same benchmark set to assess whether the additional parallelism can be obtained with only a small accuracy loss. Failure would be no increase in average tokens per forward pass or a substantial accuracy drop relative to single-block decoding; the abstract does not report ablations isolating the training objective from the decoding algorithm.

items.title: Multi-Block Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: Block Diffusion Language Models (BD-LMs) improve diffusion-based text generation with KV caching and flexible-length generation. A natural next step is to extend them from Single-Block Diffusion (SingleBD) to Multi-Block Diffusion (MultiBD), where a running-set of consecutive blocks is decoded concurrently for inter-block parallelism. However, existing BD-LMs are mostly trained under teacher forcing, where the model observes only one noisy block conditioned on a clean prefix. While the recent diffusion forcing strategy introduces visibility among multiple noisy blocks, its training states still differ from MultiBD inference, where decoding operates on a bounded running-set with heterogeneous slot-wise noise patterns. To bridge this gap, we propose Multi-Block Diffusion Language Models (MBD-LMs), obtained by post-training BD-LMs with Multi-block Teacher Forcing (MultiTF). MultiTF integrates teacher forcing and diffusion forcing by training on bounded noise-groups conditioned on clean prefixes, with randomized noise-schedulers that better match MultiBD inference states. To make MultiBD practically executable, we further introduce an optimized decoding algorithm based on the Block Buffer mechanism that preserves prefix-cache reuse, keeps input shapes static, and translates increased decoding parallelism into wall-clock acceleration. Empirically, MBD-LLaDA2-Mini increases average Tokens Per Forward pass (TPF) from 3.47 to 6.19 and improves average accuracy from 79.95% to 81.03%; when combined with DMax, MBD-LLaDA2-Mini-DMax reaches an average TPF of 9.34 with only a 1.02% accuracy drop on math and code benchmarks.

schema.problem: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, rollout generation is a dominant efficiency bottleneck because LLM decoding is autoregressive, accounting for up to 70% of total training time.
schema.motivation: Reducing rollout cost would substantially speed up RLVR training; quantizing the actor is a promising way to accelerate decoding, but naive quantization risks training instability and ineffective weight updates.
schema.proposed_approach: The method replaces the rollout actor with a quantized version to accelerate decoding. It dynamically adjusts the clipping range using the policy ratio between the full-precision actor and the quantized actor. To handle the small weight changes between RL steps, it applies a scaling procedure that reduces quantization noise and increases the effective weight update. The approach is used with INT8 and FP8 quantization.
schema.research_plan: The evidence is experimental: the quantized actor is evaluated with INT8 and FP8 quantization on DeepScaleR and DAPO, measuring rollout speed against full-precision rollouts during RL training. The dynamic clipping range is tied to the claim of avoiding long-term training collapse, while the scaling procedure is tied to mitigating the weight update problem. The abstract does not state explicit failure conditions or matched control settings.

items.title: QuRL: Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Quantized Rollout
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a trending paradigm for training reasoning large language models (LLMs). However, due to the autoregressive decoding nature of LLMs, the rollout process becomes the efficiency bottleneck of RL training, consisting of up to 70\% of the total training time. In this work, we propose Quantized Reinforcement Learning (QuRL) that uses a quantized actor for accelerating the rollout. We address two challenges in QuRL. First, we propose Adaptive Clipping Range (ACR) that dynamically adjusts the clipping ratio based on the policy ratio between the full-precision actor and the quantized actor, which is essential for mitigating long-term training collapse. Second, we identify the weight update problem, where weight changes between RL steps are extremely small, making it difficult for the quantization operation to capture them effectively. We mitigate this problem through the invariant scaling technique that reduces quantization noise and increases weight update. We evaluate our method with INT8 and FP8 quantization experiments on DeepScaleR and DAPO, and achieve 20% to 80% faster rollout during training.

schema.problem: The applicability of block-parallel generative drafting, including diffusion-based parallel drafting, to multimodal speculative decoding remains an open question. Existing multimodal speculative decoding efforts focus on input compression, adapter alignment, candidate coverage, or modality-specific verification, while block-parallel generative drafting remains largely unexplored.
schema.motivation: Block-parallel generative drafting has been shown to accelerate text-only LLMs, making it timely to assess whether these gains transfer to multimodal models.
schema.proposed_approach: The paper conducts a modality-centered survey spanning vision-language, video-language, audio, and vision-language-action architectures, analyzed from the perspectives of drafting parallelism and cross-modal information interaction. It introduces a taxonomy that separates drafter-side parallelism from orthogonal design choices such as tree construction and verification strategies. It performs an empirical comparison of existing methods under varying degrees of parallelism on standardized multimodal benchmarks covering OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning. The study then summarizes limitations, open challenges, and future directions.
schema.research_plan: (1) The taxonomy claim is supported by systematically organizing a wide spectrum of multimodal models across vision-language, video-language, audio, and vision-language-action architectures. (2) The claim about limitations and readiness is assessed through a comprehensive empirical comparison of existing methods under varying degrees of parallelism on standardized multimodal benchmarks covering OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning. Support would consist of coherent placement of methods in the taxonomy and evidence of limitations as draft parallelism increases; failure would be if existing methods transfer cleanly without uncovered challenges. The abstract does not state explicit metrics, baselines, or held-matched conditions.

items.title: Is Multimodal Speculative Decoding Ready for Diffusion-Based Parallel Drafting? A Survey and Empirical Diagnosis
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by allowing a lightweight drafter to propose future tokens while a target model verifies them in parallel. Its lossless guarantee has motivated a line of work that pushes the drafter itself toward parallel generation. The most recent paradigm is block-parallel generative drafting, including diffusion-based methods such as DFlash and DSpark, achieving up to 3.6x speedup on common daily chatting tasks. While this transition is well studied in text-only LLMs, its applicability to multimodal models remains an open question. Existing multimodal speculative decoding efforts focus on input compression, adapter alignment, candidate coverage, or modality-specific verification; however, block-parallel generative drafting remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper combines a modality-centered survey with a cross-architecture empirical study to ask: Is multimodal speculative decoding ready for diffusion-based parallel drafting? In this survey, we systematically analyze a wide spectrum of multimodal models, spanning Vision-Language, Video-Language, Audio, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, from the dual perspectives of drafting parallelism and cross-modal information interaction. We introduce a unified taxonomy that isolates drafter-side parallelism from orthogonal design choices such as tree construction and verification strategies. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive empirical comparison of existing methods under varying degrees of parallelism across standardized multimodal benchmarks, including OCR, VQA, visual reasoning, and image captioning. Finally, we summarize the limitations of current approaches, discuss open challenges, and outline promising future directions for this rapidly evolving field.

schema.problem: LLM serving systems have been built as a single general-purpose, hand-tuned stack intended to support every model and workload, and there is no automatic way to synthesize bespoke serving systems tailored to different usage scenarios.
schema.motivation: The current approach costs many engineer-years of hand-tuning, while generic systems miss optimization opportunities in non-standard scenarios; automatic generation-time specialization could reduce this effort and enable scenario-specific optimizations.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed system is a multi-agent loop that automatically synthesizes bespoke LLM serving stacks for different usage scenarios. An outer loop plans and tracks the search over candidate system designs, while an inner loop implements candidates, checks their correctness, and measures their performance on the target benchmark. The generated stacks are specialized to the target scenario, and the implementation is released as open-source code.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the generated stacks on a target benchmark by measuring performance and checking correctness. For claim (1), the standard deployment setting compares the specialized stacks against vLLM; support requires that they remain competitive with vLLM, so specialization does not cost performance. For claim (2), the non-standard setting tests six scenarios spanning non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations; support requires that the generated stacks outperform existing systems by exploiting opportunities generic systems miss. The inner-loop correctness check guards candidate viability, and the standard-setting comparison guards against overhead from generation-time specialization.

items.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?
items.abstract: For years, we have built LLM serving systems like any other critical infrastructure: a single general-purpose stack, hand-tuned over many engineer-years, meant to support every model and workload. In this paper, we take the opposite bet: a multi-agent loop that automatically synthesizes bespoke serving systems for different usage scenarios. We propose VibeServe, the first agentic loop that generates entire LLM serving stacks end-to-end. VibeServe uses an outer loop to plan and track the search over system designs, and an inner loop to implement candidates, check correctness, and measure performance on the target benchmark. In the standard deployment setting, where existing stacks are highly optimized, VibeServe remains competitive with vLLM, showing that generation-time specialization need not come at the cost of performance. More interestingly, in non-standard scenarios, VibeServe outperforms existing systems by exploiting opportunities that generic systems miss in six scenarios involving non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations. Together, these results suggest a different point in the design space for infrastructure software: generation-time specialization rather than runtime generality. Code is available at https://github.com/uw-syfi/vibe-serve.

items.title: Dr. Kernel: Reinforcement Learning Done Right for Triton Kernel Generations
items.abstract: High-quality kernel is critical for scalable AI systems, and enabling LLMs to generate such code would advance AI development. However, training LLMs for this task requires sufficient data, a robust environment, and the process is often vulnerable to reward hacking and lazy optimization. In these cases, models may hack training rewards and prioritize trivial correctness over meaningful speedup. In this paper, we systematically study reinforcement learning (RL) for kernel generation. We first design KernelGYM, a robust distributed GPU environment that supports reward hacking check, data collection from multi-turn interactions and long-term RL training. Building on KernelGYM, we investigate effective multi-turn RL methods and identify a biased policy gradient issue caused by self-inclusion in GRPO. To solve this, we propose Turn-level Reinforce-Leave-One-Out (TRLOO) to provide unbiased advantage estimation for multi-turn RL. To alleviate lazy optimization, we incorporate mismatch correction for training stability and introduce Profiling-based Rewards (PR) and Profiling-based Rejection Sampling (PRS) to overcome the issue. The trained model, Dr Kernel-14B, reaches performance competitive with Claude-4.5-Sonnet in Kernelbench. Finally, we study sequential test-time scaling for Dr Kernel-14B. On the KernelBench Level-2 subset, 31.6% of the generated kernels achieve at least a 1.2x speedup over the Torch reference, surpassing Claude-4.5-Sonnet (26.7%) and GPT-5 (28.6%). When selecting the best candidate across all turns, this 1.2x speedup rate further increases to 47.8%. All resources, including environment, training code, models, and dataset, are included in https://www.github.com/hkust-nlp/KernelGYM.
